For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

derivations.claim: Equality of measures is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; by [F2], $\sim$ is therefore an equivalence relation, so each class $[\theta]_\sim$ is defined.
If $\psi=\bar\psi\circ\mathsf P$, then $P_\theta=P_\eta$ gives $\bar\psi(P_\theta)=\bar\psi(P_\eta)$ and hence $\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)$. Thus (iii) implies identifiability.

Suppose $\psi$ is identifiable. Form the relation $G:=\{(Q,a):\text{there exists }\theta\in\Theta\text{ with }Q=P_\theta\text{ and }a=\psi(\theta)\}$. Every $Q\in\mathcal M$ has at least one such parameter by [F1]. If both $\theta$ and $\eta$ represent the same $Q$, then [F2] gives $\theta\sim\eta$, so [F4] gives $\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)$. Thus $G$ has exactly one value for each $Q\in\mathcal M$, defines a function $\bar\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal T_0$ by [F3], and satisfies $\psi=\bar\psi\circ\mathsf P$. This construction defines the graph directly and uses no choice axiom.

By [F2], $\eta\in[\theta]_\sim$ exactly when $\eta\sim\theta$. If $a,b\in[\theta]_\sim$, then $a\sim\theta$ and $b\sim\theta$, so symmetry and transitivity from step 1.1 give $a\sim b$; conversely, $\theta\sim\eta$ gives $\eta\in[\theta]_\sim$. Hence [F4] is exactly constancy of $\psi$ on every class.

If $\bar\psi_1$ and $\bar\psi_2$ both factor $\psi$, each $Q\in\mathcal M$ equals $P_\theta$ for some $\theta$ by [F1], and then $\bar\psi_1(Q)=\psi(\theta)=\bar\psi_2(Q)$ by [F3]. The factor is unique. The implication in step 1.2 and the construction in step 1.3 give (i) iff (iii), while step 2.1 gives (i) iff (ii).

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ be an estimand, and set
$\mathcal M:=\mathsf P(\Theta)$, the set of laws in the model. For
$\theta\in\Theta$, write
$$
[\theta]_\sim:=\{\eta\in\Theta:\eta\sim\theta\}.
$$
Then the following are equivalent: **(i)** $\psi$ is identifiable; **(ii)**
$\psi$ is constant on every observational equivalence class $[\theta]_\sim$;
and **(iii)** there is a unique function $\bar\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal T_0$

derivations.claim: The full power set contains $\mathcal X$ and is closed under finite unions and complements, so it is an algebra of subsets. Every countable union of its members is still a subset of $\mathcal X$, so it is a sigma-algebra by [F1] and gives a measurable space by [F2]. For any $p\in[0,1]$, both singleton masses $p$ and $1-p$ are nonnegative, and $P_p(\mathcal X)=p+(1-p)=1$. If $(A_n)$ is pairwise disjoint, each of $0$ and $1$ belongs to at most one $A_n$, so $\sum_nP_p(A_n)=p\mathbf1_{\{1\in\cup_nA_n\}}+(1-p)\mathbf1_{\{0\in\cup_nA_n\}}=P_p(\cup_nA_n)$. Hence every $P_p$ is a probability measure by [F3].

If $P_p=P_{p'}$, evaluation on $\{1\}$ gives $p=P_p(\{1\})=P_{p'}(\{1\})=p'$. Thus the model map is injective and equal laws force $\psi(p)=\psi(p')$; the target is identifiable by [F7]. By [F8] it factors uniquely through the set of Bernoulli laws.

The points $(u,v)=(1/5,1/2)$ and $(u',v')=(3/10,2/5)$ have coordinates in $[0,1]$, and their sums are $1/5+1/2=2/10+5/10=7/10$ and $3/10+2/5=3/10+4/10=7/10\le1$, so both belong to $\Theta$. An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable function
$s:X\to[0,+\infty)\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]) is a
**nonnegative simple measurable function** when it has finite range.

Equivalently, there are pairwise disjoint measurable sets
$E_1,\dots,E_m\in\mathcal A$ and coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_m\in[0,+\infty)$
such that
$$s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}.$$
Any such display is a **simple representation** of $s$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ take values in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]). Its **partial sums** are the unique sequence $(s_n)$ in $[0,+\infty]$ satisfying

$$s_0=0,\qquad s_{n+1}=s_n+a_n.$$

To apply [[thm-recursion]] with a fixed successor function, use the state space $\mathbb N\times[0,+\infty]$ and the self-map $T(n,s)=(n+1,s+a_n)$, starting from $(0,0)$. Recursion gives a unique state sequence; induction makes its first coordinate $n$, and its second coordinates are exactly the unique $(s_n)$ satisfying the displayed recurrence. Addition of two nonnegative extended reals is always defined, including when either is $+\infty$. The sequence $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing, and its **nonnegative extended sum** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n\in[0,+\infty],$$

whose existence follows from completeness of the extended real line ([[lem-extended-reals-complete]]). More generally, for $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$\sum_{k\ge m}a_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{m+j}.$$

Finite sums use the same recursion: $\sum_{k<n}a_k=s_n$, so the empty sum at $n=0$ is $0$. A double sum such as $\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}$ means that the inner nonnegative extended sum is formed first and the resulting nonnegative extended sequence is then summed.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

derivations.claim: For each $x\in\mathcal X$, the set function $C\mapsto K(x,C)$ is the Dirac measure at $T(x)$, so it is a probability measure by [F2] and [F3].

Steps 1.1 and 1.2 verify both clauses of [F4], so $K$ is a probability kernel and therefore a randomized procedure. Since each section is the point mass at $T(x)$, it takes the action $T(x)$ with probability one.

If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra

A **randomized test** is a randomized procedure with binary action space
whose action set is $\{0,1\}$, equipped with its full sigma-algebra

[[def-sigma-algebra]]), where $1$ means reject and $0$ means do not reject
([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its **test function** is
$$\varphi(x)=K(x,\{1\}),\qquad x\in\mathcal X.$$
Since $K(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure and $\{0\},\{1\}$ partition the
action set, $K(x,\{0\})+K(x,\{1\})=1$. Thus $\varphi(x)\in[0,1]$ and
$1-\varphi(x)=K(x,\{0\})$ is the probability of not rejecting. Give $[0,1]$
the trace of the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,+\infty]$, namely
$\{C\cap[0,1]:C\in\mathcal B([0,+\infty])\}$. By
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], $x\mapsto K(x,\{1\})$ is
measurable; since it has range in $[0,1]$, its preimage of $C\cap[0,1]$ equals
its preimage of $C$ and is measurable for every such $C$. Hence $\varphi$ is a
measurable map in the preimage sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Its value is the
rejection probability after observing $x$.
The convention $1=\text{reject}$ is fixed here. No null or alternative
hypothesis is part of this definition.

$$\int_{\mathsf D}g\,dQ_\theta=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}g(a)\,K(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
with nonnegative extended values allowed.

derivations.claim: The full power set on the one-point data space is a sigma-algebra by [F7], and $P_{\theta_0}=\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure by [F1]. Hence the stated family is a statistical experiment by [F2].

The full power set on $\{0,1\}$ is a sigma-algebra by [F7]. The action section assigns masses $0$, $1-p$, $p$, and $1$ to $\varnothing$, $\{0\}$, $\{1\}$, and $\{0,1\}$, respectively. They are nonnegative and have total mass one by [A1]. For any disjoint sequence of subsets of $\{0,1\}$, each of the two points occurs in at most one member, so the mass of the union equals the sum of the assigned masses. Thus $K(x_0,\cdot)$ is a probability measure.

The data space has one point, so for every action event $B$ the evaluation $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is constant; its preimages are empty or the whole data space, both measurable. Step 1.2 and this measurability verify that $K$ is a probability kernel and hence a randomized procedure.

By [F4], the test function is $\varphi(x_0)=K(x_0,\{1\})=p$. The action-law identity [F5] gives $Q_{\theta_0}(\{1\})=\int K(x,\{1\})P_{\theta_0}(dx)$. The integrand is the simple function $p1_{\mathcal X}$, whose integral is $pP_{\theta_0}(\mathcal X)=p$ by [F1] and [F6]. This includes both endpoints $p=0$ and $p=1$.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

A **randomized test** is a randomized procedure with binary action space
whose action set is $\{0,1\}$, equipped with its full sigma-algebra
$2^{\{0,1\}}$ (the power set, which is a sigma-algebra by
[[def-sigma-algebra]]), where $1$ means reject and $0$ means do not reject
([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its **test function** is
$$\varphi(x)=K(x,\{1\}),\qquad x\in\mathcal X.$$
Since $K(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure and $\{0\},\{1\}$ partition the
action set, $K(x,\{0\})+K(x,\{1\})=1$. Thus $\varphi(x)\in[0,1]$ and
$1-\varphi(x)=K(x,\{0\})$ is the probability of not rejecting. Give $[0,1]$
the trace of the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,+\infty]$, namely
$\{C\cap[0,1]:C\in\mathcal B([0,+\infty])\}$. By
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], $x\mapsto K(x,\{1\})$ is
measurable; since it has range in $[0,1]$, its preimage of $C\cap[0,1]$ equals
its preimage of $C$ and is measurable for every such $C$. Hence $\varphi$ is a
measurable map in the preimage sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Its value is the
rejection probability after observing $x$.
The convention $1=\text{reject}$ is fixed here. No null or alternative
hypothesis is part of this definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

derivations.claim: The family $\mathcal A=\{\varnothing,\mathcal X\}$ contains $\mathcal X$, and its only members have complements in $\mathcal A$; any countable union of its members is either empty or $\mathcal X$. Hence $\mathcal A$ is a sigma-algebra and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is a measurable space.
In the full action sigma-algebra, $\{1\}$ is measurable, but $\varphi^{-1}(\{1\})=\{1\}\notin\mathcal A$. Therefore $\varphi$ is not measurable by [F5].
The point mass $P_{\theta_0}=\delta_0$ is a probability measure on this measurable space by [F3]. Thus the stated one-parameter family is a statistical experiment.
In this valid experiment, the map is not a statistic by [F6] and is not a randomized test function by [F7], since step 1.2 shows it is not measurable.

If $\varphi$ were the action-1 evaluation of a procedure kernel, then $x\mapsto K(x,\{1\})=\varphi(x)$ would have to be measurable by [F8], contradicting step 1.2. Thus the map is not a randomized procedure either, proving the stated claim false.

The sampling law is the point mass δ_0, but measurability is a pointwise structural requirement and the null point 1 remains in the domain. As checked in steps 2.1 and 3.1.
The map's values are the binary endpoints 0 and 1; the failure concerns measurability, not its range. As checked in step 1.2.

These are the only two events in A, and the supplier proposition gives countable additivity; thus δ_0 is a probability measure.

risk_review.notes: Read all five counterexample steps, ten direct prerequisites and the Dirac probability proof. X={0,1}, A={empty,X} is closed under complements and countable unions; delta_0 has masses 0 and 1 on these two events and is countably additive. The preimage of the measurable action singleton {1} is the non-event {1}, so the identity map fails both statistic measurability and the [0,1] trace-Borel test-function requirement. A kernel with that rejection evaluation would contradict pointwise kernel measurability; no almost-everywhere modification is part of the claim. The witness has a nonempty one-parameter experiment, binary endpoint values and an explicit point mass, with no choice or empty-case assertion. Reader/refuter found no item defect. Formal sigma-algebra and measurability citations supply exactly these clauses; Hoff §§2–3 supplies terminology. No mathematical repair or outside supplier escalation is necessary.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $x\notin C$. Then there are $a\ne0$ and $b\in\mathbb R$ such that $\langle a,z\rangle\le b<\langle a,x\rangle$ for every $z\in C$. Thus a hyperplane strictly separates $x$ from $C$ ([[def-supporting-hyperplane-to-a-convex-set]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and convex, and let $a\in C\cap\partial C$. Then there is a nonzero vector $u$ such that $\langle u,z-a\rangle\le0$ for every $z\in C$. Thus the hyperplane through $a$ normal to $u$ supports $C$ ([[def-supporting-hyperplane-to-a-convex-set]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$ and let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and convex. The closure $\overline C$ is convex, $\operatorname{int}(C)=\operatorname{int}(\overline C)$, and $\partial C=\partial\overline C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex and let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex. Then $\partial f(a)$ is nonempty for every $a\in\operatorname{int}C$.

Let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex on a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]), and let $a\in C$. A vector $v$ is a subgradient of $f$ at $a$ when $f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle$ for every $y$ in the domain.

The **subdifferential** is the set

$$\partial f(a):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle\text{ for every }y\in C\},$$

with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The definition permits $\partial f(a)$ to be empty or to contain more than one vector.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: If $\int f\,d\mu=+\infty$, the conclusion holds because $f(b)\in[0,+\infty]$. Otherwise let $A:=\{a\in C:f(a)=+\infty\}$. For every integer $n\geq1$, the simple function $n\mathbf1_A$ is bounded above by $f$, so [F7] gives $n\mu(A)=\int n\mathbf1_A\,d\mu\leq\int f\,d\mu<\infty$. If $\mu(A)>0$, these lower bounds are unbounded as $n\to\infty$ (and are already infinite if $\mu(A)=+\infty$), a contradiction. Thus $E:=C\setminus A=\{a:f(a)<\infty\}$ has full $\mu$-measure. Let $S$ be the support of $\mu$, the set of points every relative open neighbourhood of which has positive measure. Since $C$ has a countable base inherited from rational balls in $\mathbb R^d$, the complement of $S$ is a countable union of open null basic sets, so $\mu(S)=1$. Every neighbourhood of a point of $S$ meets $E$, hence $E\cap S$ is dense in $S$.

Let $C_0$ be the closure of the set of finite convex combinations of points of $S$. Then $C_0\subseteq C$. If $b\notin C_0$, [F1] gives a linear functional $u$ and a real $\alpha$ with $\langle u,y\rangle\leq\alpha<\langle u,b\rangle$ for all $y\in C_0$. The function $\psi(a)=\alpha-\langle u,a\rangle$ is integrable by the first-moment assumption and is nonnegative on the full-measure support $S$. Hence $\psi^-=0$ almost everywhere, so [F5] gives $\int\psi^-\,d\mu=0$ and $\int\psi\,d\mu=\int\psi^+\,d\mu\geq0$. By [F6] and the coordinate definition of $b$, this says $\alpha-\langle u,b\rangle\geq0$, contradicting the strict separation. Thus $b\in C_0$.

If $b$ were on the relative boundary of $C_0$, [F2], applied in its affine hull, would give a nonzero supporting normal $v$ there with $\langle v,y-b\rangle\leq0$ for all $y\in C_0$. Set $u(a)=\langle v,b-a\rangle$. The first-moment assumption makes $u$ integrable, and [F6] gives $\int u\,d\mu=0$. Since $u\geq0$ on the full-measure support $S$, its negative part $u^-$ vanishes almost everywhere; [F5] gives $\int u^-\,d\mu=0$. The signed-integral definition in [F6] then gives $\int u^+\,d\mu=0$, so [F5] implies $u^+=0$ almost everywhere and therefore $u=0$ almost everywhere. By continuity of $u$ and the definition of support, every point of $S$ must lie in the hyperplane $\langle v,y-b\rangle=0$: otherwise a neighborhood of a support point outside it would have positive measure on which $u\ne0$. Its closed convex hull $C_0$ would lie in that hyperplane, contradicting that $v$ is nonzero in the direction space of its affine hull. Hence $b$ is in the relative interior of $C_0$.

Put $C_1=\operatorname{conv}(E\cap S)$, where $\operatorname{conv}$ denotes finite convex combinations. The extended-functional convexity inequality makes $f$ finite on $C_1$; on these finite values it is the real-valued Euclidean convexity of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]. Density from step 1.1 gives $\overline{C_1}=C_0$. By [F3], $b$ is in the relative interior of $C_1$. If this affine hull has dimension zero, then $\mu$ is concentrated at $b$ and the claim is equality. Otherwise identify the affine hull isometrically with $\mathbb R^k$; [F4] applied to $f|_{C_1}$ gives a subgradient $v$ at $b$, so $f(y)\geq f(b)+\langle v,y-b\rangle$ for every $y\in C_1$.

Let $\ell(a)=f(b)+\langle v,a-b\rangle$ and $w=(f-\ell)\mathbf1_E$, defining $w=0$ on $E^c$. The function $w$ is integrable because $f\mathbf1_E$ has finite nonnegative integral and $\ell$ is integrable by the first-moment assumption. The supporting inequality gives $w\geq0$ on $E\cap S$, a full-measure set; thus $w^-=0$ almost everywhere. By [F5], $\int w^-\,d\mu=0$, so [F6] gives $\int w\,d\mu=\int w^+\,d\mu\geq0$. Linearity [F6] now yields $\int f\mathbf1_E\,d\mu\geq\int\ell\mathbf1_E\,d\mu$. Also $f=f\mathbf1_E+f\mathbf1_{E^c}$, with $f\mathbf1_{E^c}=0$ almost everywhere; [F5] and additivity [F8] give $\int f\,d\mu=\int f\mathbf1_E\,d\mu$. The integrable function $\ell\mathbf1_{E^c}$ is likewise zero almost everywhere, so [F5] applied to its positive and negative parts and linearity [F6] give $\int\ell\,d\mu=\int\ell\mathbf1_E\,d\mu$. Finally [F6] and the barycenter definition yield $\int\ell\,d\mu=f(b)+\langle v,b-b\rangle=f(b)$. This proves the claim in the finite-integral case; the infinite-integral case was handled in step 1.1.

Suppose an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ also has a measurable
parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A
**Markov kernel** (or **probability kernel**) representation is a function
$$
K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]
$$
such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, the set function
$A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
and, for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and every Borel set $C\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$
\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta,A)\in C\}\in\mathcal T.
$$
Here the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,1]$ is generated by its relatively open
subsets $U\cap[0,1]$, where $U$ is open in $\mathbb R$. Thus the second
condition says that each event-probability map $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is
measurable. The kernel represents the given experiment exactly when
$K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A)$ for every $\theta$ and $A$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-probability-measure]]).

This is an optional parameter-measurable version of a model. An arbitrary
experiment does not include a measurable structure on $\Theta$ or imply this
kernel condition.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

derivations.claim: For each $C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, [F2] makes $C_\theta$ measurable and [F3], applied to $1_C$, makes $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,C_\theta)$ measurable. Thus $J(C)$ is defined. The empty set has $J$-mass zero, while $(\Theta\times\mathcal X)_\theta=\mathcal X$ and [F1], [F5] give $J(\Theta\times\mathcal X)=1$.

If $(C_n)_{n\geq0}$ are pairwise disjoint product-measurable sets, their sections are pairwise disjoint. Countable additivity of each $K(\theta,\cdot)$ gives $K(\theta,(\bigcup_n C_n)_\theta)=\lim_N\sum_{n=0}^N K(\theta,(C_n)_\theta)$. The partial sums increase; [F4] passes this limit through the $\pi$-integral and yields $J(\bigcup_nC_n)=\sum_nJ(C_n)$. Therefore $J$ is a probability measure.

For a rectangle $A\times B$, its section is $B$ on $A$ and empty off $A$, so the definition gives $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$. For a nonnegative simple function $h=\sum_{i=1}^m c_i1_{C_i}$ with disjoint measurable sets and $c_i\geq0$, the set formula for $J$ and [F6] give the displayed iterated-integral identity by finite addition and homogeneity.

For general nonnegative product-measurable $h$, take the increasing simple approximants of [F4]. Apply monotone convergence first under $J$, then sectionwise under each $K(\theta,\cdot)$, and finally under $\pi$. The identity for the simple functions from step 3.1 passes to the limit, including when either side is $+\infty$.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed steps 1.1–4.1 and all nine prerequisites. Kernel integration theorem applies to probability (finite) kernels; the section theorem applied to indicators gives measurable sections. J(empty)=0 and J(total)=1; disjoint sections and increasing finite sums prove countable additivity. Indicator identity extends by finite simple sums and three monotone-convergence applications to all nonnegative h, including infinite integrals. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Suppose an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ also has a measurable
parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A
**Markov kernel** (or **probability kernel**) representation is a function
$$
K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]
$$
such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, the set function
$A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
and, for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and every Borel set $C\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$
\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta,A)\in C\}\in\mathcal T.
$$
Here the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,1]$ is generated by its relatively open
subsets $U\cap[0,1]$, where $U$ is open in $\mathbb R$. Thus the second
condition says that each event-probability map $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is
measurable. The kernel represents the given experiment exactly when
$K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A)$ for every $\theta$ and $A$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-probability-measure]]).

This is an optional parameter-measurable version of a model. An arbitrary
experiment does not include a measurable structure on $\Theta$ or imply this
kernel condition.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable
parameter and data spaces, with $\Theta$ nonempty, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel, writing
$P_\theta=K(\theta,\cdot)$ for the sampling law
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). Let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable
under these hypotheses by kernel integration
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]],
[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The **Bayes risk** of
$\delta$ under $\pi$ is
$$r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Its **worst-case risk** is
$$R^*(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta,\delta)\in[0,+\infty],$$
and the **minimax value** is
$$V_{\rm mm}=\inf\{R^*(\delta):\delta\text{ is a measurable randomized rule from data to actions}\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
These suprema and infima are taken in the extended order on $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]]); they exist by
[[lem-extended-reals-complete]]. The parameter set is nonempty and the rule
class is nonempty under the action-space hypothesis, so these are suprema and
infima of nonempty sets of nonnegative extended risks.
A rule is minimax if its worst-case risk equals this infimum. These definitions
make no assertion that a minimizer exists. Nonemptiness of $\mathsf D$ ensures
the rule class is nonempty: fixing any $a_0\in\mathsf D$ gives the constant
point-mass rule $x\mapsto\delta_{a_0}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: Fix a randomized rule $\delta$ and put $h_\delta(\theta,x)=\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)$. The lifted kernel $((\theta,x),B)\mapsto\delta(x,B)$ is a probability kernel because the coordinate projection $(\theta,x)\mapsto x$ is measurable by [F12]. The lifted integrand $(\theta,x,a)\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is product-measurable because the pairing map $((\theta,x),a)\mapsto(\theta,a)$ is measurable by [F12]. By [F5], $h_\delta$ is product-measurable. The risk definition [F2], prior-risk definition [F11], and joint-law identity [F3] therefore give $r_\pi(\delta)=\int h_\delta\,dJ$.

Apply the posterior disintegration identity [F4] to $h_\delta\geq0$. If $M$ is the second marginal of $J$, then $r_\pi(\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_\Theta h_\delta(\theta,x)\,\Pi_x(d\theta)\right)M(dx)$. Every integral is an extended nonnegative integral, so no integrability beyond the stated measurability is needed.

Lift $\Pi$ to the kernel $((x,a),B)\mapsto\Pi_x(B)$ from $\mathcal X\times\mathsf D$ to $\Theta$. The pairing map $((x,a),\theta)\mapsto(\theta,a)$ is measurable by [F12], so [F5] makes $q(x,a)$ product-measurable. For each fixed $x$, [F6] applied to the product probability $\Pi_x\times\delta(x,\cdot)$ and $L(\theta,a)$ gives $\int_\Theta h_\delta(\theta,x)\,\Pi_x(d\theta)=\int_{\mathsf D}q(x,a)\,\delta(x,da)$. The right side is measurable in $x$ by [F5]. Thus step 2.1 yields $r_\pi(\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\int_{\mathsf D}q(x,a)\,\delta(x,da)\,M(dx)$.

The point-mass kernel $\delta^*(x,B)=1_B(d^*(x))$ is measurable because $d^*$ is measurable by [F10]; applying step 3.1 gives $r_\pi(d^*)=\int g\,dM$ for $g(x)=q(x,d^*(x))$. The pairing map $x\mapsto(x,d^*(x))$ is measurable by [F10, F12], so $g$ is measurable. Put $h(x)=\int q(x,a)\,\delta(x,da)$, which is measurable by [F5]. On the measurable full-measure set $E$ from the statement, $g1_E\leq h1_E$, so [F8] gives $\int g1_E\,dM\leq\int h1_E\,dM$. The complementary integrals vanish by [F7]; additivity [F9] gives $\int g\,dM\leq\int h\,dM=r_\pi(\delta)$ by step 3.1. The rule $\delta$ was arbitrary.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from

$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with

$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$ and let $C$ be a
nonempty closed convex subset of $\mathbb R^d$, with closedness in the Euclidean
topology ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]) and convexity as in
[[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]. Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on
its Borel sets, and assume $\int_C\|a\|_2\,\mu(da)<\infty$, where $\|\cdot\|_2$
is the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Define the barycenter
$b=\int_Ca\,\mu(da)$ coordinatewise and assume $b\in C$. If
$f:C\to[0,+\infty]$ is Borel measurable and convex, then
$$f(b)\leq\int_C f(a)\,\mu(da).$$
Convexity for this possibly extended-valued $f$ uses the extended-functional
convention of
[[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]], including its
endpoint convention for $0\cdot(+\infty)$. On a convex restriction where
$f$ is finite, this inequality reduces to the real-valued Euclidean convention of
[[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]], as used in the
subgradient step of the proof. The barycenter is the vector of coordinate
integrals.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

derivations.claim: Let $m(x)=\int_\mathsf D\|a\|_2\,\delta(x,da)$. By [F2], $m$ is measurable. For each coordinate $j$, $|a_j|\leq\|a\|_2$, so the signed integral $b_j(x)=\int a_j\,\delta(x,da)$ is measurable on $E_0=\{x:m(x)<\infty\}$ by [F2]; hence $b=(b_1,\ldots,b_d)$ is measurable on $E_0$.

The set $E=\{x\in E_0:b(x)\in\mathsf D\}$ is measurable because $\mathsf D$ is closed and therefore Borel. Fix one $a_0\in\mathsf D$ and define $d(x)=b(x)$ on $E$ and $d(x)=a_0$ off $E$. This is a measurable map into $\mathsf D$; the hypotheses give $P_\theta(E)=1$ for every $\theta$.

For each $\theta$ and every $x\in E$, the section $a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is nonnegative Borel convex, $\delta(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure with finite first moment, and its barycenter $b(x)$ belongs to $\mathsf D$. Applying [F3] gives $L(\theta,d(x))=L(\theta,b(x))\leq\int_\mathsf D L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)$.

Put $g_\theta(x)=L(\theta,d(x))$ and $h_\theta(x)=\int_\mathsf D L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)$. Both are nonnegative measurable functions by [F1], [F2], and measurability of $d$. Step 2.1 gives $g_\theta1_E\leq h_\theta1_E$, so monotonicity [F5] gives $\int g_\theta1_E\,dP_\theta\leq\int h_\theta1_E\,dP_\theta$. Since $P_\theta(E^c)=0$, [F4] gives zero integrals on $E^c$; additivity [F5] then yields $\int g_\theta\,dP_\theta\leq\int h_\theta\,dP_\theta$. This is $R(\theta,d)\leq R(\theta,\delta)$, and it holds for every $\theta$.

citations.quote: A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let $(\Omega,w)$ be a finite probability space and let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$.
After identifying $(\Omega,w)$ with the full-power-set probability space of
[[thm-finite-probability-spaces-are-exactly-finite-full-power-set-probability-spaces]],
the expectation defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]] agrees with
the published finite formulas:
$$\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega)=\sum_{x\in X(\Omega)}x\,\mathbb P(X=x).$$

derivations.claim: For each $\theta\in[0,1]$, define $P_\theta(A)=\theta 1_{\{1\in A\}}+(1-\theta)1_{\{0\in A\}}$ for $A\subseteq\{0,1\}$. Its singleton masses are nonnegative and sum to one; any disjoint sequence of subsets has at most two nonempty terms, and their masses add to the union mass. Thus $P_\theta$ is a probability measure by [F1]. The identity rule $d(x)=x$ is measurable on the finite full-power-set spaces and estimates the target $\psi(\theta)=\theta$ by [F2].
The finite expectation formula [F4] and risk definition [F3] give $R(\theta,d)=(1-\theta)(0-\theta)^2+\theta(1-\theta)^2=\theta(1-\theta)$.
Since $\theta(1-\theta)=\frac14-(\theta-\frac12)^2$, the risk is at most $1/4$, with equality at $\theta=1/2$; substitution gives risk zero at $\theta=0$ and $\theta=1$.

citations.quote: A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable
parameter and data spaces, with $\Theta$ nonempty, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel, writing
$P_\theta=K(\theta,\cdot)$ for the sampling law
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). Let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable
under these hypotheses by kernel integration
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]],
[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The **Bayes risk** of
$\delta$ under $\pi$ is
$$r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Its **worst-case risk** is
$$R^*(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta,\delta)\in[0,+\infty],$$
and the **minimax value** is
$$V_{\rm mm}=\inf\{R^*(\delta):\delta\text{ is a measurable randomized rule from data to actions}\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
These suprema and infima are taken in the extended order on $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]]); they exist by
[[lem-extended-reals-complete]]. The parameter set is nonempty and the rule
class is nonempty under the action-space hypothesis, so these are suprema and
infima of nonempty sets of nonnegative extended risks.
A rule is minimax if its worst-case risk equals this infimum. These definitions
make no assertion that a minimizer exists. Nonemptiness of $\mathsf D$ ensures
the rule class is nonempty: fixing any $a_0\in\mathsf D$ gives the constant
point-mass rule $x\mapsto\delta_{a_0}$.

Let $(\Omega,w)$ be a finite probability space and let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$.
After identifying $(\Omega,w)$ with the full-power-set probability space of
[[thm-finite-probability-spaces-are-exactly-finite-full-power-set-probability-spaces]],
the expectation defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]] agrees with
the published finite formulas:
$$\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega)=\sum_{x\in X(\Omega)}x\,\mathbb P(X=x).$$

derivations.claim: The one-point data law assigns mass one to its only point under either parameter, so it is a probability measure by [F1]. For each $q\in[0,1]$, define $\delta_q(*,B)=q1_{\{1\in B\}}+(1-q)1_{\{0\in B\}}$ for $B\subseteq\{0,1\}$; its two singleton masses are nonnegative and sum to one, hence it is a probability measure. Evaluations are measurable on the one-point data space, so $\delta_q$ is a probability kernel by [F2]. Deterministic rules are the cases $q=0$ and $q=1$.

By the finite expectation formula [F4] and the loss-risk definition [F3], the rule with probability $q$ of action $1$ has risks $R(0)=q$ and $R(1)=1-q$. Its worst-case risk is therefore $\max(q,1-q)\geq(q+1-q)/2=1/2$, with equality at $q=1/2$.

The two deterministic rules have $q=0$ or $q=1$, so each has worst-case risk $1$. The fair randomized rule has worst-case risk $1/2$, and step 1.2 shows no rule can do better. Thus the minimax value is $1/2$ and randomization strictly improves worst-case risk over every deterministic rule.

For two decision rules $\delta_0,\delta_1$ in one decision problem,
$\delta_1$ **dominates** $\delta_0$ if
$R(\theta,\delta_1)\leq R(\theta,\delta_0)$ for every parameter $\theta$,
with strict inequality for at least one $\theta$. A rule is **admissible** if
no decision rule dominates it; otherwise it is inadmissible. Risk is the
extended-valued function of [[def-loss-function-and-risk]]. Admissibility is
a pointwise comparison across the whole parameter set; it does not assert that
the rule minimizes risk at any particular parameter or under a global
criterion.

derivations.claim: For each $\theta\in\{0,1\}$, let $P_\theta$ be the point mass at $\theta$. In any disjoint sequence of events at most one event contains $\theta$, so this law is countably additive and has total mass one; it is a probability measure by [F1]. Both maps $d_0(x)=0$ and $d_1(x)=x$ are measurable on the finite full-power-set spaces by [F2].

Under squared-error loss, the only data value with positive $P_\theta$-mass is $x=\theta$. The finite-sum formula [F5] and risk definition [F3] therefore give $R(\theta,d_0)=\theta^2=\theta$ and $R(\theta,d_1)=(\theta-\theta)^2=0$.
The risks satisfy $R(\theta,d_1)\leq R(\theta,d_0)$ at both parameters, and the inequality is strict at $\theta=1$. Thus $d_1$ dominates the constant rule $d_0$ by [F4].

citations.quote: A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a probability
kernel from a standard-Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to a
standard-Borel data space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, where standard Borel means
measurably isomorphic to a Polish space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]). Let $\pi$ be a prior,
and let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be jointly measurable for a
measurable action space $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$. Let $J$ be the joint prior-data
law of [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]], let $M$ be its data
marginal, and let $\Pi_x(d\theta)$ be a regular posterior distribution of
$\theta$ given $x$ (the disintegration is supplied by
[[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]]).
Define posterior risk
$$q(x,a)=\int_\Theta L(\theta,a)\,\Pi_x(d\theta).$$
Suppose a measurable deterministic rule $d^*:\mathcal X\to\mathsf D$
attains the posterior minimum for $M$-almost every $x$; that is,
$q(x,d^*(x))\leq q(x,a)$ for every $a\in\mathsf D$ on one measurable
$M$-full-measure set. Then $d^*$ minimizes prior-integrated risk among all randomized decision
rules $\delta$:
$$r_\pi(d^*)\leq r_\pi(\delta).$$
No conclusion is asserted when a measurable posterior minimizer does not
exist. All risks may be $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: The prior and data law are point masses on singleton standard-Borel spaces by [F1]; their joint law is the point mass on the singleton pair. Define the posterior to be the point mass at $0$. The only conditioning events are empty or the whole singleton, and the conditional-law identity holds for both, so this is a regular conditional law by [F3]. Integrating $L(0,a)=a$ against it gives posterior risk $q(a)=a$ by [F2].

For every $a\in(0,1)$, $q(a)=a>0$, while the sequence $a_n=1/(n+1)$ lies in $(0,1)$ and has $q(a_n)\to0$. Thus $\inf_{a\in(0,1)}q(a)=0$ and the infimum is not attained. The claimed universal minimizer does not exist, which refutes the statement and illustrates the explicit existence premise in [F4].
