citations.quote:
Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be signed measures or complex measures on the same
measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. They are **mutually singular**, written
$$\mu\perp \nu,$$
when there are measurable sets $P,N\in\mathcal A$ with
$$P\cap N=\varnothing,\qquad P\cup N=X,$$
such that:

1. every measurable subset of $N$ has $\mu$-value $0$;
2. every measurable subset of $P$ has $\nu$-value $0$.

For positive measures this is equivalent to the usual condition
$\mu(N)=0$ and $\nu(P)=0$, because positivity turns vanishing on the ambient set
into vanishing on all measurable subsets.

Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on the same measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. We say that $
u$ is **absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$**, and write
$$
u\ll\mu,$$
if every measurable $\mu$-null set is also $
u$-null:
$$\mu(E)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
u(E)=0\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
Because every measurable subset of a $\mu$-null set is again $\mu$-null, this is equivalent to requiring $
u(F)=0$ for every measurable $F\subseteq E$ whenever $\mu(E)=0$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For
$E\in\mathcal A$, define its **total variation on $E$** by
$$|\nu|(E):=\sup\left\{\sum_{n=0}^\infty |\nu(E_n)|:\ (E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\text{ is a countable measurable partition of }E\right\},$$
where, for a signed measure, the term $|\nu(E_n)|$ means the ordinary absolute
value when $\nu(E_n)\in\mathbb R$ and means $+\infty$ when
$\nu(E_n)\in\{+\infty,-\infty\}$; for a complex measure it is the usual complex
modulus. A countable measurable partition of $E$ means:

1. each $E_n$ lies in $\mathcal A$;
2. the sets $E_n$ are pairwise disjoint;
3. $E=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n$.

The sum on the right is a nonnegative extended series, so it is always defined
in $[0,+\infty] \subseteq \overline{\mathbb R}$.

suffice. For complex measures, that finite-partition shortcut is not built into

u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|

$$

if every measurable $\mu$-null set is also $

Because every measurable subset of a $\mu$-null set is again $\mu$-null, this is equivalent to requiring $

$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

$(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function
$$\nu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow\mathbb C$$
such that:

1. $\nu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in
   $\mathcal A$,
   $$\nu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \nu(E_n)$$
   in $\mathbb C$.

The codomain is the field $\mathbb C$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]), so a complex measure is finite-valued by
definition: there is no complex number called $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ to allow.

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For
$E\in\mathcal A$, define its **total variation on $E$** by
$$|\nu|(E):=\sup\left\{\sum_{n=0}^\infty |\nu(E_n)|:\ (E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\text{ is a countable measurable partition of }E\right\},$$
where, for a signed measure, the term $|\nu(E_n)|$ means the ordinary absolute
value when $\nu(E_n)\in\mathbb R$ and means $+\infty$ when
$\nu(E_n)\in\{+\infty,-\infty\}$; for a complex measure it is the usual complex
modulus. A countable measurable partition of $E$ means:

1. each $E_n$ lies in $\mathcal A$;
2. the sets $E_n$ are pairwise disjoint;
3. $E=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n$.

The sum on the right is a nonnegative extended series, so it is always defined
in $[0,+\infty] \subseteq \overline{\mathbb R}$.

For signed measures, a later proposition shows that finite partitions already
suffice. For complex measures, that finite-partition shortcut is not built into
the definition here.

$|\nu|$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not

Fix $\theta$. Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Thus $K(T(x),A)$ is a common version of the conditional probability of $A$ given $T$, under every parameter. The kernel is fixed independently of $\theta$. Under AC, standard Borelness gives each law an individual conditional law through [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]]; sufficiency additionally asks that one kernel works across parameters.

A statistic $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is **complete** for $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ if, for every measurable real-valued $g$ such that $E_\theta|g(T)|<\infty$ for every $\theta$, the conditions $E_\theta[g(T)]=0$ for every $\theta$ imply $P_\theta(g(T)=0)=1$ for every $\theta$. Integrability is part of the premise; completeness is a property of the statistic relative to the specified family.

A statistic $U:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)$ is **ancillary** for $(P_\theta)$ if its pushforward probability $P_\theta\circ U^{-1}$ does not depend on $\theta$. Equivalently, for every $C\in\mathcal C$, $P_\theta(U\in C)$ is constant in $\theta$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

There is a probability kernel $K:T\to E$ such that $L(\omega,\cdot)=K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ simultaneously outside a single null set. In fact, with the stated everywhere-kernel convention, the construction below gives this equality for every $\omega$. Consequently K is a conditional law of X given Y.

There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|

E_{P_0}[g r]=E_{P_1}[g]
$$
for every nonnegative measurable $g$, and also for every real-valued

Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Thus $K(T(x),A)$ is a common version of the conditional probability of $A$ given $T$, under every parameter. The kernel is fixed independently of $\theta$. Under AC, standard Borelness gives each law an individual conditional law through [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]]; sufficiency additionally asks that one kernel works across parameters.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be standard Borel, let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite positive measure, let $h:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$ be a measurable statistic. For $\eta\in\mathbb R^k$ put

$$Z(\eta)=\int h(x)e^{\eta\cdot T(x)}\,\mu(dx),\qquad H=\{\eta:0<Z(\eta)<\infty\},\qquad A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta).$$

For a parameter set $\Omega\subseteq H$, the associated **exponential family** has laws $P_\eta$ with density

$$p_\eta(x)=h(x)\exp\{\eta\cdot T(x)-A(\eta)\}\quad(\eta\in\Omega).$$

The normalization $A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta)$ makes each density integrate to one. In this item **full-rank** means that $\Omega$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^k$ and there do not exist $b\ne0$ and $c\in\mathbb R$ with $b\cdot T=c$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{h>0\}$. A parameter set containing an open subset is also called regular in some sources; terminology varies, so this definition controls here. The condition is stronger than needed for the completeness theorem below but rules out redundant displayed coordinates.

Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Thus $K(T(x),A)$ is a common version of the conditional probability of $A$ given $T$, under every parameter. The kernel is fixed independently of $\theta$. Under AC, standard Borelness gives each law an individual conditional law through [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]]; sufficiency additionally asks that one kernel works across parameters.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be standard Borel, let $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ be a statistic. Fix $\theta_0\in\Theta$ and set $P_0=P_{\theta_0}$. Assume $P_\theta\ll P_0$ for every $\theta$. all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Thus $K(T(x),A)$ is a common version of the conditional probability of $A$ given $T$, under every parameter. The kernel is fixed independently of $\theta$. Under AC, standard Borelness gives each law an individual conditional law through [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]]; sufficiency additionally asks that one kernel works across parameters.

A statistic $T$ into a standard Borel space is **minimal sufficient** for $(P_\theta)$ if $\sigma(T)$ is a minimal sufficient $\sigma$-field in the preceding sense. Minimality is modulo sets null under every model law. It does not assert literal pointwise equality with any other minimal sufficient statistic.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every countable product of completely metrizable spaces is completely metrizable, including the empty product.
Assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a countable product of second countable spaces is second countable.

Assume AC. Let $X$ and $Y$ take values in nonempty standard-Borel spaces $(E,\mathcal S)$ and $(T,\mathcal T)$ on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. Let $L$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, everywhere a probability kernel. There is a probability kernel $K:T\to E$ such that $L(\omega,\cdot)=K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ simultaneously outside a single null set. In fact, with the stated everywhere-kernel convention, the construction below gives this equality for every $\omega$. Consequently K is a conditional law of X given Y.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ and $g : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$. Then $g$ is
$\sigma(f)$-measurable if and only if there is a Borel measurable function
$h : \mathbb{R} \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ such that

$$g = h \circ f.$$
Assume AC. Every standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal S)$ is measurably isomorphic to a Borel subset of $[0,1]$, including $E=\varnothing$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f : X \to [0,+\infty]$ be measurable. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ define

$$s_k := \sum_{j=0}^{k2^k-1} j2^{-k}\, \mathbf{1}_{\{j2^{-k} \le f < (j+1)2^{-k}\}} + k\,\mathbf{1}_{\{f \ge k\}}.$$

Then each $s_k$ is a simple measurable function,

$$0 \le s_k \le s_{k+1} \le f,$$

and $s_k(x) \to f(x)$ for every $x \in X$. If $E \subseteq X$ is a set on which
$f \le M < +\infty$, then $s_k \to f$ uniformly on $E$.

For a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a sub-$\sigma$-field $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal A$ is **sufficient** if for every bounded measurable $u:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ there is one $\mathcal G$-measurable bounded function $v_u$ such that

$$\int_A u\,dP_\theta=\int_A v_u\,dP_\theta\quad(A\in\mathcal G,\ \theta\in\Theta).$$

For each $\theta$, this says that $v_u$ is a version of $E_\theta[u\mid\mathcal G]$, with the same pointwise version used for every parameter. Define the family-null ideal $\mathcal N=\{N\in\mathcal A:P_\theta(N)=0\text{ for every }\theta\}$. We say $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal H\pmod{\mathcal N}$ if for every $A\in\mathcal G$ there is $B\in\mathcal H$ with $A\triangle B\in\mathcal N$. A sufficient $\sigma$-field $\mathcal G_*$ is **minimal sufficient** if $\mathcal G_*\subseteq\mathcal H\pmod{\mathcal N}$ for every sufficient $\mathcal H$.

derivations.claim: Since $P_k\ll Q$, [F5] gives finite-valued nonnegative Borel densities $f_k$ after changing each on its null set. Their exceptional sets have countable union $N$ with $Q(N)=0$; reset all $f_k$ to zero on $N$. By [F6], $[0,\infty)^{\mathbb N}$ is standard Borel. The coordinate maps are Borel, hence $T$ is Borel.

By [F7], choose a conditional-law kernel $K$ for $X$ given $T$ under $Q$. Its defining identity extends from indicator weights to nonnegative Borel weights by [F9]. By [F5], $P_k(A\cap T^{-1}C)=\int 1_A1_C(T)f_k\,dQ$. Since $T_k=f_k$, applying the weighted conditional identity with weight $1_C(t)t_k$ gives $P_k(A\cap T^{-1}C)=\int_CK(t,A)t_kQ^T(dt)$; taking $A=\mathcal X$ gives $P_k^T(C)=\int_Ct_kQ^T(dt)$. Thus $K$ works under every $P_k$, so [F1] gives sufficiency.

Let $S$ be any other standard Borel sufficient statistic with common kernel $L$. The same kernel is a conditional law under $Q$: its conditional identity follows by multiplying the identity under $P_k$ by $w_k$ and summing the nonnegative integrals, with [F9] justifying passage to the countable sum. It is also the common conditional law under each $P_k$. Let $Q^S$ and $P_k^S$ be the image laws. The identity $P_k^S\ll Q^S$ follows from $P_k\ll Q$; write $r_k=dP_k^S/dQ^S$. Disintegrating with $L$ and extending the conditional identity to the nonnegative weight $r_k$ by [F9] gives, for every $A$, $P_k(A)=\int L(s,A)r_k(s)Q^S(ds)=\int_A r_k(S(x))Q(dx)$. RN uniqueness yields $f_k=r_k(S)$ $Q$-almost surely.

Apply [F5] to each coordinate to obtain Borel $r_k$ (modified on $Q^S$-null sets if necessary). The map $\varphi(s)=(r_k(s))_{k\ge1}$ is Borel because its coordinate maps are Borel; step 2.2 gives $T=\varphi(S)$ $Q$-almost surely. Since every weight is positive, $Q(C)=0$ iff $P_k(C)=0$ for every $k$. For every Borel $D$ in the target of $T$, the sets $T^{-1}(D)$ and $S^{-1}(\varphi^{-1}(D))$ differ only on $\{T\ne\varphi(S)\}$, which is $Q$-null by step 2.2. Therefore $\sigma(T)\subseteq\sigma(S)$ modulo the family-null ideal, establishing the asserted comparison with $S$.

Let $\mathcal H$ be any sufficient sub-sigma-field as in [F2]. For each $k$, apply [F5] on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal H)$ to obtain a finite nonnegative $\mathcal H$-measurable density $r_k=d(P_k|_{\mathcal H})/d(Q|_{\mathcal H})$. For each $A\in\mathcal A$, sufficiency supplies one bounded $\mathcal H$-measurable $v_A$ with the conditional identities for $1_A$ under every $P_k$. Summing with weights gives those identities under $Q$. Testing on $\{v_A<0\}$ and $\{v_A>1\}$ shows $0\le v_A\le1$ $Q$-almost surely; clipping on these $\mathcal H$-measurable null sets preserves every identity because $P_k\ll Q$. Simple approximation and [F9] extend the $Q$ conditional identity to the nonnegative $\mathcal H$-measurable weight $r_k$, while the restricted RN identity extends to $v_A$. Consequently $\int_A r_k\,dQ=\int v_A r_k\,dQ=\int v_A\,dP_k=P_k(A)$. Uniqueness in [F5] gives $f_k=r_k$ $Q$-almost surely. Combining only these countably many null sets, $T=(r_k)_k$ $Q$-almost surely. The right side is $\mathcal H$-measurable, so every event in $\sigma(T)$ agrees modulo a family-null set with an event in $\mathcal H$. The kernel in step 2.1 gives sufficiency of $\sigma(T)$ by extending its event identities to bounded functions using simple approximation and [F9]. Thus [F2] proves minimality against every sufficient sub-sigma-field.

Let $\mathcal X$ be countable with its full $\sigma$-field, so it is standard Borel under the discrete metric. Let $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be dominated by a fixed $\sigma$-finite positive measure $\mu$. Choose the finite-valued densities $p_\theta=dP_\theta/d\mu$ as in [[def-likelihood-density]]. Let $X_0\subseteq\mathcal X$ satisfy $P_\theta(X_0)=1$ and $P_\theta(\{x\})>0$ for every $x\in X_0$ and every $\theta$. Write $m_\theta(x)=P_\theta(\{x\})$. For each $x\in X_0$, $0<\mu(\{x\})<\infty$ and $p_\theta(x)=m_\theta(x)/\mu(\{x\})$: positivity follows from $m_\theta(x)>0$, finiteness from sigma-finiteness, and the value is fixed by the density integral on the positive-measure singleton. Consequently

$$\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_\theta(y)}=\frac{m_\theta(x)}{m_\theta(y)}\frac{\mu(\{y\})}{\mu(\{x\})}.$$

For $x,y\in X_0$, define $x\sim y$ if there is a constant $c(x,y)>0$ such that $m_\theta(x)/m_\theta(y)=c(x,y)$ for every $\theta$. The displayed fixed singleton factor shows this is equivalent to constancy of the common-reference density ratio. This is an equivalence relation: the constants for $(x,x)$, $(y,x)$ and $(x,z)$ are respectively $1$, $c(x,y)^{-1}$ and $c(x,y)c(y,z)$. Its equivalence classes form a countable quotient. Equip that quotient with its discrete $\sigma$-field; it is standard Borel because the discrete metric is complete and the countable space itself is dense. Since $\Theta\ne\varnothing$ and $P_\theta(X_0)=1$, $X_0$ is nonempty; define the class statistic by mapping each point of $X_0$ to its class and every point off $X_0$ to any fixed class. It is measurable because $\mathcal X$ has the full $\sigma$-field, and values off $X_0$ are null under every law.

Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Thus $K(T(x),A)$ is a common version of the conditional probability of $A$ given $T$, under every parameter. The kernel is fixed independently of $\theta$. Under AC, standard Borelness gives each law an individual conditional law through [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]]; sufficiency additionally asks that one kernel works across parameters.

A statistic $T$ into a standard Borel space is **minimal sufficient** for $(P_\theta)$ if $\sigma(T)$ is a minimal sufficient $\sigma$-field in the preceding sense. Minimality is modulo sets null under every model law. It does not assert literal pointwise equality with any other minimal sufficient statistic.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

For a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a sub-$\sigma$-field $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal A$ is **sufficient** if for every bounded measurable $u:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ there is one $\mathcal G$-measurable bounded function $v_u$ such that

$$\int_A u\,dP_\theta=\int_A v_u\,dP_\theta\quad(A\in\mathcal G,\ \theta\in\Theta).$$

For each $\theta$, this says that $v_u$ is a version of $E_\theta[u\mid\mathcal G]$, with the same pointwise version used for every parameter. Define the family-null ideal $\mathcal N=\{N\in\mathcal A:P_\theta(N)=0\text{ for every }\theta\}$. We say $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal H\pmod{\mathcal N}$ if for every $A\in\mathcal G$ there is $B\in\mathcal H$ with $A\triangle B\in\mathcal N$. A sufficient $\sigma$-field $\mathcal G_*$ is **minimal sufficient** if $\mathcal G_*\subseteq\mathcal H\pmod{\mathcal N}$ for every sufficient $\mathcal H$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix a class $D\subseteq X_0$ and its first point $r_D$ in a fixed enumeration. By [F1], $w_D(x)=P_\theta(\{x\})/P_\theta(\{r_D\})$ for $x\in D$ is positive and independent of $\theta$. The sum $W_D=\sum_{x\in D}w_D(x)=P_\theta(D)/P_\theta(\{r_D\})$ is finite and positive. Hence $K(D,\{x\})=w_D(x)/W_D$ on $D$, zero off $D$, is a probability law independent of $\theta$. Give the common-null complement any fixed point-mass conditional law. The quotient is countable discrete standard Borel, so this is a measurable probability kernel.

Let $S$ be any other sufficient statistic into a standard Borel space, with common kernel $L$. If $x,y\in X_0$ and $S(x)=S(y)=s$, then $\{s\}$ is Borel and $P_\theta(S=s)>0$ for every $\theta$. The conditional identity forces $L(s,\{x\})=P_\theta(\{x\})/P_\theta(S=s)$ and $L(s,\{y\})=P_\theta(\{y\})/P_\theta(S=s)$. The common kernel has no parameter index, so their ratio is constant in $\theta$; [F1] yields $x\sim y$. Therefore $S$ is constant only within one class on $X_0$.

For every $\theta$, class $D$, and $A\subseteq\mathcal X$, the point-mass ratio definition gives $P_\theta(A\cap D)=P_\theta(D)K(D,A)$. Summing over classes proves the conditional-law identity in [F2]; thus $T$ is sufficient.

Since $X_0$ is countable, its image under $S$ is countable and Borel in the standard Borel target. Step 1.2 defines a function from that image to the countable quotient with $T=\varphi\circ S$ on $X_0$; extend $\varphi$ by one fixed class off the image. This extension is Borel because its nonconstant domain is countable. Since every model law is concentrated on $X_0$, $T=\varphi(S)$ almost surely under every parameter. This proves the comparison with every standard Borel sufficient statistic.

Let $\mathcal H$ be any sufficient sub-sigma-field of the full sigma-field on $\mathcal X$. For $x,y\in\mathcal X$ that some $\mathcal H$-event separates, choose one such event, using [A1] for this countable set of pairs. The atoms $H_x=\{y:\text{no }\mathcal H\text{-event separates }x,y\}$ are measurable: each is the countable intersection of the chosen events or their complements containing $x$. Every $\mathcal H$-measurable function is constant on each $H_x$, since unequal real values would be separated by the inverse image of a rational cut. For $x,y\in X_0$ in the same atom $H$, let $v_x,v_y$ be common bounded conditional-expectation versions of $1_{\{x\}},1_{\{y\}}$ supplied by sufficiency. Testing on $H$ gives $v_x|_H=P_\theta(\{x\})/P_\theta(H)$ and $v_y|_H=P_\theta(\{y\})/P_\theta(H)$ for every $\theta$; these constants are positive and independent of $\theta$. Thus the point-mass ratio is constant and $x\sim y$. Each class $D$ is therefore the intersection with $X_0$ of a union of $\mathcal H$-atoms. That union is countable and measurable, and differs from $T^{-1}(\{D\})$ only off $X_0$. Unions of classes give $\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathcal H$ modulo the family-null ideal. The common kernel in step 2.1 supplies bounded conditional versions for $\sigma(T)$ by summing bounded functions on the countable sample space. Hence [F3] proves minimal sufficiency in its full sigma-field sense.

boundaries.evidence: Statement inherits Θ nonempty and a common positive support from the definition.
Statement confines ratios to X₀ where every point mass is positive; the common-null complement is handled in step 1.1.
Step 1.1 gives ratio one when comparing a point with itself.

Step 1.1 includes singleton likelihood classes; step 1.2 proves any sufficient fiber stays in one class. Step 3.1 proves the full comparison required by def-minimal-sufficient-sigma-field, including sub-sigma-fields that were not presented by a standard Borel statistic.

There is no converse claiming that a minimally sufficient statistic must equal this class map pointwise. Proof 2.2 establishes factorization through each sufficient S on X_0 and permits changes on the common-null complement.

risk_review.notes: Steps 1.1–2.2 correctly give normalized class kernels and comparison with sufficient standard-Borel statistics. citations.quote: A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

derivations.claim: The endpoint laws are $P_0=\delta_0$ and $P_1=\delta_1$, so $Q=\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\delta_1$ assigns mass $1/2$ to each point. This is a probability measure.

For every $A\subseteq\{0,1\}$, if $Q(A)=0$ then $A=\varnothing$, so $P_\theta(A)=0$; hence $P_\theta\ll Q$. Define $q_\theta(0)=2(1-\theta)$ and $q_\theta(1)=2\theta$. For each subset $A$, $\int_Aq_\theta\,dQ=1_{\{0\in A\}}(1-\theta)+1_{\{1\in A\}}\theta=P_\theta(A)$. Thus $q_\theta=dP_\theta/dQ$, including its zero values at endpoints, and the displayed finite mixture directly dominates every member.

Step 2.1 identifies the empty set as the only Q-null subset.

Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Thus $K(T(x),A)$ is a common version of the conditional probability of $A$ given $T$, under every parameter. The kernel is fixed independently of $\theta$. Under AC, standard Borelness gives each law an individual conditional law through [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]]; sufficiency additionally asks that one kernel works across parameters.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: Define $K(t,A)=1_A((t,0))$. By [F5] each section is a point-mass probability, and all evaluations are measurable on the finite target, so [F6] makes $K$ a probability kernel independent of $\theta$. Every $P_\theta$ is concentrated on points $(t,0)$, so conditioning on $T=t$ gives this kernel. Hence $T$ is sufficient by [F1].

Every atom of $R$ has mass $1/4$, so $P_\theta\ll R$. The density values are $dP_\theta/dR(t,u)=4P_\theta(t,0)$ if $u=0$ and zero if $u=1$. For fixed $t$, the two points $(t,0)$ and $(t,1)$ have the same $T$ value but different derivative values. Every atom has positive $R$-mass, so no modification on an $R$-null set can change them; the derivative has no $\sigma(T)$-measurable version.

This refutes the implication with an arbitrary external reference. Taking the reference to be a member $P_{\theta_0}$ restores the common conditional law needed for the criterion: the conditional kernel at the reference is then the model’s shared kernel. The counterexample’s $R$ has conditional second coordinate uniform given $T$, while each model law has second coordinate zero, identifying the precise missing hypothesis.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be standard Borel, let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite positive measure, let $h:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$ be a measurable statistic. For $\eta\in\mathbb R^k$ put

$$Z(\eta)=\int h(x)e^{\eta\cdot T(x)}\,\mu(dx),\qquad H=\{\eta:0<Z(\eta)<\infty\},\qquad A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta).$$

For a parameter set $\Omega\subseteq H$, the associated **exponential family** has laws $P_\eta$ with density

$$p_\eta(x)=h(x)\exp\{\eta\cdot T(x)-A(\eta)\}\quad(\eta\in\Omega).$$

The normalization $A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta)$ makes each density integrate to one. In this item **full-rank** means that $\Omega$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^k$ and there do not exist $b\ne0$ and $c\in\mathbb R$ with $b\cdot T=c$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{h>0\}$. A parameter set containing an open subset is also called regular in some sources; terminology varies, so this definition controls here. The condition is stronger than needed for the completeness theorem below but rules out redundant displayed coordinates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

A statistic $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is **complete** for $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ if, for every measurable real-valued $g$ such that $E_\theta|g(T)|<\infty$ for every $\theta$, the conditions $E_\theta[g(T)]=0$ for every $\theta$ imply $P_\theta(g(T)=0)=1$ for every $\theta$. Integrability is part of the premise; completeness is a property of the statistic relative to the specified family.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $0\le s,t$ and a real random variable
$X_t-X_s$ has law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then, for every integer $m\ge1$,
$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$
where
$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be standard Borel, let $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ be a statistic. Fix $\theta_0\in\Theta$ and set $P_0=P_{\theta_0}$. Assume $P_\theta\ll P_0$ for every $\theta$. Then $T$ is sufficient if and only if for every $\theta$ the Radon–Nikodym derivative $dP_\theta/dP_0$ has a $\sigma(T)$-measurable version. Equivalently, for each $\theta$ there is a Borel $g_\theta:\mathcal Y\to[0,\infty)$ with $dP_\theta/dP_0=g_\theta(T)$ $P_0$-almost surely. The null exceptional set may depend on $\theta$. The requirement $P_0\in\{P_\theta\}$ is essential; an arbitrary external dominating probability is not covered.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

derivations.claim: The map $T$ is polynomial and hence a statistic by [F2]. Let $\lambda_B$ be one-dimensional Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$; the Borel half-open intervals $(-k,k]$ give it a sigma-finite cover of finite measure by [F5]. By [F4] and the affine change of variables [F10] for $z\mapsto\theta+\theta z$, each $X_i$ has Borel density $q_\theta(x_i)=(\sqrt{2\pi}\theta)^{-1}e^{-(x_i-\theta)^2/(2\theta^2)}$ relative to $\lambda_B$. Independence [F5] gives the joint law $P_\theta^{X_1}\times P_\theta^{X_2}$. The measure with density $q_\theta(x_1)q_\theta(x_2)$ relative to $\lambda_B\times\lambda_B$ exists by [F9]; Tonelli [F6] shows that it has total mass one and agrees with this product law on every measurable rectangle. By [F11], these rectangles generate the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^2$, so the product-measure uniqueness clause [F9] identifies this density measure with the joint law. Expanding its density gives $p_\theta(x_1,x_2)=(2\pi)^{-1}\theta^{-2}\exp\left(-S_2/(2\theta^2)+S_1/\theta-1\right)$. Put $u=1/\theta$, $h(x_1,x_2)=(2\pi)^{-1}$, $\Omega=\{(u,-u^2/2):u>0\}$, and $A(u,-u^2/2)=1-2\log u$. Then $p_\theta=h\exp\{uS_1-u^2S_2/2-A(u,-u^2/2)\}$, with normalizer $Z(u,-u^2/2)=e^{A}=e/u^2$; the normalization follows from the product normal density just derived. Thus the canonical statistic is $(S_1,S_2)$, and the natural parameter set lies on $\eta_2=-\eta_1^2/2$, so it contains no open subset of $\mathbb R^2$. Both densities are strictly positive, so $P_\theta\ll P_{\theta_0}$ for any fixed $\theta_0>0$. Their ratio is a Borel function of $T$; since $P_{\theta_0}$ is a model member, [F7] proves sufficiency.

From $X_i=\theta+\theta Z_i$ and [F4], $E_\theta X_i=\theta$ and $E_\theta X_i^2=2\theta^2$. The bound $|z|\le1+z^2$ gives $E|Z_i|\le1+E Z_i^2=2$, hence $E_\theta|X_i|<\infty$. Let $q_\theta$ be the one-dimensional normal density from step 1.1 and write $x^+=\max(x,0)$, $x^- =\max(-x,0)$. Independence [F5] identifies the joint law with the product of the two marginal laws, each having density $q_\theta$. Tonelli [F6] therefore gives, for every $a,b\in\{+,-\}$, $E_\theta[X_1^aX_2^b]=\left(\int_{\mathbb R}x^a q_\theta(x)\,dx\right)\left(\int_{\mathbb R}x^b q_\theta(x)\,dx\right)$, where all four factors are finite by $E_\theta|X_i|<\infty$. Subtracting the four finite identities yields $E_\theta[X_1X_2]=(E_\theta X_1)(E_\theta X_2)$; linearity [F8] now gives $E_\theta S_1^2=E X_1^2+E X_2^2+2E X_1E X_2=6\theta^2$, while $E_\theta S_2=4\theta^2$. Hence $E_\theta g(T)=6\theta^2-\tfrac32(4\theta^2)=0$ for every $\theta>0$. Also $|g(T)|\le S_1^2+\tfrac32S_2$, whose expectation is finite, so $g(T)$ is integrable.

At $(x_1,x_2)=(1,0)$, $g(T)=-1/2$. By continuity it is nonzero on a neighborhood. The density in step 1.1 is continuous and strictly positive at this point, so there is a smaller nondegenerate rectangle inside that neighborhood on which the density is bounded below by half its value at $(1,0)$. The rectangle has positive $\lambda_B\times\lambda_B$ measure by the one-dimensional box formula and the product rectangle formula [F5, F9], hence it has positive probability under every $\theta>0$. Therefore $g(T)$ is not zero almost surely, contradicting completeness [F3].

The witness does not claim that incompleteness forces a curved parameter set. It proves existence for the specified curve (u,-u^2/2), using g=s_1^2-3s_2/2; there is no converse direction in the Statement refuted.

Affine C1 change of variables gives each N(θ,θ²) density; independence, Tonelli and rectangle uniqueness on Borel R² give the positive product density.
