citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $0\le s,t$ and a real random variable
$X_t-X_s$ has law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then, for every integer $m\ge1$,
$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$
where
$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. For every $u \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $u \ne 0$ and every real $c$, the affine
   hyperplane
   $$H_{u,c} \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : \langle u,x\rangle = c \,\}$$
   ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(H_{u,c}) = 0$, and so is every subset of it.
2. Every proper linear subspace $W \subsetneq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-linear-subspace]]) is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(W) = 0$.

At $n = 1$ a hyperplane is the singleton $\{c/u_0\}$ and the only proper linear
subspace is $\{0\}$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be standard Borel, let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite positive measure, let $h:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$ be a measurable statistic. For $\eta\in\mathbb R^k$ put

$$Z(\eta)=\int h(x)e^{\eta\cdot T(x)}\,\mu(dx),\qquad H=\{\eta:0<Z(\eta)<\infty\},\qquad A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta).$$

For a parameter set $\Omega\subseteq H$, the associated **exponential family** has laws $P_\eta$ with density

$$p_\eta(x)=h(x)\exp\{\eta\cdot T(x)-A(\eta)\}\quad(\eta\in\Omega).$$

The normalization $A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta)$ makes each density integrate to one. In this item **full-rank** means that $\Omega$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^k$ and there do not exist $b\ne0$ and $c\in\mathbb R$ with $b\cdot T=c$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{h>0\}$. A parameter set containing an open subset is also called regular in some sources; terminology varies, so this definition controls here. The condition is stronger than needed for the completeness theorem below but rules out redundant displayed coordinates.

Assume AC. Let $(P_\eta)_{\eta\in\Omega}$ be the exponential family of [[def-exponential-family]] on a standard Borel sample space, with $\Omega\ne\varnothing$, and let $T$ be its canonical statistic. Then $T$ is sufficient.

Assume AC and let $(P_\eta)_{\eta\in\Omega}$ be a full-rank exponential family as in [[def-exponential-family]], with $\Omega$ containing a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^k$. Then its canonical statistic $T$ is complete.

A statistic $U:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)$ is **ancillary** for $(P_\theta)$ if its pushforward probability $P_\theta\circ U^{-1}$ does not depend on $\theta$. Equivalently, for every $C\in\mathcal C$, $P_\theta(U\in C)$ is constant in $\theta$.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be standard Borel, and let $T$ and $U$ be statistics from this sample space into standard Borel spaces for a family $(P_\theta)$. If $T$ is complete and sufficient and $U$ is ancillary, then $T$ and $U$ are independent under every $P_\theta$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

derivations.claim: The mean map is continuous, hence Borel by [F2] and a statistic. Use $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure $dx$ as base measure; it is sigma-finite by [F3]. By [F1] and the translation case of [F10], each coordinate has density $\phi(x_i-\mu)$. Independence [F4] gives the product joint law. For $n=1$ this is already the joint density. For $n\ge2$, repeated use of [F13] identifies $\lambda_n$ with the product of the one-dimensional Lebesgue measures. The measure with density $q(x)=\prod_i\phi(x_i-\mu)$ relative to $\lambda_n$ exists by [F11]. Repeated Tonelli [F4] and the rectangle formula [F12] show that its values on Borel rectangles are the products of the marginal probabilities; [F14] says these rectangles generate the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^n$, so repeated product-measure uniqueness [F12] identifies it with the joint law. Thus $p_\mu(x)=(2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\tfrac12\sum_i x_i^2+\mu\sum_i x_i-\tfrac n2\mu^2)$. Setting $T=\bar X$, $\eta=n\mu$, and $h(x)=(2\pi)^{-n/2}e^{-\sum_i x_i^2/2}$ writes it as $h(x)e^{\eta T(x)-A(\eta)}$ with $A(\eta)=\eta^2/(2n)$. Completing the square and using Tonelli gives $\int h e^{\eta T}dx=e^{\eta^2/(2n)}$. The natural parameter set is all $\mathbb R$, hence open. For $b\ne0$, the level set $b\bar x=c$ is a proper affine hyperplane, null by [F3], so $T$ has no affine constraint; it is full rank by [F5]. Thus [F6] and [F7] make $\bar X$ sufficient and complete.

The residual map $x\mapsto x-\bar x\mathbf1$ is continuous, hence a statistic by [F2]. Write $X_i=\mu+Z_i$ with iid $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$ by [F1]. Then $R_i=Z_i-\bar Z$, so the law of $R$ does not depend on $\mu$; it is ancillary by [F8]. Apply [F9] to conclude $\bar X$ and $R$ are independent under every $P_\mu$.

boundaries.evidence: Statement assumes n≥1; for n=1 the residual vector is identically zero and remains ancillary.
For n=1 the residual is zero, so the degenerate ancillary boundary is included in step 2.1.
The case n=1 is explicitly permitted in the Statement and yields the zero residual.
Step 2.1 allows the constant residual vector when n=1.

The normal mean ranges over all real mu, and eta=n mu also ranges over all real numbers in Proof 1.1, so neither has finite endpoints. The integer boundary n=1 is admissible: Proof 2.1 gives R_1=Z_1-bar Z=0, a constant ancillary statistic independent of the mean.
A1 states the AC hypothesis used by the normal-law suppliers in step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: The Example states completeness and sufficiency of the mean, ancillarity of R, and their independence. Proof 1.1 establishes the exponential-family hypotheses and 2.1 applies Basu; it does not formulate an equivalence between independence and those hypotheses.

Independence is the conclusion of Basu in Proof 2.1; no converse is claimed that independent statistics must be complete sufficient and ancillary. All three properties are separately asserted for this normal model.

risk_review.notes: Density verification and all cited statements checked. Translation change of variables, product-law identity, Borel product equality, Lebesgue product equality and Tonelli establish pμ on Borel R^n, treating n=1 directly. η=nμ with T=mean gives A=η²/(2n); completing the square normalizes it. Open R parameter space and null proper affine hyperplanes give full rank. Reviewed exponential-family sufficiency/completeness apply. The residual map is continuous and R_i=Z_i−mean(Z) has μ-independent joint law, so Basu applies on the standard-Borel sample R^n with standard-Borel targets R and R^n. At n=1 residual is constantly zero, still ancillary and independent. Reader’s exact product-density dependencies retained. Basu’s new sample hypothesis is met without changing this consumer.

citations.quote:
Let $\mathcal X$ be countable with its full $\sigma$-field, so it is standard Borel under the discrete metric. Let $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be dominated by a fixed $\sigma$-finite positive measure $\mu$. Choose the finite-valued densities $p_\theta=dP_\theta/d\mu$ as in [[def-likelihood-density]]. Let $X_0\subseteq\mathcal X$ satisfy $P_\theta(X_0)=1$ and $P_\theta(\{x\})>0$ for every $x\in X_0$ and every $\theta$. Write $m_\theta(x)=P_\theta(\{x\})$. For each $x\in X_0$, $0<\mu(\{x\})<\infty$ and $p_\theta(x)=m_\theta(x)/\mu(\{x\})$: positivity follows from $m_\theta(x)>0$, finiteness from sigma-finiteness, and the value is fixed by the density integral on the positive-measure singleton. Consequently

$$\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_\theta(y)}=\frac{m_\theta(x)}{m_\theta(y)}\frac{\mu(\{y\})}{\mu(\{x\})}.$$

For $x,y\in X_0$, define $x\sim y$ if there is a constant $c(x,y)>0$ such that $m_\theta(x)/m_\theta(y)=c(x,y)$ for every $\theta$. The displayed fixed singleton factor shows this is equivalent to constancy of the common-reference density ratio. This is an equivalence relation: the constants for $(x,x)$, $(y,x)$ and $(x,z)$ are respectively $1$, $c(x,y)^{-1}$ and $c(x,y)c(y,z)$. Its equivalence classes form a countable quotient. Equip that quotient with its discrete $\sigma$-field; it is standard Borel because the discrete metric is complete and the countable space itself is dense. Since $\Theta\ne\varnothing$ and $P_\theta(X_0)=1$, $X_0$ is nonempty; define the class statistic by mapping each point of $X_0$ to its class and every point off $X_0$ to any fixed class. It is measurable because $\mathcal X$ has the full $\sigma$-field, and values off $X_0$ are null under every law.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses of [[def-likelihood-ratio-equivalence-on-common-discrete-support]], let $T(x)=[x]_{\sim}$ on $X_0$, as a statistic into the countable quotient with its discrete standard-Borel structure, and assign one arbitrary class off $X_0$. Then $T$ is minimal sufficient for $(P_\theta)$, modulo $\mathcal X\setminus X_0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Every sample point has probability $m_p(x)=p^{t(x)}(1-p)^{n-t(x)}>0$, so the common support is the whole finite sample space. Counting measure assigns mass one to each point, so the densities equal these point masses; for $x,y$, their ratio is $m_p(x)/m_p(y)=[p/(1-p)]^{t(x)-t(y)}$.

If $t(x)=t(y)$, this ratio is one for all $p$. If $d=t(x)-t(y)\ne0$, its values at $p=1/2$ and $p=1/3$ are respectively $1$ and $(1/2)^d$, which differ. Thus equivalence classes are exactly the level sets of $T$. By [F2], $T$ is minimal sufficient.

boundaries.evidence: Statement assumes n≥1 and p∈(0,1), so every sample point belongs to the common support.
Step 1.1 checks every point has positive probability for the open parameter range.
Step 2.1 uses p=1/2 to distinguish unequal counts.
The fibers include count 0 and count n; the likelihood-ratio comparison in step 2.1 covers both.
Statement deliberately restricts p to (0,1); p=0 and p=1 are excluded.

The finite sample, count map, and parameters 1/2 and 1/3 are explicit. The invoked discrete-class theorem now assumes AC for countably selecting separating events of an arbitrary sufficient sigma-field; that premise is explicitly carried in Example, Given, A1 and dependencies.

The equivalence of likelihood-ratio classes and count fibers used in Proof 2.1 has this direction: if x~y, the ratio [p/(1-p)]^d must be parameter-independent. For d!=0 its values at p=1/2 and 1/3 differ, so equivalence forces equal counts.

If t(x)=t(y), Proof 1.1 gives the point-mass ratio [p/(1-p)]^0=1 for every p in (0,1), hence x~y. This proves the other direction of the class/count identification used to invoke minimal sufficiency in 2.1.

risk_review.notes: Point masses p^t(1−p)^(n−t) are positive at every finite sample point for p∈(0,1). The ratio is [p/(1−p)]^d; when d≠0 its values at p=1/2 and 1/3 differ, including negative d. Thus class fibers are exactly count levels; current repaired discrete-class theorem now establishes minimality against every sufficient sigma-field. Carried its explicit AC premise in Example, Given, fact A1 and dependencies. Endpoints are outside this family and no claim about them is used; n≥1 is in Given and the proof also works for n=0 if separately formulated. This necessary consumer assumption propagation is recorded with the supplier defect, without a separate invented mathematical defect or routed obligation.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $(P_k)_{k\ge1}$ be a countable family of probability measures on a standard Borel space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let $w_k>0$ with $\sum_kw_k=1$, and put $Q=\sum_kw_kP_k$. Choose finite-valued Borel versions $f_k=dP_k/dQ$, changed to zero on one common $Q$-null set. Then $T(x)=(f_k(x))_{k\ge1}$ is a Borel statistic into $[0,\infty)^{\mathbb N}$ and is minimal sufficient. For every standard Borel sufficient statistic $S$, there is a Borel $\varphi$ with $T=\varphi(S)$ $Q$-almost surely.

A statistic $T$ into a standard Borel space is **minimal sufficient** for $(P_\theta)$ if $\sigma(T)$ is a minimal sufficient $\sigma$-field in the preceding sense. Minimality is modulo sets null under every model law. It does not assert literal pointwise equality with any other minimal sufficient statistic.

derivations.claim: Since $Q(\{j\})=2^{-j}$ and $P_k(\{j\})=1$ exactly when $j=k$, the density is $f_k(j)=2^k1_{\{j=k\}}$. Therefore $T(j)$ has coordinate $j$ equal to $2^j$ and all other coordinates zero.

These vectors are distinct for distinct $j$, so $T$ is injective and its fibers are singletons. The family-null ideal is trivial because every $j$ has positive mass under $P_j$; hence the generated partition cannot be made coarser modulo a common null set. The theorem [F1] gives minimal sufficiency, also directly visible from the singleton fibers.

boundaries.evidence: Statement indexes the sample space by positive integers and the family by k≥1.
Step 1.1 identifies all zero coordinates and the single positive coordinate.
Step 1.1 computes the positive coordinate value 2^j for each sample point.
The model laws are point masses; step 2.1 verifies that their singleton fibers are minimal.

boundaries.reason: Sample and parameter labels are j,k>=1. Proof 1.1 includes the first label: Q({1})=1/2 and f_1(1)=2, with all other coordinates zero. There is no finite upper endpoint or real interval, and the infinite geometric sum defines Q.

boundaries.evidence: The RN representatives here are the explicit formulas f_k(j)=2^k 1_{j=k}; all Q atoms are positive, so no null-point version selection is needed locally. AC remains explicitly assumed in A1 for the vector theorem invoked in Proof 2.1.

boundaries.reason: The Example asserts injectivity and minimal sufficiency of a specified vector for P_k=delta_k. Proof 1.1 computes each coordinate and 2.1 checks distinctness and invokes the vector theorem; no iff characterization is stated.

Minimal sufficiency is not used to infer that an arbitrary model consists of point masses. The given point masses and weights 2^-k lead to singleton vector fibers in Proof 2.1, with no converse model assertion.

risk_review.notes: Geometric weights 2^{−k}, k≥1 sum to one; Q(j)=2^{−j}>0 and f_k(j)=2^k 1_{j=k}. T has one unique nonzero coordinate at each j, so is Borel and injective. The common-null ideal is trivial because every point has probability one under its own model law. The repaired vector theorem covers arbitrary sufficient sigma-fields, completing the example’s actual minimal-sufficiency use. Its explicit AC premise already supplies all supplier assumptions. No modification needed.

citations.quote:
Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable function
$s:X\to[0,+\infty)\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]) is a
**nonnegative simple measurable function** when it has finite range.

Equivalently, there are pairwise disjoint measurable sets
$E_1,\dots,E_m\in\mathcal A$ and coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_m\in[0,+\infty)$
such that
$$s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}.$$
Any such display is a **simple representation** of $s$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: If $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{A_j}$ is a nonnegative simple function with pairwise disjoint $A_j\in\mathcal A$, then [F1] and [F2] give $\int s\,d\delta_{x_0}=\sum_jc_j\delta_{x_0}(A_j)=\sum_jc_j\mathbf 1_{A_j}(x_0)=s(x_0)$.

Choose the increasing simple approximation $s_n\uparrow f$ from [F3]. By [F4] and step 1.1, $\int f\,d\delta_{x_0}=\lim_n\int s_n\,d\delta_{x_0}=\lim_ns_n(x_0)=f(x_0)$, including when the value is $+\infty$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: For each $x\in\mathcal X$, the section $B\mapsto K_T(x,B)=\delta_{T(x)}(B)$ is the probability measure $\delta_{T(x)}$ by [F2].

For each $B\in\mathcal G$, $x\mapsto K_T(x,B)=\mathbf 1_B(T(x))=\mathbf 1_{T^{-1}(B)}(x)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable by [F1]. Thus both clauses of the kernel definition [F3] hold, so $K_T$ is a probability kernel, hence a deterministic randomized procedure.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment: a measurable data space, a parameter-label set,
and a family of probability measures on the data space. Let
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be its real-valued target function (estimand). An estimator
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ is a measurable statistic
with the real Borel target ([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]). At a parameter
$\theta$ for which $T$ is integrable under $P_\theta$, its **bias** is
$$\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T):=\mathbb E_\theta[T]-\psi(\theta).$$

Its **mean squared error** (MSE) is the extended nonnegative number
$$\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T):=\mathbb E_\theta[(T-\psi(\theta))^2]\in[0,+\infty].$$
This is the risk of the deterministic rule induced by $T$ under squared-error
loss $L(\theta,a)=(a-\psi(\theta))^2$: its Dirac kernel is constructed in
[[lem-statistic-induces-deterministic-procedure]], and the risk supplier's
integral formula reduces to the displayed expectation when the action is
$T(x)$ by [[lem-dirac-integral-evaluation]]
([[def-loss-function-and-risk]]). For each fixed $\theta$, this loss is Borel
in the real action $a$; no measurable structure on $\Theta$ or measurability
of $\psi$ is required. The expectation convention is
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. If $T$ is
square-integrable under $P_\theta$, then its variance is defined by
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] and this MSE is finite. Bias is not
defined at parameters where $T$ is not integrable.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $\theta$. Since $P_\theta$ is a probability measure, the constant $1$ has $L^2(P_\theta)$ norm $1$. Applying [F4] to $T$ and $1$ gives $\mathbb E_\theta|T|\leq(\mathbb E_\theta[T^2])^{1/2}<\infty$. Put $\mu=\mathbb E_\theta[T]$ and $b=\mu-\psi(\theta)$. Then [F1] gives $b=\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T)$ and $T-\psi(\theta)=(T-\mu)+b$.

Since $T,\mu\in L^1(P_\theta)$ by step 1.1 and $P_\theta(\mathcal X)=1$, [F3] gives $\mathbb E_\theta[T-\mu]=\mathbb E_\theta[T]-\mu\mathbb E_\theta[1]=0$. For every finite $c$, $(T-c)^2\leq2T^2+2c^2$, so the centered square and squared error are integrable. Expanding $(T-\psi(\theta))^2=((T-\mu)+b)^2$ now gives $\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T)=\mathbb E_\theta[(T-\mu)^2]+b^2=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)+\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T)^2$ by [F1] and [F2].

boundaries.evidence: Statement: the conclusion is pointwise in theta and vacuous if the parameter set is empty.
When bias is zero, step 2.1 reduces MSE to variance.
For a constant estimator, step 2.1 gives zero variance and MSE equal to squared bias.
If T is almost surely constant, the centered term in step 2.1 vanishes.

boundaries.reason: The Statement assumes E_theta[T^2]<infinity and gives the additive identity MSE_theta(T)=Var_theta(T)+Bias_theta(T)^2. Proof 1.1 defines the finite mean and bias, and 2.1 expands the square and cancels the centered expectation. The equality is not a biconditional predicate.

finite_checks.result: The centered-square term in step 2.1 vanishes.

Let $T$ be an estimator of a real estimand $\psi$ in a statistical experiment.
It is **unbiased** if it is integrable under every $P_\theta$ and
$$\mathbb E_\theta[T]=\psi(\theta)\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta.$$
Equivalently, its bias from [[def-bias-and-mean-squared-error]] is zero at every
parameter. It is a **finite-variance unbiased estimator** if it is unbiased
and square-integrable under every $P_\theta$.

A finite-variance unbiased estimator $T$ is **uniformly minimum-variance
unbiased** (UMVU) for $\psi$ if, for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and every other
finite-variance unbiased estimator $U$ of the same estimand,
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U).$$
The same estimator must satisfy these inequalities throughout the parameter
space; the definition asserts no existence of a UMVU estimator. Variance has
the meaning in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Thus $K(T(x),A)$ is a common version of the conditional probability of $A$ given $T$, under every parameter. The kernel is fixed independently of $\theta$. Under AC, standard Borelness gives each law an individual conditional law through [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]]; sufficiency additionally asks that one kernel works across parameters.

Let $K$ be a randomized procedure for the experiment
$\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
with action space $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$. Give $[0,+\infty]$ its Borel
sigma-algebra. For every nonnegative $\mathcal G/\mathcal B([0,+\infty])$-
measurable function $g:\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$, the function
$$h_g(x)=\int_{\mathsf D}g(a)\,K(x,da)$$
is $\mathcal A$-measurable. In particular, $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is measurable
for every action event $B\in\mathcal G$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$, the
set function
$$Q_\theta(B)=\int_{\mathcal X}K(x,B)\,P_\theta(dx),\qquad B\in\mathcal G,$$
is a probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, and for every such $g$,
$$\int_{\mathsf D}g\,dQ_\theta=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}g(a)\,K(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
with nonnegative extended values allowed.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and assume the target $Y$ carries a Borel
sigma-algebra $\mathcal{B}(Y)$.

The **sigma-algebra generated by $f$** is

$$\sigma(f) := \{\, f^{-1}(B) : B \in \mathcal{B}(Y) \,\}.$$

Because preimages preserve complements and countable unions, this is a
sigma-algebra on $X$. It is the smallest sigma-algebra on $X$ that makes $f$
measurable.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.
Assume AC. For $1\le p\le\infty$, conditional expectation is a linear map from real $L^p(P)$ to real $L^p(P|_{\mathcal G})$ satisfying $\|E[X\mid\mathcal G]\|_p\le\|X\|_p$.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC. Real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ embeds isometrically as a closed subspace of real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. For $X\in L^2(P)$, $U=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is its orthogonal projection onto this subspace. It uniquely minimizes $E[(X-Z)^2]$ over $Z\in L^2(\mathcal G)$ as an almost-sure class.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

derivations.claim: Write $u$ for the measurable function defining $U$. For each $\theta$, $P_\theta^S$ is a probability measure: preimages under the measurable map $S$ preserve the empty set, disjoint countable unions, and the whole space. By [L1], $K$ is a parameter-independent probability kernel from the statistic space to the data space, so it is a randomized procedure for the pushforward experiment by [F15]. Thus [F2] and [F3] show that $h_+(s)=\int u^+dK(s,\cdot)$, $h_-(s)=\int u^-dK(s,\cdot)$, and $r(s)=\int|u|dK(s,\cdot)$ are Borel. Let $g=h_+-h_-$ where $r<\infty$ and $g=0$ elsewhere; [F6] makes both terms finite on this Borel set, and [F3] makes $g$ Borel.

Fix $\theta$ and a Borel statistic event $B$. For nonnegative simple functions of the data, [L1] and finite linearity give $\int_B\int s(x)K(t,dx)P_\theta^S(dt)=\mathbb E_\theta[\mathbf1_{\{S\in B\}}s(X)]$. Approximate $u^+$ and $u^-$ increasingly by simple functions using [F4]; [F5] passes each equality to the limit. Applying the same identity to $|u|$ with $B=\mathsf S$ gives $\mathbb E_\theta r(S)=\mathbb E_\theta|U|<\infty$. If $N=\{r(S)=+\infty\}$ had positive probability, then $m\mathbf1_N\leq r(S)$ for every positive integer $m$, so [F6] would give $mP_\theta(N)\leq\mathbb E_\theta r(S)$ for all $m$, a contradiction; thus $r(S)<\infty$ almost surely. By [F6], $h_+(S),h_-(S)\leq r(S)$, so $|g(S)|\leq2r(S)$ and $g(S)$ is integrable. The two finite event-integral identities may therefore be subtracted, giving $\mathbb E_\theta[\mathbf1_{\{S\in B\}}g(S)]=\mathbb E_\theta[\mathbf1_{\{S\in B\}}U]$. By [F7], [F8], and [F9], $g(S)$ is a version of $\mathbb E_\theta[U\mid\sigma(S)]$ as an almost-sure class for every $\theta$.
By [F10], $g(S)$ is square-integrable under each $P_\theta$. By [F11], $\mathbb E_\theta[g(S)]=\mathbb E_\theta[U]=\psi(\theta)$; hence it is an unbiased finite-variance estimator.

Fix $\theta$. The residual $U-g(S)$ is orthogonal in $L^2(P_\theta)$ to every square-integrable $\sigma(S)$-measurable function by [F12]. By step 3.1 and $\psi(\theta)\in\mathbb R$, $g(S)-\psi(\theta)$ is such a function. Expanding the centered square gives $\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U)=\mathbb E_\theta[(U-g(S))^2]+\operatorname{Var}_\theta(g(S))$. The first term is nonnegative, proving the variance inequality.

By [F14], equality in step 4.1 holds exactly when $U=g(S)$ $P_\theta$-almost surely. Since $g(S)$ is $\sigma(S)$-measurable, this is precisely almost-sure $\sigma(S)$-measurability: if $U$ has such a representative, its $L^2$ class lies in the projection subspace and [F12] fixes it.

For U=0 and psi=0, the construction in step 1.1 gives g=0 and step 4.1 has zero residual.
For a constant-one estimator with target one, the conditional mean is one and step 5.1 gives equality.
For degenerate sampling laws, the event identities in step 2.1 and L2 equality in step 4.1 remain valid.

Equality of variances implies U=g(S) almost surely by step 5.1.
If U is sigma(S)-measurable, the projection property in step 5.1 fixes its L2 class and gives equality.

Let $T$ be an estimator of a real estimand $\psi$ in a statistical experiment.
It is **unbiased** if it is integrable under every $P_\theta$ and
$$\mathbb E_\theta[T]=\psi(\theta)\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta.$$
Equivalently, its bias from [[def-bias-and-mean-squared-error]] is zero at every
parameter. It is a **finite-variance unbiased estimator** if it is unbiased
and square-integrable under every $P_\theta$.

A finite-variance unbiased estimator $T$ is **uniformly minimum-variance
unbiased** (UMVU) for $\psi$ if, for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and every other
finite-variance unbiased estimator $U$ of the same estimand,
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U).$$
The same estimator must satisfy these inequalities throughout the parameter
space; the definition asserts no existence of a UMVU estimator. Variance has
the meaning in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment: a measurable data space, a parameter-label set,
and a family of probability measures on the data space. Let
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be its real-valued target function (estimand). An estimator
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ is a measurable statistic
with the real Borel target ([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]). At a parameter
$\theta$ for which $T$ is integrable under $P_\theta$, its **bias** is
$$\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T):=\mathbb E_\theta[T]-\psi(\theta).$$

Its **mean squared error** (MSE) is the extended nonnegative number
$$\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T):=\mathbb E_\theta[(T-\psi(\theta))^2]\in[0,+\infty].$$
This is the risk of the deterministic rule induced by $T$ under squared-error
loss $L(\theta,a)=(a-\psi(\theta))^2$: its Dirac kernel is constructed in
[[lem-statistic-induces-deterministic-procedure]], and the risk supplier's
integral formula reduces to the displayed expectation when the action is
$T(x)$ by [[lem-dirac-integral-evaluation]]
([[def-loss-function-and-risk]]). For each fixed $\theta$, this loss is Borel
in the real action $a$; no measurable structure on $\Theta$ or measurability
of $\psi$ is required. The expectation convention is
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. If $T$ is
square-integrable under $P_\theta$, then its variance is defined by
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] and this MSE is finite. Bias is not
defined at parameters where $T$ is not integrable.

For a finite family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space,
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).$$
Equivalently, it is $\sum_{i,j\in I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$. The empty sum has variance zero, and the singleton formula is the identity.
The original finite-probability-space case is included, since every real random variable there is square-integrable and the covariance/variance definitions agree with the finite centered-product/square formulas.
In the first display, the second sum is over two-element subsets of $I$.

If $X$ and $Y$ are independent square-integrable real random variables, then
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.$$

Thus independence implies zero covariance. The converse is false in general.

For real random variables $X$ and $Y$ on one finite probability space, define
$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
The **standard deviation** of $X$ is $\sigma_X:=\operatorname{Var}(X)^{1/2}$, using the unique nonnegative square root supplied by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. Variance is nonnegative because its defining random variable is pointwise nonnegative and expectation is a sum with nonnegative weights.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

In a statistical experiment, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and let $T$ be a
real estimator with $\mathbb E_\theta[T^2]<\infty$. For every $\theta$,
$$\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T)=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)+\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T)^2.$$

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

For $p\in[0,1]$, a **Bernoulli$(p)$ random variable** takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, a **binomial$(n,p)$ random variable** is a sum $X=\sum_{i<n}X_i$ of $n$ mutually independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables. When $n=0$, this is the constant zero random variable.

A finite family of finite-valued random variables $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **mutually independent** when for every nonempty $J\subseteq I$ and every selection $x_j\in X_j(\Omega)$,
$$\mathbb P(X_j=x_j\text{ for every }j\in J)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P(X_j=x_j).$$
It is **pairwise independent** when this identity is required only for two distinct indices. The empty family is mutually independent vacuously, and a one-member family is mutually independent.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For $p\in[0,1]$, a **Bernoulli$(p)$ random variable** takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, a **binomial$(n,p)$ random variable** is a sum $X=\sum_{i<n}X_i$ of $n$ mutually independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables. When $n=0$, this is the constant zero random variable.

A finite family of finite-valued random variables $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **mutually independent** when for every nonempty $J\subseteq I$ and every selection $x_j\in X_j(\Omega)$,
$$\mathbb P(X_j=x_j\text{ for every }j\in J)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P(X_j=x_j).$$
It is **pairwise independent** when this identity is required only for two distinct indices. The empty family is mutually independent vacuously, and a one-member family is mutually independent.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

derivations.claim: For $s\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ let $F_s=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_i x_i=s\}$; it has $\binom ns\geq1$ elements. Define $K(s,A)=|A\cap F_s|/\binom ns$ for every data event $A$. Each section is the uniform probability measure on $F_s$, and every event evaluation is measurable because the statistic space is finite and discrete; thus $K$ is a probability kernel independent of $p$. By [F4], independence makes the joint law the product of the Bernoulli coordinate masses. For $0<p<1$, each vector in $F_s$ has mass $p^s(1-p)^{n-s}$ and $P_p(S=s)>0$, so $K(s,\cdot)$ is the conditional law given $S=s$. At $p=0$ or $p=1$, only $s=0$ or $s=n$ is supported, respectively, and that fiber is a singleton on which the same kernel is the conditional law. Hence $K$ is a common regular conditional law and proves sufficiency by [L1].

For $0<p<1$, the uniform fiber law is invariant under coordinate permutations, so the $n$ conditional means $\mathbb E_p[X_i\mid S=s]$ agree. Their sum is $s$, hence each is $s/n$. At $p=0,1$, $X_1=S/n$ almost surely, so the same formula holds on the support. Since $0\leq X_1\leq1$, $U=X_1$ is square-integrable; its Bernoulli law gives $\mathbb E_pX_1=p\cdot1+(1-p)\cdot0=p$ by [F4]. Both spaces are standard Borel by [F5] and $S$ is sufficient by step 1.1, so [F2] and [F1] identify $S/n$ as the Rao–Blackwellized unbiased estimator; [F3] records its conditional-expectation class convention.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment dominated by a fixed sigma-finite positive measure
$\mu$, and let $p_\theta$ be selected finite-valued measurable
Radon–Nikodym density representatives as in
[[def-likelihood-density]]. The simultaneous selection of this arbitrary-index
family uses the Axiom of Choice. No measurability of $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$
or common exceptional null set for an arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$ is
implied.

Let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and fix a parameter $\theta$ at
which the selected family $\eta\mapsto p_\eta(x)$ is differentiable for
$\mu$-almost every $x$, with measurable coordinate derivatives. On
$\{x:p_\theta(x)>0\}$, define the log-likelihood
$\ell_\theta(x)=\log p_\theta(x)$ and the **score**
$$S_\theta(x):=\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta(x) =\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\log p_\theta(x)\right)_{j=1}^d.$$
Set $S_\theta(x)=0$ where $p_\theta(x)=0$, which is $P_\theta$-null.
For $d=1$, this is $S_\theta=\partial_\theta\log p_\theta$.

For $d=1$, the scalar **Fisher information** is
$$I(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[S_\theta(X)^2]\in[0,+\infty].$$
When $d>1$ and $S_\theta$ is square-integrable, the **Fisher information
matrix** is $I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[S_\theta(X)S_\theta(X)^\mathsf T]$;
its $i,j$ entry is $\mathbb E_\theta[S_{\theta,i}S_{\theta,j}]$. No scalar
information is defined here for a vector parameter.
The information matrix is a second-moment matrix by definition; it equals the
score covariance matrix when the score has mean zero.

The derivatives, score and information are defined relative to the specified
differentiable representative family. The Radon–Nikodym definition alone
does not supply parameter differentiability or a canonical score version.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: By [F2]–[F4], every selected density has $\int p_\eta\,d\mu=P_\eta(\mathcal X)=1$. Fix a coordinate $j$ and a sequence $h_n\to0$ with $\theta+h_ne_j\in U$. For almost every $x\in S$, the mean value theorem [F6] bounds $\left|(p_{\theta+h_ne_j}(x)-p_\theta(x))/h_n\right|$ by $g_1(x)$, and the quotient converges to $\partial_jp_\theta(x)$. Dominated convergence [F7] therefore gives convergence of the quotient integrals. Linearity [F11] shows each quotient integral is $(1-1)/h_n=0$, so $\int\partial_jp_\theta\,d\mu=0$. Since $\mathbb E_\theta S_{\theta,j}^2<\infty$ and $P_\theta$ is a probability, $S_{\theta,j}$ is integrable (use $|z|\le(1+z^2)/2$). On $S$, the signed density identity [F5] and [F8] identify $\mathbb E_\theta S_{\theta,j}$ with this integral; outside $S$ the law is zero. Thus every score coordinate has mean zero.

For any coordinates $i,j$, apply the same sequence argument to $\partial_i p_{\theta+h_ne_j}$. The mean value theorem bounds its difference quotient by $g_2$, so [F7] interchanges this derivative and the integral. Step 1.1 holds at every parameter in $U$, hence $\int\partial_i p_\eta\,d\mu=0$ throughout $U$; linearity [F11] turns each difference-quotient integral into the difference of these zero integrals. Dominated convergence then gives $\int\partial_{ij}p_\theta\,d\mu=0$.

On $S\setminus N$, differentiate $\ell_\theta=\log p_\theta$ using [F9]. Multiplying the Hessian formula by $p_\theta$, integrating with the signed density identity [F5] and linearity [F11], and using step 2.1 yields $\mathbb E_\theta[\partial_{ij}\ell_\theta] =\int\partial_{ij}p_\theta\,d\mu-\mathbb E_\theta[S_{\theta,i}S_{\theta,j}] =-\mathbb E_\theta[S_{\theta,i}S_{\theta,j}]$. The terms are integrable: $\int|\partial_{ij}p_\theta|\,d\mu\le\int g_2\,d\mu$, and $2|S_{\theta,i}S_{\theta,j}|\le S_{\theta,i}^2+S_{\theta,j}^2$.
The coordinate identities in step 3.1 give the asserted matrix identity; when $d=1$ they give the scalar identity. Step 1.1 supplies the score mean-zero claim in both cases.

boundaries.reason: The statement fixes a parameter value and a probability model.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 1.1: the score may vanish, and its mean-zero identity still holds.
Statement: the scalar case d=1 is included and gives the usual information identity.
Steps 1.1–3.1: a parameter-constant density has zero derivatives and both sides of the identity vanish.

boundaries.reason: Statement: the parameter lies in an open set, so endpoint parameters are excluded.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1: AC supplies the selected density representatives used by the score.

boundaries.reason: The statement is an implication, not an equivalence.
The statement is an implication, not an equivalence.

Nonzero difference quotients are measurable and dominated; sequential DCT plus integral linearity gives integral partial_j p_eta=0 throughout U (this density-integral part needs no second score moment at eta), then integral partial_ij p_theta=0. For a scalar parameter this reads
$\mathbb E_\theta S_\theta=0$ and
$I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta S_\theta^2
=-\mathbb E_\theta[\ell_\theta''(X)]$.

This common-support, integrable-envelope setup is sufficient, not necessary:
the theorem does not claim that every model with valid score identities must
have common support or these envelopes.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

In a measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ ([[def-measure-space]]), a measurable set $N\in\mathcal A$ is **$\mu$-null** if $\mu(N)=0$.

A property $P(x)$ holds **$\mu$-almost everywhere**, or **for $\mu$-almost every $x$**, if its exceptional set is contained in a measurable $\mu$-null set: there is $N\in\mathcal A$ with $\mu(N)=0$ such that $P(x)$ holds for every $x\in X\setminus N$. Both notions are relative to the named measure $\mu$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $T$ be an estimator of a real estimand $\psi$ in a statistical experiment.
It is **unbiased** if it is integrable under every $P_\theta$ and
$$\mathbb E_\theta[T]=\psi(\theta)\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta.$$
Equivalently, its bias from [[def-bias-and-mean-squared-error]] is zero at every
parameter. It is a **finite-variance unbiased estimator** if it is unbiased
and square-integrable under every $P_\theta$.

A finite-variance unbiased estimator $T$ is **uniformly minimum-variance
unbiased** (UMVU) for $\psi$ if, for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and every other
finite-variance unbiased estimator $U$ of the same estimand,
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U).$$

space; the definition asserts no existence of a UMVU estimator. Variance has
the meaning in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Every globally finite-variance unbiased estimator in [F13] satisfies the theorem's local mean and second-moment hypotheses. For the stated broader class, if the score-covariance identity is assumed directly, it is already available. Under the sufficient density route, linearity [F6] and [F12] give $$\frac{\psi(\theta+h_n)-\psi(\theta)}{h_n}=\int T(x)\frac{p_{\theta+h_n}(x)-p_\theta(x)}{h_n}\,d\mu.$$ The mean value theorem [F9] bounds the integrand by the common integrable envelope outside $N_H$; its pointwise limit is $T(x)\partial_\theta p_\theta(x)$. Dominated convergence [F9] therefore gives $\psi'(\theta)=\int T\,\partial_\theta p_\theta\,d\mu$. On the common positive support, [F1] gives $\partial_\theta p_\theta=p_\theta S_\theta$. The product $TS_\theta$ is integrable by $2|TS_\theta|\le T^2+S_\theta^2$. By [F10], [F11], and [F12], $P_\theta=p_\theta\,d\mu$ and $\int T\partial_\theta p_\theta\,d\mu=\mathbb E_\theta[T S_\theta]$. Since $\mathbb E_\theta S_\theta=0$ by [F2] and $\mathbb E_\theta T=\psi(\theta)$, [F4] identifies this with $\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T,S_\theta)$. Thus either allowed route supplies the covariance identity.

Put $U=T-\psi(\theta)$. The $P_\theta$-almost-everywhere classes of $U$ and $S_\theta$ lie in $L^2(P_\theta)$ by [F4]–[F5]. Their product is integrable since $2|US_\theta|\le U^2+S_\theta^2$. Expectation linearity [F6] and $\mathbb E_\theta S_\theta=0$ give $\langle U,S_\theta\rangle:=\mathbb E_\theta[US_\theta] =\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T,S_\theta)=\psi'(\theta)$. The pairing $\langle V,W\rangle=\mathbb E_\theta[VW]$ is an inner product on these classes: symmetry and bilinearity follow from [F6], and positive definiteness follows from [F6].

By Cauchy–Schwarz [F8] in this real inner product space, $\psi'(\theta)^2=|\langle U,S_\theta\rangle|^2 \le\langle U,U\rangle\langle S_\theta,S_\theta\rangle =\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)I(\theta)$. Divide by $I(\theta)>0$ to obtain the stated lower bound.

Since $I(\theta)>0$, equality in step 3.1 holds exactly when the $L^2(P_\theta)$ classes of $U$ and $S_\theta$ are linearly dependent [F8]. Taking their inner product with $S_\theta$ and using step 2.1 fixes the coefficient as $\psi'(\theta)/I(\theta)$; conversely that relation gives equality by direct substitution. This is precisely the asserted almost-sure equality condition.
