citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. For every sequence
$(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets there is a sequence
$(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with $a_n\in A_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Thus the
Axiom of Choice implies the pair-local countable choice principle
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces and let $b\in W$. A vector $x\in V$ minimises $\lVert Tx-b\rVert$ if and only if

$$T^*(Tx-b)=0,$$

equivalently $T^*Tx=T^*b$. Minimisers exist, and if $x_0$ is one minimiser, then the full set of minimisers is $x_0+\ker T$.

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ have independent standard-normal coordinates, and let $U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $U^TU=I_n$. Then $UZ$ also has independent $N(0,1)$ coordinates. Here $I_n$ is the identity matrix and $U$ is orthogonal.

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an integer $k\ge1$, let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_k)$ have law $N_k(0,I_k)$, so its coordinates are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The **chi-square law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $\chi_k^2$, is the law of
$$
Q_k=\sum_{j=1}^k G_j^2=\|G\|^2.
$$
For $k=0$, define $\chi_0^2=\delta_0$, the point mass at zero. This zero-degree law records a rank-zero projection only; it is not used as a denominator in a Student or Fisher ratio. The multivariate-normal characteristic-function theorem makes the definition independent of the chosen realization of $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $k\ge1$, the law $\chi_k^2$ has density
$$
f_k(x)=c_k x^{k/2-1}e^{-x/2}\mathbf 1_{\{x>0\}},\qquad c_k=\frac{\sigma_{k-1}(S^{k-1})}{2(2\pi)^{k/2}}>0,
$$
where $\sigma_{k-1}$ is the polar surface measure on the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^k$. Consequently, $Q_k>0$ almost surely, and its cumulative distribution function is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a positive integer $k$, take the product probability law of an independent standard normal $G$ and an independent $Q_k\sim\chi_k^2$. The **Student t law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $t_k$, is the law of
$$T_k=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{G}{\sqrt{Q_k/k}},&Q_k>0,\\ 0,&Q_k=0. \end{cases}$$
For positive integers $r,s$, take independent $Q_r\sim\chi_r^2$ and $Q_s\sim\chi_s^2$. The **Fisher F law with degrees $(r,s)$**, denoted $F_{r,s}$, is the law of
$$F_{r,s}=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Q_r/r}{Q_s/s},&Q_s>0,\\ 0,&Q_s=0. \end{cases}$$
The displayed piecewise maps are Borel measurable: each quotient is continuous on its Borel positive-denominator region, and the value on the Borel zero set is constant. The positive-degree chi-square lemma proves that the denominators are positive almost surely, so these versions agree almost surely with the usual quotients. Zero degrees are excluded from both definitions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every $k\ge1$, the CDF of $t_k$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, is symmetric about zero, and has limits $0$ and $1$ at $-\infty$ and $+\infty$. For every $r,s\ge1$, the CDF of $F_{r,s}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$, is zero on $(-\infty,0]$, and is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$ with limit $1$ at $+\infty$. Consequently, for each $u\in(0,1)$ each law has exactly one $u$-quantile on its support.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

Let $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ be an orthonormal basis of a subspace $W$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. Then

$$P_Wv=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i.$$

The map $P_W$ is linear, with image $W$, kernel $W^\perp$, and $P_W^2=P_W$. Moreover, regarding both projections as endomorphisms of $V$,

$$I-P_W=P_{W^\perp}.$$

derivations.claim: By full column rank, the columns of $X$ are linearly independent. Apply [F2] to obtain orthonormal columns of $Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with the same successive spans. Expressing each column of $X$ in this basis gives $X=QR$, where $R$ is upper triangular; its diagonal entries are the nonzero Gram–Schmidt residual norms, so $R$ is invertible. By [F3], extend the columns of $Q$ to an orthonormal basis $[Q\ Q_0]$ of $\mathbb R^n$.

Set $U=[Q\ Q_0]$. Then $U$ is orthogonal. Standardizing the independent errors gives $\eta=\varepsilon/\sigma$ with independent standard-normal coordinates, so [F4] makes $U^T\eta=(Z_Q,Z_0)$ a standard-normal product vector with independent coordinate blocks. Since $X=QR$ and $X^TX=R^TR$, the normal-equation solution in [F1] is $\widehat\beta=R^{-1}Q^TY=\beta+\sigma R^{-1}Z_Q$. Substituting $X=QR$ and $(R^TR)^{-1}=R^{-1}R^{-T}$ gives $P_X=Q R(R^TR)^{-1}R^TQ^T=Q[RR^{-1}R^{-T}R^T]Q^T=QQ^T$, because $RR^{-1}=I_p$ and $R^{-T}R^T=I_p$. Since $U$ is orthogonal, $I_n-P_X=Q_0Q_0^T$. Thus $(I_n-P_X)Y=\sigma Q_0Z_0$, so $RSS_X/\sigma^2=\|Z_0\|^2\sim\chi_{n-p}^2$ by [F5]. By [A2] and [F7], the linear maps defining $\widehat\beta$ and $Q_0Z_0$, and the squared-norm map defining $RSS_X$, are Borel; hence these quantities are measurable functions of the independent coordinate blocks and $\widehat\beta$ is independent of $RSS_X$ by [F4]. The map defining $\widehat\beta$ is linear and Borel, so it is a statistic for the stated experiment. The residual map and squared norm are continuous, so $RSS_X$ and $S$ are continuous. The piecewise t version in the Statement is Borel: its quotient is continuous on the Borel set $S>0$ and its value on $S=0$ is constant. Its denominator has positive degree $n-p$, hence $S>0$ almost surely by [F5].

For $c\ne0$, put $v=R^{-T}c$. Invertibility of $R$ gives $v\ne0$. Complete $v/\|v\|$ to an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^p$ by [F3]; applying [F4] to the resulting orthogonal matrix shows $G_c=v^TZ_Q/\|v\|\sim N(0,1)$. Under [A2], the continuous linear map defining $G_c$ is Borel. It is independent of $Q_0:=\|Z_0\|^2\sim\chi_{n-p}^2$, because $Z_Q$ and $Z_0$ are independent blocks and $G_c$ and the squared-norm map are measurable functions of those blocks. Since $X^TX=R^TR$, $\|v\|^2=c^TR^{-1}R^{-T}c=c^T(X^TX)^{-1}c$. Thus on $Q_0>0$ the displayed contrast ratio is $G_c/\sqrt{Q_0/(n-p)}$; on $Q_0=0$ its version $\widetilde T_c$ is zero. This is exactly the extension in the definition of $t_{n-p}$, so [F5]–[F6] give $\widetilde T_c\sim t_{n-p}$.

For the nested models, let $W_D=W_U\cap W_R^\perp$. The finite-dimensional orthogonal decompositions in [F3] give $\mathbb R^n=W_R\oplus W_D\oplus W_U^\perp$, with dimensions $p-q,q,n-p$. Choose orthonormal bases in these three spaces and concatenate them into an orthogonal matrix $V$. By [F4], the coordinates of $V^T\varepsilon/\sigma$ in the three blocks are independent standard normals. Under the null, $P_R(X\beta)=P_U(X\beta)=X\beta$, so $(I-P_R)Y=(I-P_R)\varepsilon=P_{W_D}\varepsilon+P_{W_U^\perp}\varepsilon$ and $(I-P_U)Y=(I-P_U)\varepsilon=P_{W_U^\perp}\varepsilon$: here [F8] identifies $I-P_R=P_{W_R^\perp}$ and $I-P_U=P_{W_U^\perp}$, while the direct sum in [F3] splits the first projection into the two orthogonal components. The coordinate-block maps and the linear projections are continuous, and squared norms are continuous, so [A2] and [F7] make all these random vectors and real variables measurable. Orthogonality and [F9] give $RSS_R-RSS_U=\sigma^2\sum_{j=1}^{q}G_j^2$ and $RSS_U=\sigma^2\sum_{j=1}^{n-p}H_j^2$, where the $G$ and $H$ coordinate blocks are independent standard-normal blocks. By [F5] these sums are independent $\sigma^2\chi_q^2$ and $\sigma^2\chi_{n-p}^2$ variables; both degrees are positive. The piecewise ratio $\widetilde F$ is Borel, since it is continuous on the Borel set $RSS_U>0$ and constant on $RSS_U=0$. Its value is the scaled ratio on $Q_H:=\sum_{j=1}^{n-p}H_j^2>0$ and $0$ when $Q_H=0$; by [F6] this is exactly the defined $F_{q,n-p}$ version. The F denominator is positive almost surely by [F5], so $\widetilde F\sim F_{q,n-p}$.

boundaries.evidence: Statement requires n>p≥1 and 1≤q≤p; no empty full design/sample is allowed. It permits the reduced subspace dimension p−q=0 when q=p; step 4.1 includes the zero-dimensional reduced block.
Statement assumes σ²>0 and c≠0. Step 3.1 gives cᵀ(XᵀX)^−1c=||R^−Tc||²>0; step 2.1 gives S>0 almost surely and the piecewise definition sets the zero-denominator event to zero.
Statement allows p=q=1,n=2: numerator and residual degrees both equal one. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 use only their positivity, so this smallest design case is included.

Statement excludes rank-deficient X by linearly independent columns and excludes σ²=0. Steps 2.1/4.1 nevertheless define measurable zero-denominator versions on the corresponding probability-zero residual events.
Statement permits q=p but excludes q=0 and p=n; step 4.1 yields q and n−p positive chi-square degrees at those allowed dimension endpoints.
Step 1.1 obtains QR from a finite Gram–Schmidt list and completes a finite basis; A1/A2 carry AC and its Countable Choice consequence through normal and Borel-measurability suppliers.

boundaries.reason: The theorem supplies independent residual sums and exact t/F laws under a fixed full-rank Gaussian design, not a characterization of all error laws.
The exact ratio law is not asserted to imply Gaussian errors or full rank for an arbitrary regression experiment.

finite_checks.claim: For p=1,n=2,q=1, the t/F denominator degree n−p=1 and F numerator degree q=1.
finite_checks.result: Both chi-square components have positive degree and are positive almost surely.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all four proof steps with the actual full-rank least-squares, Gram--Schmidt, orthogonal-decomposition/basis, projection/Pythagoras and statistic supplier statements. X=QR yields invertible R and P_X=QQ^T; standardizing with sigma>0 gives independent Q and residual blocks. The coefficient statistic is linear/Borel and its residual sum has sigma^2 chi-square(n-p) law. For fixed nonzero c, v=R^{-T}c is nonzero and ||v||^2=c^T(X^TX)^{-1}c>0; the rotated standard-normal contrast is independent of the positive residual chi-square. Under the nested-model null, W_R, W_U intersect W_R-perp and W_U-perp form orthogonal blocks of dimensions p-q, q and n-p, so RSS_R-RSS_U and RSS_U are the independent scaled chi-square contributions. q=p includes the zero-dimensional reduced space; q>=1 and n>p ensure positive ratio degrees. Piecewise-zero extensions are Borel and agree almost surely with the finite ratios. AC/countable-choice assumptions are preserved. No defect.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$, and let $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be an orthogonal projection of rank $r$, where $0\le r\le n$. Then the random vectors $PZ$ and $(I_n-P)Z$ are independent, and
$$
\|PZ\|^2\sim\chi_r^2,\qquad \|(I_n-P)Z\|^2\sim\chi_{n-r}^2.
$$
The two squared norms are independent. The cases $r=0$ and $r=n$ are included, with $\chi_0^2=\delta_0$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $k\ge1$, the law $\chi_k^2$ has density
$$
f_k(x)=c_k x^{k/2-1}e^{-x/2}\mathbf 1_{\{x>0\}},\qquad c_k=\frac{\sigma_{k-1}(S^{k-1})}{2(2\pi)^{k/2}}>0,
$$
where $\sigma_{k-1}$ is the polar surface measure on the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^k$. Consequently, $Q_k>0$ almost surely, and its cumulative distribution function is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a positive integer $k$, take the product probability law of an independent standard normal $G$ and an independent $Q_k\sim\chi_k^2$. The **Student t law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $t_k$, is the law of
$$T_k=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{G}{\sqrt{Q_k/k}},&Q_k>0,\\ 0,&Q_k=0. \end{cases}$$
For positive integers $r,s$, take independent $Q_r\sim\chi_r^2$ and $Q_s\sim\chi_s^2$. The **Fisher F law with degrees $(r,s)$**, denoted $F_{r,s}$, is the law of
$$F_{r,s}=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Q_r/r}{Q_s/s},&Q_s>0,\\ 0,&Q_s=0. \end{cases}$$
The displayed piecewise maps are Borel measurable: each quotient is continuous on its Borel positive-denominator region, and the value on the Borel zero set is constant. The positive-degree chi-square lemma proves that the denominators are positive almost surely, so these versions agree almost surely with the usual quotients. Zero degrees are excluded from both definitions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every $k\ge1$, the CDF of $t_k$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, is symmetric about zero, and has limits $0$ and $1$ at $-\infty$ and $+\infty$. For every $r,s\ge1$, the CDF of $F_{r,s}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$, is zero on $(-\infty,0]$, and is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$ with limit $1$ at $+\infty$. Consequently, for each $u\in(0,1)$ each law has exactly one $u$-quantile on its support.

derivations.claim: By [A2], Countable Choice holds, so [F2] applies to the linear continuous map $x\mapsto\bar x$; hence it is a statistic on the stated Borel data space. Put $Z_i=(X_i-\mu)/\sigma$. The affine pushforward definition in [F1] gives each $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$, and [F1] preserves their independence. Thus $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ by [F4].

Define $\bar Z=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i$, $u=n^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)^T$, and $P=uu^T$. Since $u^Tu=1$, $P$ is a rank-one orthogonal projection. We have $u^TZ=\sqrt n\,\bar Z$ and $X-\bar X(1,\ldots,1)^T=\sigma(I_n-P)Z$. Therefore $\bar X=\mu+\sigma u^TZ/\sqrt n$ and $S^2=\sigma^2\|(I_n-P)Z\|^2/(n-1)$.

By [F3], $PZ$ and $(I_n-P)Z$ are independent and $Q:=\|(I_n-P)Z\|^2\sim\chi_{n-1}^2$. The continuous linear map $z\mapsto u^Tz$ is Borel by [A2] and [F2], and $u^TZ=u^TPZ$; the continuous squared-norm map on the complementary vector is likewise Borel. Thus $G:=u^TZ$ and $Q$ are measurable functions of the independent vectors in [F3], so they are independent by [F1]. By [F4], $G\sim N(0,1)$.

The formulas in step 2.1 express $\bar X$ as an affine function of $G$ and $S^2$ as $\sigma^2 Q/(n-1)$. Hence $\bar X$ and $S^2$ are independent, $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2=Q\sim\chi_{n-1}^2$, and $S>0$ almost surely by [F5].

The set $\{S>0\}$ is Borel and the displayed quotient is continuous there; assigning $0$ on $\{S=0\}$ therefore makes $\widetilde T$ measurable. Since $S=0$ exactly when $Q=0$, step 2.1 gives $\widetilde T=G/\sqrt{Q/(n-1)}$ on $\{Q>0\}$ and both versions are $0$ on $\{Q=0\}$. The variables $G$ and $Q$ are independent with laws $N(0,1)$ and $\chi_{n-1}^2$, so [F5] gives $\widetilde T\sim t_{n-1}$.

Let $q=q_{n-1}(1-\alpha/2)$. By [F5], the $t_{n-1}$ CDF is continuous and symmetric, so $F_{t_{n-1}}(0)=1/2<1-\alpha/2$ and strict increase gives $q>0$; symmetry then gives $F_{t_{n-1}}(-q)=\alpha/2$. Step 5.1 therefore gives $\mathbb P(-q\le\widetilde T\le q)=1-\alpha$. On the full-probability event $\{S>0\}$ from step 4.1, this event is exactly $\{\mu\text{ lies in the displayed interval}\}$ by multiplying by $S/\sqrt n$ and rearranging. The events agree almost surely, so the interval has exact coverage $1-\alpha$.

$$\widehat\beta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^TY,\qquad P_X=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T,\qquad RSS_X=\|(I_n-P_X)Y\|^2,\qquad S^2=\frac{RSS_X}{n-p},\qquad S=\sqrt{S^2}.$$

$$\widetilde T_c:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{c^T\widehat\beta-c^T\beta}{S\sqrt{c^T(X^TX)^{-1}c}},&S>0,\\ 0,&S=0 \end{cases} \sim t_{n-p},\qquad \frac{RSS_X}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi_{n-p}^2,$$
and $\widehat\beta$ is independent of $RSS_X$, with $S>0$ almost surely.

For nested deterministic full and reduced design spaces $W_R\subset W_U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of dimensions $p-q$ and $p$, where $q$ is an integer and $1\le q\le p<n$, let $P_R,P_U$ be the orthogonal projections onto these spaces and define $RSS_R=\|(I-P_R)Y\|^2$ and $RSS_U=\|(I-P_U)Y\|^2$. $$\widetilde F:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{(RSS_R-RSS_U)/q}{RSS_U/(n-p)},&RSS_U>0,\\ 0,&RSS_U=0 \end{cases} \sim F_{q,n-p}.$$

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment with $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let
$(S,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable space. A
family of measurable maps $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$, one for each
$\theta\in\Theta$, is a **pivot** if the pushforward law
$$\nu_\theta(B):=P_\theta(q_\theta^{-1}(B)),\qquad B\in\mathcal S$$
is the same probability measure $\nu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$.
Each section is a random element on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P_\theta)$, so
its pushforward is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].
No measurability in $\theta$ is asserted or needed.

For $S=\mathbb R$, a pivot is a real-valued statistic whose sampling
distribution is parameter-free. A pivot need not be invertible in the
parameter, and its inversion need not be an interval.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment with $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let
$(S,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable space. A
family of measurable maps $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$, one for each
$\theta\in\Theta$, is a **pivot** if the pushforward law
$$\nu_\theta(B):=P_\theta(q_\theta^{-1}(B)),\qquad B\in\mathcal S$$
is the same probability measure $\nu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$.
Each section is a random element on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P_\theta)$, so
its pushforward is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].
No measurability in $\theta$ is asserted or needed.

For $S=\mathbb R$, a pivot is a real-valued statistic whose sampling
distribution is parameter-free. A pivot need not be invertible in the
parameter, and its inversion need not be an interval.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be an
experiment with nonempty $\Theta$. Let $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$ be a
pivot with common law $\nu$, and let $B\in\mathcal S$. Define
$$C(x):=\{\theta\in\Theta:q_\theta(x)\in B\}$$
If $\nu(B)\ge1-\alpha$, then $C$ is a confidence set with coverage at
least $1-\alpha$. If $\nu(B)=1-\alpha$, its coverage is exactly
$1-\alpha$ for every parameter value. For an interval $B=[a,b]$ in
$\mathbb R$, exactness requires calibration of the actual probability
$\nu([a,b])$; quantile labels alone do not remove endpoint atoms.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

derivations.claim: Let $G$ have the standard normal law. Its density is $\phi(u)=e^{-u^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, positive everywhere and bounded above by $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$, with total mass one by [F1]. Thus $\Phi(t)=P(G\le t)$ satisfies $0<\Phi(b)-\Phi(a)=\int_a^b\phi(u)\,du\le(b-a)/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for every $a<b$, proving strict increase and continuity. u,1-\alpha/2}$, which exists uniquely by [F2]. Symmetry and continuity give $F_{t_

[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

derivations.claim: The sample sigma-algebra is the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^n$ by [F7]. The maximum map $m(x)=\max_i x_i$ satisfies $|m(x)-m(y)|\le\max_i|x_i-y_i|$, so it is continuous. The preimages of open sets are therefore open; since the Borel sigma-algebra is generated by open sets, preimages of every Borel set are Borel and $M=m(X)$ is measurable. Also $m/\theta$ is continuous because $\theta>0$. The coordinate variables are independent by [F1], and [F2] gives their product joint law.

If $0\le u\le1$, then $P_\theta(M/\theta\le u)=P_\theta(X_1\le u\theta,\ldots,X_n\le u\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n u=u^n$. For $u<0$ the probability is $0$, and for $u\ge1$ it is $1$. This law does not depend on $\theta$, so $M/\theta$ is a pivot by [F3].
The distribution function $u^n$ established in step 1.2 is continuous. Therefore $P_\theta(\alpha^{1/n}\le M/\theta\le1)=1-(\alpha^{1/n})^n=1-\alpha$. By [F5], pivot inversion gives exact coverage.

Since $\theta>0$, the inequality $\alpha^{1/n}\le M/\theta\le1$ is equivalent to $M\le\theta\le M/\alpha^{1/n}$. Thus the inverted set is $[M,M/\alpha^{1/n}]\cap(0,\infty)$, and [F4] identifies its coverage with the probability computed in step 2.1.

The model excludes theta=0 and alpha=0.

citations.quote:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For all $x,y\in R$ and $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$ (x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nkx^ky^{n-k}.$$

The natural-number coefficients act by repeated addition. The formula includes $n=0$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal Y,\mathcal G),(Q_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be an
experiment with nonempty $\Theta$, and let $0\le\alpha\le1$. For each
$\eta\in\Theta$, let $A_\eta\in\mathcal G$ be the acceptance event of a
test of the point null $\theta=\eta$, on the full observation space,
including any auxiliary randomization. Suppose
$Q_\eta(A_\eta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every $\eta\in\Theta$.
Then $C(y):=\{\eta\in\Theta:y\in A_\eta\}$
is a confidence set with coverage at least $1-\alpha$.

The probability bound is the point-null level condition written in terms of
acceptance events. For a randomized test, a rejection-probability function on
the original data space is not itself an acceptance event; the auxiliary
randomization must be part of the observation before applying this statement.

For a finite set $A$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put

$$[A]^{k} := \{\, S \subseteq A \ :\ \lvert S\rvert = k \,\},$$

the set of $k$-element subsets of $A$. Every $S \subseteq A$ is finite
([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so the condition $\lvert S\rvert = k$ makes
sense for every subset.

**$[A]^{k}$ is finite.** It is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A)$, which is finite by
[[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], so [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]] applies.

**$\lvert [A]^{k}\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** Let $h : A \to A'$ be
a bijection of finite sets. The direct image map $S \mapsto h[S]$ carries
$[A]^{k}$ into $[A']^{k}$, because $h$ restricted to $S$ is a bijection of $S$
onto $h[S]$ and so $\lvert h[S]\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = k$ by the transport
clause of [[def-finite-cardinality]]; the map $T \mapsto h^{-1}[T]$ is its
two-sided inverse, since $h^{-1}[h[S]] = S$ and $h[h^{-1}[T]] = T$ for a
bijection $h$. So $[A]^{k} \approx [A']^{k}$ and the two have the same
cardinality.

**Definition.** For $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ set

$$\binom{n}{k} := \big\lvert\, [n]^{k} \,\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$

the **binomial coefficient**. By the previous paragraph and $\lvert n\rvert = n$,

$$\big\lvert [A]^{k}\big\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k} \qquad \text{for every finite } A .$$

**$\binom{n}{k}$ is a count, so it is a natural number by construction.** It is
*not* defined as $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$: that expression involves a division, hence
lives in $\mathbb{R}$, and the assertion that its value is a natural number is a
theorem, proved in [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]. Defining the coefficient as a
count makes integrality free and leaves the closed formula something to prove.

**Boundary values, read off the definition and not stipulated.**

- $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ **for every $n$, including $n = 0$**: the subsets of $n$ of
  cardinality $0$ are exactly the subsets equal to $\varnothing$
  ([[def-finite-cardinality]], clause (b)), so $[n]^{0} = \{\varnothing\}$, a
  one-element set. No empty-product convention is involved.
- $\binom{n}{n} = 1$: if $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert = n = \lvert n\rvert$
  then $S = n$ by clause 3 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $[n]^{n} = \{n\}$.
- $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$: a subset $S \subseteq n$ has
  $\lvert S\rvert \le n$ by clause 2 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $\lvert S\rvert = k > n$ is impossible and $[n]^{k} = \varnothing$
  ([[lem-nat-trichotomy]]).
- $\binom{n}{1} = n$: a subset of cardinality $1$ is $\{x\}$ for exactly one
  $x \in n$, since $\lvert S\rvert = 1$ means $S \approx \{0\}$; so
  $S \mapsto$ its unique element is a bijection $[n]^{1} \to n$.
- $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{0}{k} = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, both instances of the
  above.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]), let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]). The words
*nondecreasing*, *increasing*, *nonincreasing* and *decreasing* are those of
[[def-monotone-function]], in which *increasing* is the strict notion.

1. If $f'(x) \ge 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nondecreasing on $I$.
2. If $f'(x) > 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is increasing on
   $I$.
3. If $f'(x) \le 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nonincreasing on $I$.
4. If $f'(x) < 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is decreasing on
   $I$.

Conversely, with no continuity hypothesis and no hypothesis at any other point:

5. If $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ is nondecreasing on $I$ and differentiable at a
   point $c \in I$ that is a limit point of $I$, then $f'(c) \ge 0$; if $f$ is
   nonincreasing and differentiable at such a $c$, then $f'(c) \le 0$.

**No strict converse is claimed here, and none is true.** Claim 5 gives the
weak inequality only, and it cannot be improved: an increasing function may have
a vanishing derivative at a point. That failure is recorded separately, as a
false statement later on this page, with its witness worked out on the companion
page. Reading claim 2 backwards is the single most common misuse of this
theorem, and this statement does not license it.

**Claims 1 to 4 need the interval; claim 5 does not.** The forward direction
runs through the mean value theorem on a segment joining two points of $I$, so
order-convexity is essential. Claim 5 is a statement about one point and uses
only that the difference quotients have a constant sign.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

derivations.claim: The full power set of $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ is an algebra closed under countable unions, hence a sigma-algebra by [F5]. The binomial theorem [F1] gives $\sum_{j=0}^n\binom njp^j(1-p)^{n-j}=(p+1-p)^n=1$; all terms are nonnegative for $p\in[0,1]$, so [F6] makes the displayed masses a probability measure, including $p=0,1$. These laws form an experiment as in [F7].

For $k<n$, count pairs consisting of a $j$-element subset of an $n$-element set and a distinguished element inside it. Counting in the two orders gives $j\binom nj=n\binom{n-1}{j-1}$ for $1\le j\le k$. Counting instead a distinguished element outside the subset gives $(n-j)\binom nj=n\binom{n-1}j$ for $0\le j\le k$, by [F4]. The first identity is not used at $j=0$: in differentiating $p^j$, that boundary term is zero, so the first derivative sum starts at $j=1$, while the second identity includes $j=0$. Since $F_p(k)$ is a polynomial, it is continuous on $[0,1]$, and for $0<p<1$ termwise differentiation and the two identities give $$\frac{d}{dp}F_p(k) =\sum_{j=1}^k j\binom njp^{j-1}(1-p)^{n-j} -\sum_{j=0}^k(n-j)\binom njp^j(1-p)^{n-j-1} =-n\binom{n-1}k p^k(1-p)^{n-k-1}<0.$$ When $k=0$, the first sum is empty and the $j=0$ term of the second sum gives the same formula. By [F9], $F_p(k)$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1]$. Also $F_0(k)=1$ and $F_1(k)=0$ because $k<n$. Applying [F10] to this continuous polynomial on $[0,1]$ gives a point $U_k\in(0,1)$ with $F_{U_k}(k)=\alpha$; strict decrease makes it unique.

For each fixed candidate $p_0$, $F_{p_0}(k)$ is nondecreasing in integer $k$. Let $k_0$ be the least $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ with $F_{p_0}(k)\ge\alpha$, which exists because $F_{p_0}(n)=1$. The deterministic test function is $\varphi_{p_0}(x)=\mathbf1_{\{F_{p_0}(x)<\alpha\}}$; it is measurable on this finite space. Its rejection event is $\{X<k_0\}$, whose probability is $0$ if $k_0=0$, and otherwise is $F_{p_0}(k_0-1)<\alpha$. The null is $\{p_0\}$, and the alternative $[0,1]\setminus\{p_0\}$ is nonempty; by [F8] the test size equals this rejection probability and is at most $\alpha$.

For an observed $x<n$, strict decrease of $F_p(x)$ in $p$ makes $\{p_0:F_{p_0}(x)\ge\alpha\}=[0,U_x]$; for $x=n$, the set is $[0,1]=[0,U_n]$. Thus $C(X)$ is precisely the inversion of those acceptance events. The level calculation in step 2.1 and [F3] imply its coverage is at least $1-\alpha$, in the sense of [F2].

The unique root is U_0=1-alpha^(1/n), including n=1.

risk_review.notes: Read all four steps and all ten cited supplier statements. Finite nonnegative masses normalize by the binomial theorem, with 0^0=1 at p=0/1. The two subset-with-distinguished-element counts are valid for their stated j ranges; their derivative sums telescope to -n C(n-1,k)p^k(1-p)^(n-k-1), strictly negative on (0,1) for k<n, including k=0 and k=n-1. Continuity and endpoint values give a unique U_k in (0,1) by IVT, without arbitrary choice. The least integer k0 with CDF>=alpha exists; rejection uses strict <alpha, so probability is 0 or F(k0-1)<alpha. Singleton null and nonempty alternative satisfy test-size Definition. Both directions of inversion give [0,U_x], including x=n. n=1 gives U0=1-alpha; p=0/1 are covered surely. n=0 and alpha endpoints excluded. MIT Lecture11 p.1 and USC Lecture14 p.20 eventwise inversion checked; no reader/refuter finding or remaining defect.

citations.quote:
A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: Let $\pi_S:S\times\mathbb R\to S$ be the first-coordinate projection and define $\widetilde K((s,t),C):=K(s,C)$. The projection is measurable because $\pi_S^{-1}(A)=A\times\mathbb R$ for every $A\in\Sigma$; hence [F1] and [F2] show that $\widetilde K$ is a probability kernel from $(S\times\mathbb R,\Sigma\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ to $\mathbb R$.

The relation $\{(t,y):y>t\}$ is $\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}(-\infty,q)\times(q,\infty)$: density in [F3] supplies a rational strictly between $t$ and $y$, and every point in a displayed rectangle has $t<y$. The relation $\{(t,y):y<t\}$ has the analogous representation $\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}(q,\infty)\times(-\infty,q)$. These are countable unions of Borel rectangles by [F3] and [F4], and the equality relation is their joint complement. Therefore all three relations belong to $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. The coordinate map $(s,t,y)\mapsto(t,y)$ is measurable because inverse images of generating rectangles are $S\times B\times C$; taking inverse images now proves the two relation indicators in the domain of $\widetilde K$ are product-measurable.

Apply [F5] to $\widetilde K$ and the two indicator functions of the relation sets in step 1.2. Their section integrals are $\int 1_{\{y>t\}}K(s,dy)=K(s,(t,\infty))=a(s,t)$ and $\int 1_{\{y=t\}}K(s,dy)=K(s,\{t\})=b(s,t)$, so both maps are product-measurable.

For $n=2,3$, fix a bijection $e:\mathbb Q\to\mathbb N$ supplied by [F3]. Each rational open box is encoded by a finite tuple of natural numbers, and iterating the injection $(a,b)\mapsto 2^a(2b+1)$ shows there are only countably many such boxes. Density of $\mathbb Q$ then shows they form a base of $\mathbb R^n$: each point of an open set lies in such a box contained in that set. Thus each open set is a countable union of rectangles in the finite product sigma-algebra, giving $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathcal B(\mathbb R)^{\otimes n}$. Conversely, each coordinate projection $\pi_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, so [F7] makes $\pi_i^{-1}(A)$ Borel for every $A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$; finite intersections show every measurable rectangle is Borel, giving the reverse inclusion. Hence the Borel product and Euclidean Borel sigma-algebras agree in both dimensions. The map $\omega\mapsto(S_0(\omega),T_0(\omega))$ is measurable because the inverse image of each generating rectangle $A\times B$ is $S_0^{-1}(A)\cap T_0^{-1}(B)$; therefore $a(S_0,T_0)$ and $b(S_0,T_0)$ are measurable by [F6] and [F7]. The sets $(t,\infty)$ and $\{t\}$ are disjoint and their union is $[t,\infty)$, so finite additivity gives $a(S_0,T_0)+b(S_0,T_0)=K(S_0,[T_0,\infty))$. The map $(x,z)\mapsto x+z$ is continuous by $|(x+z)-(x_0+z_0)|\le |x-x_0|+|z-z_0|$. The map $(x,z,u)\mapsto x+uz$ is continuous because $|(x+uz)-(x_0+u_0z_0)|\le |x-x_0|+|u|\cdot|z-z_0|+|z_0|\cdot|u-u_0|$, and $|u|$ is bounded in a sufficiently small neighborhood of $u_0$. The pairs and triples of the real measurable functions already obtained and $U$ are measurable because inverse images of generating product rectangles are finite intersections of coordinate preimages. The established Borel-product equalities make these continuous maps measurable by [F7]. Composition by [F7] proves measurability of the asserted sums.

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a real random variable. Its **cumulative distribution function** is
the function
$$F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],\qquad F_X(x):=\mathbb P(X\le x)=\mathbb P_X((-\infty,x]).$$

The second expression is the same quantity written in terms of the law
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] of $X$.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $A\subseteq B$ be measurable with $\mu(A)<+\infty$. Then

$$\mu(B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B\setminus A).$$

If $\mu(B)<+\infty$, all terms are real and hence $\mu(B\setminus A)=\mu(B)-\mu(A)$. If $\mu(B)=+\infty$, then $\mu(B\setminus A)=+\infty$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **measurable** when
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], $F$ is nondecreasing. For each real $c$, $\{x:F(x)>c\}$ is an upper set, hence is empty, all of $\mathbb R$, or a ray with or without its finite endpoint; each such ray is Borel by [F11]. Thus every strict superlevel set is Borel, and [F10] makes $F$ Borel-measurable. For each $x$, the sets $(-\infty,x+1/n]$ decrease to $(-\infty,x]$ and have finite measure, so [F4] gives right continuity. The sets $(-\infty,-n]$ decrease to $\varnothing$ and $(-\infty,n]$ increase to $\mathbb R$, so [F3] and [F4] give the limits $0$ and $1$ at the two infinities. Also $(-\infty,x-1/n]$ increases to $(-\infty,x)$, so [F3] gives $F(x-)=\mu((-∞,x))$; [F5] then gives $F(x)-F(x-)=\mu(\{x\})$.

For every $x$, step 1.1 gives $F(x-)=\lim_nF(x-1/n)$. Each translate $x\mapsto F(x-1/n)$ is measurable because translation is continuous and [F8] preserves measurability under composition; [F9] makes their increasing limit $F(x-)$ measurable. Thus $\Delta F=F-F(\cdot-)$ is measurable by [F9]. Since $Y$ is measurable, $F(Y-)$ and $\Delta F(Y)$ are measurable. Fix a bijection $e:\mathbb Q\to\mathbb N$ supplied by [F12]. Each rational open rectangle is encoded by four natural numbers, and iterating the injection $(a,b)\mapsto 2^a(2b+1)$ shows there are only countably many such rectangles. Density of $\mathbb Q$ makes them a base of $\mathbb R^2$. Every Euclidean open set is therefore a countable union of rectangles in $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. Conversely the coordinate projections are continuous, and [F8] makes the inverse image of each Borel set under either projection Borel; finite intersections then show every Borel rectangle is Euclidean Borel. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$. The pair $(U,\Delta F(Y))$ is measurable into the product sigma-algebra because preimages of generating rectangles are intersections of coordinate preimages, hence it is measurable into $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$. The map $(u,d)\mapsto ud$ is continuous, as $|ud-u_0d_0|\le |u|\cdot|d-d_0|+|d_0|\cdot|u-u_0|$ and $|u|$ is bounded near $u_0$; hence [F8] makes it Borel-measurable. Composing and then summing with $F(Y-)$ proves $V$ is measurable.

Fix $0<u<1$ and set $A_u:=\{x:F(x)\ge u\}$. The upper-tail limit in step 1.1 makes $A_u$ nonempty, and the lower-tail limit makes it bounded below. Applying [F6] to $-A_u$ gives $q:=-\sup(-A_u)=\inf A_u$. For every $n$, the infimum property gives $F(q+1/n)\ge u$, so right continuity from step 1.1 yields $F(q)\ge u$. Since $q-1/n<q$ and $q$ is a lower bound for $A_u$, $F(q-1/n)<u$; the sets $(-\infty,q-1/n]$ increase to $(-\infty,q)$, so [F3] and step 1.1 give $F(q-)=\lim_nF(q-1/n)\le u$. Put $a:=F(q-)$ and $b:=F(q)$. If $Y<q$, then $F(Y)\le a\le u$, so $V\le u$; this event has probability $a$. If $b>a$, then $P(Y=q)=b-a$ and, conditional on $Y=q$, $V=a+U(b-a)$ is uniform on $[a,b]$, contributing $(u-a)$ to $P(V\le u)$. If $b=a$, the inequalities force $a=b=u$ and $P(Y=q)=0$, so this contribution is zero.

For $Y>q$, monotonicity gives $F(Y-)\ge F(q)=b\ge u$. If $F(Y-)>u$, then $V>u$. If $F(Y-)=u$ and $\Delta F(Y)>0$, the event $V\le u$ requires $U=0$, which has probability zero by [A1]. In the remaining case $F(Y-)=F(Y)=u$, put $L:=\{y>q:F(y-)=F(y)=u\}$. By steps 1.1 and 2.1, both $F$ and $F(\cdot-)$ are Borel-measurable, so $L=\{y>q\}\cap\{F(y-)=u\}\cap\{F(y)=u\}$ is Borel and therefore $\mu$-measurable. If $L$ is empty it contributes no mass. Otherwise let $r=\sup L$, allowing $r=+\infty$ when $L$ is unbounded. For every $z$ with $q<z<r$, some $y\in L$ has $z<y$, so monotonicity gives $u=F(q)\le F(z)\le F(y-)=u$ and hence $F(z)=u$. If $r<\infty$, define $c_n=q+(r-q)n/(n+1)$; if $r=+\infty$, define $c_n=q+n$. In either case $c_n\uparrow r$ (with the limit interpreted as $+\infty$ in the second case), and [F5] gives $\mu((q,c_n])=F(c_n)-F(q)=0$. By [F3], $\mu((q,r))=0$. If finite $r$ belongs to $L$, its mass is $\Delta F(r)=0$, so $\mu(L)=0$. Thus $Y>q$ contributes no probability, and step 2.2 yields $P(V\le u)=a+(u-a)=u$.

For $u_n=1/n$, the events $\{V\le u_n\}$ decrease to $\{V\le0\}$; [F4] and the formula from step 3.1 give $P(V\le0)=0$. For $v_n=1-1/n$ with $n\ge2$, the events $\{V\le v_n\}$ increase to $\{V<1\}$; [F3] and step 3.1 give $P(V<1)=1$. Finally $0\le V\le1$ by its definition, so $P(V\le1)=1$. Thus $P(V\le u)=u$ for all $u\in[0,1]$, which is the uniform law.

Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty finite set. Its **uniform probability space** assigns every $\omega\in\Omega$ the weight $1/|\Omega|$. Thus every event $A\subseteq\Omega$ has
$$\mathbb P(A)=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}.$$
Nonemptiness is required so that the denominator is positive.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

derivations.claim: Starting from the given list, repeatedly take the maximum of the remaining entries and remove every index carrying that value. By [F2] each nonempty remaining list has a maximum, and each iteration removes at least one of the original $m$ indices, so the process ends after at most $m$ iterations. It produces distinct values $b_1>b_2>\cdots>b_k$ with block sizes $r_j$. Put $c_j:=\sum_{\ell<j}r_\ell$, so $\sum_jr_j=m$. By [F1], the event that $a_J=b_j$ has probability $r_j/m$. On that event, $R_0=(c_j+r_j)/m$ and, by [A1] and [F3], $R_U=(c_j+r_jU)/m$, uniform on the interval $I_j=[c_j/m,(c_j+r_j)/m]$ of length $r_j/m$.

By step 1.1, the intervals $I_j$ are consecutive, begin at $0$, and end at $1$. Conditional on $a_J=b_j$, $R_U=(c_j+r_jU)/m$, so for $u\in[0,1]$ its conditional CDF is $0$ below the left endpoint, $(mu-c_j)/r_j$ between the endpoints, and $1$ above the right endpoint, by [A1]. Multiplying each conditional CDF contribution by $P(a_J=b_j)=r_j/m$ gives the length of $I_j\cap[0,u]$. These lengths sum to $u$ because the intervals partition $[0,1]$ up to shared endpoints. Hence $P(R_U\le u)=u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$, so $R_U$ is uniform.

For $u\in[0,1]$, $P(R_0\le u)$ is the sum of $r_j/m$ over those blocks whose right endpoint $(c_j+r_j)/m$ is at most $u$. These blocks form an initial segment; if the last is $j$, the sum telescopes to $(c_j+r_j)/m\le u$, and if there is no such block the sum is zero. Hence $P(R_0\le u)\le u$.

Step 3.1 at u=1 sums all block weights to one; with m=1 step 1.1 gives one block and RU=U,R0=1.
Step 1.1 permits every entry equal; then k=1,r1=m,c1=0 and the two formulas become RU=U and R0=1.
