citations.quote:
Fix one null probability law $P_0$. Let $S$ be a random element of a measurable space and let $T$ be a real random variable on the same probability space. Suppose a conditional law kernel $K(s,\cdot)$ of $T$ given $S$ is supplied, in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]. On an auxiliary extension, let $U$ be independent of $(S,T)$ and have the uniform Borel probability law on $[0,1]$, characterized by $P(U\le u)=u$ for $0\le u\le1$. The **randomized conditional upper-tail p-value** is
$$p_U:=K(S,(T,\infty))+U K(S,\{T\}),$$
and its **nonrandomized upper-tail value** is
$$p_0:=K(S,[T,\infty)).$$
The strict tail and atom terms are evaluated at the realized pair $(S,T)$; the independent $U$ randomizes only within the tie mass. Their measurability, including measurability of both displayed p-values, follows from [[lem-conditional-kernel-tail-and-atom-evaluations-are-measurable]]. The inclusive tail is the sum of the strict tail and the atom at $T$. This definition asserts no existence of the conditional kernel; it is supplied as part of the input.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $Y$ be a real random variable with cumulative distribution function $F(y)=P(Y\le y)$, and let $U$ be independent of $Y$ with the uniform Borel probability law on $[0,1]$. Write $F(y-):=P(Y<y)$ and $\Delta F(y):=F(y)-F(y-)=P(Y=y)$. Then
$$V:=F(Y-)+U\Delta F(Y)$$
has the uniform distribution on $[0,1]$, for arbitrary continuous, discrete, mixed, or singular laws of $Y$.

derivations.claim: For each $s$, let $\Lambda_s:=K(s,\cdot)\otimes\lambda$, where $\lambda$ is the uniform law of $U$. By [F4] this is a probability measure with rectangle values $\Lambda_s(C\times D)=K(s,C)\lambda(D)$. For $A\in\sigma(S)$ and Borel $C,D$, the conditional-law identity [F2] gives $\int_A\Lambda_S(C\times D)\,dP_0=\lambda(D)P_0(A\cap\{T\in C\})$. Independence in [F3] makes the right side $P_0(A\cap\{T\in C,U\in D\})$. The class of product-Borel sets where the evaluation $s\mapsto\Lambda_s(E)$ is measurable and every such conditional identity holds is a Dynkin system: complements subtract from the probability-one whole-space evaluation, and disjoint unions follow by countable additivity and increasing limits. It contains the generating rectangles, so [F5] and [F6] extend measurability and the conditional identity to every product-Borel set. Thus $\Lambda_S$ is a conditional law of $(T,U)$ given $S$.

For almost every conditioning value $s$, the conditional law just constructed makes $T$ have law $K(s,\cdot)$ and keeps $U$ independent uniform. Write $F_s(t):=K(s,(-\infty,t])$ and $\Delta_s(t):=F_s(t)-F_s(t-)$. By [F7], $V=F_s(T-)+(1-U)\Delta_s(T)$ is uniform, since $1-U$ is also uniform. The p-value formula in [F1] gives $p_U=1-V$, so $p_U$ is conditionally uniform.

For the same $s$, $p_0=1-F_s(T-)$ and $p_U=1-F_s(T-)-(1-U)\Delta_s(T)\le p_0$. Hence $\{p_0\le u\}\subseteq\{p_U\le u\}$ conditionally on $S=s$. Step 2.1 gives $P_0(p_0\le u\mid S=s)\le u$. This holds for each $u\in[0,1]$ and almost every conditioning value, proving conditional superuniformity.

boundaries.evidence: Statement assumes the supplied simple null P0 and conditional probability kernel; no empty-data probability law is admitted. Step 1.1 includes empty rectangle events with zero conditional mass.
Statement covers u=0; step 2.1 conditional uniformity gives zero randomized probability and step 3.1 event inclusion gives the zero inclusive bound.
Statement covers u=1; step 2.1 gives probability one, and the two tail values in F1 lie in [0,1], so the inclusive event also has probability one.
Step 2.1 permits a point-mass K(s,·); then p_U=U and p0=1, so atoms do not prevent conditional uniformity.
Statement is for every u∈[0,1]; steps 2.1 and 3.1 use the full endpoint PIT conclusion and the comparison p_U≤p0.
Step 1.1 constructs Λs=K(s,·)⊗λ from the supplied K and uniform law, then extends its conditional identity by the generating-rectangle argument. It selects no new conditional version family.

boundaries.reason: The theorem derives conditional uniformity from a supplied conditional kernel and independent randomizer; no iff about all constructions is stated.
Conditional uniformity alone is not claimed to imply the particular tail formula or independence premise used here.

risk_review.notes: Read all three steps and all seven dependency statements/definitions. K_s⊗λ exists since both factors are probabilities; independence of U from (S,T) gives conditional rectangle identities, and the displayed Dynkin-system extension gives a conditional product kernel. For the parameter-dependent event, apply the same rectangle/Dynkin argument to sets in S×(R×[0,1]): for B×E its conditional integral is 1_B(s)Λ_s(E), so the current measurable p-value map can be substituted. This is the immediate conditional-law inference used in step 2.1, not an additional existence assumption. The reviewed arbitrary-law PIT applied with 1−U yields p_U=1−V uniform; p_U≤p_0 gives superuniformity. Checked atoms, point masses, zero-probability conditioning values and u=0,1. Each asserted conditional identity is a version interpreted almost surely for each u; no common parameter-null set or division by P(S=s) is used. No AC beyond supplied kernels.

citations.quote: A **finite-group randomization setup** consists of a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ as in [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], a finite group $G$ acting on $\Omega$ as in [[def-group-action]], a statistic $T:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and a family $\mathcal P_0$ of null probability laws on $\Omega$ that is invariant under the action. Invariance means that for every $P\in\mathcal P_0$, $g\in G$, and $A\subseteq\Omega$, $P(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P(A)$. The **orbit** of $x$ is $O(x):=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}$, a finite subset of $\Omega$. The setup itself does not assert that the action is free or that distinct group elements give distinct orbit points.

For a finite-group randomization setup with statistic $T$, the **inclusive orbit upper-tail rank** at $x\in\Omega$ is
$$p_0(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the observed data and uniform on $[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized orbit rank** is
$$p_U(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Both counts are over group elements, with multiplicity. Thus a nonfree action counts a distinct orbit point as many times as it has preimages under $g\mapsto g\cdot x$.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Let $A$ and $B$ be events in a finite probability space with $\mathbb P(B)>0$. The **conditional probability of $A$ given $B$** is
$$\mathbb P(A\mid B):=\frac{\mathbb P(A\cap B)}{\mathbb P(B)}.$$
No value is assigned to $\mathbb P(A\mid B)$ when $\mathbb P(B)=0$.

In a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$, events $A\subseteq B\subseteq\Omega$ satisfy
$$0\le\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)\le1,$$
and
$$\mathbb P(\varnothing)=0,\qquad \mathbb P(\Omega)=1,\qquad \mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A),\qquad \mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A).$$
Probability zero need not imply that an event is empty.

Let $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$ with $m\ge1$. Let $J$ be uniform on $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and let $U$ be independent of $J$ and uniform on $[0,1]$. Set
$$R_0:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i\ge a_J\}}{m},\qquad R_U:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i>a_J\}+U\#\{i:a_i=a_J\}}{m}.$$
Then $R_U$ is uniform on $[0,1]$, while $R_0$ is superuniform: $P(R_0\le u)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

derivations.claim: Fix a positive-probability orbit $O$ and points $x,y\in O$. Choose $h\in G$ with $y=h\cdot x$. Invariance gives $P(X=y)=P(h\cdot X=y)=P(X=h^{-1}\cdot y)=P(X=x)$. Thus all $|O|$ distinct points have equal mass; by [F3] their conditional probabilities given $X\in O$ are each $1/|O|$.

For fixed $x\in O$, define its stabilizer $G_x:=\{g\in G:g\cdot x=x\}$. If $y=h\cdot x$, then $\{g:g\cdot x=y\}=hG_x$: every $hg$ with $g\in G_x$ sends $x$ to $y$, and if $g\cdot x=y$ then $h^{-1}g\in G_x$. Hence every distinct point of $O$ occurs exactly $|G_x|$ times in the group-transformed list. The strict and tied counts and denominator in [F2] all have this same factor, so the group-average ranks equal the ranks computed on the distinct orbit points.

Conditional on $O$, [step 1.1] makes the observed orbit point a uniform index in the finite list $(T(y))_{y\in O}$. By [F5] and [A2], the randomizer remains independent and uniform. Apply [F4] to this list and use [step 2.1]: $p_U$ is Uniform$(0,1)$ and $P(p_0\le u\mid X\in O)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.

The positive-probability orbits form a finite partition up to null orbits. Summing the conditional superuniform bounds from step 3.1 with weights $P(X\in O)$ gives $P(p_0\le u)\le u$; summing the conditional uniform laws gives $p_U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$. The argument applies to each invariant null law. Only finite counting is used, so no choice axiom is needed.

boundaries.evidence: Statement fixes a finite probability setup and conditions only on positive-probability orbits; normalization guarantees at least one such orbit. Step 4.1 omits null orbits from its finite mixture.
Step 4.1 gives zero weight to probability-zero orbits rather than conditioning by zero. At rank threshold u=0, step 3.1 invokes the multiset zero endpoint.
Step 3.1 includes u=1, where both ranks are at most one. A singleton orbit is a list of size one and gives p_U=U,p0=1.
Steps 2.1 and 3.1 include stabilizers and repeated statistic values; a trivial action produces a singleton orbit without requiring a free group action.
Step 2.1 cancels the equal stabilizer multiplicity in both counts and denominator; step 3.1 applies the tied-rank result including interval endpoints zero and one.
Step 1.1 selects an h for one fixed pair of orbit points; step 2.1 proves the fiber formula hGx. Step 4.1 sums a finite partition, so only finite choices occur and no choice axiom is needed.

boundaries.reason: The Statement is an invariance-to-validity theorem; it does not characterize invariance by a forward iff about the rank law.
A valid orbit rank for a particular statistic is not claimed to force invariance of the null law under every action element.

risk_review.notes: Read all four steps and seven dependency interfaces. Invariance and inverse group elements force equal singleton mass on each positive-mass orbit. The fiber of g↦g·x is hG_x, with exactly |G_x| elements; its factor cancels in strict/tie counts and |G|=|O||G_x|. Independence preserves the uniform randomizer after conditioning on the finite orbit, and the reviewed tied-rank lemma applies to the uniform distinct-orbit index. Finite orbit mixture yields both unconditional claims. Checked trivial group, singleton orbit, nonfree action, all tied scores, zero-mass orbits and endpoints u=0,1. Group nonemptiness and finite probability normalization prevent zero denominators. No AC.

boundaries.evidence: Definition explicitly requires nonempty disjoint Θ0,Θ1; an empty null family is excluded rather than assigned a vacuous size convention.
Definition inequality qθ≤α at α=0 forces qθ≤0 almost surely; since it is a conditional expectation of φ≥0, zero rejection is required.
Definition takes φ into [0,1]; its conditional expectation lies in [0,1] almost surely, so α=1 permits any supplied test.
Definition permits constant φ=0 or φ=1; supplied conditional versions are those same constants under every null law.
Definition uses almost-sure bounds separately under each Pθ and asserts no pointwise condition at conditioning values of probability zero; the bounds at α=0 and α=1 use the same convention.
Definition supplies each qθ as input to the conditional-level condition and asserts no common version or common exceptional set across parameters.

The definition does not assert that an unconditional level bound yields a conditional level bound for the statistic S.

Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $K$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ given $\mathcal G$. For measurable $f:E\to[0,\infty]$, the measurable function $I_f(\omega)=\int f(x)K(\omega,dx)$ satisfies

$$\int_H I_f\,dP=\int_H f(X)\,dP\qquad(H\in\mathcal G).$$

This assertion is choice-free. Under AC, it says $I_f=E[f(X)\mid\mathcal G]$ as nonnegative almost-sure classes. If $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is measurable and $E|f(X)|<\infty$, put $D=\{I_{|f|}<\infty\}$. Then $D\in\mathcal G$, $P(D)=1$, and the signed integral on $D$, extended by zero off $D$, is a real integrable conditional-expectation version of $f(X)$. Its identification with the AC-based conditional-expectation class uses AC only for that class convention.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,\{P_\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment with nonempty disjoint null and alternative parameter sets $\Theta_0,\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta$. Let $\mathcal S$ be a topological space with its Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathcal S)$, and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathcal S$ be measurable. Write $\sigma(S):=\{S^{-1}(C):C\in\mathcal B(\mathcal S)\}$, the sigma-algebra generated by $S$ as in [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]]. A possibly randomized test is a measurable function $\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ as in [[def-test-size-and-power]]. For each $\theta\in\Theta_0$, a **conditional rejection probability given $S$** is a supplied version $q_\theta$ of $E_\theta[\varphi(X)\mid\sigma(S)]$, where conditional expectation is understood as in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The test has **conditional level at most $\alpha$ given $S$ on $\Theta_0$** if such versions can be supplied with $q_\theta\le\alpha$ $P_\theta$-almost surely for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$. The almost-sure qualification is separate under each null law; no common null set or pointwise statement at conditioning values of probability zero is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: The map $(s,x)\mapsto\varphi(x)$ is product-measurable by [F5]. Kernel integration [F2] therefore makes $q$ measurable. Since $K(s,\cdot)$ is a probability measure and $0\le\varphi\le1$, every value satisfies $0\le q(s)\le1$.

Fix $\eta\in\Theta_0$. By [A1] and [F1], $K(S,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(S)$ under $P_\eta$. Applying [F3] to the bounded function $\varphi$ shows that for every $A\in\sigma(S)$, $\int_A q(S)\,dP_\eta=\int_A\varphi(X)\,dP_\eta$. Thus $q(S)$ is a version of the conditional rejection probability under this null law. The same kernel in [A1] defines the same $q$ for every $\eta$, proving nuisance-freeness; only the individual laws' almost-sure qualifications are used.

boundaries.evidence: Statement explicitly requires nonempty Θ0,Θ1 and supplies a common probability kernel. Empty data space cannot support its null probability laws.
Step 1.1 with φ=0 yields q(s)=0 at all s. Step 2.1 interprets conditional identities under each Pη, so zero-probability conditioning values impose no extra pointwise restriction.
Step 1.1 with φ=1 uses kernel total mass one to give q(s)=1; singleton conditioning spaces are allowed by the Statement standard-Borel premise.
Statement admits a point-mass null law whenever the common kernel premise holds; step 2.1 only uses the event-integral conditional identities, not a positive density.
Step 1.1 includes both bounds 0≤q≤1, inherited from 0≤φ≤1. No scalar significance-level α occurs in this theorem.
Statement supplies one K for all nuisance values and fixes realizing Polish topologies. Step 2.1 reuses that K separately under each law without selecting versions indexed by η.

citations.quote: Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,\{P_\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment with nonempty disjoint null and alternative parameter sets $\Theta_0,\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta$. Let $\mathcal S$ be a topological space with its Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathcal S)$, and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathcal S$ be measurable. Write $\sigma(S):=\{S^{-1}(C):C\in\mathcal B(\mathcal S)\}$, the sigma-algebra generated by $S$ as in [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]]. A possibly randomized test is a measurable function $\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ as in [[def-test-size-and-power]]. For each $\theta\in\Theta_0$, a **conditional rejection probability given $S$** is a supplied version $q_\theta$ of $E_\theta[\varphi(X)\mid\sigma(S)]$, where conditional expectation is understood as in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The test has **conditional level at most $\alpha$ given $S$ on $\Theta_0$** if such versions can be supplied with $q_\theta\le\alpha$ $P_\theta$-almost surely for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$. The almost-sure qualification is separate under each null law; no common null set or pointwise statement at conditioning values of probability zero is asserted.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

derivations.claim: Fix $\theta\in\Theta_0$ and choose the conditional version $q_\theta$ supplied by [F1]. Taking $A=\Omega$ in [F2] gives $E_\theta q_\theta=E_\theta\varphi(X)$.
Since $q_\theta\le\alpha$ almost surely and both variables are integrable, [F3] gives $E_\theta q_\theta\le E_\theta\alpha=\alpha$. Combining with step 1.1 yields $E_\theta\varphi(X)\le\alpha$.

The argument holds for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$, so taking the supremum of these rejection expectations gives size at most $\alpha$ under the convention [A1]. No common exceptional null set across parameter values is needed.

citations.quote:
A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

A **finite-group randomization setup** consists of a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ as in [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], a finite group $G$ acting on $\Omega$ as in [[def-group-action]], a statistic $T:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and a family $\mathcal P_0$ of null probability laws on $\Omega$ that is invariant under the action. Invariance means that for every $P\in\mathcal P_0$, $g\in G$, and $A\subseteq\Omega$, $P(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P(A)$. The **orbit** of $x$ is $O(x):=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}$, a finite subset of $\Omega$. The setup itself does not assert that the action is free or that distinct group elements give distinct orbit points.

For a finite-group randomization setup with statistic $T$, the **inclusive orbit upper-tail rank** at $x\in\Omega$ is
$$p_0(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the observed data and uniform on $[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized orbit rank** is
$$p_U(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Both counts are over group elements, with multiplicity. Thus a nonfree action counts a distinct orbit point as many times as it has preimages under $g\mapsto g\cdot x$.

derivations.claim: For $x=1$, the transformed statistic values are $T(e\cdot1)=1$ and $T(s\cdot1)=0$, so exactly one of the two group elements has value at least $T(1)$ and $p_0(1)=1/2$. For $x=0$, both transformed values $1,0$ are at least $T(0)=0$, so $p_0(0)=1$.
Therefore $\{p_0\le1/2\}=\{X=1\}$ and $P(p_0\le1/2)=9/10>1/2$, contradicting superuniformity.

The same example also defeats tie randomization: $p_U(1)=U/2$ and $p_U(0)=(1+U)/2$. Hence $P(p_U\le1/2)=9/10$, since at $X=1$ the event always occurs and at $X=0$ it requires $U=0$, an event of probability zero under the independent uniform law in the Given.

Step 3.1 formula p_U(1)=U/2 allows value zero only at U=0, a probability-zero uniform endpoint; p_0 is never zero.
Step 1.1 gives p_0(0)=1 and p_0(1)=1/2; step 3.1 gives p_U(0)=(1+U)/2≤1.
Counterexample assigns both outcomes positive weights 1/10 and 9/10; these unequal weights violate swapping invariance and produce the failure in step 2.1.
Step 3.1 identifies the only x=0 contribution at threshold 1/2 as U=0, of probability zero; step 2.1 gives the interior threshold failure 9/10>1/2.
Counterexample displays the two outcomes, two group elements and swapping action explicitly; step 1.1 counts their images without selecting a kernel or infinite family.

boundaries.reason: The refuted assertion is universal superuniformity without invariance; step 2.1 disproves it at one threshold, rather than proving a forward characterization.
The construction does not claim that failure of invariance always implies an invalid rank; it only supplies this weighted two-point witness.

Invariance means that for every $P\in\mathcal P_0$, $g\in G$, and $A\subseteq\Omega$, $P(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P(A)$. The **orbit** of $x$ is $O(x):=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}$, a finite subset of $\Omega$. The setup itself does not assert that the action is free or that distinct group elements give distinct orbit points.

For a finite-group randomization setup with statistic $T$, the **inclusive orbit upper-tail rank** at $x\in\Omega$ is
$$p_0(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the observed data and uniform on $[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized orbit rank** is
$$p_U(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Both counts are over group elements, with multiplicity. Thus a nonfree action counts a distinct orbit point as many times as it has preimages under $g\mapsto g\cdot x$.

In a finite-group randomization setup, fix a null law invariant under the group action. Conditional on every orbit $O$ with positive probability, the data are uniform on the distinct points of $O$. For the orbit ranks of [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]], the inclusive p-value $p_0$ is superuniform under the null, and the independent-uniform tie-randomized value $p_U$ is Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on each positive-probability orbit. Consequently, $p_U$ is also Uniform$(0,1)$ unconditionally.

Let $A$ and $B$ be events in a finite probability space with $\mathbb P(B)>0$. The **conditional probability of $A$ given $B$** is
$$\mathbb P(A\mid B):=\frac{\mathbb P(A\cap B)}{\mathbb P(B)}.$$
No value is assigned to $\mathbb P(A\mid B)$ when $\mathbb P(B)=0$.

derivations.claim: The group $S_3$ permutes the three one-hot vectors transitively. Each vector has weight $1/3$, so every permutation preserves the law and the null is invariant. The permutations fixing a given coordinate position are the identity and the transposition of the other two positions; hence each orbit point is produced by exactly two of the six group elements.

At $e_1$, $T(e_1)=1$; two transformed values equal $1$ and four equal $0$. Thus $p_0(e_1)=2/6=1/3$ and $p_U(e_1)=2U/6=U/3$. At $e_2$ or $e_3$, the observed statistic is $0$; two transformed values are strictly greater and four tie, so $p_0=6/6=1$ and $p_U=(2+4U)/6=1/3+2U/3$.

Under the uniform null, $e_1$ occurs with probability $1/3$, and $e_2,e_3$ together with probability $2/3$. Conditional on the first case, $p_U$ is uniform on $[0,1/3]$; conditional on the second, it is uniform on $[1/3,1]$. For $0\le u\le1/3$, $P(p_U\le u)=(1/3)(3u)=u$. For $1/3\le u\le1$, $P(p_U\le u)=1/3+(2/3)((u-1/3)/(2/3))=u$. Hence $p_U$ is uniform on $[0,1]$. The inclusive rank is $1/3$ with probability $1/3$ and $1$ with probability $2/3$, so $P(p_0\le u)$ is $0$ for $u<1/3$, $1/3$ for $1/3\le u<1$, and $1$ for $u=1$; thus it is superuniform. These are the single-orbit conclusions of [F3].

Let $((\Omega_i,w_i))_{i\in I}$ be a finite indexed family of finite probability spaces. Their **product probability space** has outcome set
$$\Omega:=\prod_{i\in I}\Omega_i$$
and assigns $\omega=(\omega_i)_{i\in I}$ the weight
$$w(\omega):=\prod_{i\in I}w_i(\omega_i).$$
For $I=\varnothing$, the product outcome set is the singleton containing the empty function and its weight is the empty product $1$. Normalization and independence of coordinate events are proved in [[thm-product-probability-has-independent-coordinate-events]].

The weights in every finite product of finite probability spaces are nonnegative and sum to $1$. For events $A_i\subseteq\Omega_i$, the coordinate events
$$C_i:=\{\omega\in\prod_{j\in I}\Omega_j:\omega_i\in A_i\}$$
are mutually independent, and for every $J\subseteq I$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcap_{j\in J}C_j\right)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P_j(A_j).$$

A finite family of finite-valued random variables $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **mutually independent** when for every nonempty $J\subseteq I$ and every selection $x_j\in X_j(\Omega)$,
$$\mathbb P(X_j=x_j\text{ for every }j\in J)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P(X_j=x_j).$$
It is **pairwise independent** when this identity is required only for two distinct indices. The empty family is mutually independent vacuously, and a one-member family is mutually independent.

Let $A$ and $B$ be events in a finite probability space with $\mathbb P(B)>0$. The **conditional probability of $A$ given $B$** is
$$\mathbb P(A\mid B):=\frac{\mathbb P(A\cap B)}{\mathbb P(B)}.$$
No value is assigned to $\mathbb P(A\mid B)$ when $\mathbb P(B)=0$.

Fix one null probability law $P_0$. Let $S$ be a random element of a measurable space and let $T$ be a real random variable on the same probability space. Suppose a conditional law kernel $K(s,\cdot)$ of $T$ given $S$ is supplied, in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]. On an auxiliary extension, let $U$ be independent of $(S,T)$ and have the uniform Borel probability law on $[0,1]$, characterized by $P(U\le u)=u$ for $0\le u\le1$. The **randomized conditional upper-tail p-value** is
$$p_U:=K(S,(T,\infty))+U K(S,\{T\}),$$
and its **nonrandomized upper-tail value** is
$$p_0:=K(S,[T,\infty)).$$
The strict tail and atom terms are evaluated at the realized pair $(S,T)$; the independent $U$ randomizes only within the tie mass. Their measurability, including measurability of both displayed p-values, follows from [[lem-conditional-kernel-tail-and-atom-evaluations-are-measurable]]. The inclusive tail is the sum of the strict tail and the atom at $T$. This definition asserts no existence of the conditional kernel; it is supplied as part of the input.

Under the simple null and the supplied conditional law in [[def-randomized-conditional-p-value]], for every $u\in[0,1]$,
$$P_0(p_U\le u\mid\sigma(S))=u\quad P_0\text{-almost surely},$$
while the nonrandomized upper-tail value satisfies
$$P_0(p_0\le u\mid\sigma(S))\le u\quad P_0\text{-almost surely}.$$
Thus the randomized value is conditionally uniform and the inclusive-tail value is conditionally superuniform, including when the conditional law has atoms.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

Let $\varphi$ be a test for nonempty disjoint null and alternative parameter sets $\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ as in [[def-test-size-and-power]], let $S$ be a statistic, and let $\alpha\in[0,1]$. If for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$ there is a conditional-expectation version $q_\theta=E_\theta[\varphi(X)\mid\sigma(S)]$ with $q_\theta\le\alpha$ $P_\theta$-almost surely, then $E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\le\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta_0$. Consequently, the test has size at most $\alpha$, where size is the supremum of its rejection expectation over the null family as in [[def-test-size-and-power]].

derivations.claim: Write $\Omega=\{0,1\}^{N}$ and give each coordinate the two-point Bernoulli$(p)$ law. By [F1], a sequence with $s$ ones has weight $p^s(1-p)^{N-s}$; the product weights sum to $(p+(1-p))^N=1$, and [F2] gives the independent-trial model. For $0<p<1$, every sequence with $S=s$ has the same positive weight.

There are $\binom{N}{s}$ sequences with $s$ successes. Exactly $\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{s-k}$ of them have $K=k$: choose $k$ of the first $n_1$ positions and $s-k$ of the other $n_2$. These counts partition all size-$s$ subsets, so the displayed kernel weights sum to one for every $s$, and when $P_p(S=s)>0$, dividing by the total count using [F3] gives the conditional mass; the feasible range is precisely where both binomial coefficients are nonzero. At $p=0$ only $S=0$ occurs and $K=0$; at $p=1$ only $S=N$ occurs and $K=n_1$, so the supplied kernel has the required conditional law on the realized margin. At the other, probability-zero margins the same formula is simply the chosen kernel extension.

For $n_1=n_2=2$ and $s=2$, the feasible values are $k=0,1,2$, with counts $1,4,1$ among the six two-success sequences. Their probabilities are therefore $1/6,4/6,1/6$. Summing the masses at or above each observed value gives inclusive p-values $1,5/6,1/6$. The strict-tail-plus-tie formulas are respectively $5/6+U/6$, $1/6+2U/3$, and $U/6$; their intervals $[5/6,1]$, $[1/6,5/6]$, and $[0,1/6]$ have lengths matching the three conditional masses.

For each margin $s$ with $P_p(S=s)>0$, [F5] makes the nonrandomized p-value conditionally superuniform and the randomized value conditionally uniform under the null. Rejecting when the nonrandomized value is at most $\alpha$ is therefore a conditional level-$\alpha$ test, so [F6] gives unconditional size at most $\alpha$. The test function of the randomized rule is $\varphi_\alpha(x)=P_U(p_U(x,U)\le\alpha)$; it is measurable because the sample space is finite. By finite conditioning and independence of $U$, $E_p[\varphi_\alpha(X)\mid S=s]=P_p(p_U\le\alpha\mid S=s)=\alpha$, so the randomized rule has conditional and unconditional size exactly $\alpha$. At $p=0$ and $p=1$ the only observed margin has a degenerate conditional law; its inclusive value is $1$ and its randomized value is $U$, so the same validity conclusions hold.

Definition uses weak convergence of Borel laws in R^d, not a probability-level quantile. It permits point-mass limiting laws and explicitly imposes no moment-convergence conclusion.
Definition: only laws are compared; no common-space coupling is asserted.
Definition equivalently clause: weak convergence of the laws of Z_n to ν is exactly Z_n⇒Z whenever the random vector Z has law ν, by the stated law-based convergence convention.
Definition equivalently clause: Z_n⇒Z for a vector of law ν means its laws converge weakly to law(Z)=ν, recovering the displayed asymptotic-distribution condition.
For every positive n the definition supplies a probability space and a measurable random vector into Euclidean Borel R^d, with fixed d≥1; it admits neither an empty probability carrier nor n=0.
Definition: the zero-vector sequence satisfies both norm-tail criteria.
Definition permits scalar dimension d=1 and X_n≡1. Its tails vanish above M=1, so it is O_P(1), whereas the tail at ε=1/2 equals one and excludes o_P(1).
Definition: constant sequences are covered directly by the tail formulas.
Definition uses strict tail events ||X_n||>ε or >M, with positive thresholds. At ||X_n||=M the boundedness event is excluded; ε=0 is not among the vanishing-tail requirements.
Definition: the probability spaces may vary with n; no coupling or representative selection is required.

boundaries.reason: Definition gives separate formulas for o_P(1) and O_P(1). It does not state they are equivalent: the constant-one sequence satisfies the latter but not the former.
Definition independence is explicitly not implicit in either notation; the two tail formulas assert no converse that boundedness in probability forces convergence to zero.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed Definition and all four cited suppliers. Fixed positive finite dimension, Euclidean Borel measurability and positive thresholds make every norm tail an event. Varying probability spaces are allowed; no joint law or independence is asserted. Zero sequence satisfies both bounds; constant one satisfies O_P but not o_P. The limsup quantifier is eventual boundedness, sufficient for later union bounds. No choice use.

citations.quote:
For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

Random elements $X_n,X$ with values in the same metric space **converge in distribution**, written $X_n\Rightarrow X$, if their laws from [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] satisfy $P_{X_n}\Rightarrow P_X$ in [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]. They may be defined on different probability spaces. The definition specifies only their marginal laws.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open and closed sets
as in [[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]]. Then:

1. **Balls are open.** $B(x,r)$ is open, for every $x \in X$ and every $r > 0$.
2. **Arbitrary unions.** If $\mathcal{U}$ is any collection of open subsets of
   $X$, then $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$ is open.
3. **Finite intersections.** If $n \ge 1$ and $U_0, \dots, U_{n-1}$ are open,
   then $U_0 \cap \dots \cap U_{n-1}$ is open.
4. **Closed balls are closed.** $\bar B(x,r)$ is closed, for every $x \in X$ and
   every $r > 0$.

Together with the fact that $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open, recorded already in
[[def-metric-topology]], claims 2 and 3 say that $\mathcal{T}_d$ has exactly the
closure properties that the word *topology* names.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

derivations.claim: Suppose $X_n\Rightarrow X$ in $\mathbb R^d$. For positive integers $m$, set $F_m=\mathbb R^d\setminus B(0,m)=\{x:\|x\|_2\ge m\}$, where [F5] identifies the Euclidean distance with the norm and [F6] gives the metric-ball definition. By [F7] each ball is open, so [F8] makes $F_m$ closed. The sets decrease to the empty set because every vector has finite norm, and their probabilities are at most one. By [F4], $P_X(F_m)\to0$. For each $m$, [F2] and [F3] give $\limsup_nP_n(\|X_n\|_2\ge m)\le P_X(F_m)$. Choosing $m$ with right side below any prescribed $\eta>0$ proves $X_n=O_P(1)$ by [F1].

If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=o_P(1)$ in one Euclidean space, the triangle inequality gives $\{\|U_n+V_n\|_2>\varepsilon\}\subseteq\{\|U_n\|_2>\varepsilon/2\}\cup\{\|V_n\|_2>\varepsilon/2\}$. The union bound and [F1] show that the left event has probability tending to zero.

If $U_n=O_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, choose $M_U,M_V>0$ using [F1]. The event $\{\|U_n+V_n\|_2>M_U+M_V\}$ is contained in $\{\|U_n\|_2>M_U\}\cup\{\|V_n\|_2>M_V\}$, so its limiting upper probability is at most the sum of the two chosen tail bounds. Since the bounds can be arbitrarily small, $U_n+V_n=O_P(1)$.

If $C=0$, then $B(U_n,V_n)=0$ for all $n$. Suppose $C>0$, $U_n=o_P(1)$, and $V_n=O_P(1)$. For any $\eta>0$, choose $M>0$ with $\limsup_nP_n(\|V_n\|_2>M)\le\eta$. The norm bound for $B$ gives $\{\|B(U_n,V_n)\|_2>\varepsilon\}\subseteq\{\|V_n\|_2>M\}\cup\{\|U_n\|_2>\varepsilon/(CM)\}$. By [F1], the second event has probability tending to zero, so the limiting upper probability of the left event is at most $\eta$; arbitrariness of $\eta$ proves $B(U_n,V_n)=o_P(1)$. The same argument applies when the small factor is in the second coordinate.

If both inputs to $B$ are $O_P(1)$, choose $M_U,M_V>0$ so that the limiting upper probability of either input exceeding its bound is at most an arbitrary $\eta>0$. Outside the union of these two tail events, $\|B(U_n,V_n)\|_2\le C M_U M_V$. The union bound makes the limiting upper probability above this fixed bound at most $2\eta$. Letting $\eta$ decrease to zero proves $B(U_n,V_n)=O_P(1)$.

boundaries.evidence: Statement supplies random vectors on normalized probability spaces for each n; part2 explicitly uses positive integers p,q,r, excluding an empty-dimensional product-map input. No empty indexed-sum convention enters the union-bound proof.
Step 1.4 handles the bilinear norm constant C=0.
Statement includes p=q=r=1 and B(u,v)=uv with C=1; proof part2 uses |uv|≤|u||v|. Constant scalar inputs1 are O_P(1), so their product is covered without claiming it vanishes.
Steps 1.2 and 1.4 include zero and constant sequences.

Proof step 1.4 explicitly separates C=0, where the norm bound makes B(U_n,V_n)=0, from C>0 before dividing by CM. The positive ε and η tail tolerances remain those in the Statement stochastic-order conventions.
Steps 1.1 and 1.3 choose only finite tail radii from the given hypotheses.

boundaries.reason: Statement proves addition, norm-bounded-map and weak-convergence⇒boundedness rules. The words “or conversely” in part2 swap which input is o_P and which is O_P; they do not assert that a small output forces either input small.
Statement does not characterize weak convergence by O_P boundedness or input rates by an output product rate. Proof union bounds establish the listed sufficient implications only.

risk_review.notes: Read all five proof steps and eight cited suppliers. Closed exteriors F_m decrease to empty; probability continuity from above and Portmanteau closed-set limsup give the claimed eventual O_P bound. Sum events use the triangle inequality and union bound with arbitrary small budgets. Product estimates handle C=0 separately and C>0 using positive M and epsilon/(CM); reverse small-factor placement and two bounded factors both work. Composite measurability is explicitly assumed for arbitrary B, and the conditional non-Borel-set remark correctly demonstrates why a norm bound alone is insufficient. No independence, coupling across n, or AC used.

citations.quote:
Let all random vectors with index $n$ be defined on a common probability space for that $n$; the spaces may vary with $n$. In any fixed finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the following rules hold:

1. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=o_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=o_P(1)$. If $U_n=O_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=O_P(1)$.
2. For positive integers $p,q,r$, let $B:\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^r$ be a fixed map for which there is a constant $C\ge0$ with $\|B(u,v)\|_2\le C\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ for all $u,v$. Assume in each application that $B(U_n,V_n)$ is a random vector on the same probability space as $U_n,V_n$, for every $n$. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, or conversely, then $B(U_n,V_n)=o_P(1)$. If both are $O_P(1)$, then $B(U_n,V_n)=O_P(1)$.
3. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ in $\mathbb R^d$, then $X_n=O_P(1)$.

The last conclusion is finite-dimensional boundedness in probability. No independence or Axiom of Choice is assumed.

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Random elements $X_n,X$ with values in the same metric space **converge in distribution**, written $X_n\Rightarrow X$, if their laws from [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] satisfy $P_{X_n}\Rightarrow P_X$ in [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]. They may be defined on different probability spaces. The definition specifies only their marginal laws.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open and closed sets
as in [[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]]. Then:

1. **Balls are open.** $B(x,r)$ is open, for every $x \in X$ and every $r > 0$.
2. **Arbitrary unions.** If $\mathcal{U}$ is any collection of open subsets of
   $X$, then $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$ is open.
3. **Finite intersections.** If $n \ge 1$ and $U_0, \dots, U_{n-1}$ are open,
   then $U_0 \cap \dots \cap U_{n-1}$ is open.
4. **Closed balls are closed.** $\bar B(x,r)$ is closed, for every $x \in X$ and
   every $r > 0$.

Together with the fact that $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open, recorded already in
[[def-metric-topology]], claims 2 and 3 say that $\mathcal{T}_d$ has exactly the
closure properties that the word *topology* names.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $X_n=O_P(1)$. Fix a bounded continuous $f:\mathbb R^{d+k}\to\mathbb R$, and let $\eta>0$. The definition of $O_P(1)$ gives $R>0$ with $\limsup_nP_n(\|X_n\|_2>R)\le\eta$.

Let $K=\overline B_2(0,R)\times\overline B_2(c,1)\subseteq\mathbb R^{d+k}$. The factor balls are closed by [F11]. The coordinate projections are continuous because [F9] gives $d_2(x,x')\le d_2((x,y),(x',y'))$ and the analogous inequality for $y$, so $K$ is closed. For $(x,y)\in K$, [F9] and [F10] give $d_2((x,y),(0,0))^2=\|x\|_2^2+\|y\|_2^2\le R^2+(\|c\|_2+1)^2$, so $K$ is bounded. By [F4], $K$ is compact. By [F5], $f|_K$ is uniformly continuous. For any $\gamma>0$, choose $0<\delta\le1$ such that points of $K$ at distance less than $\delta$ have $f$-values differing by less than $\gamma$. By [F8], on $\{\|X_n\|_2\le R,\ \|Y_n-c\|_2\le\delta/2\}$ both pair values lie in $K$, and their Euclidean distance is at most $\delta/2$. Therefore
$$|E_nf(X_n,Y_n)-E_nf(X_n,c)|\le\gamma+2\|f\|_\infty\bigl(P_n(\|X_n\|_2>R)+P_n(\|Y_n-c\|_2>\delta/2)\bigr).$$
By [F2], the second tail tends to zero. Taking the limiting upper bound, then letting $\gamma$ and $\eta$ decrease to zero, proves that the expectation difference tends to zero.

By [F7], $X_n\Rightarrow X$ means weak convergence of its laws. The function $x\mapsto f(x,c)$ is bounded and continuous, so [F3] gives $E_nf(X_n,c)\to E f(X,c)$. Together with step 1.2, bounded-continuous-test convergence gives $(X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow(X,c)$.
The map $h$ is continuous everywhere, hence measurable with empty discontinuity set. Apply [F6] to step 2.1 to obtain $h(X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow h(X,c)$.

Statement includes d=k=m=1 and any scalar c, including1. Taking X_n≡1 and Y_n≡c gives the constant joint limiting vector (1,c), within the same bounded-continuous-test proof.

citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

For real random variables $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ on one probability space, define
$$S_0=0,\qquad S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k,\qquad \overline X_n=S_n/n\quad(n\ge1).$$
For a triangular array with finite row length $r_n\ge0$, write $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{r_n}X_{n,k}$. An empty row has sum zero. These are finite sums in [[def-finite-sum]], with its index shifted by one. Each sum and each sample mean is a real random variable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]] and [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. No independence, common law, or integrability is implicit.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

If $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ are IID real random variables and $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, then, with $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$ and $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|\longrightarrow0.$$
Consequently $S_n/n\to\mu$ in probability.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric model on a statistical experiment, and let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T$ be an estimand whose target set $\mathcal T$ is equipped with a metric $d$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]], [[def-metric-space]]). For $n\ge1$, the IID sample-size-$n$ experiment has sample space $\mathcal X^n$, product sigma-algebra $\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$, and sampling law $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $\theta$ ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product law is defined recursively from $P_\theta$; each factor is a probability measure and hence sigma-finite, so the finite product theorem supplies its existence, rectangle formula, and uniqueness ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).

A **nonrandomized estimator sequence** of $\psi$ is a sequence of measurable maps, in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]],
$$T_n:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\mathcal T,\mathcal B(\mathcal T)),\qquad n\ge1,$$
where $\mathcal B(\mathcal T)$ is the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets of the metric $d$, that is, the Borel sigma-algebra of its metric topology ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Its sampling distribution at $\theta$ and sample size $n$ is the pushforward of $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$ by $T_n$.

This definition fixes IID repeated sampling and data-measurable estimators. It imposes no measurability on the parameter map $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ or on $\psi$.

Let $(T_n)$ be an estimator sequence of an estimand $\psi$ with metric target $(\mathcal T,d)$, and fix $\theta\in\Theta$. The sequence is **consistent in probability at $\theta$** if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_\theta^{\otimes n}\bigl(\{x\in\mathcal X^n:d(T_n(x),\psi(\theta))>\varepsilon\}\bigr)\longrightarrow0.$$

The error event is measurable: by the triangle inequality, $t\mapsto d(t,\psi(\theta))$ is continuous, so its strict superlevel set at $\varepsilon$ is open in the target metric topology and hence Borel; its preimage under $T_n$ is measurable.

The consistency is **pointwise** because $\theta$ is fixed before the limit. It does not assert uniform convergence over $\Theta$ ([[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]]).

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

1. $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-metric-space]]); it is
   called the **usual metric** of $\mathbb{R}$.

derivations.claim: The experiment and model specify P_θ. Each coordinate projection on R^n is measurable because its inverse image of a Borel set is a product cylinder in the product sigma-algebra; arithmetic measurability then makes T_n measurable into the Borel target. T_n is the sample mean of F2. IID and the joint-law theorem identify the law of (X_1,...,X_n) with P_θ^⊗n. Change of variables gives E_θX_1=∫x dP_θ=μ(θ), the estimand.
The hypotheses of [F4] hold for this IID sequence, so $\overline X_n\to\mathbb E_\theta X_1=\mu(\theta)$ in probability on its given common probability space.

For each $n$, step 1.1 identifies the joint data law with $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$; applying the same measurable sample-mean map therefore gives exactly the error probabilities in [F6] for the absolute-value metric [F14]. Step 1.2 makes those probabilities tend to zero for every $\varepsilon>0$, which is consistency at $\theta$. No infinite-product extension is constructed or needed.

boundaries.evidence: Statement defines Tn=n^−1∑_{i=1}^n xi on positive IID sample sizes; n=0 is outside the stated sequence. A fixed θ and its law are supplied, so an empty parameter family has no instance.
Statement allows mean zero and constant-zero observations; step 1.2 Khinchin convergence then gives Tn=0 exactly, without a positive-variance requirement.
Step 1.1 defines T1(x1)=x1 and identifies its one-coordinate law Pθ; consistency is the sequence limit, not an assertion of zero error at n=1.
Statement includes every point-mass Pθ=δa with finite a; step 1.1 gives E X1=a and every finite average equals a.
Statement is pointwise at any fixed θ satisfying Eθ|X1|<∞ and assumes no open parameter set; step 2.1 works for any such θ including a model endpoint.

Statement explicitly supplies the IID sequence on a common probability space; step 2.1 uses its finite product joint laws and does not construct an infinite product or select parameter-dependent sequences.

boundaries.reason: The conclusion is consistency from IID integrability; it does not assert an iff involving the mean moment premise.
The theorem does not infer IID sampling or integrability from consistency of a sequence of sample means.

Fixed-theta IID infinite sequence is explicitly supplied, absolute first moment is finite, and expectation change of variables identifies its mean. Coordinate cylinder preimages and finite arithmetic give estimator measurability. Khinchin gives convergence on the supplied common space and product joint laws transfer the exact error probabilities to each finite experiment.
