citations.quote:
For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric model on a statistical experiment, and let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T$ be an estimand whose target set $\mathcal T$ is equipped with a metric $d$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]], [[def-metric-space]]). For $n\ge1$, the IID sample-size-$n$ experiment has sample space $\mathcal X^n$, product sigma-algebra $\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$, and sampling law $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $\theta$ ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product law is defined recursively from $P_\theta$; each factor is a probability measure and hence sigma-finite, so the finite product theorem supplies its existence, rectangle formula, and uniqueness ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).

A **nonrandomized estimator sequence** of $\psi$ is a sequence of measurable maps, in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]],
$$T_n:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\mathcal T,\mathcal B(\mathcal T)),\qquad n\ge1,$$
where $\mathcal B(\mathcal T)$ is the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets of the metric $d$, that is, the Borel sigma-algebra of its metric topology ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Its sampling distribution at $\theta$ and sample size $n$ is the pushforward of $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$ by $T_n$.

This definition fixes IID repeated sampling and data-measurable estimators. It imposes no measurability on the parameter map $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ or on $\psi$.

Let $(T_n)$ be an estimator sequence of an estimand $\psi$ with metric target $(\mathcal T,d)$, and fix $\theta\in\Theta$. The sequence is **consistent in probability at $\theta$** if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_\theta^{\otimes n}\bigl(\{x\in\mathcal X^n:d(T_n(x),\psi(\theta))>\varepsilon\}\bigr)\longrightarrow0.$$

The error event is measurable: by the triangle inequality, $t\mapsto d(t,\psi(\theta))$ is continuous, so its strict superlevel set at $\varepsilon$ is open in the target metric topology and hence Borel; its preimage under $T_n$ is measurable.

The consistency is **pointwise** because $\theta$ is fixed before the limit. It does not assert uniform convergence over $\Theta$ ([[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open and closed sets
as in [[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]]. Then:

1. **Balls are open.** $B(x,r)$ is open, for every $x \in X$ and every $r > 0$.
2. **Arbitrary unions.** If $\mathcal{U}$ is any collection of open subsets of
   $X$, then $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$ is open.
3. **Finite intersections.** If $n \ge 1$ and $U_0, \dots, U_{n-1}$ are open,
   then $U_0 \cap \dots \cap U_{n-1}$ is open.
4. **Closed balls are closed.** $\bar B(x,r)$ is closed, for every $x \in X$ and
   every $r > 0$.

Together with the fact that $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open, recorded already in
[[def-metric-topology]], claims 2 and 3 say that $\mathcal{T}_d$ has exactly the
closure properties that the word *topology* names.

derivations.claim: By [F4], nonidentifiability supplies $\theta_0,\theta_1\in\Theta$ with $\theta_0\sim\theta_1$ and $\psi(\theta_0)\ne\psi(\theta_1)$. Fix this pair.

Fix $n\ge1$. By [F1], the observation laws in the model are $P_\theta$. Measurable rectangles in $\mathcal X^n$ form a $\pi$-system generating $\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$ by [F7]. For every rectangle $A_1\times\cdots\times A_n$, [F8] and [F2] give $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}(A_1\times\cdots\times A_n)=\prod_{j=1}^nP_{\theta_0}(A_j)=\prod_{j=1}^nP_{\theta_1}(A_j)=P_{\theta_1}^{\otimes n}(A_1\times\cdots\times A_n)$. The full space is itself a rectangle and is an increasing exhaustion of finite mass one. Applying [F9] shows $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}=P_{\theta_1}^{\otimes n}$ on all of $\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$.

Put $\Delta=d(\psi(\theta_0),\psi(\theta_1))>0$ and $r=\Delta/3$. The two closed target balls $C_i=\{t\in\mathcal T:d(t,\psi(\theta_i))\le r\}$ are disjoint: a point in both would give $\Delta\le2r<\Delta$ by [F10].

Suppose, for contradiction, that the estimator sequence is consistent at both parameters. For $i\in\{0,1\}$ let $E_{i,n}=T_n^{-1}(C_i)$. These events are measurable because each $C_i$ is closed by [F13] and Borel by [F12], while $T_n$ is measurable by [F5] and preimages of Borel sets are measurable by [F11]. By [F6], $P_{\theta_i}^{\otimes n}(E_{i,n})\to1$ for each $i$.

For each $n$, step 2.1 gives one common sample law for both probabilities, and step 2.2 gives disjoint events, so their probabilities sum to at most one. Step 3.1 says both probabilities tend to one, so their sum tends to two, a contradiction. Therefore the estimator sequence cannot be consistent at both parameters.

boundaries.evidence: Statement nonidentifiability premise supplies an actual pair θ0,θ1 with distinct target values, fixed in step 1.1. An empty parameter set cannot satisfy that premise; every positive finite sample law used in step 2.1 is a probability law.
Steps 2.2–3.1 require only positive distance between distinct targets, including if one target is zero.

Statement cannot have the nonidentifiability premise with only one parameter, because a parameter is observationally equivalent to itself and has one target value. A one-dimensional metric target R with two different values is allowed by the proof.
The identical-law pair is the central hypothesis in the Statement.
Proof step 2.2 uses closed balls of radius Δ/3 including their boundaries; 2Δ/3<Δ keeps them disjoint. Step 3.1 consistency uses their complements as strict error events at this positive radius.
Step 1.1 fixes one existential witness pair and makes no family of choices.

boundaries.reason: Statement supplies a necessary obstruction: nonidentifiability produces a pair where simultaneous consistency is impossible. It does not assert that this pairwise impossibility characterizes nonidentifiability.
Statement gives no converse that identifiability guarantees a consistent estimator sequence; its proof only contradicts two disjoint high-probability target events under equal data laws.

risk_review.notes: Read all six proof steps and fourteen direct dependencies. Negating identifiability supplies one equivalent pair with unequal targets, requiring only finite existential instantiation. Product measures agree on generating rectangles with full-space finite exhaustion, so all finite laws coincide. The metric axioms imply nonnegativity immediately (0=d(x,x)≤2d(x,y)), and separation gives Delta>0. Closed balls of radius Delta/3 are Borel and disjoint; consistency for strict >r tails gives each complementary event probability tending to one under the same law, contradicting a sum ≤1. Empty or singleton parameter sets cannot meet nonidentifiability; no converse or AC asserted.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

Random elements $X_n,X$ with values in the same metric space **converge in distribution**, written $X_n\Rightarrow X$, if their laws from [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] satisfy $P_{X_n}\Rightarrow P_X$ in [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]. They may be defined on different probability spaces. The definition specifies only their marginal laws.

Let $d\ge1$ be fixed, and equip $\mathbb R^d$ with the Borel sigma-algebra generated by its Euclidean open sets. Let $Z_n$ be measurable random elements of this Borel space, not necessarily defined on a common probability space, and let $
u$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$. The sequence $(Z_n)$ has **asymptotic distribution** $
u$ if its laws converge weakly to $
u$; equivalently, $Z_n\Rightarrow Z$ for any random vector $Z$ with law $
u$ ([[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]], [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]).

For an estimator, any centering or scaling, such as $r_n(T_n-\psi(	heta))$, is part of the sequence whose asymptotic distribution is being specified; it is not implicit in the term. Weak convergence alone does not assert convergence of moments.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: Set $\Omega_n=\{0,1\}$, $\mathcal A_n=\mathcal P(\Omega_n)$, $P_n(\{1\})=1/n$, and $P_n(\{0\})=1-1/n$. These masses are nonnegative and sum to one. Since the space has two points, every disjoint sequence of subsets has at most two nonempty members; the mass formula is countably additive and gives zero to the empty set by [F3]. Thus [F1], [F2], and [F4] make this a probability space for each $n$. The map $X_n(0)=0$, $X_n(1)=n$ is measurable by [F5], hence a real random variable by [F6].
For any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, once $n>\varepsilon$ the event $\{|X_n|>\varepsilon\}$ is exactly $\{1\}$, so $P_n(|X_n|>\varepsilon)=1/n\to0$. Therefore $X_n=o_P(1)$ by [F7].

For bounded continuous f, put M=||f||∞ and g=f+M. The pushforward law P_{X_n} and δ_0 are probabilities. Since |f|≤M and 0≤g≤2M, every nonnegative simple minorant has simple integral at most the corresponding constant times the total mass by F3, F4 and F12; taking the nonnegative-integral suprema gives finite absolute integrals. Linearity therefore applies. Change of variables and finite simple integrals compute the shifted test-integral difference as |g(n)-g(0)|/n≤2M/n, proving weak convergence and the asymptotic-distribution claim.

The nonnegative simple-integral formula [F11]–[F12] gives $\mathbb E X_n=(1/n)n+(1-1/n)0=1$ for every $n$, while the limit variable $0$ has expectation $0$. For the finite check $n=2$, $P_2(X_2=2)=1/2$ and $\mathbb E X_2=1$, confirming the stated mass and expectation formulas.

boundaries.evidence: Example has n≥1 and proof step 1.1 constructs Ω_n={0,1}, a nonempty two-point sample space with normalized weights. Probability-zero singleton mass at n=1 does not remove the outcome from that fixed carrier.
Steps 2.1–2.2 show convergence to the constant zero and its point-mass law.
Example at n=1 gives mass1 to X_1=1 and mass0 to X_1=0; proof step 3.1 still gives E X_1=1. Degeneracy of this first marginal does not change the n→∞ limit at zero.
Example and Step 2.2 identify the limit law as δ₀.
Proof step 2.1 computes strict tail |X_n|>ε once n>ε; at ε=n the outlier is excluded by strictness. The endpoint weight1−1/n=0 at n=1 remains a normalized law in step 1.1.
Step 1.1 constructs the finite two-point spaces explicitly.

boundaries.reason: Example directly computes X_n=o_P(1), weak limitδ0 and constant expectations1 to refute expectation convergence from weak convergence. It is not a forward characterization of all rare-outlier sequences.
Example does not assert every failure of moment convergence has these masses or that the absence of moment convergence implies a δ0 weak limit; it supplies one explicit witness.

risk_review.notes: Read all four verification steps and fifteen direct suppliers. Two-point masses are nonnegative, sum to one, and give countable additivity, including n=1 with a zero-mass point. Measurability follows from the power set. For fixed epsilon the strict tail is 1/n eventually. $$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric model on a statistical experiment, and let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T$ be an estimand whose target set $\mathcal T$ is equipped with a metric $d$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]], [[def-metric-space]]). For $n\ge1$, the IID sample-size-$n$ experiment has sample space $\mathcal X^n$, product sigma-algebra $\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$, and sampling law $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $\theta$ ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product law is defined recursively from $P_\theta$; each factor is a probability measure and hence sigma-finite, so the finite product theorem supplies its existence, rectangle formula, and uniqueness ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).

A **nonrandomized estimator sequence** of $\psi$ is a sequence of measurable maps, in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]],
$$T_n:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\mathcal T,\mathcal B(\mathcal T)),\qquad n\ge1,$$
where $\mathcal B(\mathcal T)$ is the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets of the metric $d$, that is, the Borel sigma-algebra of its metric topology ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Its sampling distribution at $\theta$ and sample size $n$ is the pushforward of $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$ by $T_n$.

This definition fixes IID repeated sampling and data-measurable estimators. It imposes no measurability on the parameter map $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ or on $\psi$.

For real random variables $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ on one probability space, define
$$S_0=0,\qquad S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k,\qquad \overline X_n=S_n/n\quad(n\ge1).$$
For a triangular array with finite row length $r_n\ge0$, write $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{r_n}X_{n,k}$. An empty row has sum zero. These are finite sums in [[def-finite-sum]], with its index shifted by one. Each sum and each sample mean is a real random variable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]] and [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. No independence, common law, or integrability is implicit.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be IID square-integrable real random variables, with $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$. For $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|^2=\sigma^2/n,$$
and $S_n/n\to\mu$ in $L^2$ and in probability. Also $\mathbb P(|S_n/n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon>0$.

Let $\mathcal X=\mathbb R$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $\mathsf P$ be a parametric statistical experiment on $\mathcal X$. Define the mean estimand by $\mu(\theta)=\int x\,P_\theta(dx)$ and suppose it is finite for every $\theta$. For a fixed $\theta$, suppose an IID sequence $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ with one-observation law $P_\theta$ is given and $\mathbb E_\theta|X_1|<\infty$. The sample-mean estimator $T_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ is consistent in probability for $\mu$ at $\theta$ in the IID sample-size experiments.

The assertion is pointwise in $\theta$. The existence of a common probability space carrying the IID sequence is part of the hypothesis.

Let $(T_n)$ be an estimator sequence of an estimand $\psi$ with metric target $(\mathcal T,d)$, and fix $\theta\in\Theta$. The sequence is **consistent in probability at $\theta$** if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_\theta^{\otimes n}\bigl(\{x\in\mathcal X^n:d(T_n(x),\psi(\theta))>\varepsilon\}\bigr)\longrightarrow0.$$

The error event is measurable: by the triangle inequality, $t\mapsto d(t,\psi(\theta))$ is continuous, so its strict superlevel set at $\varepsilon$ is open in the target metric topology and hence Borel; its preimage under $T_n$ is measurable.

The consistency is **pointwise** because $\theta$ is fixed before the limit. It does not assert uniform convergence over $\Theta$ ([[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: The power set of $\{0,1\}$ is a sigma-algebra by [F1], so it defines a measurable space by [F2]. Because $0\le p\le1$, the two singleton masses are nonnegative and sum to one. For any pairwise disjoint sequence of subsets, each of $0$ and $1$ occurs in at most one set, so the mass formula is countably additive and gives zero to the empty set by [F3]. Thus $P_p$ is a probability measure by [F4], and the family is a statistical experiment with model map $p\mapsto P_p$ and target $\psi(p)=p$ by [F5, F6, F7].
For $X\sim P_p$, $X=1_{\{1\}}$ and $X^2=X$, so [F12] gives $\mathbb E_pX=p$ and $\mathbb E_pX^2=p$. By [F13], $\operatorname{Var}_p(X)=p-p^2=p(1-p)$, which is finite for all $p\in[0,1]$.

The coordinate projections are measurable by F17 and arithmetic measurability makes T_n measurable by F18. The supplied common sequence is IID, and F11 identifies its first-n joint law with P_p^⊗n. Applying F14 with variance p(1-p) from step 1.2 and transferring through this joint-law identity gives the finite-sample bound; p(1-p)=1/4-(p-1/2)^2≤1/4 yields the uniform bound.

The bound in step 2.1 tends to zero, so F16 gives consistency; it also agrees with F15. By the product rectangle formula in F8 and the joint-law identity F11, the endpoint product laws are concentrated on the all-zero or all-one sample. For n=2 and p=1/2 the same formula gives mass 1/4 to each ordered pair, so the error probability at ε=1/2 is 1/2, attaining the bound.

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

1. $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-metric-space]]); it is
   called the **usual metric** of $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric model on a statistical experiment, and let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T$ be an estimand whose target set $\mathcal T$ is equipped with a metric $d$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]], [[def-metric-space]]). For $n\ge1$, the IID sample-size-$n$ experiment has sample space $\mathcal X^n$, product sigma-algebra $\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$, and sampling law $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $\theta$ ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product law is defined recursively from $P_\theta$; each factor is a probability measure and hence sigma-finite, so the finite product theorem supplies its existence, rectangle formula, and uniqueness ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).

A **nonrandomized estimator sequence** of $\psi$ is a sequence of measurable maps, in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]],
$$T_n:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\mathcal T,\mathcal B(\mathcal T)),\qquad n\ge1,$$
where $\mathcal B(\mathcal T)$ is the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets of the metric $d$, that is, the Borel sigma-algebra of its metric topology ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Its sampling distribution at $\theta$ and sample size $n$ is the pushforward of $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$ by $T_n$.

This definition fixes IID repeated sampling and data-measurable estimators. It imposes no measurability on the parameter map $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ or on $\psi$.

Let $(T_n)$ be an estimator sequence of an estimand $\psi$ with metric target $(\mathcal T,d)$, and fix $\theta\in\Theta$. The sequence is **consistent in probability at $\theta$** if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_\theta^{\otimes n}\bigl(\{x\in\mathcal X^n:d(T_n(x),\psi(\theta))>\varepsilon\}\bigr)\longrightarrow0.$$

The error event is measurable: by the triangle inequality, $t\mapsto d(t,\psi(\theta))$ is continuous, so its strict superlevel set at $\varepsilon$ is open in the target metric topology and hence Borel; its preimage under $T_n$ is measurable.

The consistency is **pointwise** because $\theta$ is fixed before the limit. It does not assert uniform convergence over $\Theta$ ([[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]]).

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric statistical model, let $\psi:\Theta\to(\mathcal T,d)$ be a metric-valued estimand, and let $(T_n)$ be a nonrandomized estimator sequence for IID samples from this model. If $\psi$ is not identifiable, then there is a pair of observationally equivalent parameters with distinct target values, and no estimator sequence is consistent in probability at both parameters.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

derivations.claim: The power set on $\mathcal X$ is a sigma-algebra by [F1], so $(\mathcal X,\mathcal P(\mathcal X))$ is a measurable space by [F2]. For every $u\in[0,1]$, the two singleton masses $u$ and $1-u$ are nonnegative and sum to one. Any disjoint sequence of subsets of $\mathcal X$ has at most two nonempty members, so the assignment is countably additive and gives zero to the empty set by [F3]; hence each $P_{(u,v)}$ is a probability measure by [F4]. This defines the experiment and model in [F5]–[F6], and $\psi$ is the target in [F7].

At $\theta_0=(1/2,0)$ and $\theta_1=(1/2,1)$, both laws assign probability $1/2$ to each singleton and therefore are equal as measures on the power set. The target values are $0$ and $1$, whose distance is $1>0$. Thus [F8] makes the parameters observationally equivalent, while [F7] and [F9] show the target is not identifiable.

By [F11]–[F12], estimators are measurable maps on the IID sample spaces and consistency is pointwise under those sample laws. Apply [F13] to the pair from step 1.2: no estimator sequence is consistent in probability at both $\theta_0$ and $\theta_1$. For the finite check at sample size $n=2$, [F14] gives mass $(1/2)^2=1/4$ to each ordered pair under both product laws, confirming that the observation distributions remain identical.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X\in L^1(P)$, if $X$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[X\mid\mathcal G]=X$. If $P(\{X\in B\}\cap A)=P(X\in B)P(A)$ for every real Borel $B$ and $A\in\mathcal G$, then $E[X\mid\mathcal G]=EX$ almost surely.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Assume AC. Let $D\in L^1$ satisfy $\mathbb E[D\mid\mathcal G]=0$ almost surely. Let $A,B$ be finite $\mathcal G$-measurable random variables such that $A\le D\le B$ and $B-A\le c$ almost surely for a deterministic $c\ge0$. Then for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E[e^{\lambda D}\mid\mathcal G]\le e^{\lambda^2c^2/8}\quad\text{a.s.}$$

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. Then the closed bounded interval
$[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) is compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]): every family of
open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

The proof is by repeated bisection. Supposing some open cover admits no finite
subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $f$ is **bounded on $K$**: there is a real
$M \ge 0$ with

$$|f(x)| \le M \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, $f[K]$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-bounded-set]]).

**The hypothesis is compactness of $K$, not of $A$**, and it cannot be relaxed
to boundedness of $K$ or to closedness of $K$ alone: the identity is unbounded
on the closed set $[0,\infty)$, and $x \mapsto 1/x$ is unbounded on the bounded
set $(0,1)$. The general statement of that is
[[thm-compactness-is-necessary-for-evt-and-uniform-continuity]], later on this
page.

derivations.claim: Set $\mathcal F_0=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$, $\mathcal F_i=\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_i)$, $D_i=X_i-\mathbb E X_i$, and $c_i=b_i-a_i$. By [F13], $D_i$ is $\mathcal F_i$-measurable. By [F1] and [F2], $X_i$ is independent of $\mathcal F_{i-1}$; [F3] gives $\mathbb E[X_i\mid\mathcal F_{i-1}]=\mathbb E X_i$, and conditional linearity and preservation of constants in [F6] therefore give $\mathbb E[D_i\mid\mathcal F_{i-1}]=0$ almost surely.

By [F4], $a_i\le\mathbb E X_i\le b_i$. Therefore $D_i$ lies almost surely in the finite interval $[a_i-\mathbb E X_i,b_i-\mathbb E X_i]$, whose endpoints are $\mathcal F_{i-1}$-measurable, contain $0$, and have width $c_i$; in particular $|D_i|\le c_i$.
Apply [F5] to each $D_i$ and the filtration $\mathcal F_{i-1}$ from step 1.1. For every real $\lambda$, $\mathbb E[e^{\lambda D_i}\mid\mathcal F_{i-1}]\le e^{\lambda^2c_i^2/8}$ almost surely.

Let $S_k=\sum_{i=1}^kD_i$ and $S_0=0$. Step 1.2 gives $|D_i|\le c_i$, hence $S_{k-1}\in[-C,C]$ for $C:=\sum_{i<k}c_i$. This closed bounded interval is compact by [F11], and $x\mapsto e^{\lambda x}$ is continuous by [F10] and continuity of scalar multiplication, so [F12] makes $e^{\lambda S_{k-1}}$ bounded. Also $x\mapsto e^{\lambda x}$ is Borel: its open-set preimages are open, and the class of Borel sets whose preimages are Borel is a sigma-algebra containing the opens, hence contains the Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For each Borel $B$, the preimage of $B$ under $e^{\lambda S_{k-1}}$ is $S_{k-1}^{-1}( (x\mapsto e^{\lambda x})^{-1}(B))$, so this bounded factor is $\mathcal F_{k-1}$-measurable. By the addition formula in [F10], $e^{\lambda S_k}=e^{\lambda S_{k-1}}e^{\lambda D_k}$; conditional expectation preservation [F6], taking out the known factor [F7], and step 2.1 give $\mathbb E e^{\lambda S_k}\le e^{\lambda^2c_k^2/8}\mathbb E e^{\lambda S_{k-1}}$. Finite induction gives $\mathbb E e^{\lambda S_n}\le e^{\lambda^2V/8}$.

If $V=0$, every $c_i=0$, so each $X_i=a_i=b_i$ almost surely and $S=0$ almost surely. If $V>0$ and $\lambda>0$, then $e^{\lambda S}$ is nonnegative and $S\ge t$ implies $e^{\lambda S}\ge e^{\lambda t}>0$ by [F10]. Markov [F8] and step 3.1 give $\mathbb P(S\ge t)\le e^{\lambda^2V/8}/e^{\lambda t}=\exp(-\lambda t+\lambda^2V/8)$, using the reciprocal and addition formulas in [F10]. Choosing $\lambda=4t/V$ gives $\mathbb P(S\ge t)\le e^{-2t^2/V}$.

If $V>0$, substitute $-\lambda$ in the all-real MGF bound from step 3.1. Since $e^{-\lambda S}$ is nonnegative and $S\le-t$ implies $e^{-\lambda S}\ge e^{\lambda t}>0$ by [F10], Markov [F8] gives $\mathbb P(S\le-t)\le e^{\lambda^2V/8}/e^{\lambda t}$; choosing $\lambda=4t/V$ yields $e^{-2t^2/V}$. The finite union bound [F9] combines the two tails; step 4.1 already handles $V=0$. This lower-tail argument uses the same original variables and does not assert independence of their negatives.

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

derivations.claim: Let $v_i=\mathbb E[X_i^2]$. If $v=0$, then every $v_i=0$ because $v_i\ge0$. By [F6], $X_i^2=0$ almost surely for every $i$, so the finite sum is $0$ almost surely and the stated tail probability is $0$.

Suppose $v>0$. If $b=0$, every $X_i=0$ almost surely and $v=0$, a contradiction; hence $b>0$. For each fixed real $\theta$, $g_\theta(x)=e^{\theta x}$ is continuous: when $\theta\ne0$, continuity of $x\mapsto\theta x$ follows from $|\theta x-\theta y|=|\theta||x-y|$, and continuity of its composition with $e^x$ follows from [F10]; when $\theta=0$ it is constant. Thus $g_\theta$ is Borel: the Borel sets whose inverse images under $g_\theta$ are Borel form a sigma-algebra containing every open set, hence contain the sigma-algebra generated by opens ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For each Borel $B$, $\{g_\theta(X_i)\in B\}=X_i^{-1}(g_\theta^{-1}(B))$ is measurable. Now fix $i$ and $\lambda$ with $0<|\lambda|<3/b$. For $N\ge2$, the exponential series tail on $[-b,b]$ is uniformly bounded by $r_N=\sum_{k>N}(|\lambda|b)^k/k!\to0$. Each partial sum at $X_i$ is integrable; the uniform bound and [F9] give $|\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X_i}]-\mathbb E[\sum_{k=0}^N(\lambda X_i)^k/k!]|\le r_N$, so expectation passes to the series limit. Centering removes the linear term, and for every $k\ge2$, $|\mathbb E[X_i^k]|\le b^{k-2}v_i$ by [F1] and monotonicity. Also $k!\ge2\cdot3^{k-2}$ for $k\ge2$: equality holds at $k=2,3$, and each subsequent factorial factor is at least $3$. Hence the geometric-series bound and $1+x\le e^x$ from [F5] give $\mathbb E e^{\lambda X_i}\le1+\lambda^2v_i/[2(1-|\lambda|b/3)]\le\exp(\lambda^2v_i/[2(1-|\lambda|b/3)])$.

Let $S=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$, a measurable real random variable by [F11]. By the addition formula [F10], $e^{\lambda S}=\prod_i e^{\lambda X_i}$; independence [F8] and factorization [F2], applied to the nonnegative Borel functions established in step 1.2, give $\mathbb E e^{\lambda S}\le\exp(\lambda^2v/[2(1-\lambda b/3)])$ for $0<\lambda<3/b$. Since $e^x$ is positive and increasing [F10], $S\ge t$ implies $e^{\lambda S}\ge e^{\lambda t}>0$, so [F3] and the reciprocal and addition formulas in [F10] give $\mathbb P(S\ge t)\le\exp(-\lambda t+\lambda^2v/[2(1-\lambda b/3)])$. Choose $\lambda=t/(v+bt/3)$; then $\lambda b/3<1$ and direct simplification gives $\mathbb P(S\ge t)\le\exp(-t^2/[2(v+bt/3)])$.

For $0<\lambda<3/b$, the bound in step 1.2 also holds at parameter $-\lambda$. By [F10], $e^{-\lambda S}=\prod_i e^{-\lambda X_i}$; the original variables remain independent by [F8], and [F2] factors these nonnegative Borel functions, giving $\mathbb E e^{-\lambda S}\le\exp(\lambda^2v/[2(1-\lambda b/3)])$. Since $S\le-t$ implies $e^{-\lambda S}\ge e^{\lambda t}>0$, Markov [F3] and the same optimizing choice as in step 2.1 yield $\mathbb P(S\le-t)\le\exp(-t^2/[2(v+bt/3)])$. By [F7], the two one-sided bounds imply the displayed two-sided bound without asserting independence of the transformed variables $-X_i$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

For every integer $n\ge1$ and every $r\ge0$, put $\overline B_n(0,r):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, extending the positive-radius notation of [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] to $r=0$. This closed Euclidean ball is Jordan measurable; write its content as $V_n(r)$. One has $V_1(r)=2r$. For $n\ge2$ and $r\ge0$, $V_n(r)=V_{n-1}(1)\int_{-r}^{r}(r^2-t^2)^{(n-1)/2}\,dt$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be linear, with standard matrix $A$. For every bounded Jordan set $E$, the image $T(E)$ is a bounded Jordan set and
$$\operatorname{cont}(T(E))=|\det A|\operatorname{cont}(E).$$
In particular, a singular linear image has content zero.

Let $n\ge1$. For every bounded $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$, the translates $E+a$ and $E$ have equal Jordan inner and outer contents. Consequently, $E$ is Jordan measurable if and only if $E+a$ is Jordan measurable, and in that case

$$\operatorname{cont}(E+a)=\operatorname{cont}(E).$$

Here translation is as in [[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]].

If bounded Jordan measurable sets $E,F$ have $E\cap F$ of content zero, then
$$\operatorname{cont}(E\cup F)=\operatorname{cont}(E)+\operatorname{cont}(F).$$
In particular Jordan content is additive on disjoint finite families.

For bounded $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, in the metric sense of [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], its **Jordan outer content** is the infimum of $\sum_{r<q}\operatorname{vol}(R_r)$ over finite axis-parallel rectangle covers of $E$. Its **Jordan inner content** is the supremum of the same sums over finite families of rectangles contained in $E$ whose interiors are pairwise disjoint.

Metric boundedness always supplies a nondegenerate bounding rectangle. For
nonempty $E$, choose $x_0\in\mathbb R^m$ and $r>0$ with
$E\subseteq B(x_0,r)$. Since
$|x_j-(x_0)_j|\le d_\infty(x,x_0)\le d_2(x,x_0)<r$ for every coordinate
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]] clause 3, [[def-metric-ball]]), the nondegenerate box
$\prod_{j<m}[(x_0)_j-r,(x_0)_j+r]$ contains $E$. The empty set lies in
any fixed nondegenerate rectangle.

Thus the outer family is nonempty and the same bounding rectangle bounds the
inner sums; the empty family gives inner sum $0$. Refining all listed
endpoints into one grid and splitting the nested finite sums shows every
inscribed sum is at most every covering sum
([[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).
Completeness therefore supplies finite real extrema
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]],
[[lem-sup-unique]]).

The set is **Jordan measurable** when the contents agree, and their common value is its **Jordan content**. The empty set and every degenerate rectangle have content $0$.

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $r < s$
([[def-rat-order]]), with rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]].

1. **In the exponent.** If $a > 1$ then $a^{r} < a^{s}$; if $a = 1$ then $a^{r} = a^{s} = 1$; if $0 < a < 1$ then $a^{r} > a^{s}$.
2. **In the base.** If $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $r > 0$ and $0 < a < b$, then $a^{r} < b^{r}$; so $a \mapsto a^{r}$ is strictly increasing on $\{a \in \mathbb{R} : a > 0\}$.
3. **Comparison with $1$.** For rational $t > 0$: $a > 1$ implies $a^{t} > 1$, and $0 < a < 1$ implies $a^{t} < 1$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

derivations.claim: Put $V_d=\operatorname{cont}(\overline B_2(0,1))$. This number is finite by [F3] and positive by induction on $d$: $V_1=2$, and for $d\ge2$ set $\alpha=(d-1)/2>0$. On $[-1/2,1/2]$, $1-t^2\ge3/4$, so [F10] gives $(1-t^2)^\alpha\ge(3/4)^\alpha>0$; on all of $[-1,1]$ this integrand is nonnegative. By [F11], splitting the integral at $-1/2$ and $1/2$ and comparing the middle part with the constant $(3/4)^\alpha$ shows $\int_{-1}^{1}(1-t^2)^\alpha\,dt\ge(3/4)^\alpha>0$. The volume recursion [F3] then gives $V_d>0$ from $V_{d-1}>0$.

Let $E=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subseteq S^{d-1}$ have pairwise distances greater than $\epsilon$, and put $r=\epsilon/2$. The closed balls $\overline B_2(x_j,r)$ are pairwise disjoint: a point in two of them would, by the triangle inequality [F2], put the corresponding centers at distance at most $2r=\epsilon$, contrary to the separation. Each small ball lies in $\overline B_2(0,1+r)$, since $\|x_j\|_2=1$ and [F2] gives $\|y\|_2\le\|y-x_j\|_2+\|x_j\|_2\le r+1$.

By scaling and translation invariance [F4, F5], every small ball in step 1.2 has content $r^dV_d$ and the large ball has content $(1+r)^dV_d$. Finite additivity [F6] and monotonicity of outer content from [F7] give $Nr^dV_d\le(1+r)^dV_d$. Step 1.1 gives $V_d>0$, so cancellation and $r=\epsilon/2$ yield $N\le((1+r)/r)^d=(1+2/\epsilon)^d$. This also holds when $E$ is empty, for which $N=0$.

Choose an integer $M>(1+2/\epsilon)^d$ using [F8]. Let $K$ be the set of cardinalities of finite subsets of $S^{d-1}$ whose distinct points are more than $\epsilon$ apart. The first coordinate unit vector shows $K$ is nonempty, and step 2.1 shows every member of $K$ is at most $(1+2/\epsilon)^d<M$. Thus $K$ is a nonempty subset of $\{0,1,\ldots,M\}$; [F9] gives a largest member $k\in K$, attained by a finite set $\mathcal N$ by the definition of $K$.

If some $u\in S^{d-1}$ were farther than $\epsilon$ from every point of $\mathcal N$, adjoining $u$ would produce a finite set with pairwise distances greater than $\epsilon$ and cardinality $k+1$, contradicting maximality in step 3.1. Thus $\mathcal N$ is an $\epsilon$-net; step 2.1 gives its stated cardinality bound. This construction uses only a maximum in a finite set of possible cardinalities, not an axiom of choice.
