The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID random elements with law $P$. For a class $\mathcal F$ of measurable, integrable real-valued functions on $\mathcal X$, write

$$Pf:=\int f\,dP,\qquad P_nf:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(Z_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n(f):=\sqrt n\,(P_nf-Pf).$$

The map $f\mapsto P_nf-Pf$ is the centered empirical process, and $\mathbb G_n$ is its $\sqrt n$-scaled version. More generally, for independent processes $X_1(t),\ldots,X_n(t)$ whose marginal expectations are finite for each index $t\in T$, the centered process sum is

$$S_n(t):=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(X_i(t)-\mathbb E X_i(t)\bigr),\qquad t\in T.$$

On an auxiliary probability-space extension, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent signs, each taking $+1$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2$, independent of the observations. The empirical Rademacher process is

$$R_n(f):=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i),\qquad f\in\mathcal F.$$

The centered Rademacher process $\sum_i\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-Pf)$ is a distinct process; no equality between it and $R_n$ is part of this definition.

For a countable class of measurable functions, each displayed supremum of measurable sample paths is measurable. For an uncountable class, ordinary probability or expectation is used only when a specified countable subclass has the same supremum almost surely for the process in question; this is the separable-version convention used here. Otherwise state results using outer probability

$$P^*(A):=\inf\{P(B):A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$$

and, for a nonnegative possibly nonmeasurable random quantity $Y$, outer expectation

$$\mathbb E^*Y:=\inf\{\mathbb E U: U\text{ is measurable, nonnegative, and }U\ge Y\}.$$

In particular, measurability of every $f$ separately does not by itself make an uncountable supremum measurable.

For a class $\mathcal H$ of measurable real functions under a probability measure $Q$, an **envelope** $H$ means a nonnegative measurable function with $|h|\le H$ $Q$-almost surely for every $h\in\mathcal H$. Cauchy–Schwarz [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $QH\le\|H\|_{Q,2}<\infty$ when $H\in L^2(Q)$.

Let $(S,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable real-valued functions with a nonnegative measurable envelope $F$ satisfying $PF^2<\infty$. A class is **pointwise measurable** if it has a countable subclass $\mathcal F_0$ such that for each $f\in\mathcal F$ there is a sequence in $\mathcal F_0$ converging pointwise to $f$. Write $\mathbb G_n(f)=\sqrt n(P_nf-Pf)$ using [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]], and put

$$\rho_P(f,g)=\{P[(f-g)-P(f-g)]^2\}^{1/2}.$$

This is a pseudometric: distinct functions can have zero distance when their centered difference vanishes $P$-almost surely. The empirical process is **asymptotically equicontinuous in probability** with respect to $\rho_P$ if for every $\eta>0$,

$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\limsup_{n\to\infty}P^*\left(\sup_{f,g\in\mathcal F:\,\rho_P(f,g)<\delta}|\mathbb G_n(f)-\mathbb G_n(g)|>\eta\right)=0.$$

Here $P^*(A)=\inf\{P(B): A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$ is outer probability; bounded nonmeasurable functionals are handled by the corresponding outer expectation $E^*Y=\inf\{EY':Y'\text{ measurable and }Y'\ge Y\}$. For a pointwise-measurable class these conventions agree with ordinary probability whenever the displayed supremum is measurable.

Write $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$ for the bounded real-valued functions on the index set $\mathcal F$, with norm $\|z\|_{\mathcal F}=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|z(f)|$. The class is **$P$-Donsker** if $\mathbb G_n$, as a process in this space, converges weakly in the outer-expectation sense to a tight Borel law of a centered Gaussian process $\mathbb G_P$ with covariance

$$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbb G_P(f),\mathbb G_P(g))=P[(f-Pf)(g-Pg)].$$

Here outer weak convergence means $E^*H(\mathbb G_n)\to EH(\mathbb G_P)$ for every bounded uniformly continuous real function $H$ on $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$; the outer expectation is the infimum of expectations of measurable majorants. The law is tight in the sense of [[def-tight-family-of-probability-measures]]. Finite-dimensional convergence means weak convergence of the vector of process values at every finite list of indices, as in [[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]].

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty countable class of measurable real functions with a nonnegative measurable envelope $H$, so $|g|\le H$ $P$-almost everywhere for every $g\in\mathcal G$, and $0<\|H\|_{P,2}<\infty$. Use $\mathbb G_n(g)=\sqrt n(P_ng-Pg)$ as in [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]]. Suppose that for some integer $q_0\ge1$ there are nested finite partitions $\Pi_q$ of $\mathcal G$, for all $q\ge q_0$, with $m_q$ nonempty cells. For each cell $C\in\Pi_q$ choose a representative $\pi_q(C)\in C$ and define its pointwise oscillation

$$\Delta_{q,C}(x)=\sup_{g,h\in C}|g(x)-h(x)|.$$

Assume $\Delta_{q,C}$ is measurable, $0\le\Delta_{q,C}\le2H$ $P$-almost everywhere, and $\|\Delta_{q,C}\|_{P,2}\le2^{-q}\|H\|_{P,2}$. If $C'\in\Pi_{q+1}$ is contained in $C\in\Pi_q$, then $\Delta_{q+1,C'}\le\Delta_{q,C}$ pointwise by definition. Put

$$L_q=1+\log(2m_q),\qquad a_q=\frac{2^{-q}\|H\|_{P,2}}{\sqrt{L_{q+1}}},\qquad M_{\mathcal G}=\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\|g\|_{P,2}.$$

The refinement property gives $m_{q+1}\ge m_q$, so $a_q$ is nonincreasing.

There is a universal constant $C<\infty$ such that

$$\mathbb E\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}|\mathbb G_n(g)|\le C\left[(M_{\mathcal G}+2^{-q_0}\|H\|_{P,2})\sqrt{L_{q_0}}+\|H\|_{P,2}\sum_{q>q_0}2^{-q}\sqrt{L_q}+\sqrt n\,P\!\left(H\mathbf1_{\{H>\sqrt n a_{q_0}/2\}}\right)\right].$$

This is a local maximal estimate: the nested partitions and their oscillation bounds are hypotheses. Empirical-process notation uses [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]].

A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$, using the positive-base real-power convention of [[def-real-power]]. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

derivations.claim: Choose a countable pointwise-dense subclass $\mathcal F_0\subseteq\mathcal F$. For $\delta>0$, set $\mathcal H_\delta=\{(f-g)-P(f-g):f,g\in\mathcal F_0,\ \rho_P(f,g)\le\delta\}$. Every $h\in\mathcal H_\delta$ has $\|h\|_{P,2}\le\delta$ and is bounded in absolute value by $H:=2F+2PF$, with $\|H\|_{P,2}\le4\|F\|_{P,2}$.

If $f$ and $g$ lie in $L^2(P)$ brackets $[l_i,u_i]$ and $[l_j,u_j]$ of width at most $r\|F\|_{P,2}$, respectively, then $(f-g)-P(f-g)$ lies in the bracket $[l_i-u_j-P(u_i-l_j),\ u_i-l_j-P(l_i-u_j)].$ Its width is $w_i+w_j+P(w_i+w_j)$, where $w_i=u_i-l_i$ and $w_j=u_j-l_j$; Cauchy–Schwarz gives its $L^2(P)$ norm at most $2(\|w_i\|_{P,2}+\|w_j\|_{P,2})\le4r\|F\|_{P,2}$. Thus $N_{[]}(4r\|F\|_{P,2},\mathcal H_\delta,L^2(P))\le N_{[]}(r\|F\|_{P,2},\mathcal F,L^2(P))^2$.

Fix $0<\delta<\|H\|_{P,2}/2$ and choose $q_0\ge1$ with $\delta/2<2^{-q_0}\|H\|_{P,2}\le\delta$. For each $q\ge q_0$, take a finite bracketing cover of $\mathcal H_\delta$ at width $2^{-q}\|H\|_{P,2}$ and partition the class by assigning each function to the first bracket containing it. Refine these finite partitions cumulatively through level $q$; by [A1], the countable family of finite covers and their representatives can be selected. If $b_q$ is the unrefined level-$q$ count, step 1.2 gives $b_q\le N_{[]} (r_q\|F\|_{P,2},\mathcal F,L^2(P))^2$ for $r_q=2^{-q}\|H\|_{P,2}/(4\|F\|_{P,2})$, and the refined count satisfies $m_q\le\prod_{p=q_0}^q b_p$. Consequently, using $\sqrt{1+\sum x_p}\le1+\sum\sqrt{x_p}$ for $x_p\ge0$ and summing the resulting geometric weights, $\sum_{q\ge q_0}2^{-q}\sqrt{1+\log(2m_q)}\le C_1\int_0^{C_2\delta/\|F\|_{P,2}}\sqrt{1+\log N_{[]} (\epsilon\|F\|_{P,2},\mathcal F,L^2(P))}\,d\epsilon$ for universal constants $C_1,C_2$: the unrefined entropy terms at scale $r_q$ are bounded by the integrand on the adjacent dyadic interval $[r_q/2,r_q]$ by monotonicity of bracketing numbers, and cumulative refinement contributes only a geometric sum of earlier terms. The added $1$ contributes a geometric sum of order $2^{-q_0}$, which is also bounded by the displayed integral because its integrand is at least $1$. On each refined cell $C$, define $\Delta_{q,C}=\sup_{h,h'\in C}|h-h'|$ and choose $\pi_q(C)\in C$. Countability makes this pointwise supremum measurable; containment in a level-$q$ bracket gives $\Delta_{q,C}\le u-l$ $P$-almost everywhere, so it has the required $L^2(P)$ bound. Intersecting partitions makes these oscillations nonincreasing on child cells. Thus these partitions and widths satisfy the hypotheses of [F2] when the local maximal inequality is applied.

Apply [F2] to $\mathcal H_\delta$ with envelope $H$ and this nested partition. Its coarse term is at most $C\delta\sqrt{1+\log(2m_{q_0})}$, its dyadic tail is bounded by the right-hand side of step 2.1, and its final envelope-tail term tends to zero as $n\to\infty$ for this fixed $\delta$: for each fixed $a>0$, $\sqrt n P(H\mathbf1_{\{H>a\sqrt n\}})\le a^{-1}P(H^2\mathbf1_{\{H>a\sqrt n\}})\to0$ by [F4].

The entropy integral in the statement makes the integral in step 2.1 tend to zero with $\delta$. It also gives $\delta\sqrt{\log N_{[]} (c\delta\|F\|_{P,2},\mathcal F,L^2(P))}\to0$ for each fixed $c>0$: if $h(\epsilon)=\sqrt{\log N_{[]} (\epsilon\|F\|_{P,2},\mathcal F,L^2(P))}$, monotonicity yields $(\epsilon/2)h(\epsilon)\le\int_{\epsilon/2}^{\epsilon}h(u)\,du\to0$. Therefore step 3.1 implies $\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\limsup_n E\sup_{h\in\mathcal H_\delta}|\mathbb G_n(h)|=0$.

By [F5], Markov's inequality converts the expected-supremum limit in step 4.1 into asymptotic equicontinuity for pairs in $\mathcal F_0$. For arbitrary $f,g\in\mathcal F$, choose pointwise approximants $f_k,g_k\in\mathcal F_0$. The common envelope gives $L^1(P)$ convergence by [F4]; applying [F4] to $|f_k-f|^2\le4F^2$ and $|g_k-g|^2\le4F^2$ also gives $L^2(P)$ convergence. Pointwise convergence gives $P_nf_k\to P_nf$ and $P_ng_k\to P_ng$ for each fixed finite sample, so $\rho_P(f_k,g_k)\to\rho_P(f,g)$ and the empirical-process increment converges pointwise to the desired increment. Hence a pair with $\rho_P(f,g)<\delta/2$ is a limit of pairs from $\mathcal F_0$ with distance below $\delta$. The outer-probability modulus over $\mathcal F$ is therefore bounded by the countable-class modulus over $\mathcal F_0$ at radius $\delta$, proving the asserted asymptotic equicontinuity.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID random elements with law $P$. For a class $\mathcal F$ of measurable, integrable real-valued functions on $\mathcal X$, write

$$Pf:=\int f\,dP,\qquad P_nf:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(Z_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n(f):=\sqrt n\,(P_nf-Pf).$$

The map $f\mapsto P_nf-Pf$ is the centered empirical process, and $\mathbb G_n$ is its $\sqrt n$-scaled version. More generally, for independent processes $X_1(t),\ldots,X_n(t)$ whose marginal expectations are finite for each index $t\in T$, the centered process sum is

$$S_n(t):=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(X_i(t)-\mathbb E X_i(t)\bigr),\qquad t\in T.$$

On an auxiliary probability-space extension, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent signs, each taking $+1$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2$, independent of the observations. The empirical Rademacher process is

$$R_n(f):=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i),\qquad f\in\mathcal F.$$

The centered Rademacher process $\sum_i\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-Pf)$ is a distinct process; no equality between it and $R_n$ is part of this definition.

For a countable class of measurable functions, each displayed supremum of measurable sample paths is measurable. For an uncountable class, ordinary probability or expectation is used only when a specified countable subclass has the same supremum almost surely for the process in question; this is the separable-version convention used here. Otherwise state results using outer probability

$$P^*(A):=\inf\{P(B):A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$$

and, for a nonnegative possibly nonmeasurable random quantity $Y$, outer expectation

$$\mathbb E^*Y:=\inf\{\mathbb E U: U\text{ is measurable, nonnegative, and }U\ge Y\}.$$

In particular, measurability of every $f$ separately does not by itself make an uncountable supremum measurable.

A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$, using the positive-base real-power convention of [[def-real-power]]. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $d\ge1$ be fixed, and equip $\mathbb R^d$ with the Borel sigma-algebra generated by its Euclidean open sets. Let $Z_n$ be measurable random elements of this Borel space, not necessarily defined on a common probability space, and let $
u$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$. The sequence $(Z_n)$ has **asymptotic distribution** $
u$ if its laws converge weakly to $
u$; equivalently, $Z_n\Rightarrow Z$ for any random vector $Z$ with law $
u$ ([[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]], [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]).

For an estimator, any centering or scaling, such as $r_n(T_n-\psi(	heta))$, is part of the sequence whose asymptotic distribution is being specified; it is not implicit in the term. Weak convergence alone does not assert convergence of moments.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For any set $I$, standard-Borel coordinate spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)$, and consistent finite-dimensional laws $(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_I$ whose $F$-coordinate marginal is $\mu_F$ for each finite $F$.

Let $(T,d)$ be a nonempty pseudometric space that is totally bounded in the following sense: for every $r>0$ there is a finite set $E_r\subseteq T$ such that $T\subseteq\bigcup_{e\in E_r}\{t\in T:d(t,e)\le r\}$. Its diameter is $D:=\sup_{s,t\in T}d(s,t)<\infty$. For each $t\in T$, let $X_t$ be a real random variable. Assume the process is separable: a specified countable dense subset $T_0\subseteq T$, equipped with a fixed listing, has the property that the supremum of every process increment over $T$ equals its supremum over $T_0$ almost surely. Suppose all increments are centered and sub-Gaussian with their $d$-scale, meaning that for every $s,t\in T$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(X_s-X_t)\}\le\exp\{\lambda^2d(s,t)^2/2\}.$$

If

$$\int_0^D\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,T,d)}\,d\epsilon<\infty,$$

where $N(\epsilon,T,d)$ is the least number of closed $d$-balls of radius $\epsilon$ covering $T$ ([[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]]), then for every $t_0\in T$,

$$\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}|X_t-X_{t_0}|\le C\int_0^D\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,T,d)}\,d\epsilon$$

for a universal constant $C$. If $D=0$, the integral and the supremum are both zero.

For a class $\mathcal H$ of measurable real functions under a probability measure $Q$, an **envelope** $H$ means a nonnegative measurable function with $|h|\le H$ $Q$-almost surely for every $h\in\mathcal H$. Cauchy–Schwarz [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $QH\le\|H\|_{Q,2}<\infty$ when $H\in L^2(Q)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty pointwise-measurable class of measurable functions with a nonnegative envelope $F$ satisfying $PF^2<\infty$. Assume $0<\|F\|_{P,2}<\infty$ and

$$\int_0^1\sqrt{\log N_{[]}\bigl(\epsilon\|F\|_{P,2},\mathcal F,L^2(P)\bigr)}\,d\epsilon<\infty.$$

Use the empirical process $\mathbb G_n$ and semimetric $\rho_P$ from [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]] and [[def-donsker-class-and-asymptotic-equicontinuity]]. Then $\mathbb G_n$ is asymptotically equicontinuous in probability with respect to $\rho_P$.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for assertion 5 and the consequent
existence claim ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of all Cauchy sequences
in $X$ ([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]). Then:

1. For all $x = (x_n)$ and $y = (y_n)$ in $\mathcal{C}$ the real sequence
   $\big(d(x_n,y_n)\big)_n$ converges, so
   $$\rho(x,y) \;:=\; \lim_{n} d(x_n,y_n)$$
   is a single well-determined real ([[thm-cauchy-criterion-via-lub]],
   [[lem-limit-unique]]).
2. The relation $x \sim y :\Longleftrightarrow \rho(x,y) = 0$ is an equivalence
   relation on $\mathcal{C}$. Write $\widehat{X} := \mathcal{C}/\!\sim$ for the
   set of its classes and $[x]$ for the class of $x$.
3. $\widehat{d}\big([x],[y]\big) := \rho(x,y)$ does not depend on the chosen
   representatives, and $\widehat{d}$ is a metric on $\widehat{X}$.
4. The map $\iota : X \to \widehat{X}$ sending $p$ to the class of the constant
   sequence at $p$ is an isometric embedding with dense image
   ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]],
   [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).
5. $(\widehat{X}, \widehat{d})$ is complete.

Consequently $\big((\widehat{X},\widehat{d}), \iota\big)$ is a completion of
$(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-completion]]), and **every metric space has a
completion**.

**The notation is kept honest.** A Cauchy sequence in $X$ need not converge in
$X$, so no symbol $\lim_n x_n$ appears anywhere below; the only limits taken are
limits of *real* sequences, and each is written only after its existence has been
proved. The equivalence relation is defined and verified here rather than cited, as was
done for [[def-integers]], so that the construction is self-contained and its
transitivity argument is visible at the point of use.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$
be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) that is complete
([[def-complete-metric-space]]) and totally bounded ([[def-totally-bounded]]).
Then $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]).

**Where the axiom is spent, and why the weaker principle suffices.**
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used exactly once, at step 3.1, to fix one finite
$1/(n+1)$-net **together with a listing of it** for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ at
once. The family of sets being chosen from is written down before any selection
is made and does not depend on the earlier selections, which is precisely the
situation countable choice covers and dependent choice
([[def-dependent-choice]]) is not needed for. Everything after step 3.1 is
canonical: at each stage the construction takes the **least** admissible index in
the listing already fixed.

As always on this page, the claim is an upper bound on the cost of the proof
given here, not an assertion that $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is necessary for the
theorem.

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space. Every member of
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is bounded, so the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(f,g):=\sup_{x\in K}|f(x)-g(x)|$$

is defined on $C(K,\mathbb{R})$. With this metric,
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is complete.
Assume AC. For a compact metric K, $C(K;\mathbb R)$ has a countable uniformly dense subset in the supremum norm.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.
Assume AC. Every Borel probability on a Polish space S is tight.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If dimension zero is admitted, interpret $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton empty tuple; both conclusions then hold as well.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

derivations.claim: If $\|F\|_{P,2}=0$, every member of a countable pointwise-dense subclass is zero $P$-almost surely. By [F15], countable subadditivity gives a probability-one event on which all those functions vanish at every observation. Pointwise approximation then makes every $f\in\mathcal F$ vanish at the observations; dominated convergence gives $Pf=0$ for each $f$. Thus $\mathbb G_n$ is the zero process in outer probability and the conclusion holds with the zero Gaussian bridge.

Assume $\|F\|_{P,2}>0$. Each finite $L^2(P)$ bracket of width $r$ has $\rho_P$-diameter at most $r$, because $\rho_P(f,g)\le\|f-g\|_{P,2}\le\|u-l\|_{P,2}$. The entropy integral being finite forces $N_{[]}(r,\mathcal F,L^2(P))<\infty$ for every $r>0$: if it were infinite at one positive scale, monotonicity would make the integral infinite on an interval below that scale. Therefore the quotient of $\mathcal F$ by zero $\rho_P$-distance is totally bounded. The countable pointwise-dense subclass is dense in this quotient, since $|f_k-f|^2\le4F^2$ and [F7] gives $\|f_k-f\|_{P,2}\to0$.

Enumerate the countable dense subclass as $\mathcal F_0=\{f_j:j\in J\}$. For any finite list $f_{j_1},\ldots,f_{j_m}$, the covariance matrix $\Sigma_{ab}=K(f_{j_a},f_{j_b})$ is positive semidefinite, since $c^T\Sigma c=P[\sum_a c_a(f_{j_a}-Pf_{j_a})]^2\ge0$. [F3] supplies the centered Gaussian law $N_m(0,\Sigma)$. For any sublist, both the corresponding marginal and the Gaussian law constructed from its covariance have, in every direction, the same centered normal projection; [F14] makes the laws equal. Thus these finite-dimensional laws are consistent.

The coordinate space $\mathbb R$ with its Borel sigma-algebra is standard Borel by [F13], so [F4] extends the consistent Gaussian laws to a centered Gaussian process $\mathbb G_0$ indexed by $\mathcal F_0$, with covariance $K$. Each increment $\mathbb G_0(f)-\mathbb G_0(g)$ is centered normal with variance $\rho_P(f,g)^2$.

For any centered normal $Y$ with variance $\sigma^2$, if $\sigma=0$ then $Y=0$ almost surely and $\mathbb E e^{\lambda Y}=1$. If $\sigma>0$, the normal-density representation and density-integration identity in [F12] give $$\mathbb E e^{\lambda Y}=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{\lambda\sigma x}\phi(x)\,dx=e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\int_{\mathbb R}\phi(x-\lambda\sigma)\,dx,$$ by completing the square. To evaluate the last integral, for $a=\lambda\sigma$ and $R>|a|$, one-dimensional substitution from [F12] gives $\int_{-R}^R\phi(x-a)\,dx=\int_{-R-a}^{R-a}\phi(u)\,du$. These translated intervals increase to $\mathbb R$, so monotone convergence [F12] and $\int\phi=1$ give $\int_{\mathbb R}\phi(x-a)\,dx=1$. Thus every centered Gaussian increment with variance $\sigma^2$ has MGF proxy $\sigma^2$, as needed for chaining.

For $\delta>0$, index the Gaussian increment process by pairs $(f,g)\in\mathcal F_0^2$ with $\rho_P(f,g)\le\delta$, and write $Y_{f,g}=\mathbb G_0(f)-\mathbb G_0(g)$. Its canonical pseudometric is $d_Y((f,g),(f',g'))=\{E[(Y_{f,g}-Y_{f',g'})^2]\}^{1/2}$. The triangle inequality in $L^2(P)$ gives $d_Y\le\rho_P(f,f')+\rho_P(g,g')$, while every $Y_{f,g}$ has standard deviation at most $\delta$, so the $d_Y$-diameter of this pair set is at most $2\delta$. By step 4.1 its increments are centered sub-Gaussian with their $d_Y$-scale. A product of two $\epsilon/4$-nets of $\mathcal F_0$ covers the pair set within $d_Y$-distance $\epsilon/2$. Its centers might lie outside the restricted pair set; from each product ball that meets the pair set, choose one pair inside it. The triangle inequality then gives an $\epsilon$-net with centers in the pair set and cardinality at most $N(\epsilon/4,\mathcal F_0,\rho_P)^2$. Applying [F5] with the diagonal base point $(f_*,f_*)$ yields $E\sup_{f,g\in\mathcal F_0:\,\rho_P(f,g)\le\delta}|\mathbb G_0(f)-\mathbb G_0(g)|\le C\int_0^{C'\delta}\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F_0,\rho_P)}\,d\epsilon,$ which tends to zero as $\delta\downarrow0$ by the bracketing cover bound in step 1.2.

Choose rational $\delta_k\downarrow0$ so that the expectation in step 5.1 is at most $2^{-3k}$. By [F11], the probability that the corresponding modulus exceeds $2^{-k}$ is at most $2^{-2k}$, and the first Borel–Cantelli lemma makes only finitely many such events occur almost surely. Thus the Gaussian sample paths are uniformly $\rho_P$-continuous on $\mathcal F_0$ almost surely. By [A2], Countable Choice is available for the metric-completion construction in [F8], so the metric quotient embeds densely in a complete metric completion $T$; compactness and the pathwise extension are established below.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and take a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net in the totally bounded metric quotient from step 1.2. Its image in $T$ is still a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net for the dense embedded quotient. For any $x\in T$, density gives a quotient point $q$ with $d(x,q)<\varepsilon/2$, and some net point $y$ satisfies $d(q,y)\le\varepsilon/2$; hence $d(x,y)<\varepsilon$. Thus $T$ is totally bounded, and it is compact by its completeness from [F8] and the complete-plus-totally-bounded theorem in [F8]. To extend a path $G_0$ that is uniformly $\rho_P$-continuous on the listed dense subset $\mathcal F_0$, for each $x\in T$ and $n\ge1$ let $f_n(x)$ be the first listed point of $\mathcal F_0$ within $1/n$ of $x$. The sequence $G_0(f_n(x))$ is Cauchy by uniform continuity and therefore has a real limit by [F13]. Any two sequences from $\mathcal F_0$ converging to $x$ have pairwise distances tending to zero, so uniform continuity makes their value limits equal. Define $\overline G_0(x)$ by this common limit. To verify continuity, given $\eta>0$ choose $\tau>0$ so that $d(u,v)<\tau$ for $u,v\in\mathcal F_0$ implies $|G_0(u)-G_0(v)|<\eta/2$. If $d(x,y)<\tau/3$, approximating sequences $u_n\to x$ and $v_n\to y$ eventually satisfy $d(u_n,v_n)<\tau$; passing to their value limits gives $|\overline G_0(x)-\overline G_0(y)|\le\eta/2<\eta$. Density makes this extension unique.

Uniform continuity on the countable set $\mathcal F_0$ is a measurable path event: for each integer $m$, the condition that some positive rational radius makes every coordinate increment below $1/m$ for pairs in $\mathcal F_0$ closer than that radius is a countable union and intersection of measurable coordinate events. By step 6.1 this event has probability one. On it use the extension from step 7.1, and define the function to be zero off it. The resulting map is a Borel random element of $C(T,\mathbb R)$: evaluations at the countable dense set $\mathcal F_0$ are measurable, and for continuous functions the supremum distance is the supremum over $\mathcal F_0$, so preimages of open balls are measurable; separability makes every open set a countable union of such balls. By [F9], $C(T,\mathbb R)$ is complete and separable; [F10] makes it Polish and its Gaussian law tight. For any finite list $f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\mathcal F$, choose pointwise approximants $f_{i,k}\in\mathcal F_0$ for each $i$. By [F7], $\|f_{i,k}-f_i\|_{P,2}\to0$. Fix coefficients $c_1,\ldots,c_m$ and put $S_k=\sum_i c_i\mathbb G_0(f_{i,k})$ and $S=\sum_i c_i\overline G_0([f_i])$. Step 7.1 gives $S_k\to S$ almost surely. Each $S_k$ is centered normal with variance $\sigma_k^2\to\sigma^2=\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jK(f_i,f_j)=P[\sum_i c_i(f_i-Pf_i)]^2\ge0$. Dominated convergence [F7] applied to $e^{itS_k}$, whose modulus is one, gives convergence of characteristic functions. By [F12], the limit is $e^{-t^2\sigma^2/2}$ and determines the centered normal law of variance $\sigma^2$. Every linear combination of the limiting vector is therefore centered normal; [F3] identifies that vector as multivariate normal with covariance $(K(f_i,f_j))$. This proves that the pathwise extension has the required Gaussian finite-dimensional laws. Define $R:C(T,\mathbb R)\to\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$ by $R(z)(f)=z([f])$, where $[f]$ is the image of $f$ in the metric quotient and its completion. Since these images are dense in $T$ and $z-w$ is continuous, $\|R(z)-R(w)\|_{\mathcal F}=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|z([f])-w([f])|=\sup_{t\in T}|z(t)-w(t)|$, so $R$ is an isometry and is continuous. Its pushforward of the tight Borel law on $C(T,\mathbb R)$ is a tight Borel Gaussian bridge on $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$.

Fix any finite $f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\mathcal F$. The vectors $(f_1(X_i)-Pf_1,\ldots,f_m(X_i)-Pf_m)$ are iid and have finite second moments, bounded in squared norm by $2m(F(X_i)^2+(PF)^2)$ almost surely. [F2] gives convergence of their normalized sums to $N_m(0,(K(f_a,f_b))_{a,b})$, the corresponding finite-dimensional law of the Gaussian bridge from step 8.1. This proves finite-dimensional convergence, with the asymptotic-distribution convention of [F1].

By [F6], the empirical processes are asymptotically equicontinuous in $\rho_P$. For each $\epsilon>0$, the totally bounded quotient from step 1.2 has a finite $\epsilon/2$-net with centers in the dense subset $\mathcal F_0$; density then makes it an $\epsilon$-net for all of $\mathcal F$. List its finitely many centers and assign to each $f$ the first center within distance $\epsilon$, obtaining $\pi_\epsilon(f)$. Define $\mathbb G_{n,\epsilon}(f)=\mathbb G_n(\pi_\epsilon(f))$ and $\mathbb G_{\epsilon}(f)=\mathbb G_P(\pi_\epsilon(f))$. Their ranges lie in a finite-dimensional subspace of $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$; the linear map from the selected coordinate vector to that subspace is continuous in the supremum norm. Thus the finite-dimensional convergence in step 9.1, tested after composition with any bounded continuous functional, gives $\mathbb G_{n,\epsilon}\Rightarrow\mathbb G_\epsilon$ for each fixed $\epsilon$.

The sup-norm error $\|\mathbb G_n-\mathbb G_{n,\epsilon}\|_{\mathcal F}$ is bounded by the empirical-process modulus over pairs at $\rho_P$-distance at most $\epsilon$; it is therefore bounded by the modulus at radius $2\epsilon$ in [F6], which tends to zero in outer probability as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. This gives $|E^*H(Z)-E^*H(Z')|\le\omega_H(r)+2\|H\|_\infty p$ by measurable majorants. AC is used in [F2], [F4], [F10], and the countable-choice completion in [F8]; no finite-dimensional limit is used as a substitute for the process-level equicontinuity step.

citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID random elements with law $P$. For a class $\mathcal F$ of measurable, integrable real-valued functions on $\mathcal X$, write

$$Pf:=\int f\,dP,\qquad P_nf:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(Z_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n(f):=\sqrt n\,(P_nf-Pf).$$

The map $f\mapsto P_nf-Pf$ is the centered empirical process, and $\mathbb G_n$ is its $\sqrt n$-scaled version. More generally, for independent processes $X_1(t),\ldots,X_n(t)$ whose marginal expectations are finite for each index $t\in T$, the centered process sum is

$$S_n(t):=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(X_i(t)-\mathbb E X_i(t)\bigr),\qquad t\in T.$$

On an auxiliary probability-space extension, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent signs, each taking $+1$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2$, independent of the observations. The empirical Rademacher process is

$$R_n(f):=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i),\qquad f\in\mathcal F.$$

The centered Rademacher process $\sum_i\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-Pf)$ is a distinct process; no equality between it and $R_n$ is part of this definition.

For a countable class of measurable functions, each displayed supremum of measurable sample paths is measurable. For an uncountable class, ordinary probability or expectation is used only when a specified countable subclass has the same supremum almost surely for the process in question; this is the separable-version convention used here. Otherwise state results using outer probability

$$P^*(A):=\inf\{P(B):A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$$

and, for a nonnegative possibly nonmeasurable random quantity $Y$, outer expectation

$$\mathbb E^*Y:=\inf\{\mathbb E U: U\text{ is measurable, nonnegative, and }U\ge Y\}.$$

In particular, measurability of every $f$ separately does not by itself make an uncountable supremum measurable.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

Use the empirical-measure convention of [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]]: for iid observations $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ with common law $P$, $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)$ and $Pf=\int f\,dP$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable real-valued functions with a nonnegative measurable integrable envelope $F$, meaning $|f|\le F$ $P$-almost surely for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $PF<\infty$. It is **pointwise measurable** if there is a countable subclass $\mathcal F_0$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ is the pointwise limit of a sequence from $\mathcal F_0$. For a pointwise-measurable class, dominated convergence [[thm-dominated-convergence]] gives $Pf_k\to Pf$ along the approximating sequence, and finite empirical averages converge pointwise, so the supremum defining the uniform law is determined by $\mathcal F_0$. The class is **$P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if

$$\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\longrightarrow0$$

in probability. It is **strongly $P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if the same convergence holds almost surely. For an uncountable class with a countable pointwise-dense subclass, the supremum is interpreted using outer probability unless the chosen version makes it measurable. For a pointwise-measurable class the supremum is determined by the countable subclass and is measurable. That subclass has a common conull envelope bound, so the supremum is finite almost surely; after choosing a real-valued version, almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability by [[thm-almost-sure-convergence-implies-convergence-in-probability]].

derivations.claim: Fix a finite set $A\subseteq[0,1]$. If $A=\varnothing$, then $P(A)=0$. Otherwise write $m=|A|\ge1$. Given $\epsilon>0$, for each $x\in A$ let $I_x=\{y\in[0,1]:|y-x|<\epsilon/(2m)\}$. These $m$ intervals cover $A$, and each has length at most $\epsilon/m$. By [A1] and finite subadditivity [F2], $0\le P(A)\le\sum_{x\in A}P(I_x)\le\epsilon$. Since this holds for every $\epsilon>0$, $P(A)=0$. By [F1], each event $\{X_i\in A\}$ has probability zero; countable subadditivity [F2] gives $P(\exists i\ge1:X_i\in A)=0$. Hence with probability one $P_n(A)=0=P(A)$ for every $n$. This proves the pointwise strong law for this fixed $A$, without asserting one common event for all finite sets.

For any realized finite sample $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the set $A_n=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ is finite, so $A_n\in\mathcal A$, $P_n(A_n)=1$, and $P(A_n)=0$. Every indicator deviation is at most one, so the supremum over $\mathcal A$ equals one for every sample. This supremum is the constant measurable function one; by [F4] it does not converge to zero in probability.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Use the empirical-measure convention of [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]]: for iid observations $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ with common law $P$, $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)$ and $Pf=\int f\,dP$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable real-valued functions with a nonnegative measurable integrable envelope $F$, meaning $|f|\le F$ $P$-almost surely for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $PF<\infty$. It is **pointwise measurable** if there is a countable subclass $\mathcal F_0$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ is the pointwise limit of a sequence from $\mathcal F_0$. For a pointwise-measurable class, dominated convergence [[thm-dominated-convergence]] gives $Pf_k\to Pf$ along the approximating sequence, and finite empirical averages converge pointwise, so the supremum defining the uniform law is determined by $\mathcal F_0$. The class is **$P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if

$$\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\longrightarrow0$$

in probability. It is **strongly $P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if the same convergence holds almost surely. For an uncountable class with a countable pointwise-dense subclass, the supremum is interpreted using outer probability unless the chosen version makes it measurable. For a pointwise-measurable class the supremum is determined by the countable subclass and is measurable. That subclass has a common conull envelope bound, so the supremum is finite almost surely; after choosing a real-valued version, almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability by [[thm-almost-sure-convergence-implies-convergence-in-probability]].

A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$, using the positive-base real-power convention of [[def-real-power]]. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID random elements with law $P$. For a class $\mathcal F$ of measurable, integrable real-valued functions on $\mathcal X$, write

$$Pf:=\int f\,dP,\qquad P_nf:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(Z_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n(f):=\sqrt n\,(P_nf-Pf).$$

The map $f\mapsto P_nf-Pf$ is the centered empirical process, and $\mathbb G_n$ is its $\sqrt n$-scaled version. More generally, for independent processes $X_1(t),\ldots,X_n(t)$ whose marginal expectations are finite for each index $t\in T$, the centered process sum is

$$S_n(t):=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(X_i(t)-\mathbb E X_i(t)\bigr),\qquad t\in T.$$

On an auxiliary probability-space extension, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent signs, each taking $+1$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2$, independent of the observations. The empirical Rademacher process is

$$R_n(f):=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i),\qquad f\in\mathcal F.$$

The centered Rademacher process $\sum_i\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-Pf)$ is a distinct process; no equality between it and $R_n$ is part of this definition.

For a countable class of measurable functions, each displayed supremum of measurable sample paths is measurable. For an uncountable class, ordinary probability or expectation is used only when a specified countable subclass has the same supremum almost surely for the process in question; this is the separable-version convention used here. Otherwise state results using outer probability

$$P^*(A):=\inf\{P(B):A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$$

and, for a nonnegative possibly nonmeasurable random quantity $Y$, outer expectation

$$\mathbb E^*Y:=\inf\{\mathbb E U: U\text{ is measurable, nonnegative, and }U\ge Y\}.$$

In particular, measurability of every $f$ separately does not by itself make an uncountable supremum measurable.

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty pointwise-measurable class of measurable real functions with a nonnegative integrable envelope $F$. Suppose $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^1(P))<\infty$ for every $\epsilon>0$. Then $\mathcal F$ is $P$-Glivenko–Cantelli: $\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\to0$ in probability. If Countable Choice is assumed, then the stronger conclusion holds that this convergence is almost sure. The terms $P_n$, $P$, and the outer-probability convention are those of [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]], and the class notion is [[def-glivenko-cantelli-class]].

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Let $A$ be at most countable ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then
$B$ is at most countable.

The proof establishes the sharper statement about subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ from
which this follows: **a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is finite if it is
bounded above, and countably infinite if it is not.**

**No choice principle is used.** This is the point of the lemma rather than a
footnote to it. The enumeration of an unbounded $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is built
by always taking the *least* element of $S$ above the previous one, and the least
element of a nonempty set of naturals is canonical
([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): it is determined by $S$, not selected from it.
Replacing "least" by "some" would turn the construction into an appeal to
dependent choice.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

derivations.claim: The class is pointwise measurable. Since $1\in\mathbb Q$, the rational thresholds together with $1$ are indexed by $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$, a countable set by [F5]–[F6]. Then $q_k\to t$ from above, so $\mathbf1_{[0,q_k]}(x)\to\mathbf1_{[0,t]}(x)$ for every $x\in[0,1]$.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

Otherwise state results using outer probability

$$P^*(A):=\inf\{P(B):A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$$

and, for a nonnegative possibly nonmeasurable random quantity $Y$, outer expectation

$$\mathbb E^*Y:=\inf\{\mathbb E U: U\text{ is measurable, nonnegative, and }U\ge Y\}.$$

In particular, measurability of every $f$ separately does not by itself make an uncountable supremum measurable.

For a class $\mathcal H$ of measurable real functions under a probability measure $Q$, an **envelope** $H$ means a nonnegative measurable function with $|h|\le H$ $Q$-almost surely for every $h\in\mathcal H$. Cauchy–Schwarz [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $QH\le\|H\|_{Q,2}<\infty$ when $H\in L^2(Q)$.

Let $(S,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable real-valued functions with a nonnegative measurable envelope $F$ satisfying $PF^2<\infty$. A class is **pointwise measurable** if it has a countable subclass $\mathcal F_0$ such that for each $f\in\mathcal F$ there is a sequence in $\mathcal F_0$ converging pointwise to $f$. Write $\mathbb G_n(f)=\sqrt n(P_nf-Pf)$ using [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]], and put

$$\rho_P(f,g)=\{P[(f-g)-P(f-g)]^2\}^{1/2}.$$

This is a pseudometric: distinct functions can have zero distance when their centered difference vanishes $P$-almost surely. The empirical process is **asymptotically equicontinuous in probability** with respect to $\rho_P$ if for every $\eta>0$,

$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\limsup_{n\to\infty}P^*\left(\sup_{f,g\in\mathcal F:\,\rho_P(f,g)<\delta}|\mathbb G_n(f)-\mathbb G_n(g)|>\eta\right)=0.$$

Here $P^*(A)=\inf\{P(B): A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$ is outer probability; bounded nonmeasurable functionals are handled by the corresponding outer expectation $E^*Y=\inf\{EY':Y'\text{ measurable and }Y'\ge Y\}$. For a pointwise-measurable class these conventions agree with ordinary probability whenever the displayed supremum is measurable.

Write $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$ for the bounded real-valued functions on the index set $\mathcal F$, with norm $\|z\|_{\mathcal F}=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|z(f)|$. The class is **$P$-Donsker** if $\mathbb G_n$, as a process in this space, converges weakly in the outer-expectation sense to a tight Borel law of a centered Gaussian process $\mathbb G_P$ with covariance

$$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbb G_P(f),\mathbb G_P(g))=P[(f-Pf)(g-Pg)].$$

Here outer weak convergence means $E^*H(\mathbb G_n)\to EH(\mathbb G_P)$ for every bounded uniformly continuous real function $H$ on $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$; the outer expectation is the infimum of expectations of measurable majorants. The law is tight in the sense of [[def-tight-family-of-probability-measures]]. Finite-dimensional convergence means weak convergence of the vector of process values at every finite list of indices, as in [[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]].

A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$, using the positive-base real-power convention of [[def-real-power]]. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

For a class $\mathcal H$ of measurable real functions under a probability measure $Q$, an **envelope** $H$ means a nonnegative measurable function with $|h|\le H$ $Q$-almost surely for every $h\in\mathcal H$. Cauchy–Schwarz [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $QH\le\|H\|_{Q,2}<\infty$ when $H\in L^2(Q)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$ on a measurable space, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty pointwise-measurable class of measurable real functions with a measurable envelope $F\ge0$ satisfying $PF^2<\infty$. If $\|F\|_{P,2}=0$, the empirical process is the zero process almost surely. Otherwise assume

$$\int_0^1\sqrt{\log N_{[]}\bigl(\epsilon\|F\|_{P,2},\mathcal F,L^2(P)\bigr)}\,d\epsilon<\infty,$$

where $N_{[]}(r,\mathcal F,L^2(P))$ is the least number of measurable brackets $[l,u]$ with $l\le f\le u$ $P$-almost surely and $\|u-l\|_{P,2}\le r$ that cover $\mathcal F$. Then $\mathcal F$ is $P$-Donsker in the sense of [[def-donsker-class-and-asymptotic-equicontinuity]]: the empirical process $\mathbb G_n=\sqrt n(P_n-P)$ converges weakly in outer expectation in $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$ to a tight centered Gaussian bridge with covariance

$$K(f,g)=P[(f-Pf)(g-Pg)].$$

The $L^2(P)$ bracketing number and width use [[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]].

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Let $A$ be at most countable ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then
$B$ is at most countable.

The proof establishes the sharper statement about subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ from
which this follows: **a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is finite if it is
bounded above, and countably infinite if it is not.**

**No choice principle is used.** This is the point of the lemma rather than a
footnote to it. The enumeration of an unbounded $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is built
by always taking the *least* element of $S$ above the previous one, and the least
element of a nonempty set of naturals is canonical
([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): it is determined by $S$, not selected from it.
Replacing "least" by "some" would turn the construction into an appeal to
dependent choice.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

derivations.claim: The class $\mathcal F=\{f_t:t\in[0,1]\}$ is pointwise measurable. Since $1\in\mathbb Q$, the rational thresholds together with $1$ are indexed by $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$, which is countable by [F5]–[F6]. For each fixed $t<1$, [A2] and [F7] give rationals $q_k\in\mathbb Q\cap(t,\min(1,t+1/k))$, so $q_k\to t$ from above and $f_{q_k}(x)\to f_t(x)$ for every $x\in[0,1]$. The envelope $F\equiv1$ is measurable and square-integrable.

For an integer $m\ge1$, the $m$ brackets $[f_{j/m},f_{(j+1)/m}]$ have $L^2(P)$ width $\sqrt{1/m}$, since their endpoint difference is the indicator of an interval of length $1/m$. Thus for $0<\epsilon\le1$, choosing $m=\lceil\epsilon^{-2}\rceil$ gives $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^2(P))\le m$.

Consequently $\log N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^2(P))\le\log(1+\epsilon^{-2})\le\log2+2\log(1/\epsilon)$ for $0<\epsilon\le1$. Since $\log(1/\epsilon)\le1/\epsilon$, the square-root entropy is bounded by $\sqrt{\log2}+\sqrt2\epsilon^{-1/2}$, an integrable function on $(0,1]$. All hypotheses of [F4] hold.

Applying [F4] gives a tight centered Gaussian limit. For $s,t\in[0,1]$, $P(f_sf_t)=P([0,\min(s,t)])=\min(s,t)$ and $Pf_sPf_t=st$, so [F2] gives covariance $\min(s,t)-st$. This is precisely the defining covariance of the standard Brownian bridge stated in the example, proving the claimed limit. AC is carried from [F4].
