citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For every admissible input to [[alg-constrained-l0-least-squares]], its finite
scan terminates and returns a support minimizing $\|y-P_{V_S}y\|_2^2$ over all
supports of size at most $s$. Among tied minimizers, it returns the earliest
support in the prescribed order.

Moreover, let $n,d$ be positive integers, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ be fixed, and
let $\theta^*\in\mathbb R^d$ have at most $s$ nonzero coordinates, where
$1\le s\le d/2$. Suppose $Y=X\theta^*+\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon$ is centered
sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2\ge0$ in the linear-functional sense of
[[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]]. Let $\widehat\mu_s$ be the fitted vector
returned by [[alg-constrained-l0-least-squares]]. For $0<\delta<1$, with
$C:=32(4+2\log6)$,

$$\mathbb E\left[\frac1n\|\widehat\mu_s-X\theta^*\|_2^2\right] \le C\frac{\sigma^2s\log(ed/s)}{n},$$

and

$$\mathbb P\!\left(\frac1n\|\widehat\mu_s-X\theta^*\|_2^2 \le C\frac{\sigma^2\left[s\log(ed/s)+\log(1/\delta)\right]}{n}\right) \ge1-\delta.$$
No design-rank, incoherence, or column-normalization condition is assumed. The
claim concerns fitted values; it gives no coefficient-error bound.

Let $n,N\ge1$ and let $P_1,\ldots,P_N$ be orthogonal projections in
$\mathbb R^n$ onto fixed finite-dimensional subspaces $V_1,\ldots,V_N$. Let
$c_1,\ldots,c_N\in\mathbb R$ be fixed. For $y\in\mathbb R^n$, define
$q_i(y):=n^{-1}\|y-P_i y\|_2^2+c_i$, choose the least index attaining
$\min_{1\le i\le N}q_i(y)$, and return its fitted vector $P_i y$. The resulting
map $\widehat m:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ is Borel measurable. The index map
is Borel measurable when $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ has its discrete sigma-algebra.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $\sigma\ge0$, and let
$\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,\sigma^2I_n)$ be a centered multivariate normal vector.
Then for every $u\in\mathbb R^n$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E\exp(\lambda\langle u,\varepsilon\rangle) =\exp\!\left(\frac{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2}{2}\right).$$
In particular, $\varepsilon$ is sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$ in the
linear-functional sense of [[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]].

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n,d\ge1$, $\sigma>0$, and let
$1\le s\le d/2$ be integers. Observe $Z\in\mathbb R^d$ with independent
coordinates $Z_j\sim N(\theta_j,\sigma^2/n)$ for a parameter
$$\Theta_{s,d}:=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^d: |\{j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}:\theta_j\ne0\}|\le s\}.$$
For every Borel estimator $T:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$,
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{s,d}} \mathbb E_\theta\|T(Z)-\theta\|_2^2 \ge \frac{\sigma^2s\log(ed/s)}{200000n}.$$

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: By [F3], the noise satisfies the centered vector proxy condition required by [F1]. The support-search fitted vector is Borel by [F2], so it is an admissible estimator for [F6]. Applying [F1] at each $\theta\in\Theta_s$ and taking the supremum and then the infimum gives the upper bound.

Fix any Borel fitted-vector estimator $T$. Put $Z=Y/\sqrt n$ and $S(z)=T(\sqrt n z)/\sqrt n$, which is Borel by [F8]. Under the independent realization in [F4], the coordinates of $Z$ are coordinatewise measurable affine transforms of independent standard normals. By [F7], they remain independent and have laws $N(\theta_j,\sigma^2/n)$, exactly the sequence experiment in [F5]. Applying [F5] to the Borel estimator $S$ gives $$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_s}\mathbb E_\theta\|S(Z)-\theta\|_2^2 \ge\frac{\sigma^2s\log(en/s)}{200000n}.$$

Since $X=\sqrt n I_n$, pointwise $$\frac1n\|T(Y)-X\theta\|_2^2 =\left\|\frac{T(Y)}{\sqrt n}-\theta\right\|_2^2 =\|S(Z)-\theta\|_2^2.$$ By [F6] these pointwise losses define the respective risks. Thus every Borel $T$ has supremum fitted-value risk at least the lower bound in step 1.2. Taking the infimum over $T$ proves the minimax lower bound.
The upper bound in step 1.1 and the lower bound in step 2.1 give the displayed comparison, with universal constants $1/200000$ and $C$.

matrix, and write $V_X:=\{X\theta:\theta\in\mathbb R^d\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$
for its column space. For an observed vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, the **fixed-design
least-squares fitted vector** is

$$\widehat\mu_X(y):=P_{V_X}y,$$

where $P_{V_X}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $V_X$, as defined in
[[def-orthogonal-projection]]. It is uniquely defined even when $X$ is rank
deficient. The nearest-point characterization in
[[thm-orthogonal-projection-is-the-unique-nearest-point]] says that
$\widehat\mu_X(y)$ minimizes $\|y-v\|_2$ over $v\in V_X$. This item defines the
fitted vector; it does not select a coefficient representation $\widehat\theta$.

Let $n,d\ge1$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ be fixed, and put
$V=\operatorname{col}(X)$ and $r=\dim V$. Let $P_V$ be the orthogonal
projection and let $\mu\in\mathbb R^n$ be fixed. Let
$\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_n)$ be a centered random vector
with square-integrable coordinates satisfying
$\mathbb E[\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j]=\sigma^2\mathbf 1_{i=j}$ for
$\sigma^2\ge0$. For $Y=\mu+\varepsilon$ and
$\widehat\mu=\widehat\mu_X(Y)$ as in
[[def-fixed-design-projection-estimator]],

$$\mathbb E\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|_2^2=\|P_V\mu-\mu\|_2^2+r\sigma^2.$$

In particular, when $\mu\in V$, the expected squared fitted-value error is
exactly $r\sigma^2$. The moment assumptions hold for centered Gaussian noise
with covariance matrix $\sigma^2 I_n$; Gaussianity is not otherwise needed.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

derivations.claim: Both coefficient vectors are distinct, but $X_n\theta_1=\mathbf 1_n=X_n\theta_2$. Thus the asserted injectivity fails, and the observation distributions under $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are identical because the additive noise law is common.

Let $T(Y)\in\mathbb R^2$ be any measurable coefficient estimator. For every $a\in\mathbb R^2$, completing squares gives $$\|a-\theta_1\|_2^2+\|a-\theta_2\|_2^2 =2\left\|a-\left(\frac12,\frac12\right)\right\|_2^2+1\ge1.$$ Integrating under the common observation law and using [F3] shows that the sum of the two coefficient risks is at least $1$, so their maximum is at least $1/2$ for every $n$.

The common fitted mean $\mu=\mathbf 1_n$ lies in $\operatorname{col}(X_n)$, which has rank $1$. By [F2], its projected least-squares fit has expected squared fitted-value risk $\sigma^2$, or $\sigma^2/n$ per observation by [F4]. This vanishes as $n$ grows while the coefficient-risk lower bound in step 1.2 stays at least $1/2$.

**Input:** naturals $n,d\ge1$, a fixed design $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, a data
vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and a natural $s$ with $0\le s\le d$.

**Candidate supports:** list all subsets $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ with
$|S|\le s$ in lexicographic order of their length-$d$ indicator vectors,
using $0<1$. This is a finite nonempty list because it contains $\varnothing$
and is contained in the finite power set of $\{1,\ldots,d\}$.

**Procedure:** for each candidate $S$, let $V_S$ be the span of the columns of
$X$ indexed by $S$ and compute $\widehat\mu_S=P_{V_S}y$. Compute its residual
score $q_S=\|y-\widehat\mu_S\|_2^2$. Initialize the incumbent at the first
candidate. Scan the remaining candidates in the stated order, replacing the
incumbent exactly when a strictly smaller score is found; retain the earlier
candidate on a tie. Return the selected support and its fitted vector
$\widehat\mu_s$.

Each $V_S$ is finite-dimensional, so the projections are defined by
[[def-fixed-design-projection-estimator]]. The fitted-vector selection is Borel
measurable by [[lem-finite-support-projection-selection-is-borel]]. The procedure
performs a finite exhaustive support search; no computational-efficiency claim is
made.

For every admissible input to [[alg-constrained-l0-least-squares]], its finite
scan terminates and returns a support minimizing $\|y-P_{V_S}y\|_2^2$ over all
supports of size at most $s$. Among tied minimizers, it returns the earliest
support in the prescribed order.

Moreover, let $n,d$ be positive integers, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ be fixed, and
let $\theta^*\in\mathbb R^d$ have at most $s$ nonzero coordinates, where
$1\le s\le d/2$. Suppose $Y=X\theta^*+\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon$ is centered
sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2\ge0$ in the linear-functional sense of
[[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]]. Let $\widehat\mu_s$ be the fitted vector
returned by [[alg-constrained-l0-least-squares]]. For $0<\delta<1$, with
$C:=32(4+2\log6)$,

$$\mathbb E\left[\frac1n\|\widehat\mu_s-X\theta^*\|_2^2\right] \le C\frac{\sigma^2s\log(ed/s)}{n},$$

and

$$\mathbb P\!\left(\frac1n\|\widehat\mu_s-X\theta^*\|_2^2 \le C\frac{\sigma^2\left[s\log(ed/s)+\log(1/\delta)\right]}{n}\right) \ge1-\delta.$$
No design-rank, incoherence, or column-normalization condition is assumed. The
claim concerns fitted values; it gives no coefficient-error bound.

Use the real random variable convention of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and the expectation convention of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. A real random variable $X$ is **centered** when it is integrable and $\mathbb E X=0$. A vector random element $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)$ in $\mathbb R^d$, for an integer $d\ge1$, is centered when each coordinate is integrable and $\mathbb E Z_j=0$. For $u,z\in\mathbb R^d$, write $\langle u,z\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^d u_jz_j$ and $\|u\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d u_j^2)^{1/2}$, using the Euclidean convention in [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]].

For $\sigma^2\ge0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$
A centered vector random element $Z\in\mathbb R^d$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\langle u,Z\rangle}\le e^{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R^d\text{ and }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$

For $\nu^2\ge0$ and $b>0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu^2,b)$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\nu^2/2}\qquad\text{whenever }|\lambda|\le1/b.$$

The parameters $\sigma^2$ and $\nu^2$ are moment-generating-function upper-bound proxies; they are not asserted to equal the variance. The vector condition controls every one-dimensional projection and does not assert independence of coordinates.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

derivations.claim: The three candidate supports are $\varnothing,\{1\},\{2\}$. Their fitted vectors are $0$, $(\varepsilon_1,0)$, and $(0,\varepsilon_2)$, with residual squares $\varepsilon_1^2+\varepsilon_2^2$, $\varepsilon_2^2$, and $\varepsilon_1^2$, respectively. Hence the chosen fitted vector has squared norm $\max(\varepsilon_1^2,\varepsilon_2^2)$, including a tie.

Pointwise, $\varepsilon_1^2\le\max(\varepsilon_1^2,\varepsilon_2^2) \le\varepsilon_1^2+\varepsilon_2^2$. Taking expectations and using [F4] gives $\sigma^2\le\mathbb E\|\widehat\mu_s\|_2^2\le2\sigma^2$. Division by $n=2$ proves the stated interval for fitted-value error.

Here $s=1$, $d=2$, and $n=2$, and the noise satisfies [F3], so [F2] gives expected error at most $C\sigma^2\log(2e)/2$. This is consistent with the direct calculation; the example makes no separate minimax lower-bound claim. By [F5], this expectation is the squared fitted-value risk.

for its column space. For an observed vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, the **fixed-design
least-squares fitted vector** is

$$\widehat\mu_X(y):=P_{V_X}y,$$

where $P_{V_X}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $V_X$, as defined in
[[def-orthogonal-projection]]. It is uniquely defined even when $X$ is rank
deficient. The nearest-point characterization in
[[thm-orthogonal-projection-is-the-unique-nearest-point]] says that
$\widehat\mu_X(y)$ minimizes $\|y-v\|_2$ over $v\in V_X$. This item defines the
fitted vector; it does not select a coefficient representation $\widehat\theta$.

Let $n,d\ge1$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ be fixed, and put
$V=\operatorname{col}(X)$ and $r=\dim V$. Let $P_V$ be the orthogonal
projection and let $\mu\in\mathbb R^n$ be fixed. Let
$\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_n)$ be a centered random vector
with square-integrable coordinates satisfying
$\mathbb E[\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j]=\sigma^2\mathbf 1_{i=j}$ for
$\sigma^2\ge0$. For $Y=\mu+\varepsilon$ and
$\widehat\mu=\widehat\mu_X(Y)$ as in
[[def-fixed-design-projection-estimator]],

$$\mathbb E\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|_2^2=\|P_V\mu-\mu\|_2^2+r\sigma^2.$$

In particular, when $\mu\in V$, the expected squared fitted-value error is
exactly $r\sigma^2$. The moment assumptions hold for centered Gaussian noise
with covariance matrix $\sigma^2 I_n$; Gaussianity is not otherwise needed.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment: a measurable data space, a parameter-label set,
and a family of probability measures on the data space. Let
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be its real-valued target function (estimand). An estimator
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ is a measurable statistic
with the real Borel target ([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]). At a parameter
$\theta$ for which $T$ is integrable under $P_\theta$, its **bias** is
$$\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T):=\mathbb E_\theta[T]-\psi(\theta).$$

Its **mean squared error** (MSE) is the extended nonnegative number
$$\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T):=\mathbb E_\theta[(T-\psi(\theta))^2]\in[0,+\infty].$$
This is the risk of the deterministic rule induced by $T$ under squared-error
loss $L(\theta,a)=(a-\psi(\theta))^2$: its Dirac kernel is constructed in
[[lem-statistic-induces-deterministic-procedure]], and the risk supplier's
integral formula reduces to the displayed expectation when the action is
$T(x)$ by [[lem-dirac-integral-evaluation]]
([[def-loss-function-and-risk]]). For each fixed $\theta$, this loss is Borel
in the real action $a$; no measurable structure on $\Theta$ or measurability
of $\psi$ is required. The expectation convention is
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. If $T$ is
square-integrable under $P_\theta$, then its variance is defined by
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] and this MSE is finite. Bias is not
defined at parameters where $T$ is not integrable.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

derivations.claim: Since $\operatorname{col}(X)=\mathbb R$, [F1] gives $\widehat\mu=Y=\varepsilon$. Therefore the training residual $|Y-\widehat\mu|^2$ is zero for every outcome.
By [F2], the expected squared error for estimating the true mean is $\mathbb E|\widehat\mu-\mu|^2=\sigma^2$. This is the scalar MSE and squared-loss risk by [F5].

The test-response error is $Y'-\widehat\mu=\varepsilon'-\varepsilon$. Expanding its square and using [F3] and [F4], $\mathbb E|\varepsilon'-\varepsilon|^2 =\mathbb E[(\varepsilon')^2]+\mathbb E[\varepsilon^2] -2\mathbb E[\varepsilon']\mathbb E[\varepsilon] =2\sigma^2$.
The training residual, mean-estimation error, and fresh-response test error are respectively $0$, $\sigma^2$, and $2\sigma^2$ in this model, so these quantities are distinct.

For $n,d\ge1$, a deterministic design $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, response $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and penalty $\tau>0$, define the Lasso objective
$$Q_y(\theta)=\frac1n\|y-X\theta\|_2^2+2\tau\|\theta\|_1.$$
Its minimizer set is $\mathcal M(y)=\operatorname{argmin}_{\theta\in\mathbb R^d}Q_y(\theta)$. The penalty is strictly positive; no full-rank condition on $X$ is imposed. The nonemptiness, compactness, and convexity of this set are proved separately; this page defines the objective and minimizer set but does not select one minimizer.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

derivations.claim: The function $Q_y$ is continuous. For $0\le t\le1$, the identity $\|ta+(1-t)b\|_2^2=t\|a\|_2^2+(1-t)\|b\|_2^2-t(1-t)\|a-b\|_2^2$ proves convexity of the squared-residual term, while $|tu+(1-t)v|\le t|u|+(1-t)|v|$ in each coordinate proves convexity of $\|\cdot\|_1$. Since $\|\theta\|_1=\sum_j|\theta_j|\ge\|\theta\|_2$ (squaring both sides reduces this to nonnegative cross terms $2|\theta_j||\theta_k|$), $Q_y(\theta)\ge2\tau\|\theta\|_2\to\infty$ as $\|\theta\|_2\to\infty$. Choose $R>0$ with $2\tau R>Q_y(0)$. By [F2], $Q_y$ attains a minimum on the closed radius-$R$ ball; every point outside that ball has objective greater than $Q_y(0)$, so a global minimum is attained inside the ball.

The minimizer set is closed as the inverse image $Q_y^{-1}(\{\min Q_y\})$ of a closed singleton under a continuous function, and it is contained in the closed radius-$R$ ball from step 1.1. Hence it is compact by [F2]. If $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are minimizers and $0\le t\le1$, convexity gives $Q_y(t\theta_1+(1-t)\theta_2)\le tQ_y(\theta_1)+(1-t)Q_y(\theta_2)=\min Q_y$; by minimality equality holds, so the minimizer set is convex.

Let $n,d\ge1$ be integers, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ be deterministic, and let $\theta^\ast\in\mathbb R^d$. The fixed-design regression model is
$$Y=X\theta^\ast+\varepsilon,$$
where $Y,\varepsilon$ are random vectors in $\mathbb R^n$. For $\sigma^2\ge0$, the noise is centered sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$ when
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\langle u,\varepsilon\rangle}\le e^{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/2}\qquad(u\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lambda\in\mathbb R),$$
using the vector convention of [[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]]. No independence among the coordinates of $\varepsilon$ is assumed. The parameter is $s$-sparse when $1\le s\le d$ and $|\{j:\theta^\ast_j\ne0\}|\le s$.

Fix integers $n,d\ge1$, a deterministic matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, a response $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and a penalty $\tau>0$. The minimizer set $\mathcal M(y)$ of [[def-lasso-estimator]] is nonempty, compact, and convex.

Let $n,d\ge1$, $1\le s\le d$, and $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$. For $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, let $v_S$ be the vector agreeing with $v\in\mathbb R^d$ on $S$ and equal to zero off $S$; write $\|v\|_1=\sum_j|v_j|$ and use the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ of [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]. The cone associated to $S$ is
$$\mathcal C(S)=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:\|v_{S^c}\|_1\le3\|v_S\|_1\}.$$
The design satisfies the restricted eigenvalue condition with constant $\kappa^2>0$ at sparsity $s$ when
$$\frac{\|Xv\|_2^2}{n}\ge\kappa^2\|v_S\|_2^2$$
for every $S$ with $|S|\le s$ and every nonzero $v\in\mathcal C(S)$. The denominator is the norm of the supported component; this condition does not assert a lower bound for all vectors in $\mathbb R^d$.

derivations.claim: By [F4] choose any minimizer $\hat\theta$. Comparison with $\theta^\ast$ in [F1] and substitution from [F2] give $\frac{\|X\Delta\|_2^2}{n}+2\tau(\|\hat\theta\|_1-\|\theta^\ast\|_1)\le\frac{2}{n}\langle\varepsilon,X\Delta\rangle.$ This follows by expanding $\|\varepsilon-X\Delta\|_2^2$ and cancelling $\|\varepsilon\|_2^2$.

By [A1], writing $g=X^{\mathsf T}\varepsilon/n$, the finite-coordinate calculation $|\langle g,\Delta\rangle|\le\sum_j|g_j||\Delta_j|\le(\max_j|g_j|)\sum_j|\Delta_j|=\|g\|_\infty\|\Delta\|_1$ bounds the right side of step 1.1 by $\tau(\|\Delta_S\|_1+\|\Delta_{S^c}\|_1)$. The reverse triangle inequality in [F3] gives $\|\hat\theta\|_1-\|\theta^\ast\|_1\ge-\|\Delta_S\|_1+\|\Delta_{S^c}\|_1$. Substitution and rearrangement yield the displayed bound. The bound implies $\|\Delta_{S^c}\|_1\le3\|\Delta_S\|_1$, which is precisely $\Delta\in\mathcal C(S)$ by [F5].

For integers $n,d,s$ with $n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le d$, and a deterministic matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, write $G=X^{\mathsf T}X/n$. The design satisfies the incoherence condition at sparsity $s$ if
$$\max_{1\le j,k\le d}|G_{jk}-\mathbf 1_{\{j=k\}}|\le\frac1{14s}.$$
Here the maximum is entrywise, $\mathbf 1_{\{j=k\}}$ is $1$ when $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise, and no probabilistic assumption on $X$ is made. The constant $1/(14s)$ is the exact premise used in the local restricted-eigenvalue derivation; it is not a generic definition of design compatibility.

Let $n,d\ge1$, $1\le s\le d$, and $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$. For $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, let $v_S$ be the vector agreeing with $v\in\mathbb R^d$ on $S$ and equal to zero off $S$; write $\|v\|_1=\sum_j|v_j|$ and use the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ of [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]. The cone associated to $S$ is
$$\mathcal C(S)=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:\|v_{S^c}\|_1\le3\|v_S\|_1\}.$$
The design satisfies the restricted eigenvalue condition with constant $\kappa^2>0$ at sparsity $s$ when
$$\frac{\|Xv\|_2^2}{n}\ge\kappa^2\|v_S\|_2^2$$
for every $S$ with $|S|\le s$ and every nonzero $v\in\mathcal C(S)$. The denominator is the norm of the supported component; this condition does not assert a lower bound for all vectors in $\mathbb R^d$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

derivations.claim: Write $v=v_S+v_{S^c}$. Since $v_S$ and $v_{S^c}$ have disjoint supports, [F1] gives $v_S^{\mathsf T}Gv_S\ge\|v_S\|_2^2-\frac{1}{14s}\|v_S\|_1^2\ge\frac{13}{14}\|v_S\|_2^2,$ where the second inequality uses [F3].

The same disjoint-support fact makes $v_S^{\mathsf T}Iv_{S^c}=0$. Thus $|v_S^{\mathsf T}Gv_{S^c}|\le\frac{1}{14s}\|v_S\|_1\|v_{S^c}\|_1\le\frac{3}{14s}\|v_S\|_1^2\le\frac{3}{14}\|v_S\|_2^2,$ using [F1], [F2] and [F3]. Also $v_{S^c}^{\mathsf T}Gv_{S^c}\ge0$ by [F4].

Expanding $v^{\mathsf T}Gv$ and using steps 1.1–1.2 gives $v^{\mathsf T}Gv\ge\left(\frac{13}{14}-2\frac{3}{14}\right)\|v_S\|_2^2=\frac12\|v_S\|_2^2.$ This is the stated restricted eigenvalue inequality, including $v_S=0$ (then the cone condition forces $v=0$, for which both sides are zero).

Let $n,d\ge1$ be integers, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ be deterministic, and let $\theta^\ast\in\mathbb R^d$. The fixed-design regression model is
$$Y=X\theta^\ast+\varepsilon,$$
where $Y,\varepsilon$ are random vectors in $\mathbb R^n$. For $\sigma^2\ge0$, the noise is centered sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$ when
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\langle u,\varepsilon\rangle}\le e^{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/2}\qquad(u\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lambda\in\mathbb R),$$
using the vector convention of [[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]]. No independence among the coordinates of $\varepsilon$ is assumed. The parameter is $s$-sparse when $1\le s\le d$ and $|\{j:\theta^\ast_j\ne0\}|\le s$.

Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ be centered sub-Gaussian real random variables with a common proxy $\sigma^2\ge0$, where $m\ge1$. No independence is assumed. For $t>0$, if $\sigma^2>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\left(\max_{1\le j\le m}|Y_j|\ge t\right)\le2m\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),$$
and if $\sigma^2=0$ the probability is $0$.

Let $Z$ be a centered sub-Gaussian vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with proxy $\sigma^2$, where $d\ge1$. For $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\mathcal N$ be the sphere net supplied by [[lem-epsilon-net-of-unit-sphere-has-cardinality-bound]]. Then for $t>0$, if $\sigma^2>0$,
$$\mathbb P(\|Z\|_2\ge t)\le2(1+2/\epsilon)^d\exp\!\left(-\frac{(1-\epsilon)^2t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),$$
and if $\sigma^2=0$ this probability is $0$. The deterministic reduction is $\|z\|_2\le(1-\epsilon)^{-1}\max_{u\in\mathcal N}|\langle u,z\rangle|$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^d$.

For integers $n,d,s$ with $n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le d$, and a deterministic matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, write $G=X^{\mathsf T}X/n$. The design satisfies the incoherence condition at sparsity $s$ if
$$\max_{1\le j,k\le d}|G_{jk}-\mathbf 1_{\{j=k\}}|\le\frac1{14s}.$$
Here the maximum is entrywise, $\mathbf 1_{\{j=k\}}$ is $1$ when $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise, and no probabilistic assumption on $X$ is made. The constant $1/(14s)$ is the exact premise used in the local restricted-eigenvalue derivation; it is not a generic definition of design compatibility.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

For $n,d\ge1$, a deterministic design $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, response $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and penalty $\tau>0$, define the Lasso objective
$$Q_y(\theta)=\frac1n\|y-X\theta\|_2^2+2\tau\|\theta\|_1.$$
Its minimizer set is $\mathcal M(y)=\operatorname{argmin}_{\theta\in\mathbb R^d}Q_y(\theta)$. The penalty is strictly positive; no full-rank condition on $X$ is imposed. The nonemptiness, compactness, and convexity of this set are proved separately; this page defines the objective and minimizer set but does not select one minimizer.

Fix integers $n,d\ge1$, a deterministic matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, a response $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and a penalty $\tau>0$. The minimizer set $\mathcal M(y)$ of [[def-lasso-estimator]] is nonempty, compact, and convex.

Let $Y=X\theta^\ast+\varepsilon$ be the fixed-design model of [[def-subgaussian-fixed-design-regression-model]], let $S=\{j:\theta^\ast_j\ne0\}$, and let $\hat\theta$ be any minimizer of the objective in [[def-lasso-estimator]] with $\tau>0$. Write $\Delta=\hat\theta-\theta^\ast$. If
$$\left\|X^{\mathsf T}\varepsilon/n\right\|_\infty\le\tau/2,$$
then
$$\frac{\|X\Delta\|_2^2}{n}+\tau\|\Delta_{S^c}\|_1\le3\tau\|\Delta_S\|_1.$$
In particular, $\|\Delta_{S^c}\|_1\le3\|\Delta_S\|_1$, so $\Delta\in\mathcal C(S)$ for the cone in [[def-restricted-eigenvalue-condition]].

Let $n\ge1$, $1\le s\le d$, and let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ satisfy the incoherence condition of [[def-fixed-design-incoherence-condition]]. For every $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ with $|S|\le s$ and every $v\in\mathcal C(S)$,
$$\frac{\|Xv\|_2^2}{n}\ge\frac12\|v_S\|_2^2.$$
Consequently the restricted eigenvalue condition of [[def-restricted-eigenvalue-condition]] holds with $\kappa^2=1/2$.

Let $Y=X\theta^\ast+\varepsilon$ be as in [[def-subgaussian-fixed-design-regression-model]], with $n\ge1$, $d\ge1$, noise proxy $\sigma^2\ge0$, and $X$ satisfying the incoherence condition of [[def-fixed-design-incoherence-condition]] at some $1\le s\le d$. For $\delta\in(0,1)$ define
$$\tau=4\sigma\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log(2d)}{n}}+\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{n}}\right).$$
Then
$$P\!\left(\left\|X^{\mathsf T}\varepsilon/n\right\|_\infty\le\tau/2\right)\ge1-\delta.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric, where $p\ge1$. Then
$$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_{\|v\|_2=1}|v^{\mathsf T}Av|=\max_j|\lambda_j|,$$
where $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p$ are the eigenvalues of $A$.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and $0<\epsilon<1$. There is a finite set $\mathcal N\subseteq S^{d-1}$ such that every $u\in S^{d-1}$ has some $v\in\mathcal N$ with $\|u-v\|_2\le\epsilon$, and
$$|\mathcal N|\le(1+2/\epsilon)^d.$$
Here $S^{d-1}=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\|u\|_2=1\}$ by [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]. Such a set is called an $\epsilon$-net of the sphere.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

$$\Sigma=\mathbb E[(X_1-\mu)(X_1-\mu)^{\mathsf T}].$$
The oracle-centered sample covariance and the sample-centered covariance are respectively
$$\widehat\Sigma_\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)(X_i-\mu)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \widehat\Sigma^\ast=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)(X_i-\bar X)^{\mathsf T},\quad \bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
For a matrix estimate $A$, squared operator loss is $\|A-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$, with the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. This definition distinguishes the known-mean raw second moment from the estimator that removes an unknown mean.

Use the real random variable convention of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and the expectation convention of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. A real random variable $X$ is **centered** when it is integrable and $\mathbb E X=0$. A vector random element $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)$ in $\mathbb R^d$, for an integer $d\ge1$, is centered when each coordinate is integrable and $\mathbb E Z_j=0$. For $u,z\in\mathbb R^d$, write $\langle u,z\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^d u_jz_j$ and $\|u\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d u_j^2)^{1/2}$, using the Euclidean convention in [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]].

For $\sigma^2\ge0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$
A centered vector random element $Z\in\mathbb R^d$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\langle u,Z\rangle}\le e^{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R^d\text{ and }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$

For $\nu^2\ge0$ and $b>0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu^2,b)$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\nu^2/2}\qquad\text{whenever }|\lambda|\le1/b.$$

The parameters $\sigma^2$ and $\nu^2$ are moment-generating-function upper-bound proxies; they are not asserted to equal the variance. The vector condition controls every one-dimensional projection and does not assert independence of coordinates.

Let $U,V$ be centered real random variables, not necessarily independent, each sub-Gaussian with proxy $K^2>0$ as in [[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]]. Then $W=UV-\mathbb E[UV]$ is sub-exponential with parameters $(256K^4,16K^2)$ under the restricted-MGF convention of that definition.

Put $v=\sum_{i=1}^n\nu_i^2$, $b=\max_{1\le i\le n}b_i$, and $S=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. For $t>0$, if $v>0$ then
$$\mathbb P(|S|\ge t)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac12\min\!\left\{\frac{t^2}{v},\frac{t}{b}\right\}\right),$$
and if $v=0$ then $\mathbb P(|S|\ge t)=0$.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and $0<\epsilon<1$. There is a finite set $\mathcal N\subseteq S^{d-1}$ such that every $u\in S^{d-1}$ has some $v\in\mathcal N$ with $\|u-v\|_2\le\epsilon$, and
$$|\mathcal N|\le(1+2/\epsilon)^d.$$
Here $S^{d-1}=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\|u\|_2=1\}$ by [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]. Such a set is called an $\epsilon$-net of the sphere.

$$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\max_{v\in\mathcal N}|v^{\mathsf T}Av|.$$
The operator norm is the finite-dimensional norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].

Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ be centered sub-Gaussian real random variables with a common proxy $\sigma^2\ge0$, where $m\ge1$. No independence is assumed. For $t>0$, if $\sigma^2>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\left(\max_{1\le j\le m}|Y_j|\ge t\right)\le2m\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),$$
and if $\sigma^2=0$ the probability is $0$.

Let $Z$ be a centered sub-Gaussian vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with proxy $\sigma^2$, where $d\ge1$. For $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\mathcal N$ be the sphere net supplied by [[lem-epsilon-net-of-unit-sphere-has-cardinality-bound]]. Then for $t>0$, if $\sigma^2>0$,
$$\mathbb P(\|Z\|_2\ge t)\le2(1+2/\epsilon)^d\exp\!\left(-\frac{(1-\epsilon)^2t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),$$
and if $\sigma^2=0$ this probability is $0$. The deterministic reduction is $\|z\|_2\le(1-\epsilon)^{-1}\max_{u\in\mathcal N}|\langle u,z\rangle|$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^d$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

derivations.claim: If $L=0$, [F2] and [F6] imply $P(\|Z_i\|_2\ge1/m)=0$ for each $i$ and positive integer $m$. By [F8], the countable union over $i,m$ shows that every $Z_i=0$ almost surely; then [F9] gives $\Sigma=0$, and both estimators are exact. Assume $L>0$. Fix a unit vector $u$ and set $W_i=(u^{\mathsf T}Z_i)^2-E[(u^{\mathsf T}Z_i)^2]$. By [F2]–[F3], each $W_i$ is centered sub-exponential with parameters $(256L^2,16L)$; [F10] gives that these variables are iid across $i$.

By [F10] the sample vectors are independent, and [F7] gives, for every $u\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, $E e^{\lambda\langle u,\bar Z\rangle}=\prod_{i=1}^n E e^{(\lambda/n)\langle u,Z_i\rangle}\le e^{L\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/(2n)}.$ Thus $\bar Z$ is centered sub-Gaussian with proxy $L/n$. Applying the vector clause of [F6] with a $1/2$-net at $s=4\sqrt{Lr}$ gives $P(\|\bar Z\|_2^2>16Lr)\le2\cdot5^p e^{-2(p+x)}\le\delta/2,$ since $r=(p+x)/n$ and $x=\log(4/\delta)$.

Applying [F4] to $\sum_iW_i$ gives, for every $t>0$, $P\left(\left|u^{\mathsf T}(\widehat\Sigma_0-\Sigma)u\right|>t\right)\le2\exp\left[-\frac12\min\left\{\frac{nt^2}{256L^2},\frac{nt}{16L}\right\}\right].$ This is uniform over unit $u$.

Take a $1/4$-net with at most $9^p$ points and put $x=\log(4/\delta)$, so $r=(p+x)/n$. With $C_0=80$ and $t=C_0L(\sqrt r+r)$, the exponent in step 2.1 is at least $\frac12\min\{80^2/256,80/16\}(p+x)=\frac52(p+x)\ge p\log9+x$. A union bound gives probability at least $1-\delta/2$ that every net quadratic form is at most $t$ in absolute value.
By [F9], $\widehat\Sigma_0-\Sigma$ is symmetric. On the event in step 3.1, [F5] gives $\|\widehat\Sigma_0-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2t=160L(\sqrt r+r)$. This proves the first estimate.

Expanding [F1] gives $\widehat\Sigma^*=\widehat\Sigma_0-\bar Z\bar Z^{\mathsf T}$. For $w\ne0$ and unit $v$, [F12] gives $\|ww^{\mathsf T}v\|_2=\|w\|_2|\langle w,v\rangle|\le\|w\|_2^2$, with equality at $v=w/\|w\|_2$; if $w=0$, both sides vanish. Thus [F11] gives $\|\bar Z\bar Z^{\mathsf T}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|\bar Z\|_2^2$. For vectors $a,b$, [F12] and $\|a+b\|_2^2=\|a\|_2^2+2\langle a,b\rangle+\|b\|_2^2$ give $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2$; applying this inside the maximum in [F11] gives $\|A+B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Let $p\ge2$ be an integer, $0\le q<1$, $c_{n,p}\ge0$, and $\tau>0$. For a symmetric covariance matrix $\Sigma=(\sigma_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le p}$, write
$$|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(1)}\ge\cdots\ge|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(p-1)}$$
for the magnitudes of the off-diagonal entries in column $j$, arranged in nonincreasing order. Define
$$G_q(c_{n,p})=\left\{\Sigma:\max_{1\le j\le p}\max_{1\le k\le p-1} k|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(k)}^q\le c_{n,p}\right\}\quad(0<q<1).$$
For $q=0$, define $G_0(c_{n,p})$ to be the symmetric covariance matrices with at most $c_{n,p}$ nonzero off-diagonal entries in each column. The corresponding law class $\mathcal P_q(\tau,c_{n,p})$ consists of iid laws of $X\in\mathbb R^p$ whose covariance lies in $G_q(c_{n,p})$ and which satisfy
$$P(|v^{\mathsf T}(X-\mathbb E X)|>t)\le e^{-t^2/(2\tau)}
$$
for every unit vector $v$ and every $t>0$. This is a clean sub-Gaussian model; it assumes neither coordinate independence nor robustness to contamination.

Input: observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n\in\mathbb R^p$, with integers $n\ge1$, $p\ge2$, and a fixed threshold constant $\gamma_\tau>0$ determined by the directional sub-Gaussian tail parameter $\tau$.

Compute the sample-centered covariance $\widehat\Sigma^\ast$ from [[def-sample-covariance-and-operator-norm-loss]] and put $\lambda=\gamma_\tau\sqrt{\log(p)/n}$. Output the symmetric matrix $\widehat\Sigma$ defined by
$$\widehat\sigma_{jj}=\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jj},\qquad \widehat\sigma_{jk}=\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}\mathbf 1\{|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}|\ge\lambda\}\quad(j\ne k).$$
The diagonal is unchanged; an off-diagonal entry at threshold equality is retained. This procedure is a definition and makes no risk or positive-semidefiniteness guarantee.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric, where $p\ge1$. Then
$$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_{\|v\|_2=1}|v^{\mathsf T}Av|=\max_j|\lambda_j|,$$
where $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p$ are the eigenvalues of $A$.

derivations.claim: On the event in the Statement, each diagonal error is at most $\lambda/2$. For an off-diagonal entry that is retained, $|\sigma_{jk}|\ge\lambda/2$ and $|\widehat\sigma_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}|\le\lambda/2\le\min\{|\sigma_{jk}|,\lambda\}$. If it is removed, then $|\sigma_{jk}|\le|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}|+|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}|<3\lambda/2$, and its error is $|\sigma_{jk}|\le(3/2)\min\{|\sigma_{jk}|,\lambda\}$.

For $q=0$, [F1] and step 1.1 bound every off-diagonal column error sum by $(3/2)c_{n,p}\lambda$. For $0<q<1$, fix a column, put $a_k=|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(k)}$, $T=c_{n,p}\lambda^{-q}$, and $B_q:=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}2^{r(1-1/q)}=\frac1{1-2^{1-1/q}}<\infty.$ The class bound in [F1] gives $a_k\le(c_{n,p}/k)^{1/q}$. If $T<1$, then $\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\min(a_k,\lambda)\le c_{n,p}^{1/q}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k^{-1/q}\le B_qc_{n,p}^{1/q}\le B_qc_{n,p}\lambda^{1-q},$ because grouping $2^r\le k<2^{r+1}$ gives at most $2^r(2^r)^{-1/q}$ per block, and $c_{n,p}<\lambda^q$. If $T\ge1$, let $m=\lfloor T\rfloor\ge T/2$. The first $m$ terms contribute at most $m\lambda\le c_{n,p}\lambda^{1-q}$. Grouping the tail into blocks $2^rm<k\le2^{r+1}m$ gives $\sum_{k>m}k^{-1/q}\le B_qm^{1-1/q},$ so the tail contributes at most $B_qc_{n,p}^{1/q}m^{1-1/q}\le B_q2^{1/q-1}c_{n,p}\lambda^{1-q}$; here the exponent $1-1/q$ is negative and $m\ge T/2$. Thus for either case each off-diagonal column error sum is at most $C_qc_{n,p}\lambda^{1-q}$ for a finite constant $C_q$ depending only on $q$. Adding the diagonal error bound $\lambda/2$ from step 1.1 bounds every row sum by $C_q(c_{n,p}\lambda^{1-q}+\lambda)$. For $q=0$, the same total is at most $(3/2)c_{n,p}\lambda+\lambda/2\le2(c_{n,p}\lambda+\lambda)$.

For any unit vector $v$, [F3] identifies the operator norm with the maximum absolute Rayleigh quotient. With $A=\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma$, symmetry and $2|v_jv_k|\le v_j^2+v_k^2$ give $|v^{\mathsf T}(\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma)v| \le\sum_{j,k}|A_{jk}||v_j||v_k| \le\frac12\sum_{j,k}|A_{jk}|(v_j^2+v_k^2) \le\max_j\sum_k|A_{jk}|,$ because $A$ is symmetric, its absolute column sums equal its row sums, and $\sum_jv_j^2=1$. Taking the maximum over unit $v$ and using step 2.1 yields the claimed operator bound.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $X$ be an
integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so
its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$
In the nonnegative case the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Use the real random variable convention of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and the expectation convention of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. A real random variable $X$ is **centered** when it is integrable and $\mathbb E X=0$. A vector random element $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)$ in $\mathbb R^d$, for an integer $d\ge1$, is centered when each coordinate is integrable and $\mathbb E Z_j=0$. For $u,z\in\mathbb R^d$, write $\langle u,z\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^d u_jz_j$ and $\|u\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d u_j^2)^{1/2}$, using the Euclidean convention in [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]].

For $\sigma^2\ge0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$
A centered vector random element $Z\in\mathbb R^d$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\langle u,Z\rangle}\le e^{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R^d\text{ and }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$

For $\nu^2\ge0$ and $b>0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu^2,b)$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\nu^2/2}\qquad\text{whenever }|\lambda|\le1/b.$$

The parameters $\sigma^2$ and $\nu^2$ are moment-generating-function upper-bound proxies; they are not asserted to equal the variance. The vector condition controls every one-dimensional projection and does not assert independence of coordinates.

derivations.claim: The tail bound and [F1] imply $\mathbb E e^{a|X|}=1+a\int_0^\infty e^{at}\mathbb P(|X|>t)\,dt\le1+2a\int_0^\infty e^{at-t^2/(2\tau)}\,dt<\infty$ for every $a>0$, since completing the square gives $at-t^2/(2\tau)=-(t-a\tau)^2/(2\tau)+a^2\tau/2$. Thus all MGFs below are finite.

Let $X_1,X_2$ be the coordinate variables on the product of two copies of the law of $X$; [F2] gives this probability space, and its rectangle formula makes them independent with law equal to that of $X$. Set $D=X_1-X_2$. Independence [F3] gives $\mathbb E e^{\lambda D}=(\mathbb E e^{\lambda X})(\mathbb E e^{-\lambda X})$. By [F4], the second factor is at least $1$, so $\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le\mathbb E e^{\lambda D}$. The product is unchanged when $\lambda$ is replaced by $-\lambda$, hence $\mathbb E e^{\lambda D}=\mathbb E\cosh(\lambda D)$.

A union bound gives $\mathbb P(|D|>t)\le4e^{-t^2/(8\tau)}$ because $|D|>t$ implies $|X_1|>t/2$ or $|X_2|>t/2$. For $m\ge1$, [F1] and the substitution $u=t^2/(8\tau)$ yield $\mathbb E|D|^{2m}=2m\int_0^\infty t^{2m-1}\mathbb P(|D|>t)\,dt\le4(8\tau)^m m!.$ The integral is evaluated using $\int_0^\infty t^{2m-1}e^{-t^2/(8\tau)}dt=\tfrac12(8\tau)^m(m-1)!$.

By [F5], the nonnegative power series for $\cosh$ may be integrated term by term. With $x=8\tau\lambda^2$, step 2.1 and $(2m)!\ge(m!)^2$ give $\mathbb E\cosh(\lambda D)\le1+4\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{x^m}{m!}=4e^x-3\le e^{4x}.$ For the last inequality, $f(x)=e^{4x}-4e^x+3$ satisfies $f(0)=0$ and $f'(x)=4(e^{4x}-e^x)\ge0$ for $x\ge0$. Therefore $\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{32\tau\lambda^2}$ for every $\lambda$, which is the proxy-$64\tau$ assertion by [F6].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

derivations.claim: Applying [F1] to $U^2,V^2$ gives $\mathbb E U^2,\mathbb E V^2\le2\tau$. Since $2|UV|\le U^2+V^2$, $UV$ is integrable and $|\mathbb E UV|\le2\tau$. Also, for $x>0$, $|UV|>x$ implies $|U|>\sqrt x$ or $|V|>\sqrt x$, so $\mathbb P(|UV|>x)\le2e^{-x/(2\tau)}$.

Put $W=UV-\mathbb E UV$. If $t\ge4\tau$, then $|W|>t$ implies $|UV|>t-|\mathbb E UV|\ge t/2$, so step 1.1 gives $\mathbb P(|W|>t)\le2e^{-t/(4\tau)}\le4e^{-t/(8\tau)}$. If $0<t<4\tau$, then $4e^{-t/(8\tau)}>4e^{-1/2}>1$, so the same final bound follows from $\mathbb P(|W|>t)\le1$. Thus for all $t>0$, $\mathbb P(|W|>t)\le4e^{-t/(8\tau)}$.

By [F1] and step 2.1, for every integer $m\ge2$, $\mathbb E|W|^m=m\int_0^\infty t^{m-1}\mathbb P(|W|>t)\,dt\le4(8\tau)^m m!.$ The identity follows from substitution $u=t/(8\tau)$ and $\int_0^\infty u^{m-1}e^{-u}du=(m-1)!$.

Fix $|\lambda|\le1/(16\tau)$ and put $x=8\tau|\lambda|\le1/2$. The variable $W$ is integrable and centered by step 1.1. The nonnegative measurable partial sums $A_N=\sum_{m=0}^N|\lambda W|^m/m!$ increase pointwise to $e^{|\lambda W|}$. Finite linearity [F5] and monotone convergence [F3], applied only to these nonnegative partial sums, give $$\mathbb E e^{|\lambda W|}=1+|\lambda|\mathbb E|W|+\sum_{m\ge2}\frac{|\lambda|^m\mathbb E|W|^m}{m!}\le1+|\lambda|\mathbb E|W|+4\sum_{m\ge2}x^m<\infty.$$ Thus $e^{|\lambda W|}$ is an integrable dominating variable.

The signed partial sums $S_N=\sum_{m=0}^N(\lambda W)^m/m!$ converge pointwise to $e^{\lambda W}$ and satisfy $|S_N|\le A_N\le e^{|\lambda W|}$. Dominated convergence [F4] and finite linearity [F5] justify taking expectations termwise; the scalar series of expectations is absolutely convergent by step 4.1. Since $\mathbb EW=0$, step 3.1 gives $$\mathbb E e^{\lambda W}=1+\sum_{m\ge2}\frac{\lambda^m\mathbb EW^m}{m!}\le1+4\sum_{m\ge2}x^m=1+\frac{4x^2}{1-x}\le1+8x^2\le e^{8x^2}=e^{512\tau^2\lambda^2}.$$ By [F2] the parameters remain $\nu^2=1024\tau^2$ and $b=16\tau$.

Let $p\ge2$ be an integer, $0\le q<1$, $c_{n,p}\ge0$, and $\tau>0$. For a symmetric covariance matrix $\Sigma=(\sigma_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le p}$, write
$$|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(1)}\ge\cdots\ge|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(p-1)}$$
for the magnitudes of the off-diagonal entries in column $j$, arranged in nonincreasing order. Define
$$G_q(c_{n,p})=\left\{\Sigma:\max_{1\le j\le p}\max_{1\le k\le p-1} k|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(k)}^q\le c_{n,p}\right\}\quad(0<q<1).$$
For $q=0$, define $G_0(c_{n,p})$ to be the symmetric covariance matrices with at most $c_{n,p}$ nonzero off-diagonal entries in each column. The corresponding law class $\mathcal P_q(\tau,c_{n,p})$ consists of iid laws of $X\in\mathbb R^p$ whose covariance lies in $G_q(c_{n,p})$ and which satisfy
$$P(|v^{\mathsf T}(X-\mathbb E X)|>t)\le e^{-t^2/(2\tau)}
$$
for every unit vector $v$ and every $t>0$. This is a clean sub-Gaussian model; it assumes neither coordinate independence nor robustness to contamination.

Let $U,V$ be real random variables on one probability space, not necessarily independent, and suppose for some $\tau>0$ that
$$\mathbb P(|U|>t)\le e^{-t^2/(2\tau)},\qquad \mathbb P(|V|>t)\le e^{-t^2/(2\tau)}\quad(t>0).$$
Then $W=UV-\mathbb E[UV]$ is well-defined, centered, and sub-exponential with parameters $(1024\tau^2,16\tau)$ in the convention of [[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]].

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent centered real random variables, with $X_i$ sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu_i^2,b_i)$ as defined in [[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]], where $n\ge1$ and $b_i>0$. Put $v=\sum_{i=1}^n\nu_i^2$, $b=\max_{1\le i\le n}b_i$, and $S=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. For $t>0$, if $v>0$ then
$$\mathbb P(|S|\ge t)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac12\min\!\left\{\frac{t^2}{v},\frac{t}{b}\right\}\right),$$
and if $v=0$ then $\mathbb P(|S|\ge t)=0$.

Let $X$ be a centered real random variable and let $\tau>0$. If
$$\mathbb P(|X|>t)\le2e^{-t^2/(2\tau)}\qquad(t>0),$$
then $X$ is sub-Gaussian with proxy $64\tau$ in the MGF convention of [[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]]:
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{32\tau\lambda^2}\qquad(\lambda\in\mathbb R).$$

Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ be centered sub-Gaussian real random variables with a common proxy $\sigma^2\ge0$, where $m\ge1$. No independence is assumed. For $t>0$, if $\sigma^2>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\left(\max_{1\le j\le m}|Y_j|\ge t\right)\le2m\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),$$
and if $\sigma^2=0$ the probability is $0$.

Let $Z$ be a centered sub-Gaussian vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with proxy $\sigma^2$, where $d\ge1$. For $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\mathcal N$ be the sphere net supplied by [[lem-epsilon-net-of-unit-sphere-has-cardinality-bound]]. Then for $t>0$, if $\sigma^2>0$,
$$\mathbb P(\|Z\|_2\ge t)\le2(1+2/\epsilon)^d\exp\!\left(-\frac{(1-\epsilon)^2t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),$$
and if $\sigma^2=0$ this probability is $0$. The deterministic reduction is $\|z\|_2\le(1-\epsilon)^{-1}\max_{u\in\mathcal N}|\langle u,z\rangle|$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^d$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $n,p\ge1$ be integers and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent identically distributed random vectors in $\mathbb R^p$ with finite second moments, mean $\mu=\mathbb E X_1$, and covariance matrix
$$\Sigma=\mathbb E[(X_1-\mu)(X_1-\mu)^{\mathsf T}].$$
The oracle-centered sample covariance and the sample-centered covariance are respectively
$$\widehat\Sigma_\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)(X_i-\mu)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \widehat\Sigma^\ast=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)(X_i-\bar X)^{\mathsf T},\quad \bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
For a matrix estimate $A$, squared operator loss is $\|A-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$, with the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. This definition distinguishes the known-mean raw second moment from the estimator that removes an unknown mean.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

derivations.claim: Put $U_i=X_i-\mu$. For coordinate unit vectors $e_j,e_k$, [F1] gives the required tail bounds for $U_{ij}$ and $U_{ik}$. Hence [F2] makes $W_i^{jk}=U_{ij}U_{ik}-\sigma_{jk}$ centered sub-exponential with parameters $(1024\tau^2,16\tau)$. For fixed $(j,k)$ these variables are independent across $i$ by [F6].

By [F4], each $U_{ij}$ is sub-Gaussian with proxy $64\tau$. Independence across $i$ and [F7] give $\mathbb E e^{\lambda n^{-1}\sum_iU_{ij}}\le\prod_i e^{32\tau\lambda^2/n^2}=e^{32\tau\lambda^2/n},$ so each $\bar U_j=n^{-1}\sum_iU_{ij}$ has proxy $64\tau/n$. Apply [F5] at $s=\sqrt{128\tau u/n}$ to obtain $\mathbb P\!\left(\max_j|\bar U_j|>s\right)\le2p e^{-u}.$

Set $r=u/n$ and $t=64\tau(\sqrt r+r)$. Applying [F3] to $n^{-1}\sum_iW_i^{jk}$ gives $\mathbb P\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_iW_i^{jk}\right|>t\right)\le2\exp\!\left[-\frac12\min\!\left\{\frac{nt^2}{1024\tau^2},\frac{nt}{16\tau}\right\}\right]\le2e^{-2u},$ because each expression inside the minimum is at least $4u$. Expanding [F8] gives $\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}=n^{-1}\sum_iU_{ij}U_{ik}-\bar U_j\bar U_k$. Let $\Sigma\in G_q(c_{n,p})$ from [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]], let $\widehat\Sigma$ be the output of [[alg-entrywise-thresholded-sample-covariance]] with threshold $\lambda>0$, and suppose
$$\max_{1\le j,k\le p}|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}|\le\lambda/2.$$
Then
$$\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C_q\left(c_{n,p}\lambda^{1-q}+\lambda\right),$$
where $C_q<\infty$ depends only on $q$; for $q=0$, the class means at most $c_{n,p}$ nonzero off-diagonal entries per column and one may take $C_0=2$.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid from $\mathcal P_q(\tau,c_{n,p})$ of [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]], with $n\ge1$, $p\ge2$, and $\tau>0$. Let $u>0$ and let $\widehat\Sigma^\ast$ be the sample-centered covariance. Then
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le j,k\le p}|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}| \le192\tau\left(\sqrt{\frac un}+\frac un\right)\right)\ge1-2pe^{-u}-2p^2e^{-2u}.$$
In particular $u=\log(8p^4)$ gives the original probability $1-p^{-2}$.
No independence between coordinates of a single observation is assumed.

Input: observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n\in\mathbb R^p$, with integers $n\ge1$, $p\ge2$, and a fixed threshold constant $\gamma_\tau>0$ determined by the directional sub-Gaussian tail parameter $\tau$.

Compute the sample-centered covariance $\widehat\Sigma^\ast$ from [[def-sample-covariance-and-operator-norm-loss]] and put $\lambda=\gamma_\tau\sqrt{\log(p)/n}$. Output the symmetric matrix $\widehat\Sigma$ defined by
$$\widehat\sigma_{jj}=\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jj},\qquad \widehat\sigma_{jk}=\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}\mathbf 1\{|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}|\ge\lambda\}\quad(j\ne k).$$
The diagonal is unchanged; an off-diagonal entry at threshold equality is retained. This procedure is a definition and makes no risk or positive-semidefiniteness guarantee.

derivations.claim: Put $m=\log p/n$ and $r=u/n$. Since $p\ge2$, $\log 8=3\log2\le3\log p$, so $u=\log8+4\log p\le7\log p$ and $r\le7m\le7$. Thus $\sqrt r+r\le(1+\sqrt7)\sqrt r<4\sqrt r<12\sqrt m$. On the event in step 1.1, [F1] applies to the thresholded estimator of [F3] and yields $\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C_q(c_{n,p}\lambda^{1-q}+\lambda).$ Substituting $\lambda=8192\tau\sqrt m$ and absorbing the fixed factor $8192^{1-q}$ into a finite constant depending only on $q$ gives the stated bound. The event probability is at least $1-p^{-2}$.

Let $p\ge2$ be an integer, $0\le q<1$, $c_{n,p}\ge0$, and $\tau>0$. For a symmetric covariance matrix $\Sigma=(\sigma_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le p}$, write
$$|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(1)}\ge\cdots\ge|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(p-1)}$$
for the magnitudes of the off-diagonal entries in column $j$, arranged in nonincreasing order. Define
$$G_q(c_{n,p})=\left\{\Sigma:\max_{1\le j\le p}\max_{1\le k\le p-1} k|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(k)}^q\le c_{n,p}\right\}\quad(0<q<1).$$
For $q=0$, define $G_0(c_{n,p})$ to be the symmetric covariance matrices with at most $c_{n,p}$ nonzero off-diagonal entries in each column. The corresponding law class $\mathcal P_q(\tau,c_{n,p})$ consists of iid laws of $X\in\mathbb R^p$ whose covariance lies in $G_q(c_{n,p})$ and which satisfy
$$P(|v^{\mathsf T}(X-\mathbb E X)|>t)\le e^{-t^2/(2\tau)}
$$
for every unit vector $v$ and every $t>0$. This is a clean sub-Gaussian model; it assumes neither coordinate independence nor robustness to contamination.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

Let $n,p\ge1$ be integers and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent identically distributed random vectors in $\mathbb R^p$ with finite second moments, mean $\mu=\mathbb E X_1$, and covariance matrix
$$\Sigma=\mathbb E[(X_1-\mu)(X_1-\mu)^{\mathsf T}].$$
The oracle-centered sample covariance and the sample-centered covariance are respectively
$$\widehat\Sigma_\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)(X_i-\mu)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \widehat\Sigma^\ast=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)(X_i-\bar X)^{\mathsf T},\quad \bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
For a matrix estimate $A$, squared operator loss is $\|A-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$, with the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. This definition distinguishes the known-mean raw second moment from the estimator that removes an unknown mean.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric, where $p\ge1$. Then
$$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_{\|v\|_2=1}|v^{\mathsf T}Av|=\max_j|\lambda_j|,$$
where $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p$ are the eigenvalues of $A$.

Let $\mathcal Q$ be a family of probability laws on a common measurable sample space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)$, and let $\Sigma(Q)\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be a specified matrix parameter for each $Q\in\mathcal Q$, with fixed $p\ge1$. Give $\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ its usual Euclidean topology and Borel sigma-algebra. An estimator is a measurable map $\widehat\Sigma:(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)\to(\mathbb R^{p\times p},\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{p\times p}))$. Define its squared operator risk at $Q$ and the minimax risk over $\mathcal Q$ by
$$R_Q(\widehat\Sigma)=\mathbb E_Q\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(Q)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2,\qquad\mathfrak R(\mathcal Q)=\inf_{\widehat\Sigma}\sup_{Q\in\mathcal Q}R_Q(\widehat\Sigma).$$

For a family $\mathcal P$ of one-observation laws on a common measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and an integer $n\ge1$, the $n$-observation experiment observes $n$ independent observations, each with law $P$. Its sample space is $(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})$ and its sample law is the finite product probability measure $P^{\otimes n}$; this is the joint law of the IID family in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and [[def-independent-random-elements]]. For estimators $\widehat\Sigma:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\mathbb R^{p\times p},\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{p\times p}))$, define
$$R_{n,P}(\widehat\Sigma)=\mathbb E_{P^{\otimes n}}\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2,\qquad\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal P)=\inf_{\widehat\Sigma}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}R_{n,P}(\widehat\Sigma).$$

An infinite expectation is allowed, so every measurable estimator has an extended nonnegative risk. Suprema of risks are taken in the ordered range $[0,\infty]$, with $\sup\varnothing:=0$, its least element. Thus when $\mathcal Q$ or $\mathcal P$ is empty the corresponding supremum is zero for every estimator, and its minimax risk is zero. The estimator class is nonempty because the constant zero matrix map is measurable. The operator norm is from [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].

derivations.claim: Since $\log p_n\ge n^2$, $c_{n,p_n}\le M n^{-5/2}<1$ for all sufficiently large $n$; also $p_n\ge e^{n^2}\ge n^2$. The point mass at zero has zero covariance, zero off-diagonal entries, and directional tail probability zero, so it belongs to $\mathcal P_0(\tau,c_{n,p_n})$. Thus this class is nonempty. For any $P$ in it and any unit vector $v$, set $Y=v^{\mathsf T}(X-EX)$. By [F1]–[F2], $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(P)v=E_PY^2=\int_0^\infty P(Y^2>u)\,du \le\int_0^\infty e^{-u/(2\tau)}\,du=2\tau.$ By [F3], $\Sigma(P)$ is symmetric and $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(P)v=E_P[(v^{\mathsf T}(X-EX))^2]\ge0$. Taking the maximum over unit $v$ and using [F4] gives $\|\Sigma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\tau$.

The constant estimator $\widehat\Sigma\equiv0$ is measurable on the n-sample space. By [F5] and step 1.1, $\mathfrak R_n\bigl(\mathcal P_0(\tau,c_{n,p_n})\bigr) \le\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_0}E_{P^{\otimes n}}\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2 \le4\tau^2.$ This bound is independent of $n$ and $p_n$.

Since $e^{n^2}\le p_n<e^{n^2}+1\le2e^{n^2}$, we have $n\le\log p_n/n\le n+(\log2)/n$, so $\log p_n/n\sim n$. Hence $c_{n,p_n}^2\frac{\log p_n}{n}+\frac{\log p_n}{n} \ge\frac{\log p_n}{n}\longrightarrow\infty.$ No positive comparison constant independent of $n$ can make this diverging expression a lower bound for the uniformly bounded minimax risk in step 2.1. This contradicts the claimed equivalence.
