Let $d\ge1$, let $I$ be an invertible real symmetric matrix such that $v^TIv>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^d$, let $z\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty and closed in the Euclidean metric. Define $q_z(h):=z^Th-\tfrac12h^TIh$. Then there is a constant $\lambda>0$ such that $h^TIh\ge\lambda\|h\|_2^2$ for all $h$, $q_z$ attains its maximum on $C$, and

$$\sup_{h\in C}q_z(h)=\tfrac12z^TI^{-1}z-\tfrac12d_I^2(I^{-1}z,C).$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Let $(X_n)$ and $(Y_n)$ be real random variables on one probability space, and let $X$ be a real random variable (possibly on another space). If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n\to c$ in probability for $c\in\mathbb R$, then $X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c$ and $X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX$. If $c\ne0$, define $Q_n=X_n/Y_n$ on $\{Y_n\ne0\}$ and give $Q_n$ any fixed value on $\{Y_n=0\}$. Then $Q_n\Rightarrow X/c$.

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

Random elements $X_n,X$ with values in the same metric space **converge in distribution**, written $X_n\Rightarrow X$, if their laws from [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] satisfy $P_{X_n}\Rightarrow P_X$ in [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]. They may be defined on different probability spaces. The definition specifies only their marginal laws.

derivations.claim: With the supplied QMD information $I$ of [F1], write $q_z(h)=h^Tz-\tfrac12h^TIh$ and $m_A(z)=\sup_{h\in A}q_z(h)$ for $A=C,C_0$. By [F6], $m_A(z)=\tfrac12z^TI^{-1}z-\tfrac12d_I^2(I^{-1}z,A)$. If $h_A(z)$ is a maximizer, then $q_z(h_A(z))\ge q_z(0)=0$. The lower bound in [F6] and [F5] imply $\|h_A(z)\|_2\le2\|z\|_2/\lambda$ (with the bound immediate when $h_A(z)=0$).

Let $\lambda$ be from [F6], fix $M>0$, and choose $R>2M/\lambda+1$. For $A_n=C_n$, $A=C$ (and likewise for $A_n=C_{0n}$, $A=C_0$), write $m_{A_n,R}(z)=\sup_{h\in A_n\cap\overline B_2(0,R)}q_z(h)$. For every $\|z\|_2\le M$, [F6] gives a maximizer $h(z)$ of $q_z$ on $A$ with $\|h(z)\|_2\le2M/\lambda<R-1$. Local set convergence supplies points of $A_n$ within $\delta_{n,R-1}+1/n$ of $h(z)$, hence inside the radius-$R$ ball for all large $n$. Conversely, every point of $A_n\cap\overline B_2(0,R)$ is within $\delta_{n,R}+1/n$ of a point of $A$. With $B_I=\sum_{j,k=1}^d|I_{jk}|$, [F3] and [F5] give $|q_z(h)-q_z(h')|\le(M+B_I(R+1))\|h-h'\|_2$ for $\|h\|_2,\|h'\|_2\le R+1$ and $\|z\|_2\le M$. These two directions show $\sup_{\|z\|_2\le M}|m_{A_n,R}(z)-m_A(z)|\to0$. The same bounds apply to both full and null sets.

The sequence $Z_n$ is tight. Indeed, for any $\eta>0$ choose $R$ with $P(\|Z\|_2\ge R)<\eta$, possible because [F7] supplies a Borel probability law on finite-dimensional $\mathbb R^d$. The set $\{z:\|z\|_2\ge R\}$ is closed, so [F8] bounds $\limsup_nP(\|Z_n\|_2\ge R)$ by $\eta$. step 1.1 then makes the maximizers of $q_{Z_n}$ over $C$ and $C_0$ tight as well.

For $A_n=C_n$ or $C_{0n}$, put $L_{A_n,R}:=\sup_{h\in A_n\cap\overline B_2(0,R)}\{\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)\}$. Given $\eta>0$, tightness of $Z_n$ lets us choose $M$ so that $\|Z_n\|_2\le M$ with limiting probability at least $1-\eta/3$. Choose $R>2M/\lambda+1$ large enough that the joint event that both local likelihood maximizers lie in the radius-$R$ ball has limiting probability at least $1-\eta/3$. By step 1.1 both quadratic maximizers also lie in that ball whenever $\|Z_n\|_2\le M$. Thus all four full and truncated suprema agree except on events with total limiting upper probability at most $2\eta/3$. step 2.2 and arbitrariness of $\eta$ give $T_n-2(m_C(Z_n)-m_{C_0}(Z_n))\to_P0$.

The form $\langle u,v\rangle_I=u^TIv$ is an inner product; its Cauchy–Schwarz inequality follows by requiring $(u-tv)^TI(u-tv)\ge0$ for every real $t$. Thus the induced norm satisfies the triangle inequality, and taking infima gives $|d_I(x,C)-d_I(y,C)|\le\|x-y\|_I$. Also $v^TIv\le B_I\|v\|_2^2$, where $B_I$ is the finite entry sum from step 1.2, so the distance map is Euclidean Lipschitz after composition with the fixed linear map $I^{-1}$. Therefore $g(z):=d_I^2(I^{-1}z,C_0)-d_I^2(I^{-1}z,C)$ is continuous. The formula in step 1.1 gives $2[m_C(z)-m_{C_0}(z)]=g(z)$. By [F9], $g(Z_n)\Rightarrow g(Z)$. step 3.1 and [F10] then give $T_n\Rightarrow g(Z)$, which is the stated distance-difference law.

citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on

associated with this QMD score is

$$F_{X_n}(x)\longrightarrow F_X(x)$$
at every continuity point $x$ of $F_X$. Here $F_X$ is the CDF from
[[def-cumulative-distribution-function-of-a-random-variable]] and continuity
points are those of [[def-atom-and-continuity-point-of-a-law]].

$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

derivations.claim: On the probability-one event $0<X_{(n)}\le\theta$, the likelihood at a candidate $u>0$ is $L_n(u)=\prod_{i=1}^np_u(X_i)=u^{-n}\mathbf1\{X_{(n)}\le u\}$. Thus $X_{(n)}$ maximizes the likelihood almost surely; on the null event $X_{(n)}=0$, use the arbitrary positive assignment specified above.

For $0\le t<n\theta$, independence and the uniform CDF give $P_\theta\{n(\theta-X_{(n)})>t\}=P_\theta\{X_i<\theta-t/n\text{ for every }i\}=(1-t/(n\theta))^n$. For fixed $t\ge0$ this formula applies for all sufficiently large $n$, and its limit is $e^{-t/\theta}$.

For every $h>0$ small enough that $\theta+h>0$, the gained support interval $(\theta,\theta+h]$ has $p_\theta=0$ and $p_{\theta+h}=1/(\theta+h)$. If the model were QMD at $\theta$, the score term in [F2] would vanish on this interval and the squared remainder integral would be at least $\int_\theta^{\theta+h}p_{\theta+h}(x)\,dx=h/(\theta+h)$. But $[h/(\theta+h)]/h^2=1/[h(\theta+h)]\to\infty$, contradicting the required $o(h^2)$ remainder. Thus the model is not QMD at $\theta$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an integer $k\ge1$, let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_k)$ have law $N_k(0,I_k)$, so its coordinates are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The **chi-square law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $\chi_k^2$, is the law of
$$
Q_k=\sum_{j=1}^k G_j^2=\|G\|^2.
$$
For $k=0$, define $\chi_0^2=\delta_0$, the point mass at zero. This zero-degree law records a rank-zero projection only; it is not used as a denominator in a Student or Fisher ratio. The multivariate-normal characteristic-function theorem makes the definition independent of the chosen realization of $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and let $\theta_0\in\Theta_0$. Assume the full-model parameter set $\Theta$ is open in $\mathbb R^d$, so $\theta_0$ is interior for the QMD model. Under $P_{\theta_0}$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID and let $\ell_n(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log p_\theta(X_i)$ be their sample log-likelihood. Define local parameter sets $C_n:=\sqrt n(\Theta-\theta_0)$ and $C_{0n}:=\sqrt n(\Theta_0-\theta_0)$. Assume the model is QMD at $\theta_0$ as in [[def-qmd-path]], and write $I:=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$ for its Fisher information; assume $I$ is positive definite, meaning $v^TIv>0$ for every nonzero $v$. Suppose $C_n$ and $C_{0n}$ are closed in the Euclidean metric (their complements are open), contain $0$, and converge locally to nonempty closed convex cones $C$ and $C_0$ with $C_0\subseteq C$. A cone contains $0$ and is closed under multiplication by every nonnegative scalar; convex means that the set contains the line segment between each pair of its points. Local convergence means that, for every $R>0$, there are $\delta_{n,R}\to0$ such that every point of $C_n\cap\overline B_2(0,R)$ or $C\cap\overline B_2(0,R)$ is within $\delta_{n,R}$ in Euclidean distance of the other set, and likewise for $C_{0n}$ and $C_0$. Here a point $x$ is within $\delta$ of a set $A$ when $\inf_{a\in A}\|x-a\|_2\le\delta$.

Assume a uniform local quadratic likelihood expansion: for $h\in C_n$,

$$\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)=h^TZ_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+r_n(h),$$

where $Z_n\Rightarrow Z\sim N_d(0,I)$ under $P_{\theta_0}$ and, for every $R>0$, $\sup\{|r_n(h)|:h\in C_n,\ \|h\|_2\le R\}\to_P0$. Assume the full and null local log-likelihoods attain maxima at $\hat h_n\in C_n$ and $\hat h_{0n}\in C_{0n}$ and that both maximizer sequences are tight, meaning that for every $\eta>0$ some $R<\infty$ makes the limiting upper probability of either norm exceeding $R$ at most $\eta$. For

$$T_n:=2\left[\sup_{h\in C_n}\{\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)\}-\sup_{h\in C_{0n}}\{\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)\}\right],$$

the likelihood-ratio statistic satisfies

$$T_n\Rightarrow d_I^2(I^{-1}Z,C_0)-d_I^2(I^{-1}Z,C),$$

where $d_I$ is the Fisher-information distance of [[def-fisher-information-metric-distance]]. QMD alone is not asserted to imply the uniform expansion or tightness hypotheses.
Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid real random variables with mean $m$ and variance $0<\sigma^2<\infty$. Then $$\frac{\sum_{k=1}^nX_k-nm}{\sigma\sqrt n}\ \Rightarrow\ N(0,1).$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying

The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $0\le s,t$ and a real random variable
$X_t-X_s$ has law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then, for every integer $m\ge1$,
$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$
where
$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Put $q_\mu(x)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(4\sigma^2)}$. Direct differentiation gives $q'_\mu=(x-\mu)q_\mu/(2\sigma^2)$ and $q''_\mu=((x-\mu)^2/(4\sigma^4)-1/(2\sigma^2))q_\mu$. Its square is a polynomial times $p_\mu=q_\mu^2$. By [F8] and [F9], $\int (x-\mu)^2p_\mu\,dx=\sigma^2$ and $\int (x-\mu)^4p_\mu\,dx=3\sigma^4$, so $\|q''_\mu\|_2^2=3/(16\sigma^4)<\infty$. Also $s_\mu=2q'_\mu/q_\mu=(x-\mu)/\sigma^2$ has second moment $1/\sigma^2$. The identity $q''_a(x)=q''_0(x-a)$ and [F12] give the same norm for every real shift $a$. With $\sigma=1$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F13] gives $E|X-\mu|\le1$, so the even normal density [F1] gives $E(X-\mu)=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=1$. The two-variable functions $(x,v)\mapsto q''_{\mu+v}(x)$ and $(x,u)\mapsto q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ are continuous. To verify the needed product measurability locally, the rectangles $(a,b)\times(c,d)$ with rational endpoints form a countable base of $\mathbb R^2$: inside any open ball about a point, density of the rationals gives a rational rectangle containing that point and contained in the ball. Every open subset is therefore the union of the subfamily of these rectangles contained in it, hence a countable union of measurable product rectangles. Thus preimages of open subsets under these continuous functions belong to $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, and also to the product of the Lebesgue sigma-algebras. Their squares and restrictions to compact parameter intervals are consequently product measurable, as required by Tonelli below.

For fixed $x$, the functions $v\mapsto q''_{\mu+v}(x)$ and $u\mapsto q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ are continuous on each compact interval. By [F10] they are Riemann integrable, by [F15] their integrals are respectively $q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ and $q_{\mu+t}(x)-q_\mu(x)-tq'_\mu(x)$, and [F11] identifies these with their Lebesgue integrals under the assumed AC. Reversed endpoints give the same identities for negative $u,t$.

Cauchy–Schwarz [F13] on the interval between $0$ and $u$, then Tonelli [F14] and step 1.1, gives $\|q'_{\mu+u}-q'_\mu\|_2^2\le u^2\|q''_0\|_2^2$. The second identity of step 2.1 and another Cauchy–Schwarz/Tonelli application give $\|q_{\mu+t}-q_\mu-tq'_\mu\|_2^2\le |t|\int_0^{|t|}u^2\|q''_0\|_2^2du=|t|^4\|q''_0\|_2^2/3=o(t^2)$. For negative $t$ use $q'_{\mu-u}$ on the length-$|t|$ interval; the same first bound holds. This proves QMD with the explicitly supplied normal densities, score $s_\mu$, and positive information $1/\sigma^2$ by [F7].

Under $\mu=0$, the local sets are $C_n=\mathbb R$ and $C_{0n}=(-\infty,0]$ for every $n$, so they are already their limiting closed convex cones. Direct expansion gives $\ell_n(h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(0)=hZ_n-h^2/2$ with $Z_n=\sqrt n\bar X_n$ and zero remainder. The full and null local maximizers are $Z_n$ and $\min(0,Z_n)$. By [F4] and the mean and variance from step 1.1, $Z_n\Rightarrow G\sim N(0,1)$. Choose a large $R$ with $P(|G|\ge R)$ small and apply [F5] to the closed tails to see that both maximizer sequences are tight. Thus all hypotheses of [F3] hold with $I=1$.

Completing the square in $\ell_n(\mu)$ gives the full MLE $\bar X_n$ and the constrained MLE $\min(0,\bar X_n)$. Hence the finite-sample likelihood-ratio statistic is $T_n=2[\ell_n(\bar X_n)-\ell_n(\min(0,\bar X_n))]=n(\bar X_n\vee0)^2=(Z_n\vee0)^2$. By [F5], $T_n\Rightarrow(G\vee0)^2$. Its CDF is $0$ for $t<0$ and $P(G\le\sqrt t)=\Phi(\sqrt t)$ for $t\ge0$, so it has mass $1/2$ at zero. By symmetry, $P(G^2\le t)=2\Phi(\sqrt t)-1$ for $t\ge0$, while [F1] gives $P(G=0)=0$; hence $(G\vee0)^2$ has the mixture law $\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\mathcal L(G^2)=\tfrac12\chi_0^2+\tfrac12\chi_1^2$, not $\chi_1^2$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on it, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, and let $\mu$ be a fixed sigma-finite measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Suppose $(p_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ is a specified family of nonnegative measurable densities with $\int p_\theta\,d\mu=1$. Let $P$ be the actual data probability measure; it need not equal any model law $p_\theta\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Assume $p_\theta(X)>0$ $P$-almost surely and $\ell_\theta(X):=\log p_\theta(X)$ is integrable under $P$ for every parameter considered. Expectation means integration against $P$ ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

The population log-likelihood criterion is $M_P(\theta):=\mathbb E_P[\ell_\theta(X)]$. A **pseudo-true parameter** is any maximizer $\theta^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta\in\Theta}M_P(\theta)$. It is unique when this argmax set is the singleton $\{\theta^*\}$. The model is **misspecified relative to $P$** when $P\ne p_\theta\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$. This definition does not assert existence, uniqueness, interiority, or separation of the maximizer; those are theorem hypotheses when needed.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID from a probability law $P$ that is misspecified relative to the density family $p_\theta$, and let $\ell_\theta=\log p_\theta$ be as in [[def-pseudo-true-parameter-under-misspecification]]. Write $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nf(X_i)$ and $M(\theta)=\mathbb E_P\ell_\theta(X)$. Assume that $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, and that $\theta^*$ is the unique separated interior maximizer of $M$, where interior means that some Euclidean open ball about $\theta^*$ lies in $\Theta$: for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\eta_\varepsilon>0$ such that $M(\theta^*)-M(\theta)\ge\eta_\varepsilon$ whenever $\theta\in\Theta$ and $\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2\ge\varepsilon$. Assume the uniform law $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|P_n\ell_\theta-M(\theta)|\to_P0$, and let $\hat\theta_n\in\Theta$ be a measurable approximate maximizer with $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_n\ell_\theta-P_n\ell_{\hat\theta_n}\to_P0$.

Let $S_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta(x)$ be continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $\theta^*$. Assume $\mathbb E_PS_{\theta^*}=0$, $\mathbb E_P\|S_{\theta^*}\|_2^2<\infty$, and set $J=\mathbb E_P[S_{\theta^*}S_{\theta^*}^{T}]$. Suppose $H=\mathbb E_P[\nabla_\theta S_{\theta^*}]$ is nonsingular, $D(\theta):=\mathbb E_P[\nabla_\theta S_\theta]$ exists and is continuous at $\theta^*$, and for every sufficiently small fixed $\delta>0$,

$$\sup_{\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2\le\delta}\|P_n\nabla_\theta S_\theta-D(\theta)\|_{op}\to_P0,$$

where $\|A\|_{op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2\le1}\|Av\|_2$. Finally assume the approximate score equation $\sqrt n\,P_nS_{\hat\theta_n}=o_P(1)$. Then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta^*)\Rightarrow N_d\!\left(0,H^{-1}JH^{-T}\right).$$

The covariance is the sandwich matrix formed from the Hessian $H$ under $P$ and the score second moment $J$ under $P$. The theorem does not assert that it equals the inverse Fisher information of the fitted model.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: Let $Z\sim N(0,1)$, so $X\overset{d}=\tau Z$. Direct integration gives $E|Z|=2(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_0^\infty z e^{-z^2/2}dz=\sqrt{2/\pi}<\infty$, so symmetry gives $E Z=0$. Since $\phi'(z)=-z\phi(z)$ and $z^k\phi(z)\to0$ at both tails, integration by parts gives $E Z^2=\int z^2\phi(z)dz=1$ and $E Z^4=\int z^4\phi(z)dz=3\int z^2\phi(z)dz=3$. Hence $E_PX=0$, $E_PX^2=\tau^2$, and $E_PX^4=3\tau^4$. The fitted log-density is $\ell_\theta(x)=-\tfrac12\log(2\pi)-\tfrac12(x-\theta)^2$. The functions $1$, $X$, and $X^2$ are integrable by the finite absolute first and second moments just established. Thus the expanded log-density is a finite linear combination of integrable functions, and [F9] gives $E_P(X-\theta)^2=E_PX^2-2\theta E_PX+\theta^2$. Therefore $M(\theta)=E_P\ell_\theta(X)=-\tfrac12\log(2\pi)-\tfrac12(\tau^2+\theta^2)$, so $\theta^*=0$ is the unique separated maximizer, and $H=E_P\partial_\theta S_{\theta^*}(X)=-1$.

The uniform criterion error is bounded by $\sup_{\theta\in[-1,1]}|P_n\ell_\theta-M(\theta)|\le\tfrac12|P_nX^2-\tau^2|+|P_nX|$. Put $Y_i=X_i$ and $W_i=X_i^2-\tau^2$. All terms of the following single-variable expansions are integrable by the finite first, second, and fourth moments in step 1.1. Linearity [F9] therefore gives $\mathbb E_PY_i=\mathbb E_PW_i=0$, $\mathbb E_PY_i^2=\tau^2$, and $\mathbb E_PW_i^2=3\tau^4-2\tau^2\mathbb E_PX_i^2+\tau^4=2\tau^4$. Moreover $\mathbb E_P|Y_i|=\tau\mathbb E|Z|<\infty$ and $\mathbb E_P|W_i|\le\mathbb E_PX_i^2+\tau^2=2\tau^2$, so [F8] applies to these variables. By independence and [F8], all cross expectations $\mathbb E_P[Y_iY_j]$ and $\mathbb E_P[W_iW_j]$ vanish for $i\ne j$. For either centered family $V_i=Y_i$ or $V_i=W_i$, $|V_iV_j|\le(V_i^2+V_j^2)/2$ makes every mixed product integrable. Thus [F9] permits termwise expectation of each finite square expansion and gives $\mathbb E_P[(P_nX)^2]=\tau^2/n$ and $\mathbb E_P[(P_nX^2-\tau^2)^2]=2\tau^4/n$. Applying [F5] to these squared deviations gives $P_nX\to_P0$ and $P_nX^2\to_P\tau^2$ by [F7], proving the required uniform law.

The exact constrained MLE is $\hat\theta_n=\Pi_{[-1,1]}(\bar X_n)$, the projection of the sample mean onto $[-1,1]$. step 2.1 and [F7] give $\bar X_n\to_P0$, hence $\hat\theta_n\to_P0$ and the separated-criterion consistency condition holds. On $\{|\bar X_n|\le1\}$ the score equation is exact: $P_nS_{\hat\theta_n}=\bar X_n-\hat\theta_n=0$. The complementary event has probability tending to zero, so $\sqrt nP_nS_{\hat\theta_n}\to_P0$. The score is $S_\theta(x)=x-\theta$, its second moment at $\theta^*=0$ under $P$ is $J=\tau^2$, and the sample Hessian is identically $-1$, so the Hessian law holds with $H=-1$.

All hypotheses of [F4] now hold. It gives $\sqrt n\hat\theta_n\Rightarrow N(0,H^{-1}JH^{-T})=N(0,\tau^2)$. The fitted model's score second moment at $\theta=0$ is $E_{N(0,1)}[(X-0)^2]=1$, so the sandwich variance $\tau^2$ differs from the inverse fitted-model information $1$ because $\tau^2\ne1$.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. A **density version** on $\mathbb R^d$ is a Borel
function $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,d\lambda_d=1.$$
Write $P_f=f\,d\lambda_d$ for its probability law
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Let $\Theta$ be any set of such density
versions. For sample size $n\ge1$, the iid experiment has data space
$$\left((\mathbb R^d)^n,\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\right)$$
and sampling law $P_f^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $f\in\Theta$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]],
[[def-independent-random-elements]],
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
The pointwise target at $x\in\mathbb R^d$ is the estimand
$$\psi_x(f)=f(x):\Theta\to\mathbb R$$
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

A **normalized kernel** is a Borel function $K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with
$K\in L^1(\lambda_d)$ and $\int K\,d\lambda_d=1$. It may be signed. For
bandwidth $h>0$ and observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the kernel density estimate
is the indexed family
$$\widehat f_h(x)=\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For each fixed $x$, this is intended as a real-valued estimator of $\psi_x$;
the next local lemma supplies its measurability
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]).

Assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if $K$ is pointwise nonnegative the estimate
is a probability density for every sample, as proved in
[[lem-nonnegative-kde-integrates-to-one]]. For a signed kernel the estimate
need not be nonnegative. Point evaluation depends on the selected density
version: this definition does not assert that $f\mapsto f(x)$ is
identifiable from the law $P_f$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability

([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

$K\in L^1(\lambda_d)$ and $\int K\,d\lambda_d=1$. It may be signed. For
bandwidth $h>0$ and observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the kernel density estimate

$$\widehat f_h(x)=\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

the next local lemma supplies its measurability
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]).

is a probability density for every sample, as proved in
[[lem-nonnegative-kde-integrates-to-one]]. For a signed kernel the estimate
need not be nonnegative. Point evaluation depends on the selected density
version: this definition does not assert that $f\mapsto f(x)$ is

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.

   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose

and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is

page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable

the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for

Integration by parts and the second fundamental theorem [F5] give $q(1)-q(0)-q'(0)=\int_0^1(1-t)q''(t)dt.$ Since $|q''(t)|\le C\|y\|^2$ and $\int_0^1(1-t)dt=1/2$, this yields $\left|f(x+y)-M-g\cdot y\right|\le\frac C2\|y\|^2,$ so both the upper and lower Taylor bounds with this remainder hold. Taking $y=-g/C$ and using $f\ge0$ yields $0\le f(x-g/C)\le M-\|g\|^2/(2C)$; hence $\|g\|\le\sqrt{2CM}$.

If $M>0$, put $r=\tfrac18\sqrt{M/C}$. For every $y$ with $\|y\|\le r$, the corresponding lower Taylor bound and step 1.1 give $f(x+y)\ge M-\|g\|r-\frac C2r^2\ge M\left(1-\frac{\sqrt2}{8}-\frac1{128}\right)\ge\frac12M.$ The cube $Q=x+[-r/\sqrt d,r/\sqrt d]^d$ lies in that ball and has measure $\lambda_d(Q)=(2r/\sqrt d)^d=(M/(16Cd))^{d/2}$ by [A1] and [F2].

Monotonicity [F3] and $\int f=1$ now imply $1\ge\int_Qf\,d\lambda_d\ge\frac12M\left(\frac{M}{16Cd}\right)^{d/2}.$ Thus $M^{1+d/2}\le2(16Cd)^{d/2}$ for every $x$ with $f(x)>0$; points where $f(x)=0$ satisfy the same resulting finite bound. Therefore $f$ is bounded.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by

**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the

$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose

and $u'v$ are integrable and

then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable

differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does

continuous integrands.

Integration by parts and the second fundamental theorem [F7] give $g(x-hu)=g(x)-h\nabla g(x)\cdot u+ h^2\int_0^1(1-t)\,u^TD^2g(x-thu)u\,dt.$ The first moments are absolutely integrable since $|u_j|\le1+\|u\|^2$ and $K\in L^1$ with $M_2(K)<\infty$. statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. A **density version** on $\mathbb R^d$ is a Borel
function $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,d\lambda_d=1.$$
Write $P_f=f\,d\lambda_d$ for its probability law
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Let $\Theta$ be any set of such density
versions. For sample size $n\ge1$, the iid experiment has data space
$$\left((\mathbb R^d)^n,\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\right)$$
and sampling law $P_f^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $f\in\Theta$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]],
[[def-independent-random-elements]],
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
The pointwise target at $x\in\mathbb R^d$ is the estimand
$$\psi_x(f)=f(x):\Theta\to\mathbb R$$
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

A **normalized kernel** is a Borel function $K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with
$K\in L^1(\lambda_d)$ and $\int K\,d\lambda_d=1$. It may be signed. For
bandwidth $h>0$ and observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the kernel density estimate
is the indexed family
$$\widehat f_h(x)=\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For each fixed $x$, this is intended as a real-valued estimator of $\psi_x$;
the next local lemma supplies its measurability
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]).

Assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if $K$ is pointwise nonnegative the estimate
is a probability density for every sample, as proved in
[[lem-nonnegative-kde-integrates-to-one]]. For a signed kernel the estimate
need not be nonnegative. Point evaluation depends on the selected density
version: this definition does not assert that $f\mapsto f(x)$ is
identifiable from the law $P_f$.

Fix $x\in\mathbb R^d$, $h>0$, $n\ge1$, and a Borel normalized kernel $K$.
The evaluation map
$$T_x:(\mathbb R^d)^n\to\mathbb R,\qquad (z_1,\ldots,z_n)\mapsto\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^nK\!\left(\frac{x-z_i}{h}\right)$$
is measurable for the finite product Borel sigma-algebra. Hence it is a
statistic on the iid density experiment.

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be a density version with all partial
derivatives through order two existing and continuous, so
$\int f\,d\lambda_d=1$. If its Hessian satisfies
$H:=\sup_x\|D^2f(x)\|_{op}<\infty$, then $f$ is bounded.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Apply [F5] separately to $g^+$ and $g^-$, then subtract their finite integrals using [F7]: $\mathbb EZ_i=\int g^+f-\int g^-f=\int gf$. This derives the signed density identity without applying the nonnegative density theorem directly to $g$. Since the $X_i$ have the same law, the $Z_i$ have the same expectation. Linearity [F7] and the signed substitution in [F6] therefore yield $\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)=\frac1{h^d}\mathbb E Z_1 =\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(u)f(x-hu)du.$

For fixed $u$, set $q(t)=f(x-thu)$ on $[0,1]$. By [F9], $q'(0)=-h
abla f(x)\cdot u$ and $q''(t)=h^2u^TD^2f(x-thu)u$. Integration by parts with $1-t$ and $q'$, then the second fundamental theorem, gives $f(x-hu)=f(x)-h
abla f(x)\cdot u+ h^2\int_0^1(1-t)u^TD^2f(x-thu)u\,dt.$ For $u
e0$, subtracting $ rac{h^2}{2}u^TD^2f(x)u$ defines a remainder $h^2\|u\|^2ho(h,u)$, where $ho(h,u)=\int_0^1(1-t)  rac{u^T(D^2f(x-thu)-D^2f(x))u}{\|u\|^2}dt.$ Continuity of the Hessian at $x$ gives $ho(h,u)	o0$ for each fixed $u$; the global Hessian bound gives $|ho(h,u)|\le H$ uniformly in $h,u$. Set $ho(h,0)=0$.

Substitute the expansion from step 1.2 into the convolution in step 1.1. Statement: The expansion remains valid when f(x)=0 or the Hessian at x vanishes.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all three steps and fourteen direct suppliers. C2 nonnegative density with bounded Hessian is bounded by the independently reviewed lemma. This gives finite absolute kernel moments against the sampling density for each h; signed expectation is rigorously derived from nonnegative parts and finite linearity. The affine substitution has determinant magnitude h^d. Integral Taylor remainder tends to zero after division by h^2*||u||^2 for each u and is uniformly bounded by H. Absolute second moment dominates the remainder, and DCT applies along any h sequence tending to zero; unit mass and absolutely finite centered first moments cancel constant/linear terms. u=0 is explicitly defined and every mu_jk is absolutely finite. The result is at each fixed x, not uniform in x. AC_omega is carried; reader locator repair accepted.

$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: Put $Z_i=K((x-X_i)/h)$. By [F2] and [F7], and using the nonnegative substitution $u\mapsto x-hu$ from [F8], $\mathbb E[Z_i^2]=h^d\int K(u)^2f(x-hu)du \le h^d\|f\|_\infty\|K\|_2^2<\infty.$ Likewise $\mathbb E|Z_i|\le h^d\|f\|_\infty\|K\|_1<\infty$, so each $Z_i$ is integrable and square-integrable. The maps $z\mapsto K((x-z)/h)$ preserve independence by [F4]; identical laws of $X_i$ give identical laws of $Z_i$.

Let $W_i=Z_i-\mathbb E Z_i$. For $i\ne j$, [F5] applied to the independent integrable variables $W_i,W_j$ gives $\mathbb E[W_iW_j]=\mathbb E[W_i]\mathbb E[W_j]=0$. Expanding the finite square and using expectation linearity [F11] therefore gives $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_h(x)) =\frac{1}{nh^{2d}}\left(\mathbb E[Z_1^2]-(\mathbb EZ_1)^2\right).$

Step 1.1 shows that $t\mapsto K((x-t)/h)f(t)$ is integrable. Put $g(t)=K((x-t)/h)$ and decompose $g=g^+-g^-$ into its nonnegative parts. The density integrals of both parts are finite because $\int|g|f<\infty$ by step 1.1. Apply the nonnegative density identity [F7] to each part and subtract using [F11], obtaining $\mathbb EZ_1=\int gf$. Applying the signed substitution [F9] to this integrable product gives $\mathbb E Z_1=h^d\int K(u)f(x-hu)du$, so $|\mathbb EZ_1|\le h^d\|f\|_\infty\|K\|_1$. Along any sequence $h_n\to0$, [F10] gives $\int K(u)^2f(x-h_nu)du\longrightarrow f(x)\|K\|_2^2.$ Thus the first term in step 2.1 is $f(x)\|K\|_2^2/(nh_n^d)+o((nh_n^d)^{-1})$. The subtracted mean-square term is $O(n^{-1})=o((nh_n^d)^{-1})$ because $h_n^d\to0$. The additional $nh_n^d\to\infty$ condition places the expansion in the vanishing-variance regime. This proves the formula.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all three proof steps and thirteen direct suppliers. Bounded continuous f and K in L1 intersect L2 imply finite first and square moments for every h>0, including signed K. Measurable transforms preserve independence; product factorization gives zero centered cross terms. Exact variance is (E Z1^2-(E Z1)^2)/(n*h^(2d)). DCT with ||f||infinity*K^2 gives the leading term, and the mean-square subtraction is O(1/n), hence little-o of 1/(n*h^d) since h->0. The displayed nh^d->infinity is sufficient for vanishing variance though not required for the expansion itself. At f(x)=0 the absolute little-o statement still holds. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. A **density version** on $\mathbb R^d$ is a Borel
function $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,d\lambda_d=1.$$
Write $P_f=f\,d\lambda_d$ for its probability law
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Let $\Theta$ be any set of such density
versions. For sample size $n\ge1$, the iid experiment has data space
$$\left((\mathbb R^d)^n,\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\right)$$
and sampling law $P_f^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $f\in\Theta$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]],
[[def-independent-random-elements]],
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
The pointwise target at $x\in\mathbb R^d$ is the estimand
$$\psi_x(f)=f(x):\Theta\to\mathbb R$$
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

A **normalized kernel** is a Borel function $K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with
$K\in L^1(\lambda_d)$ and $\int K\,d\lambda_d=1$. It may be signed. For
bandwidth $h>0$ and observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the kernel density estimate
is the indexed family
$$\widehat f_h(x)=\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For each fixed $x$, this is intended as a real-valued estimator of $\psi_x$;
the next local lemma supplies its measurability
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]).

Assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if $K$ is pointwise nonnegative the estimate
is a probability density for every sample, as proved in
[[lem-nonnegative-kde-integrates-to-one]]. For a signed kernel the estimate
need not be nonnegative. Point evaluation depends on the selected density
version: this definition does not assert that $f\mapsto f(x)$ is
identifiable from the law $P_f$.

For a Borel normalized kernel $K$, $h>0$ and $n\ge1$, the map
$$Q_h:(\mathbb R^d)^n\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R,\qquad (z_1,\ldots,z_n,x)\mapsto\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-z_i}{h}\right)$$
is Borel measurable for the finite product Borel sigma-algebra.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f$ be a density version in
$W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d)$, and let $K$ be a normalized Borel kernel with
$K\in L^1$, $\int u_jK(u)\,du=0$ for every $j$, and
$$M_2(K):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|K(u)|\,\|u\|^2du<\infty.$$
Define the convolution $S_hf=\int K(u)f(\cdot-hu)du$ as an $L^2$ equivalence
class. With
$$\|D^2f\|_{2,F}^2:=\sum_{j,k=1}^d\|\partial_{jk}f\|_{L^2}^2,$$
one has, for every $h>0$,
$$\|S_hf-f\|_{L^2}\le\frac{h^2}{2}M_2(K)\,\|D^2f\|_{2,F}.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

If $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable and $\int f\,d\mu<+\infty$, then
$f(x)<+\infty$ for almost every $x$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: For fixed $h$, [F2] makes $(z,x)\mapsto\widehat f_h(x)$ Borel, and [F1] makes $f(x)$ Borel as a function of $(z,x)$. Arithmetic measurability in [F2] therefore makes the squared error product-measurable and nonnegative. Tonelli [F6] identifies MISE with the integral over $x$ of its expected pointwise squared error, even before finiteness has been established.

Write $q_h(x,z)=h^{-d}K((x-z)/h)$. By Tonelli and the substitution $z+hu$ in [F8], $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbb E|q_h(x,X_1)|dx=\|K\|_1, \qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbb E[q_h(x,X_1)^2]dx =h^{-d}\|K\|_2^2.$ Consequently, [F9] makes the summands integrable and square-integrable for almost every $x$. For such $x$, put $g(z)=q_h(x,z)$ and $g^+=\max(g,0)$, $g^-=\max(-g,0)$. The nonnegative density formula [F7] applied to $|g|$ shows $\int|g|f<\infty$. Thus both parts have finite density integrals, and [F7] applied separately to them, followed by subtraction using [F11], gives $\mathbb E q_h(x,X_1)=\int g(z)f(z)dz$. Signed substitution [F8] then identifies this integral with $S_hf(x)$, and identical laws plus finite-sum linearity [F11] give $\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)=S_hf(x)$.

At almost every $x$ from step 2.1, the variables $q_h(x,X_i)$ are iid and square-integrable. Set $W_i=q_h(x,X_i)-\mathbb E q_h(x,X_i)$. These are independent, integrable and square-integrable by [F5] and step 2.1; for $i\ne j$, [F5] makes $W_iW_j$ integrable and gives $\mathbb E[W_iW_j]=\mathbb EW_i\,\mathbb EW_j=0$. Expanding the finite square in the variance definition [F10] and applying [F11] gives $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_h(x))=n^{-2}\sum_i\mathbb EW_i^2=\operatorname{Var}(q_h(x,X_1))/n$. Expanding one centered square using [F10]–[F11] gives $\operatorname{Var}(q_h(x,X_1))=\mathbb E[q_h(x,X_1)^2]-(\mathbb E q_h(x,X_1))^2\le\mathbb E[q_h(x,X_1)^2]$. Integrating and using step 2.1 bounds the integrated variance by $\|K\|_2^2/(nh^d)$.

For almost every $x$, step 2.1 identifies the bias with $S_hf(x)-f(x)$. The $L^2$ bound [F3] therefore gives $\int_{\mathbb R^d}(\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))^2dx \le\frac{h^4}{4}M_2(K)^2\|D^2f\|_{2,F}^2.$

At almost every $x$, expand $\widehat f_h(x)-f(x)=(\widehat f_h(x)-\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x))+(\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))$. The centered term has expectation zero, so [F10]–[F11] give $\mathbb E[(\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))^2] =\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_h(x)) +(\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))^2.$ Integrate this nonnegative identity using step 1.1, then apply steps 3.1 and 3.2 to obtain the displayed MISE bound. For $h_n=n^{-1/(d+4)}$, both $h_n^4$ and $(nh_n^d)^{-1}$ equal $n^{-4/(d+4)}$, which proves the stated upper rate.

boundaries.evidence: The statement assumes n,d≥1 and a density of integral one.
Statement: A vanishing bias term leaves the variance bound; h=0 is excluded.
Statement: The inequality applies at n=1; the rate choice is asymptotic in n.
Statement: The bound permits zero target values and signed kernels with the stated moments.

boundaries.reason: All norms and integrals range over R^d.

boundaries.reason: Joint measurability, integrated variance and the Sobolev convolution estimate give the MISE upper bound and balanced bandwidth rate in step 4.1.
The upper rate is explicitly not a minimax lower bound and does not characterize all densities with that risk rate.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all five steps and eighteen direct suppliers. Joint Borel measurability licenses Tonelli before finiteness. Integrated absolute and square summand moments are exactly ||K||1 and h^(-d)||K||2^2; hence a common full-measure set has finite moments. Positive/negative parts derive the signed density formula, and affine substitution identifies expectation with the L2 convolution. Independence kills centered cross terms, bounding integrated variance by ||K||2^2/(n*h^d). The reviewed W2,2 bias supplier gives h^4*M2^2*||D2f||2,F^2/4; pointwise bias-variance identity holds almost everywhere and Tonelli yields finite MISE. n=1, every h>0, signed K and arbitrary Borel density versions in the Sobolev class are covered; no boundedness of f is assumed. h=n^(-1/(d+4)) balances the two powers exactly. This is only an upper rate, not a lower bound. AC_omega is explicit. Reader APTS locator correction is sound.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The nonnegative improper plane Gaussian integral satisfies

$$\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,d(x,y)=\pi.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid with a Borel
probability density version $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$. Let
$K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be Borel with $K\in L^1\cap L^2$,
$\int K(u)du=1$, $\int u_jK(u)du=0$ for each $j$, and
$\int|K(u)|\|u\|^2du<\infty$. Suppose $f$ has continuous second partial
derivatives and a globally bounded continuous Hessian. At each fixed
$x\in\mathbb R^d$, as $h\downarrow0$,
$$\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x) =\frac{h^2}{2}\sum_{j,k=1}^d\mu_{jk}\,\partial_{jk}f(x)+o(h^2), \qquad \mu_{jk}:=\int_{\mathbb R^d}u_ju_kK(u)du.$$
Here $r(h)=o(h^2)$ means $r(h)/h^2\to0$ as $h\downarrow0$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid with bounded
continuous Borel density version $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$. Let
