The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. A **density version** on $\mathbb R^d$ is a Borel
function $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,d\lambda_d=1.$$
Write $P_f=f\,d\lambda_d$ for its probability law
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Let $\Theta$ be any set of such density
versions. For sample size $n\ge1$, the iid experiment has data space
$$\left((\mathbb R^d)^n,\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\right)$$
and sampling law $P_f^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $f\in\Theta$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]],
[[def-independent-random-elements]],
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
The pointwise target at $x\in\mathbb R^d$ is the estimand
$$\psi_x(f)=f(x):\Theta\to\mathbb R$$
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

A **normalized kernel** is a Borel function $K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with
$K\in L^1(\lambda_d)$ and $\int K\,d\lambda_d=1$. It may be signed. For
bandwidth $h>0$ and observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the kernel density estimate
is the indexed family
$$\widehat f_h(x)=\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For each fixed $x$, this is intended as a real-valued estimator of $\psi_x$;
the next local lemma supplies its measurability
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]).

Assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if $K$ is pointwise nonnegative the estimate
is a probability density for every sample, as proved in
[[lem-nonnegative-kde-integrates-to-one]]. For a signed kernel the estimate
need not be nonnegative. Point evaluation depends on the selected density
version: this definition does not assert that $f\mapsto f(x)$ is
identifiable from the law $P_f$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

The nonnegative improper plane Gaussian integral satisfies

$$\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,d(x,y)=\pi.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim: Put $I=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-t^2}dt$. Tonelli [F5] and [F4] give $I^2=\pi$, so $I=\sqrt\pi$. Scaling by $s=t/\sqrt2$ with [F6] yields $\int (2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}dt=1$; repeated Tonelli gives $\int K_d=1$. Since $f_\tau(x)=\tau^{-d}K_d(x/\tau)$, [F6] with $x=\tau u$ gives $\int f_\tau=1$.

By [F1] and [F2], expectation of one KDE summand is integration of its Gaussian kernel against $f_\tau$. The summand is bounded for fixed $h$, hence integrable. The integrand is nonnegative; using [F6] with $T(u)=x-hu$ changes variables to $\int K_d(u)f_\tau(x-hu)du$. All summands have this expectation, so linearity [F3] gives $\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}K_d(u)f_\tau(x-hu)du.$ The integral is finite because both Gaussian densities are bounded and integrable.

In the integrand of step 2.1, combine exponents using $\|u\|^2+\tau^{-2}\|x-hu\|^2 =\frac{\tau^2+h^2}{\tau^2} \left\|u-\frac{h x}{\tau^2+h^2}\right\|^2 +\frac{\|x\|^2}{\tau^2+h^2}.$ The remaining translated Gaussian integral is $(2\pi\tau^2/ (\tau^2+h^2))^{d/2}$ by [F4], [F5], and affine scaling [F6]. Multiplying the normalizing constants gives the displayed formula.
At $x=0$, $\mathbb E\widehat f_h(0)=(2\pi(\tau^2+h^2))^{-d/2} <(2\pi\tau^2)^{-d/2}=f(0),$ because $h>0$. Therefore a finite positive bandwidth has nonzero bias in this example.

Example: At x=0 positive bandwidth increases covariance and strictly lowers the Gaussian peak.

Assume AC as used to select the regression version. Fix a statistical experiment indexed by $\theta$, a point $x$, a real
regression target $m_\theta(x)$, and a real-valued estimator
$T_x$ of that target, meaning a measurable statistic with target space
$\mathbb R$ as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. At this point, use the
squared-error loss
$$L_x(\theta,a)=(a-m_\theta(x))^2,\qquad a\in\mathbb R.$$
Its **pointwise squared-error risk** is the possibly infinite quantity
$$R_x(\theta,T_x)=\int (T_x(z)-m_\theta(x))^2\,P_\theta(dz)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is the deterministic-rule specialization of the risk in
[[def-loss-function-and-risk]]: the action space is $\mathbb R$ with its
Borel sigma-algebra, the action is $T_x(z)$, and the loss section is
measurable because it is continuous in $a$. The integral is nonnegative, so
it is defined without a finite-moment assumption.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

derivations.claim: For the general assertion truncate $L$ to $L_A=L\mathbf1_{\{|u|\le A,\ |L(u)|\le A\}}$. The expectation of $(nh)^{-1}\sum_iL_A(U_i)$ is $\int L_A(u)f(x-hu)\,du\to f(x)\int L_A$ by uniform density convergence on its fixed compact support. Its variance is at most $(nh)^{-1}\int L_A(u)^2f(x-hu)\,du=O_A((nh)^{-1})\to0$. The elementary bound $\mathbb P(|V-\mathbb EV|>\epsilon)\le\operatorname{Var}(V)/\epsilon^2$ follows by integrating $\epsilon^2\mathbf1_{\{|V-\mathbb EV|>\epsilon\}}\le(V-\mathbb EV)^2$. Thus the truncated average converges in probability.

The expectation of the absolute difference between the full and truncated averages is at most $C\int|L-L_A|$, using the global density bound or its bound on the shrinking image of the compact support of $L$. This tends to zero as $A\to\infty$. Markov's bound, obtained from $\epsilon\mathbf1_{\{Z>\epsilon\}}\le Z$ for $Z\ge0$, makes this difference uniformly small in probability. Also $\int L_A\to\int L$. First choosing $A$ large and then $n$ large proves the general assertion.

For the rapid-tail case and $L(u)=u^jK(u)$, $j=0,1,2$, restrict first to $|x-X_i|\le\delta$, where the density is bounded. The same truncation proof works there. The expected absolute contribution of the remaining observations is at most $\epsilon_h h^{2-j}\int_{|z-x|>\delta}|z-x|^{j-3}f(z)\,dz\to0$, where $\epsilon_h=\sup_{|u|\ge\delta/h}|u|^3K(u)\to0$. Thus the same scalar limits hold for these three moments without a global density bound.

$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure

whose measure property is supplied by

Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix a sample size $n\ge1$,
a prediction point $x\in\mathbb R$, a bandwidth $h>0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$, and a fixed fallback
$a_0\in\mathbb R$. For data $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$, put
$$D_{n,h}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h).$$
The **Nadaraya–Watson estimator** of the pointwise target $m(x)$ is
$$\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h}(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h)Y_i}{D_{n,h}(x)},&D_{n,h}(x)>0,\\[6pt] a_0,&D_{n,h}(x)=0. \end{cases}$$
For fixed $x,h,n$, this is a Borel statistic on $(\mathbb R^2)^n$ with its
product Borel sigma-algebra: each weight, product, and finite sum is Borel;
the positive-denominator set is Borel, and division is continuous there. In
any statistical experiment on this sample space whose pointwise regression
estimand is $\psi_x(\theta)=m_\theta(x)$, with $m_\theta$ the selected
version from [[def-regression-target-version]], it is an estimator of
$\psi_x$ in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The fallback is
part of the definition. Kernel regularity and bandwidth assumptions used for
bias or variance results are stated in those results.

Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix $n\ge1$, a point
$x\in\mathbb R$, bandwidth $h>0$, degree $p\in\mathbb N_0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K$, and fallback $a_0\in\mathbb R$. Set
$u_i=(x-X_i)/h$, $r_p(u)=(1,u,\ldots,u^p)^\mathsf T$, let $Z$ be the matrix
whose $i$th row is $r_p(u_i)^\mathsf T$, let
$W=\operatorname{diag}(K(u_1),\ldots,K(u_n))$, and put
$M=Z^\mathsf TWZ$. If $M$ is nonsingular, define
$$\widehat\beta=M^{-1}Z^\mathsf TW(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^\mathsf T,\qquad \widehat m_{p,h}(x)=\widehat\beta_0.$$
If $M$ is singular, define $\widehat m_{p,h}(x)=a_0$. For fixed $x,h,n,p$
and Borel $K$, this is a real statistic on $(\mathbb R^2)^n$ with its product
Borel sigma-algebra: the matrix entries are Borel, the nonsingular-matrix set
is Borel, matrix inversion is continuous there, and the fixed fallback gives
the other branch. In any statistical experiment on this sample space whose
pointwise regression estimand is $\psi_x(\theta)=m_\theta(x)$, with
$m_\theta$ the selected version from [[def-regression-target-version]], it
estimates $\psi_x$ in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The case
$p=1$ is the **local-linear estimator**. No claim that $M$ is nonsingular for
a given sample is implicit in this definition.

Let $X_i$ be iid real random variables with density $f$ continuous and
positive at a fixed point $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative,
symmetric, with $\int K=1$ and $0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$.
Assume compact kernel support, a globally bounded density $f$, or a bounded
rapid-tail kernel satisfying $\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)\to0$.
For $h=h_n\to0$ with $nh_n\to\infty$, set $U_i=(x-X_i)/h_n$ and
$$M_n=\frac1{nh_n}\sum_{i=1}^nK(U_i)\begin{pmatrix}1\\U_i\end{pmatrix}(1,U_i).$$
Then
$$M_n\longrightarrow f(x)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\mu_2\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{in probability},$$
and $\mathbb P(M_n\text{ is nonsingular})\to1$.
More generally, the proof establishes $(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_i L(U_i)\to f(x)\int L$
for any integrable Borel function $L$, if $f$ is bounded globally or $L$
has compact support. Boundedness or square integrability of $L$ is unnecessary.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Assume AC. Let X,Y take values in standard-Borel E,T, and let K be a disintegration kernel giving the conditional law of X given Y. For measurable $f:E\to[0,\infty]$, put $h(y)=\int_E f(x)K(y,dx)$. Then h is measurable and
$$E[f(X)\mid\sigma(Y)]=h(Y)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

For measurable real f with $E|f(X)|<\infty$, define $D=\{y:\int|f(x)|K(y,dx)<\infty\}$ and use the signed integral for h on D, zero off D. Then $P_Y(D)=1$, h is real measurable, and the same identity holds.

derivations.claim: By [F3], $M_n=(nh)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)(1,U_i)^\mathsf T(1,U_i)\to f(x)\operatorname{diag}(1,\mu_2)$ in probability. Put $V_n=(nh)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)^2\sigma^2(X_i)(1,U_i)^\mathsf T(1,U_i)$. The scalar generalization proved in [F3] applies also to a continuous multiplier $\sigma^2(x-hu)$: on fixed truncated support this multiplier converges uniformly to $\sigma^2(x)$ and is bounded, and the tail expectation is bounded by $C\int_{\mathrm{tail}}|L|$. Thus, for $L=K^2$ the $(0,0)$ entry tends to $f(x)\sigma^2(x)R(K)$. In the rapid-tail alternative, local truncation remains valid. For $j=0,1,2$ the expected absolute far contribution to $V_{n,j}$ is bounded by $C h^{5-j}\int_{|z-x|>\delta}|z-x|^{j-6}\sigma^2(z)f(z)\,dz=o(1)$, since [F7] gives $\int\sigma^2f\le\mathbb EY^2$. Also $\int(1+u^2)K^2<\infty$ follows from boundedness and the rapid tail. For the local-linear conclusion, $\int(1+u^2)K^2<\infty$ permits $L=K^2u^j$, $j=0,1,2$, by the same truncation argument. All entries then converge to $f(x)\sigma^2(x)\int K^2u^{j+k}$; symmetry makes the off-diagonal limit zero. Terms with $K(U_i)=0$ are interpreted as zero. Every active response-law variance is finite almost surely; these are variances under the specified conditional response laws, without an assumption of unconditional square integrability.

On the event $\sum_iK(U_i)>0$, [F1], conditional response independence, and [F4] give $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h_n}(x)\mid X_{1:n})=\dfrac{\sum_iK(U_i)^2\sigma^2(X_i)}{(\sum_iK(U_i))^2}$. Writing $M_{n,00}=(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)$ and $V_{n,00}=(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)^2\sigma^2(X_i)$ makes the scaled variance $V_{n,00}/M_{n,00}^2$, which converges to $f(x)\sigma^2(x)R(K)/f(x)^2$. The zero-denominator event has probability tending to zero by [F3]'s $(0,0)$ entry, so the same convergence holds with the fallback.

On a nonsingular local-linear design matrix, weighted least squares gives conditional variance $(nh_n)^{-1}e_0^\mathsf TM_n^{-1}V_nM_n^{-1}e_0$, where $e_0=(1,0)^\mathsf T$. The limit matrix is diagonal with entries $f(x)$ and $f(x)\mu_2$, so its inverse has first diagonal entry $1/f(x)$; the $(0,0)$ limit of $V_n$ is $f(x)\sigma^2(x)R(K)$. Matrix inversion is continuous at this invertible limit, because its entries are quotients of entries of the adjugate by the nonzero determinant. Thus the scaled conditional variance converges to $R(K)\sigma^2(x)/f(x)$. By [F3] the singular-design event has probability tending to zero, and the fallback does not change convergence in probability.

For the extra Nadaraya–Watson clause, choose $A,\kappa>0$ with $J=\{|u|\le A,K(u)\ge\kappa\}$ of positive measure, possible since $\int K=1$. Its predictor count is binomial with success probability $p_h\asymp h$. On $G_n=\{N\ge np_h/2\}$, $T_n=n^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)\ge c_1h$, whereas Markov's bound applied to $e^{-N}$ gives $\mathbb P(G_n^c)\le\exp(-c_2nh)$. The truncation argument of step 1.1 also proves $V_{n,00}\to f(x)\sigma^2(x)R(K)$ in $L^1$: the bounded truncated average converges in $L^2$, while the expected absolute tail is uniformly small. On $G_n$, $(T_n/h)^{-2}$ is bounded and converges in probability to $f(x)^{-2}$. It follows that the expectation of the scaled conditional variance on $G_n$ has the stated limit: separate $V_{n,00}$ into its constant limit and an $L^1$ error, and use bounded convergence in probability for the reciprocal factor. On $G_n^c$, the conditional variance is at most the active-region bound on $\sigma^2$, since the weights are nonnegative and sum to one, or the fallback is deterministic. Hence its scaled expectation is $O(nh e^{-c_2nh})\to0$ in those alternatives. Under rapid tails, the conditional variance is at most $\sum_i\sigma^2(X_i)$; the count among the other $n-1$ observations is independent of $X_i$ and is below $np_h/2$ on $G_n^c$. Its binomial lower-tail bound gives $\mathbb E[\sigma^2(X_i);G_n^c]\le\mathbb EY^2 e^{-c_3nh}$. Thus the contribution to the expected scaled conditional variance is at most $n^2h\mathbb EY^2e^{-c_3nh}$. Under the stated $nh^3\to\infty$ condition, $nh\ge n^{2/3}$ eventually, so this polynomial factor times the exponential tends to zero.

Let $A_n$ be the response-law mean of the Nadaraya–Watson fit, including its fallback, and let $m_h=\int Kmf/\int Kf$. The kernel integrals and localization or global bounds imply $m_h\to m(x)$. Put $Z_i=K(U_i)$ and $R_n=n^{-1}\sum_i Z_i(m(X_i)-m_h)$. Then $\mathbb ER_n=0$ and $\mathbb ER_n^2\le n^{-1}\mathbb E[Z_1^2(m(X_1)-m_h)^2]=o(h/n)$: after change of variables, continuity at $x$ handles a fixed compact $u$-set and the integrable $K^2$ tail is dominated by bounded $f,m$. On $G_n$, $A_n-m_h=R_n/T_n$, so its expected square is $o((nh)^{-1})$. On $G_n^c$, $A_n$ and $m_h$ are bounded in the compact/global alternatives. Under rapid tails, [F7] gives $\int m^2f<\infty$; the far part of the second-moment integral is $O(h^6)\int m^2f=o(h)$, and the leave-one-out binomial argument in step 3.1 gives $\mathbb E[A_n^2;G_n^c]\le n\mathbb EY^2e^{-c_4nh}+a_0^2\mathbb P(G_n^c)$. Its expected squared bad-event contribution is therefore negligible in all stated cases, and $\operatorname{Var}(A_n)\le\mathbb E(A_n-m_h)^2=o((nh)^{-1})$. Bounded active-region means and variances, or the bound $\widehat m^2\le\sum_iY_i^2+a_0^2$ under rapid tails, make the Nadaraya–Watson fit square-integrable. Expanding its centered square and integrating first under the response laws gives total variance equal to the expected conditional variance plus $\operatorname{Var}(A_n)$. Step 3.1 therefore proves the unconditional Nadaraya–Watson expansion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real random variables on a probability
space, with $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$, and choose a regular conditional law
$Q(x,dy)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$. On
$D=\{x:\int |y|\,Q(x,dy)<\infty\}$ define
$m(x)=\int y\,Q(x,dy)$, and put $m(x)=0$ off $D$. By
[[cor-conditional-expectation-as-a-measurable-function-of-the-conditioning-variable]],
$m$ is Borel measurable and $m(X)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E[Y\mid\sigma(X)]$. A **regression target** is the resulting
$P_X$-almost-sure equivalence class; a **chosen regression-function version**
is the particular Borel function selected by the specified conditional law.

Pointwise smoothness is an additional hypothesis on the chosen version. It is
not implied by existence of conditional expectation, and statements about
$m(x)$ at a specified point use that selected version.

derivations.claim: With $u_i=(x-X_i)/h$, the design row is $(1,u_i)$ and $X_i=x-hu_i$, so $Y_i=(a+bx)-bh\,u_i$. Thus the response vector is exactly $Z\gamma$ for $\gamma=(a+bx,-bh)^\mathsf T$.

The weighted least-squares formula gives $\widehat\beta=(Z^\mathsf TWZ)^{-1}Z^\mathsf TWZ\gamma=\gamma$. By the chosen-version convention in [F2], the specified conditional law in [A2] fixes $m(x)=a+bx$ at this evaluation point. Thus its intercept is $a+bx=m(x)$, proving exact reproduction of that chosen version.

Then
$$M_n\longrightarrow f(x)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\mu_2\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{in probability},$$
and $\mathbb P(M_n\text{ is nonsingular})\to1$.
More generally, the proof establishes $(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_i L(U_i)\to f(x)\int L$
for any integrable Borel function $L$, if $f$ is bounded globally or $L$

$Q(x,dy)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$. On

derivations.claim: Put $h=h_n$, $U_i=(x-X_i)/h$, $S_j=(nh)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)U_i^j$ and $r_h(u)=m(x-hu)-m(x)+hu m'(x)$. Then $S_0\to f(x)$, $S_2\to f(x)\mu_2$ by [F2]. Symmetry and the first-order density expansion give $\mathbb ES_1=-hf'(x)\mu_2+o(h)$; the tail is controlled by $u^2K$ under the global alternative. Also $\operatorname{Var}(S_1)\le C(nh)^{-1}\int u^2K^2$, using localization or the global density bound. In the rapid-tail alternative its local part has this bound, and the far contribution to $\operatorname{Var}(S_1)$ is at most $C h^2n^{-1}\int_{|z-x|>\delta}f(z)|z-x|^{-4}\,dz$, hence no larger than $O((nh)^{-1})$. Since $nh^3\to\infty$, $(S_1-\mathbb ES_1)/h\to0$ in probability by the variance bound, so $S_1=O_P(h)$.

Set $R_j=(nh)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)U_i^jr_h(U_i)$. Taylor's integral formula gives $|r_h(u)|\le Ch^2u^2$ and $r_h(u)/h^2\to\tfrac12m''(x)u^2$. The truncation proof of [F2] applies to this varying integrand: on any fixed set where $|u|$ and $K(u)$ are bounded it converges uniformly, its average has variance $O_A((nh)^{-1})$, and the absolute tail expectation is at most $C\int_{\mathrm{tail}}u^2K$. Hence $R_0/h^2\to\tfrac12m''(x)f(x)\mu_2$ in probability. Furthermore $|r_h(u)|\le Ch|u|$ and $r_h(u)/(h|u|)\to0$ pointwise. Splitting the integral as before gives $\mathbb E|R_1|/h\le\int K(u)|u||r_h(u)|f(x-hu)/h\,du\to0$. Markov's bound yields $R_1=o_P(h)$. Under the rapid-tail alternative [F5] gives $\int|m|f<\infty$; first apply these arguments on $|X_i-x|\le\delta$. For the far part put $\epsilon_h=\sup_{|u|\ge\delta/h}|u|^3K(u)\to0$ and expand $r=m(z)-m(x)-m'(x)(z-x)$. Its expected absolute contributions to $R_0/h^2$ and $R_1/h$ are bounded by $C_\delta\epsilon_h\int(1+|m|)f\to0$. The same tail estimate gives the stated expectation expansion for $S_1$. Thus all limits hold without global smoothness.

On a nonsingular design, [F1] and [F3] give $b_n-m(x)=(S_2R_0-S_1R_1)/(S_0S_2-S_1^2)$, since the constant and slope terms cancel exactly in the intercept. The singular-design event has probability tending to zero by [F2]; even after scaling by $h^{-2}$ the probability of any nonzero fallback contribution is at most that event probability, so it does not change convergence in probability. citations.quote: Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval and let $a\le t_1<\cdots<t_r\le b$ with $r\ge2$. A natural cubic spline with knots $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ is a $C^2$ function on $[a,b]$ that is a polynomial of degree at most three on every $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, has second derivative zero at $t_1$ and $t_r$, and is extended linearly on $[a,t_1]$ and $[t_r,b]$ when those intervals are nonempty. The knots $t_j$ are the distinct breakpoints; repeated observations at the same input do not create additional knots.

derivations.claim: Put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i$ and $d_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/h_i$. For $r=2$ there are no interior second derivatives to solve. For $r\ge3$, let $A$ be the $(r-2)\times(r-2)$ symmetric tridiagonal matrix with diagonal entry $2(h_{i-1}+h_i)$ in row $i$ and adjacent off-diagonal entries $h_i$. For a nonzero vector $v=(v_2,\ldots,v_{r-1})$, using $2v_iv_{i+1}\ge-v_i^2-v_{i+1}^2$ gives $v^TAv\ge\sum_{i=2}^{r-1}(h_{i-1}+h_i)v_i^2>0.$ Thus $A$ is positive definite and invertible, so the displayed system has exactly one solution $M_2,\ldots,M_{r-1}$.

On each interval define the displayed cubic. Direct substitution gives its endpoint values and second derivatives. Its left and right endpoint slopes are respectively d_i−M_i h_i/3−M_{i+1}h_i/6 and d_i+M_i h_i/6+M_{i+1}h_i/3. Equating the right slope from s_{i−1} and the left slope from s_i gives the tridiagonal equation. Hence the pieces join C^1; their second derivatives are linear with the same nodal values, so they join C^2. At the extreme knots M_1=M_r=0, so adjoining the tangent line gives the required linear tails and preserves C^2. For r=2, the formula is the straight line between the two values.

Any natural cubic interpolant has nodal second derivatives with $M_1=M_r=0$. Equality of its adjacent endpoint slopes forces the displayed tridiagonal equations, so by step 1.1 its nodal second derivatives equal the constructed ones. On each interval, the difference from $s_i$ is a cubic with zero second derivative at both endpoints; its second derivative is affine and therefore zero throughout, so the difference is affine and vanishes at both endpoint values. It is identically zero. Thus the interpolant is unique.

boundaries.reason: Statement and A1 require r>=2 strictly increasing knots. Step 1.1 handles the minimal r=2 case with an empty interior second-derivative system, rather than an empty data set.

Step 1.1 obtains the unique nodal second derivatives by inverting a positive-definite finite tridiagonal matrix; step 2.1 gives the cubic formula. This is explicit finite construction, not family selection.

citations.quote:
Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $n\ge p+1$, and $a<b$. A clamped knot vector is a nondecreasing finite sequence
$$\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_{p+1}=a<\xi_{p+2}\le\cdots\le\xi_n<\xi_{n+1}=\cdots=\xi_{n+p+1}=b,$$
with $\xi_j<\xi_{j+p+1}$ for every $1\le j\le n$. Empty interior ranges are omitted. The multiplicity $\mu(\eta)$ of an interior knot $\eta$ is its number of occurrences among $\xi_{p+2},\ldots,\xi_n$.

Write $\mathcal P_p$ for the real polynomials of degree at most $p$. The degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ consists of functions that restrict to a member of $\mathcal P_p$ on each nonempty knot interval and whose derivatives through order $p-\mu(\eta)$ agree across each interior knot $\eta$. The convention $C^{-1}$ means that no matching condition is imposed. For this piecewise definition, take knot cells left-closed and right-open; at a knot with no matching condition, the value is the one from the cell on its right, and at $b$ use the left limit. Thus the function value at a discontinuous knot is specified.

For each degree $d\in\{0,\ldots,p\}$, the functions $B_{j,d,\xi}$ are indexed by $1\le j\le n+p-d$. Set
$$B_{j,0,\xi}(x)=\mathbf 1_{[\xi_j,\xi_{j+1})}(x),\qquad 1\le j\le n+p.$$
For $1\le d\le p$ and $1\le j\le n+p-d$, define recursively
$$B_{j,d,\xi}(x)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}B_{j,d-1,\xi}(x)+\frac{\xi_{j+d+1}-x}{\xi_{j+d+1}-\xi_{j+1}}B_{j+1,d-1,\xi}(x),$$
where a term with zero denominator is defined to be zero. For every degree $d$ and every allowed index $j$, set $B_{j,d,\xi}(b)$ equal to its left limit. In particular, the degree-$p$ family has indices $1\le j\le n$. Its basis and regularity properties are proved in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]].

derivations.claim: For $p=0$, support, piecewise degree, and nonnegativity follow from the indicator definition in [F1]. Inductively, each degree-$p$ term is a lower-degree spline multiplied by an affine factor; on the lower-degree spline's support that factor is nonnegative, and the two supports lie inside $[\xi_j, \xi_{j+p+1}]$. Thus support, degree at most $p$, and nonnegativity hold for every $p$.

Define $\psi_{j,0}(y)=1$ and $\psi_{j,p}(y)=\prod_{r=1}^{p}(y-\xi_{j+r})$. Factoring $\psi_{j,p-1}$ gives $(y-x)\psi_{j,p-1}(y)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}\psi_{j,p}(y)+\frac{\xi_{j+p}-x}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}\psi_{j-1,p}(y),$ with zero-denominator terms omitted. For $p=0$, $(y-x)^p=1$ is the local identity on any nonempty knot interval. If the identity holds for degree $p-1$, multiply it by $y-x$, apply the displayed dual-polynomial identity to each summand, and regroup the two contributions to each coefficient using the recurrence in [F1]. The endpoint terms vanish by local support. Hence, for $x\in[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, $(y-x)^p=\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}\psi_{i,p}(y)B_{i,p,\xi}(x).$

Let the distinct interior knots be $\eta_1<\cdots<\eta_s$ with multiplicities $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_s$. For $k\ge1$ set $u_{r,k}(x)=(x-\eta_r)^k\mathbf1_{[\eta_r,\infty)}(x)$ and set $u_{r,0}(x)=\mathbf1_{[\eta_r,\infty)}(x)$; the value at $\eta_r$ follows the right-cell convention of [F1]. The functions $1,x,\ldots,x^p$ together with $u_{r,k}$ for $p-\mu_r+1\le k\le p$ span $S_{p,\xi}$: start with the polynomial on the first interval, then at each knot the difference of adjacent pieces has its derivatives through $p-\mu_r$ equal to zero, so it is a linear combination of the listed powers, including the right-continuous step when $\mu_r=p+1$. They are independent because restriction to successive knot intervals first forces the initial polynomial coefficients, then each new knot's coefficients, to vanish. Thus $\dim S_{p,\xi}=p+1+\sum_r\mu_r=n$.

Differentiate the identity in step 1.2 exactly $p-k$ times in $y$ and set $y=0$, for each $0\le k\le p$. Since $\frac{d^{p-k}}{dy^{p-k}}(y-x)^p|_{y=0}=\frac{p!}{k!}(-x)^k$, this yields $x^k=\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}\left[(-1)^k\frac{k!}{p!}\psi_{i, p}^{(p-k)}(0)\right]B_{i,p,\xi}(x).$ The coefficients do not depend on $m$, so this is a single expansion valid on every knot interval. Linear combination proves reproduction of every member of $\mathcal P_p$.

For $p=1$, differentiating the two affine pieces gives the derivative formula below. For $p\ge2$, differentiate the recurrence in [F1] and substitute the degree-$(p-1)$ formula inductively. The coefficients of $B_{j,p-2,\xi}$ and $B_{j+2,p-2,\xi}$ become respectively $p(x-\xi_j)/((\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)(\xi_{j+p-1}-\xi_j))$ and $-p(\xi_{j+p+1}-x)/((\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+2}))$; the middle coefficient is the sum $\frac{\xi_{j+p}-x-(p-1)(x-\xi_j)}{(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})}+\frac{-(x-\xi_{j+1})+(p-1)(\xi_{j+p+1}-x)}{(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})},$ The target middle coefficient from expanding the right side of the claimed formula with [F1] is $\frac{p(\xi_{j+p}-x)}{(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})}-\frac{p(x-\xi_{j+1})}{(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})}.$ The first summand in the previous display differs from the first target summand by $-(p-1)/(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})$, while the second differs from the second target summand by $+(p-1)/(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_{j+1})$; these excess terms cancel. Zero-denominator terms vanish by [F1]. Thus, on each open knot interval, $B'_{j,p,\xi}=p\left(\frac{B_{j,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}-\frac{B_{j+1,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1}}\right).$

Taking $k=0$ in step 2.1 gives $\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}B_{i,p,\xi}(x)=1$. Step 2.1 also shows that these $p+1$ active functions span $\mathcal P_p$ on the interval. Because $\dim\mathcal P_p=p+1$, they are linearly independent there and are a local basis.

Induct on $p$. If the knot multiplicity $\mu\le p-1$, the lower-degree splines in the recurrence are continuous there by induction, so the recurrence makes $B_{j,p,\xi}$ continuous; the derivative formula then makes its derivative $C^{p-1-\mu}$, hence $B_{j,p,\xi}\in C^{p-\mu}$. If $\mu=p$, a B-spline whose support crosses the repeated knot has one nonzero piece on either side, namely $(x-\xi_j)^p/(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)^p$ and $(\xi_{j+p+1}-x)^p/(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})^p$; both one-sided limits equal $1$, while any B-spline not crossing it has zero endpoint value there. If $\mu=p+1$, the required order is $C^{-1}$ and no matching is asserted.

The smoothness and piecewise-degree properties from steps 1.1 and 3.2 put every B-spline in $S_{p,\xi}$. If a linear combination of all $n$ B-splines is zero, then on every nonempty knot interval its active coefficients vanish by the local basis property in step 3.1. Each B-spline has a nonempty support interval by the clamped-knot hypothesis, so every coefficient occurs on at least one such interval and is zero. The B-splines are therefore $n$ independent members of the $n$-dimensional space in step 1.3, hence form its basis. The unique global expansion includes every polynomial from step 2.1.

boundaries.evidence: Given clamped knots allow no interior knots; step 1.3 then has zero knot sum and dimension p+1=n. The empty-interior-range case is included.
Step 1.1 handles degree p=0 explicitly; step 2.1 reproduces the zero polynomial and constant polynomial as members of P_p.
For p=0,n=1, step 1.1 indicator and step 3.1 local partition give the sole constant basis element; a<b is retained.
Step 3.2 separately treats knot multiplicity μ=p+1 with no continuity requirement, while step 2.2 omits zero-denominator terms by the definition.

A polynomial having an expansion does not alone characterize admissible clamping or knot multiplicity; those hypotheses remain inputs to the recurrence theorem.

risk_review.notes: Read every step: support induction, Marsden dual-polynomial identity with zero-span terms omitted on nonempty cells, monomial coefficients, derivative recurrence and multiplicity smoothness agree. Local reproduction implies local independence; truncated-power dimension n plus each final support nonempty proves global basis. Checked p=0, no interior knots, full multiplicity p+1, right-cell values and b left limits. Source: Lyche–Manni–Speleers sections 1.1–1.2, Definition 2 and Marsden identity Theorem 16. No defect.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Let $r\ge2$, $a\le x_1<\cdots<x_r\le b$, and $y_1,\ldots,y_r\in\mathbb R$. There is exactly one natural cubic spline $s$ on $[a,b]$ with $s(x_i)=y_i$ for each $i$. On each interval $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ it is the cubic with endpoint values $y_i,y_{i+1}$ and endpoint second derivatives $M_i,M_{i+1}$, where $M_1=M_r=0$ and the interior values solve the positive-definite tridiagonal system
$$h_{i-1}M_{i-1}+2(h_{i-1}+h_i)M_i+h_iM_{i+1}=6\left(\frac{y_{i+1}-y_i}{h_i}-\frac{y_i-y_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}\right),\quad 2\le i\le r-1,$$
with $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$. The interpolant is linear outside $[x_1,x_r]$.

Assume AC. Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval, let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n\in([a,b]\times\mathbb R)^n$, assume at least two distinct input values, and let $\lambda>0$. For $g\in W^{2,2}(a,b)$ use its unique continuous representative on $[a,b]$ supplied by the one-dimensional Sobolev representative theorem. The natural cubic smoothing spline is the unique minimizer, whose existence and uniqueness are proved in [[thm-natural-cubic-smoothing-spline-exists-uniquely]], of
$$J(g)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-g(x_i))^2+\lambda\int_a^b|D^2g(t)|^2\,dt.$$

The requirement of two distinct inputs is essential. The penalty is the squared $L^2$ norm of the second weak derivative; the data term uses the distinct-input interpolation convention in [[def-natural-cubic-spline]].

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

derivations.claim: Let $g\in W^{2,2}(a,b)$ and use the continuous representative in [F2] for $g$ and $g'$. The Countable Choice convention in [F1] and the choice hypotheses for [F2] are available by [F5] and [A1]. Interpolate the values $g(t_j)$ by the natural cubic $s$ from [F3], and put $h=g-s$. Then $h(t_j)=0$ for every $j$. On each interval between distinct knots, $s'''$ is constant; on the two linear tails, $s''=s'''=0$.

The natural spline with knots $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ is uniquely determined by its nodal vector $z=(s(t_1),\ldots,s(t_r))\in\mathbb R^r$ by [F3]. The tridiagonal system in the interpolation proof is linear in its data, and the interval formula is linear in the nodal values and second derivatives; hence $z\mapsto s_z''$ is linear into the finite-dimensional space of piecewise-linear functions. Therefore $R(z)=\int|s_z''|^2$ is a finite nonnegative quadratic form. In these coordinates $J(s)=\sum_j\sum_{i:x_i=t_j}(y_i-z_j)^2+\lambda R(z)$. The data term has positive-definite diagonal quadratic part because every $t_j$ occurs at least once. Adding the nonnegative quadratic form $\lambda R$ leaves a positive-definite quadratic objective, which has a unique minimizer by completing the square.

On each knot interval, the product $s''h'$ is absolutely continuous, so the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $\int s''h''=[s''h']-\int s'''h'$. Summing over the intervals, the interior boundary terms cancel because $s''$ and $h'$ are continuous. At each outer endpoint, $s''=0$ either on a linear tail or by the natural condition when that endpoint is a knot. The remaining terms are $-s'''|_{(t_j,t_{j+1})}(h(t_{j+1})-h(t_j))=0$. Thus $\int_a^b s''h''=0$.

Since $g=s+h$, expanding the square and applying step 2.1 yields $\int_a^b|g''|^2=\int_a^b|s''|^2+\int_a^b|h''|^2.$ Also $s(x_i)=g(x_i)$ for every observed input, so their data residual terms agree. Therefore $J(g)=J(s)+\lambda\int_a^b|h''|^2\ge J(s)$, with equality only if $h''=0$ almost everywhere.

Let $s_*$ be this finite-dimensional minimizer. Step 3.1 shows $J(g)\ge J(s_*)$ for every $g\in W^{2,2}$. If equality holds, then $h''=0$ almost everywhere, so by [F2] $h$ is affine; its zero values at the two distinct knots $t_1,t_r$ force $h=0$. Thus $s_*$ is the unique minimizer over the full Sobolev class, and its natural cubic form and linear tails are those of [F3].

boundaries.reason: A2 requires at least two distinct inputs and positive lambda. Step 1.2 uses at least one observation at every distinct knot to make the nodal data quadratic positive definite; an empty sample cannot satisfy it.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.2 and 4.1 cover arbitrary response values, including zero, in the positive-definite finite-dimensional objective.
The theorem includes exactly two distinct input locations; steps 1.1 and 4.1 use those two knots to eliminate the affine nullspace.
The lower boundary of two distinct inputs is included in step 4.1; the one-input failure is separately exhibited by the companion counterexample.
Step 2.1 handles data knots at a or b by the natural endpoint condition and handles nonempty linear tails.
Statement and A1 require AC; step 1.1 identifies its Sobolev representative and Countable Choice uses.

boundaries.reason: Two distinct inputs and positive lambda yield a unique Sobolev minimizer by nodal positive definiteness and the roughness orthogonality identity.
A natural cubic function is not automatically the minimizing fit; step 1.2 must optimize its nodal quadratic criterion, and step 4.1 proves that particular solution is unique.

risk_review.notes: Read all five steps and exact Sobolev/AC and distinct-knot interpolation interfaces. Each repeated input has positive observation count, so the nodal residual Hessian is positive definite; curvature adds a nonnegative quadratic form. Piecewise integration by parts is valid for AC h-prime; s-double-prime is continuous, zero at external endpoints and zero on tails. Orthogonality preserves observations and reduces J, and h-double-prime=0 with two distinct zero values forces h=0. Checked r=2, repeated observations, endpoints and lambda>0. Tibshirani section 2.3 supplies the same orthogonality argument; no defect.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

Fix a bounded interval $[a,b]$, a degree $p\in\mathbb N_0$, an exponent $1\le q\le\infty$, an integer $0\le l\le p$, and a nonempty family $\mathcal T$ of clamped degree-$p$ knot meshes on $[a,b]$. A **mesh-uniform bounded local quasi-interpolant** is a family of real-linear maps $Q_\xi:C([a,b];\mathbb R)\to S_{p,\xi}$, one for each $\xi\in\mathcal T$, for which there are common constants $M\in\mathbb N$ and $0\le C_Q<\infty$ such that the following hold for every $\xi\in\mathcal T$ and every nonempty cell $I_m$ of its mesh: there is a neighborhood $J_{\xi,m}\subseteq[a,b]$ containing $I_m$ and formed from at most $M$ adjacent knot cells; each point of $[a,b]$ belongs to at most $M$ of the neighborhoods $J_{\xi,m}$; (i) if $f=g$ almost everywhere on $J_{\xi,m}$, then $Q_\xi f=Q_\xi g$ almost everywhere on $I_m$; (ii) $Q_\xi v=v$ for every $v\in\mathcal P_l$; and (iii) $\|Q_\xi f\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le C_Q\|f\|_{L^q(J_{\xi,m})}$. The constants $M$ and $C_Q$ are independent of $\xi$. The derivative and continuous-representative conventions for Sobolev inputs are those of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]].

For a fixed mesh, the coefficient-functional formulation in Lyche–Manni–Speleers is one sufficient way to obtain these local stability and reproduction properties. Uniform constants in that construction give a family as defined here; this definition records the operator hypotheses used in the approximation proof.

derivations.claim: On any neighborhood J=[c,d], use the continuous representatives of D^j f, 0≤j≤l, supplied by [F2]. Their Sobolev-class convention [F1] and the choice hypotheses for [F2] are available under [A1] by [F5]. Repeated integration by parts for absolutely continuous functions gives the Taylor identity f(x)−T_{c,l}f(x)=1/l!∫_c^x(x−t)^lD^{l+1}f(t)dt, where T_{c,l}f(x)=Σ_{j=0}^lD^j f(c)(x−c)^j/j!. Hölder bounds the pointwise remainder and then its L^q norm by |J|^{l+1}||D^{l+1}f||_{L^q(J)}/l!, including q=1 and q=∞.

Choose c as the left endpoint of J_m and write T=T_{c,l}f. Since Q reproduces P_l, QT=T. The triangle inequality and local stability give ||f−Qf||_{L^q(I_m)}≤||f−T||_{L^q(I_m)}+||Q(f−T)||_{L^q(I_m)}≤(1+C_Q)||f−T||_{L^q(J_m)}, using I_m⊆J_m. Since |J_m|≤Mh_m by the neighborhood definition, step 1.1 gives the local estimate.

Raise the local estimates to the $q$th power and sum over the disjoint mesh cells. Each point belongs to at most $M$ neighborhoods, so $\sum_m\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q(J_m)}^q\le M\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q([a,b])}^q$. Taking the $q$th root and using $h_m\le h$ gives the stated global bound for finite $q$. For $q=\infty$, take the maximum of the local bounds; the factor $M^{1/q}$ is $1$.

On each cell, the real L^2(I) pairing is finite by Hölder and positive definite on a.e. classes. The Gram matrix of 1,x,…,x^p is positive definite because a nonzero polynomial has only finitely many roots. Solving its Gram system defines a linear cellwise projector that fixes P_p and has orthogonal residual, so Pythagoras gives L^2 contractivity. With the right-cell knot convention, these operators form a mesh-uniform local family with one-cell neighborhoods, M=1 and C_Q=1. Applying the theorem with l=s−1 gives the stated h^s bound.

boundaries.evidence: Local bounds quantify over nonempty cells; zero-length knot intervals are omitted. On a positive-length cell, Jm contains that cell and has positive h_m, permitting the Taylor remainder in step 1.1.
Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 give zero error when the derivative remainder vanishes and include every reproduced polynomial.
The order l=0 and exponent endpoints q=1 and q=infinity are covered in steps 1.1, 3.1 and 4.1.
The hypotheses allow p=l=0; step 2.1 also treats the one-cell full-multiplicity mesh.
Steps 1.1 and 3.1 use closed cell neighborhoods intersected with [a,b], including boundary cells.
Statement and A1 assume AC, and step 1.1 uses the AC-dependent one-dimensional Sobolev representatives.

boundaries.reason: Local stability and polynomial reproduction bound the Taylor residual, and controlled neighborhood overlap yields the global h-to-l-plus-one estimate.
The displayed approximation estimate is not claimed to imply locality or exact polynomial reproduction of an arbitrary operator Q.

risk_review.notes: Read all four steps, Lyche–Manni–Speleers Definitions 29–30, Theorem 32 proof and Example 33, and exact Sobolev, Holder, Pythagoras and finite-dimensional projection interfaces. Taylor integral remainder is valid for the AC representatives of derivatives through l; q=1 and infinity give the displayed (loose) constants. Cell containment and at most M adjacent cells yield length<=Mh; overlap summation gives M^(1/q). Gram matrix positive definiteness constructs the cellwise real L2 projector directly, without applying finite-dimensional ambient projection to L2. It fixes Pp, is contractive, has one-cell neighborhoods and respects right-cell/left-b values. Checked p=0, l=0, s=p+1 and zero derivative. AC used only through stated Sobolev interfaces; no defect.

citations.quote:
Let $p_K(x)=(B_{1,p,\xi}(x),\ldots,B_{K,p,\xi}(x))^T$ be a specified degree-$p$ B-spline basis on the data domain, and let $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be observed real-valued data. Form the design matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times K}$ with row $p_K(X_i)^T$. The **series least-squares fitted training vector** is
$$\widehat{\mathbf g}_K=\Pi_{\operatorname{col}(P)}\mathbf Y,$$
the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^T$ onto the column space of $P$. Conditional on the realized design, this is the fixed-design least-squares fitted vector of [[def-fixed-design-projection-estimator]]. Equivalently, it is $P\widehat\beta$ for any minimizer $\widehat\beta$ of $\|\mathbf Y-P\beta\|_2^2$; all such minimizers have the same fitted training vector. The training prediction loss relative to a specified target vector $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$ is $n^{-1}\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2$. This definition specifies training fitted values and makes no test-risk assertion.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. For every $v\in V$, the vector $P_Wv$ is the unique point of $W$ nearest to $v$: for every $w\in W$,

$$\lVert v-P_Wv\rVert\le\lVert v-w\rVert,$$

with equality if and only if $w=P_Wv$.

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

Let $n,d\in\mathbb N$ with $n,d\ge1$, and let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ be a fixed design
matrix, and write $V_X:=\{X\theta:\theta\in\mathbb R^d\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$
for its column space. For an observed vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, the **fixed-design
least-squares fitted vector** is

$$\widehat\mu_X(y):=P_{V_X}y,$$

where $P_{V_X}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $V_X$, as defined in
[[def-orthogonal-projection]]. It is uniquely defined even when $X$ is rank
deficient. The nearest-point characterization in
[[thm-orthogonal-projection-is-the-unique-nearest-point]] says that
$\widehat\mu_X(y)$ minimizes $\|y-v\|_2$ over $v\in V_X$. This item defines the
fitted vector; it does not select a coefficient representation $\widehat\theta$.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Write $\mathbf X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ and $\epsilon_i=Y_i-g_0(X_i)$. For fixed $\mathbf x$, set $\kappa_1=\kappa(x_1,\cdot)$ and, for $1\le m<n$, apply [F10] to $\kappa_m$ and $\kappa(x_{m+1},\cdot)$ to obtain $\kappa_{m+1}$; both factors are probability measures, so the rectangle formula gives total mass one at each stage. Induction gives the finite product probability measure $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\cdot)$ with rectangle values $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\prod_iB_i)=\prod_i\kappa(x_i,B_i)$. The response rectangles form a pi-system because intersections of rectangles are rectangles, and [F5] says they generate the response product sigma-algebra. On response rectangles the evaluation is Borel in $\mathbf x$ by [F4] and [F10]. Because $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, the class of sets with Borel evaluation contains the whole space, is closed under complements by subtraction from $1$, and is closed under disjoint countable unions by limits of partial sums; [F11] therefore gives measurability for every response Borel set. For rectangles $A=\prod_iA_i$ and $B=\prod_iB_i$, iid sampling gives $P(\mathbf X\in A,\mathbf Y\in B)=\prod_i\int_{A_i}\kappa(x,B_i)P_X(dx)$, and repeated Tonelli [F13] gives $\int_A\kappa_n(\mathbf x,B)P_X^{\otimes n}(d\mathbf x)=\prod_i\int_{A_i}\kappa(x,B_i)P_X(dx).$ For fixed response Borel $B$, the left side of the target identity is a finite measure in $A$; the right side is also a measure by [F12], applied to the nonnegative measurable function $\mathbf x\mapsto\kappa_n(\mathbf x,B)$. Design rectangles form a pi-system because intersections are rectangles and generate the design product sigma-algebra by [F5], so [F11] extends the equality to every design Borel $A$. For each such $A$, both sides are finite measures in $B$: countable additivity on the right follows from countable additivity of $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\cdot)$ and monotone convergence, and their common total mass is $P_X^{\otimes n}(A)$ because the joint design marginal is $P_X^{\otimes n}$ and $\kappa_n$ is a probability kernel. Thus the response sets $B$ for which the identity holds for every $A$ form a Dynkin system (complements use the common total mass); they contain the response rectangles, so [F11] gives equality for every response Borel set. Hence $\kappa_n$ is a conditional law of $\mathbf Y$ given $\mathbf X$. Under this product law the residuals are conditionally independent, have conditional means zero by [A2], and conditional second moments at most $\Delta$. Hence $E[\epsilon_i\epsilon_j\mid\mathbf X]=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $E[\epsilon_i^2\mid\mathbf X]\le\Delta$.

Let $Q=\Pi_{\operatorname{col}(D)}$. The matrix $Q$ is a Borel function of $D$: partition the finite-dimensional matrix space by rank and, within each positive-rank stratum, by the lexicographically first nonzero maximal minor; on each resulting Borel piece, the corresponding independent columns form a matrix $C$. The Gram matrix $C^TC$ is positive definite, and $C(C^TC)^{-1}C^T$ is symmetric, idempotent, and has image $\operatorname{col}(C)=\operatorname{col}(D)$, so it is the orthogonal projection; at rank zero put $Q=0$. These finitely many Borel formulas show that $Q$ is measurable with respect to $\mathbf X$. Its rank $r$ is at most $K$. Scanning the finitely many columns and retaining a column precisely when it is not in the span of those already retained gives a basis of $\operatorname{col}(D)$; applying Gram–Schmidt [F7] gives an $n\times r$ matrix $U$ with orthonormal columns spanning that subspace. For any $v$, $UU^Tv$ belongs to $\operatorname{col}(D)$ and $U^T(v-UU^Tv)=0$, so its residual is orthogonal to the columns of $U$ and hence to $\operatorname{col}(D)$. By the uniqueness in [F9], $Q=UU^T$; therefore $\operatorname{tr}(Q)=\operatorname{tr}(U^TU)=r\le K$. Since $Q_{ii}=\|Qe_i\|_2^2\ge0$, step 1.1 gives $E[\epsilon^TQ\epsilon\mid\mathbf X]=\sum_iQ_{ii}E[\epsilon_i^2\mid\mathbf X]\le\Delta\operatorname{tr}(Q)\le\Delta K.$

Write $\mathbf g=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$. From [F1] and [F8], $\widehat{\mathbf g}_K=Q\mathbf Y$, and $\mathbf Y=\mathbf g+\epsilon$. In the orthogonal decomposition $\mathbb R^n=\operatorname{col}(D)\oplus\operatorname{col}(D)^\perp$, the projection [F9] is identity on the first summand and zero on the second, so $Q^T=Q=Q^2$, $\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g\|_2^2=\|Q\epsilon-(I-Q)\mathbf g\|_2^2=\epsilon^TQ\epsilon+\|(I-Q)\mathbf g\|_2^2,$ because $Q(I-Q)=0$. For $\bar{\mathbf g}=D\bar\beta_K\in\operatorname{col}(D)$, $(I-Q)\bar{\mathbf g}=0$; the nearest-point property [F6] therefore gives $\|(I-Q)\mathbf g\|_2^2\le\|\mathbf g-\bar{\mathbf g}\|_2^2$.

Taking expectations in step 3.1, applying step 2.1 and iid sampling with [A3] yields E||ĝ_K−g||_2^2≤ΔK+∑_i∫{g_0(x)−p_K(x)^Tβ̄_K}^2P_X(dx)≤ΔK+nC^2K^(−2γ). Divide by n to obtain the claimed expected empirical training-risk bound.

boundaries.reason: Statement explicitly fixes n,K>=1. Step 4.1 divides by n, and the deterministic approximation vector lives in R^K; no empty-observation risk is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1 and 4.1 include conditional variance Delta=0 and approximation constant C=0.
The hypotheses allow n=1 and K=1; steps 2.1–3.1 use only n,K≥1.
Step 2.1 includes rank zero and every rank r≤K, so rank-deficient sample designs are covered.
The design support is the closed interval [a,b]; the product-kernel argument in step 1.1 includes its Borel endpoints.

A1 supplies the one-observation conditional kernel and A3 supplies a deterministic approximation coefficient. Step 2.1 builds the sample projection using the lexicographically first nonzero maximal minor, so no simultaneous arbitrary selections are hidden.

boundaries.reason: The supplied conditional kernel and deterministic approximation give the Delta-K-over-n plus squared approximation bound via projection noise and orthogonal bias.
Small training risk does not imply the supplied conditional-law hypotheses or independent test-risk control; the conclusion explicitly names empirical training-design loss.

risk_review.notes: Read all four steps and exact kernel, product-law, product-measure, pi-lambda, Tonelli, projection and Gram–Schmidt supplier statements. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $n,K\ge1$, and let $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be iid random elements of $([a,b]\times\mathbb R,\mathcal B([a,b])\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Write $P_X$ for the law of $X_1$ and suppose the one-observation law is $P_X(dx)\kappa(x,dy)$ for a supplied Borel probability kernel $\kappa$ from $([a,b],\mathcal B([a,b]))$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Assume a Borel function $g_0:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is supplied such that, for $P_X$-almost every $x$, $\int |y|\,\kappa(x,dy)<\infty$, $g_0(x)=\int y\,\kappa(x,dy)$, and $\int (y-g_0(x))^2\,\kappa(x,dy)\le\Delta$ for a finite $\Delta\ge0$. Let $p_K:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^K$ be a fixed Borel $K$-dimensional spline basis and assume a deterministic $\bar\beta_K\in\mathbb R^K$, a constant $C\ge0$, and $\gamma>0$ satisfy
$$\int_{[a,b]}\{g_0(x)-p_K(x)^T\bar\beta_K\}^2\,P_X(dx)\le C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
Then, with the fitted training vector $\widehat{\mathbf g}_K$ from [[def-series-spline-least-squares]] and $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$,
$$E\left[\frac1n\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2\right]\le\frac{\Delta K}{n}+C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
This is expected empirical training-design loss.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $0\le l\le p$, and $1\le q\le\infty$. Let $\mathcal T$ be a nonempty family of clamped degree-$p$ knot meshes on $[a,b]$, and let $(Q_\xi)_{\xi\in\mathcal T}$ be a mesh-uniform bounded local quasi-interpolant family as in [[def-local-spline-quasi-interpolant]], with common constants $M$ and $C_Q$. Fix $\xi\in\mathcal T$, write $Q=Q_\xi$, and let $f\in W^{l+1,q}(a,b;\mathbb R)$ with its continuous Sobolev representative. For each nonempty cell $I_m$ of $\xi$, let $J_m$ be its corresponding neighborhood and let $h_m$ be the largest cell length in $J_m$. Then
$$\|f-Qf\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le (1+C_Q)\frac{M^{l+1}}{l!}h_m^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q(J_m)}.$$
Writing $h=\max_m h_m$, the global bound is
$$\|f-Qf\|_{L^q([a,b])}\le (1+C_Q)\frac{M^{l+1+1/q}}{l!}h^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q([a,b])},$$
where $1/q=0$ for $q=\infty$. In particular, on a uniform mesh with interior knots of multiplicity $p+1$, the cellwise $L^2$ projector onto $\mathcal P_p$ is a local quasi-interpolant and gives the order-$h^s$ approximation bound for every integer $1\le s\le p+1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real random variables on a probability
space, with $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$, and choose a regular conditional law
$Q(x,dy)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$. On
$D=\{x:\int |y|\,Q(x,dy)<\infty\}$ define
$m(x)=\int y\,Q(x,dy)$, and put $m(x)=0$ off $D$. By
[[cor-conditional-expectation-as-a-measurable-function-of-the-conditioning-variable]],
$m$ is Borel measurable and $m(X)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E[Y\mid\sigma(X)]$. A **regression target** is the resulting
$P_X$-almost-sure equivalence class; a **chosen regression-function version**
is the particular Borel function selected by the specified conditional law.

Pointwise smoothness is an additional hypothesis on the chosen version. It is
not implied by existence of conditional expectation, and statements about
$m(x)$ at a specified point use that selected version.

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $n\ge p+1$, and $a<b$. A clamped knot vector is a nondecreasing finite sequence
$$\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_{p+1}=a<\xi_{p+2}\le\cdots\le\xi_n<\xi_{n+1}=\cdots=\xi_{n+p+1}=b,$$
with $\xi_j<\xi_{j+p+1}$ for every $1\le j\le n$. Empty interior ranges are omitted. The multiplicity $\mu(\eta)$ of an interior knot $\eta$ is its number of occurrences among $\xi_{p+2},\ldots,\xi_n$.

Write $\mathcal P_p$ for the real polynomials of degree at most $p$. The degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ consists of functions that restrict to a member of $\mathcal P_p$ on each nonempty knot interval and whose derivatives through order $p-\mu(\eta)$ agree across each interior knot $\eta$. The convention $C^{-1}$ means that no matching condition is imposed. For this piecewise definition, take knot cells left-closed and right-open; at a knot with no matching condition, the value is the one from the cell on its right, and at $b$ use the left limit. Thus the function value at a discontinuous knot is specified.

For each degree $d\in\{0,\ldots,p\}$, the functions $B_{j,d,\xi}$ are indexed by $1\le j\le n+p-d$. Set
$$B_{j,0,\xi}(x)=\mathbf 1_{[\xi_j,\xi_{j+1})}(x),\qquad 1\le j\le n+p.$$
For $1\le d\le p$ and $1\le j\le n+p-d$, define recursively
$$B_{j,d,\xi}(x)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}B_{j,d-1,\xi}(x)+\frac{\xi_{j+d+1}-x}{\xi_{j+d+1}-\xi_{j+1}}B_{j+1,d-1,\xi}(x),$$
where a term with zero denominator is defined to be zero. For every degree $d$ and every allowed index $j$, set $B_{j,d,\xi}(b)$ equal to its left limit. In particular, the degree-$p$ family has indices $1\le j\le n$. Its basis and regularity properties are proved in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]].

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.

citations.quote: Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval and let $a\le t_1<\cdots<t_r\le b$ with $r\ge2$. A natural cubic spline with knots $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ is a $C^2$ function on $[a,b]$ that is a polynomial of degree at most three on every $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, has second derivative zero at $t_1$ and $t_r$, and is extended linearly on $[a,t_1]$ and $[t_r,b]$ when those intervals are nonempty. The knots $t_j$ are the distinct breakpoints; repeated observations at the same input do not create additional knots.

Let $r\ge2$, $a\le x_1<\cdots<x_r\le b$, and $y_1,\ldots,y_r\in\mathbb R$. There is exactly one natural cubic spline $s$ on $[a,b]$ with $s(x_i)=y_i$ for each $i$. On each interval $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ it is the cubic with endpoint values $y_i,y_{i+1}$ and endpoint second derivatives $M_i,M_{i+1}$, where $M_1=M_r=0$ and the interior values solve the positive-definite tridiagonal system
$$h_{i-1}M_{i-1}+2(h_{i-1}+h_i)M_i+h_iM_{i+1}=6\left(\frac{y_{i+1}-y_i}{h_i}-\frac{y_i-y_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}\right),\quad 2\le i\le r-1,$$
with $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$. The interpolant is linear outside $[x_1,x_r]$.

every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

derivations.claim: For any continuous real input g, the cellwise linear interpolant is the convex combination of its endpoint values. It is contractive in L^∞ on the cell, depends only on that cell, reproduces affine functions and is a continuous piecewise-linear spline. Across all uniform meshes these operators form a mesh-uniform local family with one-cell neighborhoods, M=1 and C_Q=1.

Let $M_2=\|D^2f\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}$. On a cell $[u,v]$ of length $h$, put $a_x=x-u$ and $b_x=v-x$. By [F3] applied to $f$ and $Df$, let $f^*$ and $g^*$ be their absolutely continuous representatives; $(g^*)'=D^2f$ almost everywhere and $f^*(x)-f^*(u)=\int_u^xg^*(s)\,ds$. The absolutely continuous function $t\mapsto(x-t)g^*(t)$ has derivative $-g^*(t)+(x-t)D^2f(t)$ almost everywhere, so the fundamental theorem for absolutely continuous functions gives $f^*(x)=f^*(u)+a_xg^*(u)+\int_u^x(x-t)D^2f(t)\,dt$, and the same formula at $v$. Since $I_hf(x)=f^*(u)+(a_x/h)(f^*(v)-f^*(u))$, subtraction and simplification yield $f^*(x)-I_hf(x)=-\int_u^x\frac{b_x(t-u)}hD^2f(t)\,dt-\int_x^v\frac{a_x(v-t)}hD^2f(t)\,dt$. Hence $|f^*(x)-I_hf(x)|\le M_2\{b_xa_x^2/(2h)+a_xb_x^2/(2h)\}=M_2a_xb_x/2\le M_2h^2/8$, since $a_x+b_x=h$ and $a_xb_x\le h^2/4$. This holds on every cell and at every point, so taking the supremum gives $\|f-I_hf\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}\le h^2\|D^2f\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}/8$.
