Let $p_K(x)=(B_{1,p,\xi}(x),\ldots,B_{K,p,\xi}(x))^T$ be a specified degree-$p$ B-spline basis on the data domain, and let $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be observed real-valued data. Form the design matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times K}$ with row $p_K(X_i)^T$. The **series least-squares fitted training vector** is
$$\widehat{\mathbf g}_K=\Pi_{\operatorname{col}(P)}\mathbf Y,$$
the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^T$ onto the column space of $P$. Conditional on the realized design, this is the fixed-design least-squares fitted vector of [[def-fixed-design-projection-estimator]]. Equivalently, it is $P\widehat\beta$ for any minimizer $\widehat\beta$ of $\|\mathbf Y-P\beta\|_2^2$; all such minimizers have the same fitted training vector. The training prediction loss relative to a specified target vector $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$ is $n^{-1}\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2$. This definition specifies training fitted values and makes no test-risk assertion.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $n,K\ge1$, and let $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be iid random elements of $([a,b]\times\mathbb R,\mathcal B([a,b])\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Write $P_X$ for the law of $X_1$ and suppose the one-observation law is $P_X(dx)\kappa(x,dy)$ for a supplied Borel probability kernel $\kappa$ from $([a,b],\mathcal B([a,b]))$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Assume a Borel function $g_0:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is supplied such that, for $P_X$-almost every $x$, $\int |y|\,\kappa(x,dy)<\infty$, $g_0(x)=\int y\,\kappa(x,dy)$, and $\int (y-g_0(x))^2\,\kappa(x,dy)\le\Delta$ for a finite $\Delta\ge0$. Let $p_K:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^K$ be a fixed Borel $K$-dimensional spline basis and assume a deterministic $\bar\beta_K\in\mathbb R^K$, a constant $C\ge0$, and $\gamma>0$ satisfy
$$\int_{[a,b]}\{g_0(x)-p_K(x)^T\bar\beta_K\}^2\,P_X(dx)\le C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
Then, with the fitted training vector $\widehat{\mathbf g}_K$ from [[def-series-spline-least-squares]] and $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$,
$$E\left[\frac1n\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2\right]\le\frac{\Delta K}{n}+C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
This is expected empirical training-design loss.

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $n\ge p+1$, and $a<b$. A clamped knot vector is a nondecreasing finite sequence
$$\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_{p+1}=a<\xi_{p+2}\le\cdots\le\xi_n<\xi_{n+1}=\cdots=\xi_{n+p+1}=b,$$
with $\xi_j<\xi_{j+p+1}$ for every $1\le j\le n$. Empty interior ranges are omitted. The multiplicity $\mu(\eta)$ of an interior knot $\eta$ is its number of occurrences among $\xi_{p+2},\ldots,\xi_n$.

Write $\mathcal P_p$ for the real polynomials of degree at most $p$. The degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ consists of functions that restrict to a member of $\mathcal P_p$ on each nonempty knot interval and whose derivatives through order $p-\mu(\eta)$ agree across each interior knot $\eta$. The convention $C^{-1}$ means that no matching condition is imposed. For this piecewise definition, take knot cells left-closed and right-open; at a knot with no matching condition, the value is the one from the cell on its right, and at $b$ use the left limit. Thus the function value at a discontinuous knot is specified.

For each degree $d\in\{0,\ldots,p\}$, the functions $B_{j,d,\xi}$ are indexed by $1\le j\le n+p-d$. Set
$$B_{j,0,\xi}(x)=\mathbf 1_{[\xi_j,\xi_{j+1})}(x),\qquad 1\le j\le n+p.$$
For $1\le d\le p$ and $1\le j\le n+p-d$, define recursively
$$B_{j,d,\xi}(x)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}B_{j,d-1,\xi}(x)+\frac{\xi_{j+d+1}-x}{\xi_{j+d+1}-\xi_{j+1}}B_{j+1,d-1,\xi}(x),$$
where a term with zero denominator is defined to be zero. For every degree $d$ and every allowed index $j$, set $B_{j,d,\xi}(b)$ equal to its left limit. In particular, the degree-$p$ family has indices $1\le j\le n$. Its basis and regularity properties are proved in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]].

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.

derivations.claim: On the clamped knot vector $(0,0,1,1)$, the only nonzero degree-zero spline on $(0,1)$ is $B_{2,0}=1$; the recurrence in [F3] gives $B_{1,1}=1-x$ and $B_{2,1}=x$, so $p(1/2)=(1/2,1/2)$. Therefore $p(1/2)^T\widehat\beta=(1/2,1/2)(0,2)^T=1$, the training residual and empirical training loss are zero, and the fitted vector equals the projection in [F1]. The chosen coefficient vector is one admissible representation of it.

The independent test squared error has expectation $E\{\widehat g(X')-g_0(X')\}^2=\int_0^1(2x-1)^2dx=\frac43-2+1=\frac13>0.$ Thus zero training loss does not imply zero independent test loss, consistent with the scope of [F2].

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Here $L^2(P)$ is the real space of square-integrable measurable functions modulo equality $P$-almost surely, with its usual quotient norm ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]). For $f\in L^2(P)$, the integral $Pf:=\int f\,dP$ is finite and independent of the representative: Cauchy–Schwarz on the probability space gives $\int|f|\,dP\le\|f\|_2$, and the expectation of integrable representatives is invariant under almost-sure equality ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[lem-expectation-is-independent-of-the-ae-representative]]).

Define the **mean-zero square-integrable space** by

$$L^2_0(P):=\{f\in L^2(P):Pf=0\}.$$

It carries the norm inherited from $L^2(P)$. Countable Choice is not needed for this definition; a later local Hilbert-space argument uses it only to inherit completeness from the library's general $L^2$ Hilbert-space result.

derivations.claim: The constant function $1$ belongs to $L^2(P)$ and has norm $1$, since $P(\mathcal X)=1$. For each $f\in L^2(P)$, the pairing in [F1] satisfies $Pf=\langle f,1\rangle_P$, so [F2] gives $|Pf|\le\|f\|_2$. Thus $f\mapsto Pf$ is a bounded linear functional, and its kernel is exactly $L^2_0(P)$ by [F3].

The kernel is linear. If $f_n\in L^2_0(P)$ and $f_n\to f$ in $L^2(P)$, then $|Pf|=|P(f-f_n)|\le\|f-f_n\|_2\to0$ by step 1.1 and linearity of the pairing [F1], so $f\in L^2_0(P)$. Hence the kernel is closed.

Every Cauchy sequence in $L^2_0(P)$ is Cauchy in $L^2(P)$, which is complete by [F1] under the Countable Choice assumption [A1]; its $L^2(P)$ limit lies in $L^2_0(P)$ by step 2.1. The restricted inner product is therefore complete, proving the asserted Hilbert-space property.

Let $\mathcal M$ be a model of probability measures on a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let $\epsilon>0$, and let $t\mapsto P_t\in\mathcal M$ be a path for $0\le t<\epsilon$ with $P_0=P$. It is **dominated by a common measure** when one supplied sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ satisfies $P_t\ll\mu$ for every $t$ ([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]). Write $p_t=dP_t/d\mu$ and $p=p_0$ for simultaneously supplied nonnegative density versions; the existence and normalization of each density are the Radon–Nikodym properties in [[def-likelihood-density]] and [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]. The Axiom of Choice is the library convention for selecting such a family of versions along a path ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The DQM property below is unchanged by replacing any $p_t$ by another version, since each $L^2(\mu)$ norm is unchanged by a $\mu$-null modification.

The path is **differentiable in quadratic mean at $0$**, with **score** $s\in L^2(P)$, when

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

Here $o(t)$ means that the displayed norm divided by $t$ tends to $0$ as $t\downarrow0$; $L^2(P)$ and $L^2(\mu)$ are quotient spaces modulo almost-everywhere equality ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The definition is directional. A two-sided regular submodel qualifies by restricting it to $t\ge0$. No mean-zero condition is assumed in this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: Put $q=\sqrt p$, $q_t=\sqrt{p_t}$, and $r_t=q_t-q-(t/2)sq$. By [F1], $\|r_t\|_2=o(t)$, while [F2] gives $\|q\|_2^2=\int p\,d\mu=1$ and $\|q_t\|_2^2=\int p_t\,d\mu=1$.
If $s'$ is another score with remainder $r'_t=o_{L^2}(t)$, subtracting its expansion from [F1] gives $\|(t/2)(s-s')q\|_2\le\|r_t\|_2+\|r'_t\|_2=o(t)$.

Set $u_t=(t/2)sq+r_t$. Since $\|sq\|_2^2=\int s^2p\,d\mu=Ps^2<\infty$, we have $\|u_t\|_2=O(t)$ and $q_t=q+u_t$. The products $q r_t$ and $u_t^2$ are integrable by [F3]. Pointwise expansion and linearity [F4] give $0=\int(q+u_t)^2d\mu-\int q^2d\mu=t\,Ps+2\int q r_t\,d\mu+\|u_t\|_2^2$. By [F3], $|\int q r_t\,d\mu|\le\|q\|_2\|r_t\|_2=o(t)$ and $\|u_t\|_2^2=O(t^2)=o(t)$. Dividing by $t>0$ and taking $t\downarrow0$ gives $Ps=0$.
Divide by $t/2$ and let $t\downarrow0$. Then $\|(s-s')q\|_2^2=P[(s-s')^2]=0$, so $s=s'$ as an element of $L^2(P)$. Together with step 2.1 this proves mean zero and uniqueness.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) so that $L^2_0(P)$ is the real Hilbert space established by [[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]. For a tangent set $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)\subseteq L^2_0(P)$, its **linear span** is the set of all finite real linear combinations of elements of $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$; the span of the empty set is $\{0\}$. Its **tangent space** $\mathcal T(P)$ is the closure of that span in the $L^2(P)$ norm. The closure consists of limits of sequences from the span, equivalently of points every positive-radius norm ball around which meets the span.

The tangent set itself is retained separately and may be a cone rather than a vector space.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For any probability measure $P$, the space $L^2_0(P)$ of [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]] is a closed real linear subspace of real $L^2(P)$ with pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_P:=\int fg\,dP$; consequently it is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). The only choice use is the Countable Choice assumption already required by the general $L^2(P)$ completeness supplier.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). A subset
$W \subseteq V$ is a **linear subspace** of $V$ when

- **(W1)** $0_V \in W$;
- **(W2)** $W$ is closed under the vector addition: $u, v \in W$ implies
  $u + v \in W$;
- **(W3)** $W$ is closed under scalar multiplication: $\lambda \in F$ and
  $v \in W$ imply $\lambda v \in W$.

Every vector space $V$ has the two **trivial linear subspaces** $\{0_V\}$ and $V$
itself; a linear subspace $W$ with $W \ne V$ is called **proper**.

**The restricted operations are the required data, and $W$ is a vector space.**
By (W2) the vector addition of $V$ restricts to a binary operation
$W \times W \to W$, and by (W3) the scalar multiplication restricts to a map
$F \times W \to W$. With these and the element $0_V$, the set $W$ is a vector
space over $F$:

- axioms (V2)–(V5) are equations required of elements of $W$, which are in
  particular elements of $V$, so they are inherited from $V$; likewise
  associativity and commutativity of the restricted addition;
- $0_V$ lies in $W$ by (W1) and is a two-sided identity for the restricted
  addition, since it is one in $V$;
- for $v \in W$ the vector $(-1_F)v$ lies in $W$ by (W3), and
  $(-1_F)v = -v$ ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so $-v \in W$
  and $v + (-v) = 0_V$ holds in $W$.

So $(W,+,0_V)$ is an abelian group, which is axiom (V1), and $W$ is a vector
space over $F$ **whose zero vector and whose additive inverses are those of
$V$**. In the language of [[def-subgroup]], the three displayed conditions
(S1) $0_V \in W$, (S2) closure under addition and (S3) closure under additive
inverses all hold, so $W$ is a subgroup of the abelian group $(V,+,0_V)$
([[def-group]]); that reading, and its converse, are recorded as
[[lem-linear-subspace-is-a-subgroup]] and are cited from there rather than
re-argued below.

derivations.claim: Let $V$ be the finite real span in [F1]. By collecting coefficients of each score, the sum of two finite linear combinations is another finite linear combination; scalar multiples have the same form, and $0$ is the empty sum. Thus $V$ is a linear subspace by [F3].

If $x\notin\overline V$, some $r>0$ has $B(x,r)\cap V=\varnothing$. For any $y$ with $\|y-x\|_2<r/2$, the triangle inequality gives $B(y,r/2)\subset B(x,r)$, so $y\notin\overline V$. Hence the complement of $\overline V$ is open and $\overline V$ is closed.

Write $\overline V=\mathcal T(P)$. If $x,y\in\overline V$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose $u,v\in V$ with $\|x-u\|_2<\varepsilon/2$ and $\|y-v\|_2<\varepsilon/2$. Then $u+v\in V$ and $\|(x+y)-(u+v)\|_2<\varepsilon$, so $x+y\in\overline V$. For $a\in\mathbb R$, if $a=0$ then $ax=0\in V$; if $a\ne0$, choose $u\in V$ with $\|x-u\|_2<\varepsilon/|a|$, giving $au\in V$ and $\|ax-au\|_2<\varepsilon$. Thus $\overline V$ is linear.

A Cauchy sequence in $\overline V$ converges in $L^2_0(P)$ by [F2] under [A1]. Since $\overline V$ is closed by step 1.2, that limit lies in $\overline V$. Therefore the tangent space is complete as well as a closed linear subspace, as asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\mathcal M$ be a model of probability measures on a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let $\epsilon>0$, and let $t\mapsto P_t\in\mathcal M$ be a path for $0\le t<\epsilon$ with $P_0=P$. It is **dominated by a common measure** when one supplied sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ satisfies $P_t\ll\mu$ for every $t$ ([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]). Write $p_t=dP_t/d\mu$ and $p=p_0$ for simultaneously supplied nonnegative density versions; the existence and normalization of each density are the Radon–Nikodym properties in [[def-likelihood-density]] and [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]. The Axiom of Choice is the library convention for selecting such a family of versions along a path ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The DQM property below is unchanged by replacing any $p_t$ by another version, since each $L^2(\mu)$ norm is unchanged by a $\mu$-null modification.

The path is **differentiable in quadratic mean at $0$**, with **score** $s\in L^2(P)$, when

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

Here $o(t)$ means that the displayed norm divided by $t$ tends to $0$ as $t\downarrow0$; $L^2(P)$ and $L^2(\mu)$ are quotient spaces modulo almost-everywhere equality ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The definition is directional. A two-sided regular submodel qualifies by restricting it to $t\ge0$. No mean-zero condition is assumed in this definition.

Assume the density-version convention for the path in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]]. If $s\in L^2(P)$ is a DQM score, then $Ps=0$, so $s\in L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]). Moreover, any two scores satisfying the same DQM expansion agree $P$-almost surely. The normalization argument itself uses no choice beyond the density versions already supplied in the definition.

Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Here $L^2(P)$ is the real space of square-integrable measurable functions modulo equality $P$-almost surely, with its usual quotient norm ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]). For $f\in L^2(P)$, the integral $Pf:=\int f\,dP$ is finite and independent of the representative: Cauchy–Schwarz on the probability space gives $\int|f|\,dP\le\|f\|_2$, and the expectation of integrable representatives is invariant under almost-sure equality ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[lem-expectation-is-independent-of-the-ae-representative]]).

Define the **mean-zero square-integrable space** by

$$L^2_0(P):=\{f\in L^2(P):Pf=0\}.$$

It carries the norm inherited from $L^2(P)$. Countable Choice is not needed for this definition; a later local Hilbert-space argument uses it only to inherit completeness from the library's general $L^2$ Hilbert-space result.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) so that $L^2_0(P)$ is the real Hilbert space established by [[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]. For a tangent set $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)\subseteq L^2_0(P)$, its **linear span** is the set of all finite real linear combinations of elements of $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$; the span of the empty set is $\{0\}$. Its **tangent space** $\mathcal T(P)$ is the closure of that span in the $L^2(P)$ norm. The closure consists of limits of sequences from the span, equivalently of points every positive-radius norm ball around which meets the span.

The tangent set itself is retained separately and may be a cone rather than a vector space.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For any probability measure $P$, the space $L^2_0(P)$ of [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]] is a closed real linear subspace of real $L^2(P)$ with pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_P:=\int fg\,dP$; consequently it is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). The only choice use is the Countable Choice assumption already required by the general $L^2(P)$ completeness supplier.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: Every allowed score is in $L^2_0(P)$ by [F2]; because $L^2_0(P)$ is closed in $L^2(P)$ by [F7] under [A2], its closed tangent space is contained in $L^2_0(P)$.

Let $M=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|s(x)|<\infty$ for the bounded representative in Given, and choose $0<\epsilon<(1+M)^{-1}$. For $0\le t<\epsilon$, let $a_t=1+ts/2$, $c_t=P(a_t^2)=1+t^2Ps^2/4$, and $p_t=a_t^2/c_t$. The bound on $t$ makes $a_t\ge0$; $c_t>0$ and $Pp_t=1$, so $p_t$ is a probability density with respect to $P$.

Let $f\in L^2_0(P)$ and choose a measurable representative. Define $u_m=(-m)\vee(f\wedge m)$. Then $|u_m-f|^2\le f^2\mathbf 1_{\{|f|>m\}}$, whose right side tends pointwise to zero and is dominated by the integrable $f^2$. By [F5], $\|u_m-f\|_2\to0$. Put $s_m=u_m-Pu_m$; it is bounded and $Ps_m=0$ by [F8] and $P1=1$. Also [F6] and [F8] give $|Pu_m|=|P(u_m-f)|\le\|u_m-f\|_2$. Therefore $\|s_m-f\|_2\le2\|u_m-f\|_2\to0$.

Since $\|a_t\|_2=\sqrt{c_t}$, $\|\sqrt{p_t}-1-(t/2)s\|_2=\|a_t/\sqrt{c_t}-a_t\|_2=|1-\sqrt{c_t}|=O(t^2)=o(t)$. The density family is explicit, so it fits [A1]'s general convention without any selection. Thus $P_t=p_tP$ is an allowed DQM path with score $s$, and every bounded mean-zero score lies in the tangent set.

Each $s_m$ is a tangent score by step 2.1, and the sequence converges to the arbitrary $f\in L^2_0(P)$ by step 1.3. Hence the tangent space contains $L^2_0(P)$ by [F4]; step 1.1 gives the reverse inclusion. Thus the tangent space is exactly $L^2_0(P)$.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all five verification steps and the actual dominated-convergence, integral-linearity and Cauchy–Schwarz suppliers. The model consists of probability laws Q≪P, with the finite common dominator P. For bounded centered s, ε<(1+M)⁻¹ ensures 1+ts/2≥0 and c_t=1+t²Ps²/4>0, so p_t is nonnegative and normalized with P_0=P. The exact remainder is |1−√c_t|≤t²Ps²/4=o(t), including s=0. Truncations have squared error bounded by the integrable f² and tending to zero; centering changes the L² error by at most its original norm, so s_m→f with total error ≤2‖u_m−f‖₂. Each bounded centered class has a bounded measurable version (truncate an essentially bounded version on its measurable null exceptional set). Every s_m is an allowed score, giving one inclusion; centering and closedness give the other. Explicit path/truncation formulas add no selections; AC and Countable Choice conventions are retained. $f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

Moreover, any two scores satisfying the same DQM expansion agree $P$-almost surely. The normalization argument itself uses no choice beyond the density versions already supplied in the definition.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

Let $X$ be a set. The **counting set function** on $\mathcal P(X)$ is

$$\#_X(E):=\begin{cases}|E|,&E\text{ is finite},\\+\infty,&E\text{ is infinite},\end{cases}$$

where finite means equinumerous with a natural number ([[def-countable]]) and $+\infty$ belongs to the extended real line ([[def-extended-reals]]). The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a measure, and hence deserves the name **counting measure**, is proved in [[prop-counting-measure-is-a-measure]].
For every set $X$, the counting set function $\#_X$ of [[def-counting-measure]] is a measure on $(X,\mathcal P(X))$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

derivations.claim: Every subset of $\{0,1\}$ and its complement lie in the full power set, and every countable union of such subsets is still a subset; thus the power set is a sigma-algebra by [F4], and with this sigma-algebra the sample set is a measurable space by [F4]. Counting measure on this two-point set is a measure of total mass two by [F5, F6], hence sigma-finite by the constant sequence of covers $E_n=\{0,1\}$ in [F6]. Its only null set is empty, so each $P_t$ is absolutely continuous with respect to it. The choice of $\delta$ ensures $p+t>0$ and $1-p-t>0$ throughout $|t|<\delta$; the displayed masses sum to one, so each $P_t$ is a probability measure.

Since $p,1-p>0$, [F7] and the definition of derivative give $\sqrt{p+t}=\sqrt p+t/(2\sqrt p)+o(t)$ and $\sqrt{1-p-t}=\sqrt{1-p}-t/(2\sqrt{1-p})+o(t)$. These are exactly the two coordinates of $\sqrt{p}+(t/2)s\sqrt p+o(t)$ for the stated $s$; because counting-measure $L^2$ on two points is the Euclidean norm, the combined remainder is $o(t)$. The density versions are explicit, so the calculation uses [A1]'s convention without a selection. Thus the path is DQM with this score by [F1].
Direct calculation gives $Ps=p(1/p)+(1-p)(-1/(1-p))=0$ and $Ps^2=p/p^2+(1-p)/(1-p)^2=1/[p(1-p)]<\infty$. Hence the score is in $L^2_0(P)$ and has the stated variance.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\mathcal M$ be a model of probability measures on a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let $\epsilon>0$, and let $t\mapsto P_t\in\mathcal M$ be a path for $0\le t<\epsilon$ with $P_0=P$. It is **dominated by a common measure** when one supplied sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ satisfies $P_t\ll\mu$ for every $t$ ([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]). Write $p_t=dP_t/d\mu$ and $p=p_0$ for simultaneously supplied nonnegative density versions; the existence and normalization of each density are the Radon–Nikodym properties in [[def-likelihood-density]] and [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]. The Axiom of Choice is the library convention for selecting such a family of versions along a path ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The DQM property below is unchanged by replacing any $p_t$ by another version, since each $L^2(\mu)$ norm is unchanged by a $\mu$-null modification.

The path is **differentiable in quadratic mean at $0$**, with **score** $s\in L^2(P)$, when

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

Here $o(t)$ means that the displayed norm divided by $t$ tends to $0$ as $t\downarrow0$; $L^2(P)$ and $L^2(\mu)$ are quotient spaces modulo almost-everywhere equality ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The definition is directional. A two-sided regular submodel qualifies by restricting it to $t\ge0$. No mean-zero condition is assumed in this definition.

Assume the density-version convention for the path in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]]. If $s\in L^2(P)$ is a DQM score, then $Ps=0$, so $s\in L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]). Moreover, any two scores satisfying the same DQM expansion agree $P$-almost surely. The normalization argument itself uses no choice beyond the density versions already supplied in the definition.

Fix a model $\mathcal M$ containing a law $P$ and designate a collection of allowed submodels through $P$. Each allowed submodel is a one-sided DQM path as in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]]. Its score is the $P$-almost-sure equivalence class proved unique by [[thm-dqm-score-mean-zero]], and it belongs to $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]).

The **tangent set** $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$ is the set of scores of the designated paths. The model specification determines which paths are allowed. In particular, the tangent set need not be a linear space: it may be a **cone**, meaning it is closed under multiplication by nonnegative real scalars, while failing closure under negative scalars. One-sided restrictions can produce this behavior. The closed linear span of the tangent set is a separate construction.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) so that $L^2_0(P)$ is the real Hilbert space established by [[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]. For a tangent set $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)\subseteq L^2_0(P)$, its **linear span** is the set of all finite real linear combinations of elements of $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$; the span of the empty set is $\{0\}$. Its **tangent space** $\mathcal T(P)$ is the closure of that span in the $L^2(P)$ norm. The closure consists of limits of sequences from the span, equivalently of points every positive-radius norm ball around which meets the span.

The tangent set itself is retained separately and may be a cone rather than a vector space.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

Let $X$ be a set. The **counting set function** on $\mathcal P(X)$ is

$$\#_X(E):=\begin{cases}|E|,&E\text{ is finite},\\+\infty,&E\text{ is infinite},\end{cases}$$

where finite means equinumerous with a natural number ([[def-countable]]) and $+\infty$ belongs to the extended real line ([[def-extended-reals]]). The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a measure, and hence deserves the name **counting measure**, is proved in [[prop-counting-measure-is-a-measure]].
For every set $X$, the counting set function $\#_X$ of [[def-counting-measure]] is a measure on $(X,\mathcal P(X))$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For any probability measure $P$, the space $L^2_0(P)$ of [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]] is a closed real linear subspace of real $L^2(P)$ with pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_P:=\int fg\,dP$; consequently it is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). The only choice use is the Countable Choice assumption already required by the general $L^2(P)$ completeness supplier.

derivations.claim: Every subset of $\{-1,+1\}$ and its complement lie in the full power set, and every countable union of such subsets is still a subset; thus the power set is a sigma-algebra by [F4], and with this sigma-algebra the sample set is a measurable space by [F4]. Counting measure on the two-point set is a measure of total mass two by [F5, F6], hence sigma-finite by the constant sequence of covers $E_n=\{-1,+1\}$; its only null set is empty. For every $\theta\in[0,1]$, the masses $(1+\theta)/2$ and $(1-\theta)/2$ are nonnegative and sum to one, so $P_\theta$ is a probability measure dominated by counting measure. At $\theta=0$ both masses are $1/2$, so $\sqrt{p_0(x)}=1/\sqrt2$.
If a one-sided DQM path has score $s$, [F1] on each atom gives $\sqrt{P_{\theta(t)}\{x\}}=1/\sqrt2+t s(x)/(2\sqrt2)+o(t)$. Squaring each expansion yields $P_{\theta(t)}\{x\}=1/2+t s(x)/2+o(t)$.

Conversely, for each $a\ge0$, take $\theta(t)=at$ for sufficiently small $t\ge0$. Then $P_{\theta(t)}\{x\}=(1+atx)/2$, and [F7] at $1/2$ gives $\sqrt{P_{\theta(t)}\{x\}}=1/\sqrt2+t ax/(2\sqrt2)+o(t)$ on each atom. The two-coordinate counting-measure $L^2$ remainder is $o(t)$, so this path has score $aX$. Its densities are explicit, so [A1] requires no selection in this construction. Thus every vector on the nonnegative ray is an allowed score.

Subtract the two mass expansions from step 2.1. Since $\theta(t)=P_{\theta(t)}\{+1\}-P_{\theta(t)}\{-1\}$, we get $\theta(t)/t\to(s(+1)-s(-1))/2$. By [F2], $P_0s=(s(+1)+s(-1))/2=0$, so this limit equals $s(+1)$. The constraints $\theta(t)\ge0$ and $t>0$ force the limit $a:=s(+1)$ to be nonnegative, and $s(-1)=-a$; hence every score is $s(x)=ax$ with $a\ge0$.

The real span of $\{aX:a\ge0\}$ is $\{bX:b\in\mathbb R\}$, and every mean-zero function on the equiprobable two-point space has values $(b,-b)$, so this span is $L^2_0(P_0)$. This space is closed in $L^2(P_0)$ by [F8], hence its closure—and therefore the tangent space by [F3]—is $L^2_0(P_0)$. It strictly contains the non-linear score cone because $X$ is in the cone but $-X$ is not.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space. Vectors $x,y\in V$ are
**orthogonal**, written $x\perp y$, when

$$\langle x,y\rangle=0 .$$

For a subset $S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^\perp:=\{\,v\in V : \langle v,s\rangle=0 \text{ for every } s\in S\,\}.$$

**Orthogonality is symmetric.** If $\langle x,y\rangle=0$, then
$\langle y,x\rangle=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle}=0$, so $x\perp y$ exactly
when $y\perp x$; in particular the condition defining $S^\perp$ is symmetric in
its two arguments.

**$S^\perp$ is a linear subspace.** Let $s\in S$ and scalars $a,b$; then
$\langle 0,s\rangle=0$, and if $u,v\in S^\perp$ then
$\langle au+bv,s\rangle=a\langle u,s\rangle+b\langle v,s\rangle=0$ by linearity
in the first argument, so $au+bv\in S^\perp$. Thus $S^\perp$ is a linear
subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) for every subset $S$, whether or not
$S$ is a subspace. Moreover $0\in S^\perp$ always, and $v\in V$ lies in
$\{0\}^\perp$ for every $v$, so $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

**Monotonicity.** If $S\subseteq T\subseteq V$, then every vector orthogonal to
all of $T$ is orthogonal to all of $S$, so $T^\perp\subseteq S^\perp$.

**Nontriviality of orthogonality.** By positive definiteness
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2=0$ exactly for $v=0$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]),
so a vector orthogonal to itself is zero, and $\{0\}^\perp=V$, $V^\perp=\{0\}$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $\phi\in H^k$ is any other representer, then for every $s\in\mathcal T$ and coordinate $j$, $\langle\phi_j-\phi_{0,j},s\rangle_H=0$, so $\phi_j-\phi_{0,j}\in\mathcal T^\perp$ by [F3]. Thus every representer lies in $\phi_0+(\mathcal T^\perp)^k$.

Apply [F2] coordinatewise to write $\phi_0=\Pi_{\mathcal T}\phi_0+h$ with $\Pi_{\mathcal T}\phi_0\in\mathcal T^k$ and $h\in(\mathcal T^\perp)^k$. Countable Choice is used only in this projection step through [F2] and [A1].

Conversely, if $h\in(\mathcal T^\perp)^k$, then $\langle\phi_0+h,s\rangle_H=\langle\phi_0,s\rangle_H+\langle h,s\rangle_H=\dot\psi(s)$ for every $s\in\mathcal T$, so $\phi_0+h$ is a representer. Hence the full representer set is exactly the stated affine class.

By step 1.2, $\Pi_{\mathcal T}\phi_0$ is a representer. If two representers lie in $\mathcal T^k$, step 1.1 places their difference in $(\mathcal T^\perp)^k$ as well; each coordinate then lies in $\mathcal T\cap\mathcal T^\perp$ and has squared norm zero by positive definiteness in [F1], so the difference is zero. This proves existence and uniqueness of the canonical representer.

Let $\theta\in\mathbb R^p$, $p\ge1$ finite, be a parameter of interest at a law $P$. Assume its score vector $S_\theta=(S_{\theta,1},\ldots,S_{\theta,p})^T$ has components in $L^2_0(P)$; under a dominated differentiable parametric submodel these are the coordinate log-density scores of [[def-score-and-fisher-information]]. Let $\mathcal T_\eta\subseteq L^2_0(P)$ be the closed nuisance tangent space of [[def-nuisance-tangent-space]]. The ambient $L^2_0(P)$ is as in [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The score-density convention uses the Axiom of Choice, while Hilbert projection uses Countable Choice; both dependencies are retained separately.

The Hilbert decomposition [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]] defines $\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}f$ as the unique $g\in\mathcal T_\eta$ with $f-g\in\mathcal T_\eta^\perp$, where orthogonality and $\mathcal T_\eta^\perp$ have the meanings in [[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. The **efficient score vector** and **efficient information matrix** are

$$S_{\mathrm{eff}}=S_\theta-\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}S_\theta,\qquad I_{\mathrm{eff}}=E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}S_{\mathrm{eff}}^T],$$

where $\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}$ is the Hilbert-space orthogonal projection applied coordinatewise. This projection exists and is unique because $\mathcal T_\eta$ is a closed linear subspace; the projection theorem used by [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]] assumes Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $P$ be a probability law for one observation, let $\mathcal P$ be a model of laws containing $P$, and let $\psi:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a target functional, where $k\ge1$ is finite. A one-sided path $t\mapsto P_t$, $0\le t<\epsilon$, through $P=P_0$ is **differentiable in quadratic mean (DQM)** with score $s\in L^2(P)$ when its densities $p_t,p$ relative to one common sigma-finite measure $\mu$ satisfy

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

The score initially belongs to $L^2(P)$; [[thm-dqm-score-mean-zero]] proves it is unique modulo $P$-almost-sure equality and has mean zero, so it lies in $L^2_0(P)$ as defined by [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The allowed scores form the **tangent set** of the designated paths ([[def-tangent-set]]); their **tangent space** $\mathcal T$ is the closure of their real linear span in $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-tangent-space]]). It is a closed linear subspace by [[thm-tangent-space-is-closed-linear-subspace]], and hence a Hilbert space under Countable Choice ([[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]).

The functional $\psi$ is **pathwise differentiable at $P$ relative to $\mathcal T$** if the right derivative $\dot\psi_P(s):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\psi(P_t)-\psi(P))/t$ exists for every allowed path, depends only on its score, and extends to a continuous linear map $\dot\psi_P:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$. A vector $\phi\in L^2_0(P)^k$ is a **parameter influence curve** (or representer) when

$$\dot\psi_P(s)=E_P[\phi s]\qquad(s\in\mathcal T),$$

with the expectation interpreted coordinatewise. The Hilbert-space Riesz theorem gives a unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$; it is the **canonical gradient**. This representation requires Countable Choice, as in [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] and [[def-countable-choice]]. The supplied density versions along a path use the separate Axiom of Choice in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]] and [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. The full set of ambient representers and its projection characterization are proved in [[thm-influence-curve-representers]].

Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\mathcal T\subseteq H$ be a closed linear subspace, and let $\dot\psi:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$ be continuous linear with an ambient representer $\phi_0\in H^k$, meaning $\dot\psi(s)=\langle\phi_0,s\rangle_H$ coordinatewise for all $s\in\mathcal T$. Assume Countable Choice. Then all ambient representers are exactly

$$\phi_0+(\mathcal T^\perp)^k.$$

The unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$ is $\phi_{\mathrm{can}}=\Pi_{\mathcal T}\phi_0$; when $\dot\psi$ is a statistical path derivative, this is its canonical gradient. Projection is applied coordinatewise.

Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Here $L^2(P)$ is the real space of square-integrable measurable functions modulo equality $P$-almost surely, with its usual quotient norm ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]). For $f\in L^2(P)$, the integral $Pf:=\int f\,dP$ is finite and independent of the representative: Cauchy–Schwarz on the probability space gives $\int|f|\,dP\le\|f\|_2$, and the expectation of integrable representatives is invariant under almost-sure equality ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[lem-expectation-is-independent-of-the-ae-representative]]).

Define the **mean-zero square-integrable space** by

$$L^2_0(P):=\{f\in L^2(P):Pf=0\}.$$

It carries the norm inherited from $L^2(P)$. Countable Choice is not needed for this definition; a later local Hilbert-space argument uses it only to inherit completeness from the library's general $L^2$ Hilbert-space result.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For any probability measure $P$, the space $L^2_0(P)$ of [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]] is a closed real linear subspace of real $L^2(P)$ with pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_P:=\int fg\,dP$; consequently it is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). The only choice use is the Countable Choice assumption already required by the general $L^2(P)$ completeness supplier.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$ be any tangent set in the real Hilbert space $L^2_0(P)$. Its tangent space $\mathcal T(P)$, defined as the norm closure of its finite real linear span ([[def-tangent-space]]), is a closed linear subspace of $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space. Vectors $x,y\in V$ are
**orthogonal**, written $x\perp y$, when

$$\langle x,y\rangle=0 .$$

For a subset $S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^\perp:=\{\,v\in V : \langle v,s\rangle=0 \text{ for every } s\in S\,\}.$$

**Orthogonality is symmetric.** If $\langle x,y\rangle=0$, then
$\langle y,x\rangle=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle}=0$, so $x\perp y$ exactly
when $y\perp x$; in particular the condition defining $S^\perp$ is symmetric in
its two arguments.

**$S^\perp$ is a linear subspace.** Let $s\in S$ and scalars $a,b$; then
$\langle 0,s\rangle=0$, and if $u,v\in S^\perp$ then
$\langle au+bv,s\rangle=a\langle u,s\rangle+b\langle v,s\rangle=0$ by linearity
in the first argument, so $au+bv\in S^\perp$. Thus $S^\perp$ is a linear
subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) for every subset $S$, whether or not
$S$ is a subspace. Moreover $0\in S^\perp$ always, and $v\in V$ lies in
$\{0\}^\perp$ for every $v$, so $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

**Monotonicity.** If $S\subseteq T\subseteq V$, then every vector orthogonal to
all of $T$ is orthogonal to all of $S$, so $T^\perp\subseteq S^\perp$.

**Nontriviality of orthogonality.** By positive definiteness
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2=0$ exactly for $v=0$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]),
so a vector orthogonal to itself is zero, and $\{0\}^\perp=V$, $V^\perp=\{0\}$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: By the orthogonal-projection definition in [F1] and [F7], $R\in\mathcal T_\eta^p$ and each coordinate of $S_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is orthogonal to every element of $\mathcal T_\eta$ by [F8]. Since $\mathcal T_\eta\subseteq\mathcal T$, both $S_\theta$ and $R$ belong to $\mathcal T^p$, hence $S_{\mathrm{eff}}\in\mathcal T^p$. The projection exists by the Hilbert and closed-subspace hypotheses [F5] and [F6] under [A2]; [A1] is carried through the selected score definition.

Because $S_\theta=S_{\mathrm{eff}}+R$ and $R$ is nuisance-tangent-valued, orthogonality [F8] gives $E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}S_\theta^T]=E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}S_{\mathrm{eff}}^T]=I_{\mathrm{eff}}$. Therefore for every $a\in\mathbb R^p$ and $t\in\mathcal T_\eta$, $E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}(a^TS_\theta+t)]=I_{\mathrm{eff}}a$.

If $a^TS_\theta+t=a'^TS_\theta+t'$ for $t,t'\in\mathcal T_\eta$, step 2.1 applied to the difference gives $I_{\mathrm{eff}}(a-a')=0$. Nonsingularity forces $a=a'$, so the target derivative assigned to a score in the allowed score set is well-defined.

Set $\phi=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}S_{\mathrm{eff}}$. For a score $s=a^TS_\theta+t$, step 2.1 gives $E_P[\phi s]=a$. Moreover $\phi\in\mathcal T^p$ by step 1.1 and [F4]. Direct multiplication gives $E_P[\phi\phi^T]=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}I_{\mathrm{eff}}I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}$. No existence of an estimator is used.

Let $P$ be a probability law for one observation, let $\mathcal P$ be a model of laws containing $P$, and let $\psi:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a target functional, where $k\ge1$ is finite. A one-sided path $t\mapsto P_t$, $0\le t<\epsilon$, through $P=P_0$ is **differentiable in quadratic mean (DQM)** with score $s\in L^2(P)$ when its densities $p_t,p$ relative to one common sigma-finite measure $\mu$ satisfy

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

The score initially belongs to $L^2(P)$; [[thm-dqm-score-mean-zero]] proves it is unique modulo $P$-almost-sure equality and has mean zero, so it lies in $L^2_0(P)$ as defined by [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The allowed scores form the **tangent set** of the designated paths ([[def-tangent-set]]); their **tangent space** $\mathcal T$ is the closure of their real linear span in $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-tangent-space]]). It is a closed linear subspace by [[thm-tangent-space-is-closed-linear-subspace]], and hence a Hilbert space under Countable Choice ([[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]).

The functional $\psi$ is **pathwise differentiable at $P$ relative to $\mathcal T$** if the right derivative $\dot\psi_P(s):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\psi(P_t)-\psi(P))/t$ exists for every allowed path, depends only on its score, and extends to a continuous linear map $\dot\psi_P:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$. A vector $\phi\in L^2_0(P)^k$ is a **parameter influence curve** (or representer) when

$$\dot\psi_P(s)=E_P[\phi s]\qquad(s\in\mathcal T),$$

with the expectation interpreted coordinatewise. The Hilbert-space Riesz theorem gives a unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$; it is the **canonical gradient**. This representation requires Countable Choice, as in [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] and [[def-countable-choice]]. The supplied density versions along a path use the separate Axiom of Choice in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]] and [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. The full set of ambient representers and its projection characterization are proved in [[thm-influence-curve-representers]].

Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Here $L^2(P)$ is the real space of square-integrable measurable functions modulo equality $P$-almost surely, with its usual quotient norm ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]). For $f\in L^2(P)$, the integral $Pf:=\int f\,dP$ is finite and independent of the representative: Cauchy–Schwarz on the probability space gives $\int|f|\,dP\le\|f\|_2$, and the expectation of integrable representatives is invariant under almost-sure equality ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[lem-expectation-is-independent-of-the-ae-representative]]).

Define the **mean-zero square-integrable space** by

$$L^2_0(P):=\{f\in L^2(P):Pf=0\}.$$

It carries the norm inherited from $L^2(P)$. Countable Choice is not needed for this definition; a later local Hilbert-space argument uses it only to inherit completeness from the library's general $L^2$ Hilbert-space result.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

derivations.claim: For $r>1$ and $k\ge2$, monotonicity gives $k^{-r}\le\int_{k-1}^k x^{-r}dx$, so $\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-r}\le1+\int_1^\infty x^{-r}dx<\infty$. Taking $r=3$ shows $c$ is well-defined and the displayed masses sum to one; taking $r=2$ gives $\mu=c\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-2}<\infty$, so $P\in\mathcal M_X$. But $E_PX^2=c\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-1}=\infty$, because each dyadic block $2^{j-1}<k\le2^j$ contributes at least $1/2$.

For bounded centered $s$, choose $t\ge0$ small enough that $1+ts\ge0$. By [F7], $E_P(1+ts)=1$, so [F9] gives a probability law $P_{t,s}$ with density $1+ts$. The identity $\sqrt{1+u}-1-u/2=-u^2/[2(1+\sqrt{1+u})^2]$ bounds the square-root remainder for $u=ts$ in $L^2(P)$ by $t^2\|s^2\|_2/2=o(t)$, since $s$ is bounded. Thus these paths are DQM with score $s$ under [F1]. To see their scores are dense in $L^2_0(P)$, take $g\in L^2_0(P)$ and truncate to $g_m=\max(-m,\min(g,m))$. Dominated convergence gives $g_m\to g$ in $L^2(P)$ because $|g_m-g|^2\le g^2$ and the difference tends pointwise to zero. Cauchy--Schwarz and $\|1\|_2=1$ give $E_Pg_m\to0$, so $g_m-E_Pg_m$ are bounded centered scores converging to $g$. Hence the tangent space is $L^2_0(P)$.

Step 1.1 gives $P\in\mathcal M_X$ and $E_PX<\infty$; since $s$ is bounded, [F8] gives the finite expectation $E_{P_{t,s}}X=E_P[X(1+ts)]$, so every designated path lies in $\mathcal M_X$. Linearity [F7] then gives $\psi(P_{t,s})=E_{P_{t,s}}X=\mu+tE_P[Xs]$, so the right derivative on each allowed score is $\dot\psi_P(s)=E_P[Xs]$.

For $m\ge2$ let $s_m=(X\wedge m)-E_P[X\wedge m]$. These are bounded centered scores. Their norms are positive because $X\wedge m$ takes the distinct values $1$ and $2$ on the positive-mass points $k=1$ and $k=2$. Direct summation gives $E_P[Xs_m]=cH_m+cm\sum_{k>m}k^{-2}-\mu E_P[X\wedge m]\ge cH_m-\mu^2$, since $0\le X\wedge m\le X$. Also $$\|s_m\|_2^2=E_P[(X\wedge m)^2]-(E_P[X\wedge m])^2\le cH_m+cm^2\sum_{k>m}k^{-3}\le cH_m+c/2,$$ where the last bound follows from $\sum_{k>m}k^{-3}\le\int_m^\infty x^{-3}dx=1/(2m^2)$. The dyadic-block argument in step 1.1 shows $H_m\to\infty$, so $|E_P[Xs_m]|/\|s_m\|_2\to\infty$. The derivative on the dense score set is therefore unbounded in the tangent norm and cannot extend continuously, contrary to the requirement in [F1].

If a finite-variance influence curve $\phi\in L^2_0(P)$ represented this derivative, then for every $m\ge2$ Cauchy--Schwarz would give $|E_P[Xs_m]|=|E_P[\phi s_m]|\le\|\phi\|_2\|s_m\|_2$, contradicting step 3.1. Thus no such influence curve exists.

derivations.claim: Since $X\in L^2(P)$ and $P$ is a probability, Cauchy--Schwarz [F5] gives $\mu=E_PX<\infty$. For bounded centered $s$ and sufficiently small $t\ge0$, $1+ts\ge0$ and $E_P(1+ts)=1+tE_Ps=1$, so $P_{t,s}$ is a probability law with density $1+ts$ by [F9]. Direct rationalization gives $\sqrt{1+u}-1-u/2=-u^2/[2(1+\sqrt{1+u})^2]$; for $u=ts$ the $L^2(P)$ norm of the DQM remainder in [F10] is at most $t^2\|s^2\|_2/2=o(t)$ because $s$ is bounded. Thus the score is $s$.

Every bounded mean-zero $s$ is an allowed score. If $g\in L^2_0(P)$, truncate it to $g_m=\max(-m,\min(g,m))$. Then $g_m\to g$ in $L^2(P)$ by [F6], since $|g_m-g|^2\le g^2$ and the difference tends pointwise to zero. Also $E_Pg_m\to E_Pg=0$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and [F3], [F5]. Hence $s_m=g_m-E_Pg_m$ is bounded and mean-zero, and $s_m\to g$ in $L^2(P)$. Thus the score closure is exactly $L^2_0(P)$ by the tangent-space convention [F10].

Since $P\in\mathcal M_X$, $E_PX<\infty$; with bounded $s$, [F8] gives the finite expectation $E_{P_{t,s}}X=E_P[X(1+ts)]$, so every designated path lies in $\mathcal M_X$. Linearity [F7] then yields $\psi(P_{t,s})=E_{P_{t,s}}X=\mu+tE_P[Xs]$. Since $E_Ps=0$, the right derivative is $E_P[(X-\mu)s]$.

Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|E_P[(X-\mu)s]|\le\|X-\mu\|_2\|s\|_2$, so the derivative extends continuously to $\mathcal T$. The vector $X-\mu$ is mean-zero and square-integrable, hence belongs to $\mathcal T$. If another $\tilde\varphi\in\mathcal T$ represents the same derivative, then $h=\tilde\varphi-(X-\mu)\in\mathcal T$ is orthogonal to every bounded mean-zero score; by density and continuity it is orthogonal to itself, so $E_Ph^2=0$ and $h=0$. By [F10], $X-\mu$ is the unique representer in $\mathcal T$ and therefore the canonical gradient.

For iid observations, $(P_n-P)(X-\mu)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)=\overline X_n-\mu$ exactly. The remainder is zero, so the sample mean is asymptotically linear with estimator influence function $X-\mu$ under [F2]. This algebraic identity invokes no central limit theorem.

citations.quote:
Let $\theta\in\mathbb R^p$, $p\ge1$ finite, be a parameter of interest at a law $P$. Assume its score vector $S_\theta=(S_{\theta,1},\ldots,S_{\theta,p})^T$ has components in $L^2_0(P)$; under a dominated differentiable parametric submodel these are the coordinate log-density scores of [[def-score-and-fisher-information]]. Let $\mathcal T_\eta\subseteq L^2_0(P)$ be the closed nuisance tangent space of [[def-nuisance-tangent-space]]. The ambient $L^2_0(P)$ is as in [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The score-density convention uses the Axiom of Choice, while Hilbert projection uses Countable Choice; both dependencies are retained separately.

The Hilbert decomposition [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]] defines $\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}f$ as the unique $g\in\mathcal T_\eta$ with $f-g\in\mathcal T_\eta^\perp$, where orthogonality and $\mathcal T_\eta^\perp$ have the meanings in [[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. The **efficient score vector** and **efficient information matrix** are

$$S_{\mathrm{eff}}=S_\theta-\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}S_\theta,\qquad I_{\mathrm{eff}}=E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}S_{\mathrm{eff}}^T],$$

where $\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}$ is the Hilbert-space orthogonal projection applied coordinatewise. This projection exists and is unique because $\mathcal T_\eta$ is a closed linear subspace; the projection theorem used by [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]] assumes Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $P$ be a probability law for one observation, let $\mathcal P$ be a model of laws containing $P$, and let $\psi:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a target functional, where $k\ge1$ is finite. A one-sided path $t\mapsto P_t$, $0\le t<\epsilon$, through $P=P_0$ is **differentiable in quadratic mean (DQM)** with score $s\in L^2(P)$ when its densities $p_t,p$ relative to one common sigma-finite measure $\mu$ satisfy

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

The score initially belongs to $L^2(P)$; [[thm-dqm-score-mean-zero]] proves it is unique modulo $P$-almost-sure equality and has mean zero, so it lies in $L^2_0(P)$ as defined by [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The allowed scores form the **tangent set** of the designated paths ([[def-tangent-set]]); their **tangent space** $\mathcal T$ is the closure of their real linear span in $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-tangent-space]]). It is a closed linear subspace by [[thm-tangent-space-is-closed-linear-subspace]], and hence a Hilbert space under Countable Choice ([[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]).

The functional $\psi$ is **pathwise differentiable at $P$ relative to $\mathcal T$** if the right derivative $\dot\psi_P(s):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\psi(P_t)-\psi(P))/t$ exists for every allowed path, depends only on its score, and extends to a continuous linear map $\dot\psi_P:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$. A vector $\phi\in L^2_0(P)^k$ is a **parameter influence curve** (or representer) when

$$\dot\psi_P(s)=E_P[\phi s]\qquad(s\in\mathcal T),$$

with the expectation interpreted coordinatewise. The Hilbert-space Riesz theorem gives a unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$; it is the **canonical gradient**. This representation requires Countable Choice, as in [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] and [[def-countable-choice]]. The supplied density versions along a path use the separate Axiom of Choice in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]] and [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. The full set of ambient representers and its projection characterization are proved in [[thm-influence-curve-representers]].

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment dominated by a fixed sigma-finite positive measure
$\mu$, and let $p_\theta$ be selected finite-valued measurable
Radon–Nikodym density representatives as in
[[def-likelihood-density]]. The simultaneous selection of this arbitrary-index
family uses the Axiom of Choice. No measurability of $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$
or common exceptional null set for an arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$ is
implied.

Let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and fix a parameter $\theta$ at
which the selected family $\eta\mapsto p_\eta(x)$ is differentiable for
$\mu$-almost every $x$, with measurable coordinate derivatives. On
$\{x:p_\theta(x)>0\}$, define the log-likelihood
$\ell_\theta(x)=\log p_\theta(x)$ and the **score**
$$S_\theta(x):=\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta(x) =\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\log p_\theta(x)\right)_{j=1}^d.$$
Set $S_\theta(x)=0$ where $p_\theta(x)=0$, which is $P_\theta$-null.
For $d=1$, this is $S_\theta=\partial_\theta\log p_\theta$.

For $d=1$, the scalar **Fisher information** is
$$I(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[S_\theta(X)^2]\in[0,+\infty].$$
When $d>1$ and $S_\theta$ is square-integrable, the **Fisher information
matrix** is $I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[S_\theta(X)S_\theta(X)^\mathsf T]$;
its $i,j$ entry is $\mathbb E_\theta[S_{\theta,i}S_{\theta,j}]$. No scalar
information is defined here for a vector parameter.
The information matrix is a second-moment matrix by definition; it equals the
score covariance matrix when the score has mean zero.

The derivatives, score and information are defined relative to the specified
differentiable representative family. The Radon–Nikodym definition alone
does not supply parameter differentiability or a canonical score version.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $H=L^2_0(P)$, let $S_\theta\in H^p$ be a finite-dimensional interest-score vector, and let $\mathcal T_\eta\subseteq\mathcal T\subseteq H$ be closed linear nuisance and full tangent spaces, with $\mathcal T_\eta$ a subspace of $\mathcal T$. Assume the designated allowed score set is exactly

$$\mathcal S=\{a^TS_\theta+t:a\in\mathbb R^p,\ t\in\mathcal T_\eta\},\qquad \mathcal T=\overline{\mathcal S}^{\,L^2(P)},$$

and every allowed one-sided path with score $a^TS_\theta+t\in\mathcal S$ has right target derivative $a$ for the parameter $\theta$. If $I_{\mathrm{eff}}=E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}S_{\mathrm{eff}}^T]$ is nonsingular, then $\theta$ is pathwise differentiable and its canonical gradient is

$$\phi_{\mathrm{can}}=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}S_{\mathrm{eff}}.$$

Its covariance matrix is $E_P[\phi_{\mathrm{can}}\phi_{\mathrm{can}}^T]=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}$. This theorem does not assert that an estimator attaining the covariance bound exists.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For each parameter in the stated domain, $|\theta(u+v)+\eta u|\le2|\theta|+|\eta|<1$, so each mass is positive. Their sum is one because $\sum_{u,v}(u+v)=\sum_{u,v}u=0$ and the four constant terms sum to four. Thus the family consists of probability laws by [F5].

Finite averaging, using [F6], gives $E_PU=E_PV=0$, $E_PU^2=E_PV^2=1$, and $E_PUV=0$. Thus $w=a(U+V)+bU$ is bounded and centered. Along $(\theta_t,\eta_t)=(at,bt)$ the likelihood ratio is $1+tw$, which is nonnegative and integrates to one for sufficiently small $t\ge0$. The square-root identity $\sqrt{1+z}-1-z/2=-z^2/[2(1+\sqrt{1+z})^2]$ gives an $L^2(P)$ remainder bounded by $t^2\|w^2\|_2/2=o(t)$, so the path is DQM with score $w$ by [F2]. Direct differentiation of the log density gives interest score $U+V$ and nuisance score $U$ by [F3]. Thus the designated nuisance scores span $\{U\}$, which is closed since $\|cU\|_2=|c|$, and all designated scores $a(U+V)+bU$ span $\{U,V\}$, which is closed because $\|aU+bV\|_2^2=a^2+b^2$.

Since $U\in\mathcal T_\eta$ and $E_P[(U+V-U)U]=E_P[VU]=0$, $U$ is the orthogonal projection of $S_\theta=U+V$ onto $\mathcal T_\eta$. Hence $S_{\mathrm{eff}}=V$ and $I_{\mathrm{eff}}=E_PV^2=1$ by [F1].

Along each direction $(at,bt)$, the target parameter is $\theta_t=at$, so its right derivative is $a$. Step 1.2 gives the full score-space decomposition $\mathcal T=\overline{\{aS_\theta+bU:a,b\in\mathbb R\}}$; step 2.1 gives nonsingular $I_{\mathrm{eff}}=1$. The finite densities are explicit, and the theorem's stated axiom inputs are Axiom of Choice [A1] and Countable Choice [A2]. Therefore the hypotheses of [F4] apply, and the canonical gradient is $I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}S_{\mathrm{eff}}=V$.

Fix a law $P$ and an iid sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$. For a measurable vector function $\varphi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$, write $P\varphi=E_P[\varphi(X)]$ and $P_n\varphi=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\varphi(X_i)$, where $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}$ is the empirical measure. For a vector remainder $R_n$, $R_n=o_P(n^{-1/2})$ means $\sqrt n R_n\to0$ in $P$-probability.

A measurable estimator sequence $\widehat\psi_n$ of $\psi(P)\in\mathbb R^k$ is **asymptotically linear at $P$** with **estimator influence function** $\varphi$ if

$$\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P)=(P_n-P)\varphi+o_P(n^{-1/2}),$$

where $\varphi\in L^2_0(P)^k$: $E_P\varphi=0$ and $E_P\|\varphi\|^2<\infty$. The space $L^2_0(P)$ and its almost-sure equivalence convention are as in [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. This definition alone does not assert regularity under local alternatives, pathwise differentiability of $\psi$, or asymptotic normality.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Let $(X_n)$ and $(Y_n)$ be real random variables on one probability space, and let $X$ be a real random variable (possibly on another space). If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n\to c$ in probability for $c\in\mathbb R$, then $X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c$ and $X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX$. If $c\ne0$, define $Q_n=X_n/Y_n$ on $\{Y_n\ne0\}$ and give $Q_n$ any fixed value on $\{Y_n=0\}$. Then $Q_n\Rightarrow X/c$.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If dimension zero is admitted, interpret $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton empty tuple; both conclusions then hold as well.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Put $Z_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\varphi(X_i)$ and $R_n=\sqrt n\{\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P)\}-Z_n$. By [F1], $R_n\to0$ in probability. The vectors $\varphi(X_i)$ are iid, centered, and have finite second moment, so [F2] gives $Z_n\Rightarrow Z\sim N_k(0,\Sigma_\varphi)$. The covariance is positive semidefinite by $a^T\Sigma_\varphi a=P[(a^T\varphi)^2]\ge0$ for every $a\in\mathbb R^k$.
Fix any $a\in\mathbb R^k$. By [F3], $a^TZ_n\Rightarrow a^TZ$. Also $|a^TR_n|\le\|a\|\|R_n\|$, so $a^TR_n\to0$ in probability. Apply [F4] to obtain $a^T(Z_n+R_n)\Rightarrow a^TZ$.

Step 2.1 holds for every $a$, and $Z$ is the specified Borel Gaussian law from step 1.1. [F5] therefore gives $Z_n+R_n\Rightarrow Z$, which is the asserted limit. No nonsingularity of $\Sigma_\varphi$ is used.
