Let $F$ be a Borel probability law on $\mathbb R$, let $\psi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, and let $\theta\in\mathbb R$ satisfy

$$J(\theta):=\int\psi(y-\theta)\,dF(y)=0.$$

Assume $\int|\psi(y-\theta)|\,dF(y)<\infty$ and that there is an open interval $I$ containing $\theta$ and a nonnegative $g\in L^1(F)$ such that $|\psi'(y-t)|\le g(y)$ for $F$-almost every $y$ and every $t\in I$. Put $A:=\int\psi'(y-\theta)\,dF(y)$ and assume $A\ne0$. For each fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, let $\theta_x(\epsilon)$ be the locally unique root near $\theta$ of

$$\int\psi(y-t)\,dF_{\epsilon,x}(y)=0,\qquad F_{\epsilon,x}=(1-\epsilon)F+\epsilon\delta_x.$$

Then, for all sufficiently small $\epsilon\ge0$, this local root exists and

$$\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\frac{\theta_x(\epsilon)-\theta}{\epsilon}=\frac{\psi(x-\theta)}{A}.$$

Here $T(F_{\epsilon,x})$ denotes this local root. In the special case $\psi(u)=u$ and $F$ has a finite first absolute moment, $\theta=\mu:=\int y\,dF(y)$ and $\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)=x-\mu$.

For a statistical functional $T$ at a law $F$, let $D_{T,F}:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\text{ exists as a finite vector}\}$. When $D_{T,F}\ne\varnothing$, its **gross-error sensitivity** is the extended nonnegative number

$$\gamma^*(T,F):=\sup_{x\in D_{T,F}}\|\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\|_2.$$

For a real-valued functional the norm is absolute value. This supremum only ranges over directions where the influence function exists; it makes no claim that the derivative exists in every direction.

For any fixed sample $x\in\mathbb R^n$, the sample mean $\bar x=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ has finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction $1/n$. Let $F$ be a Borel probability law on $\mathbb R$, let $m=m(F)$ be its lower median, and assume $F(m)=1/2$. Suppose that on an open interval $I$ containing $m$ there is a continuous density version $f$ satisfying

$$F((s,t])=\int_s^t f(u)\,du\quad(s<t,\ s,t\in I),\qquad f(m)>0.$$

For each fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, the right point-contamination influence function of the lower-median functional is

$$\operatorname{IF}(x;m,F)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac1{2f(m)},&x<m,\\[4pt]0,&x=m,\\[4pt]+\dfrac1{2f(m)},&x>m.\end{cases}$$

Consequently, its gross-error sensitivity is $\gamma^*(m,F)=1/(2f(m))$.

For any fixed sample $x\in\mathbb R^n$, the sample mean $\bar x=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ has finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction $1/n$. If $n=2r+1$ is odd and the conventional sample median is the $(r+1)$-st order statistic, its finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction is $(r+1)/n=\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor/n$.

Since $1/[2(2r+1)]\to0$ as $r\to\infty$, the odd-sample median breakdown fractions tend to $1/2$.
The bounded pointwise sensitivity and the separate replacement count follow from different definitions and theorems; here the median has both properties under the stated density hypothesis.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $G$ be a probability measure on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R$, and put $F_G(t):=G(( -\infty,t])$. For any $G$ such that $S_G:=\{t\in\mathbb R:F_G(t)\ge1/2\}$ is nonempty and bounded below, define its **lower median** by

$$m(G):=\inf S_G.$$

The stated condition makes $m(G)$ a finite real number. This convention chooses the left endpoint when the set of medians is an interval; it assumes neither a density nor uniqueness.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $n\ge1$, and let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$. Define

$$P_n(A):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}(A),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$

Then $P_n$ is a probability measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $\mathcal P$ be a collection of probability measures on it, and let $T:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a single-valued map with finite $k\ge1$. Such a map is a **statistical functional**. For $F\in\mathcal P$ and $x\in\mathcal X$, suppose the point-contamination path $F_{\epsilon,x}=(1-\epsilon)F+\epsilon\delta_x$ belongs to $\mathcal P$ for all sufficiently small $\epsilon\ge0$ ([[def-gross-error-path]]). The **gross-error influence function** at $(x;T,F)$ is

$$\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F):=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\frac{T(F_{\epsilon,x})-T(F)}{\epsilon}\in\mathbb R^k,$$

when this finite right limit exists. Its domain may be a proper subset of $\mathcal X$.

For probability measures $F,H$ on a common measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]) and $0\le\epsilon\le1$, the gross-error path is $F_{\epsilon,H}=(1-\epsilon)F+\epsilon H$, a probability measure by [[lem-convex-mixture-of-probability-laws]]. For any $x\in X$, its point-contamination direction at $x$ is the specialization $H=\delta_x$ ([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]). The path is used for a derivative at $\epsilon=0$; the definition alone gives no uniform-in-$H$ remainder.

For a statistical functional $T$ at a law $F$, let $D_{T,F}:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\text{ exists as a finite vector}\}$. When $D_{T,F}\ne\varnothing$, its **gross-error sensitivity** is the extended nonnegative number

$$\gamma^*(T,F):=\sup_{x\in D_{T,F}}\|\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F)\|_2.$$

For a real-valued functional the norm is absolute value. This supremum only ranges over directions where the influence function exists; it makes no claim that the derivative exists in every direction.

Let $n\ge1$, let $T_n:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be a total statistic, and fix a sample $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. For $0\le m\le n$, define its maximum replacement displacement by

$$B_m(T_n,x):=\sup\bigl\{|T_n(y)-T_n(x)|:y\in\mathbb R^n,\ \#\{i:y_i\ne x_i\}\le m\bigr\}\in[0,+\infty].$$

When the set is nonempty, the finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction is

$$\epsilon_n^*(T_n,x):=\frac1n\min\{m\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:B_m(T_n,x)=+\infty\}.$$

Only coordinate replacements are counted, and the replacement values range over all of $\mathbb R$. This is a property of the statistic at the fixed sample; it is not a probability or contamination-neighborhood statement.

Let $F$ be a Borel probability law on $\mathbb R$, let $m=m(F)$ be its lower median, and assume $F(m)=1/2$. Suppose that on an open interval $I$ containing $m$ there is a continuous density version $f$ satisfying

$$F((s,t])=\int_s^t f(u)\,du\quad(s<t,\ s,t\in I),\qquad f(m)>0.$$

For each fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, the right point-contamination influence function of the lower-median functional is

$$\operatorname{IF}(x;m,F)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac1{2f(m)},&x<m,\\[4pt]0,&x=m,\\[4pt]+\dfrac1{2f(m)},&x>m.\end{cases}$$

Consequently, its gross-error sensitivity is $\gamma^*(m,F)=1/(2f(m))$.

Let $n=2r+1\ge1$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R$. Let $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i}$ be their empirical probability law and write $x_{(1)}\le\cdots\le x_{(n)}$ for the sorted sample. Then the lower median $m(P_n)$ is $x_{(r+1)}$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

derivations.claim: By [F14], every Borel set is Lebesgue measurable; since [F5] makes $[-1,1]$ Borel and Lebesgue measurable with measure $2$, each $A\cap[-1,1]$ is measurable for Borel $A$. For pairwise disjoint Borel sets $A_j$, these intersections are disjoint, so countable additivity of $\lambda$ gives countable additivity of $P(A)=\lambda(A\cap[-1,1])/2$. Also $P(\varnothing)=0$ because $\lambda(\varnothing)=0$, and $P(\mathbb R)=1$ by [F5]. Thus [F1] and [F2] make $P$ a Borel probability law. For $-1\le t\le1$, [F5] gives $F_P(t)=P((-\infty,t])=(t+1)/2$; for $t<-1$ the intersection $(-\infty,t]\cap[-1,1]$ is empty. It follows that $m(P)=0$, the density near zero is $f=1/2$, and $P$ has no atoms, the latter by the degenerate-interval case of [F5].

Fix any point $z\in\mathbb R$. By [F9], $P_{\epsilon,z}$ is carried by a bounded interval containing $[-1,1]$ and $z$, and its only possible atom location is $z$, because [F5] gives $P(\{z\})=0$. The trigger in $T$ requires two distinct atom locations, so it is false and $T(P_{\epsilon,z})=m(P_{\epsilon,z})$ for all sufficiently small $\epsilon\ge0$. Therefore [F8] and [F12] give $\operatorname{IF}(z;T,P)=\operatorname{IF}(z;m,P)$, equal to $-1$ for $z<0$, $+1$ for $z>0$, and $0$ for $z=0$.

Fix odd $n=2r+1\ge5$ and a clean sample $x\in[-1,1]^n$. Its empirical median is the middle order statistic by [F13] and lies in $[-1,1]$, so every atom location of $P_n$ is within distance $2$ of that median. The trigger is false and $T_n(x)$ is the sample median.

After at most one replacement, at least $n-1=2r$ observations remain in $[-1,1]$. At least $r+1$ resulting observations are at most $1$ and at least $r+1$ are at least $-1$, so the middle order statistic, hence the lower empirical median by [F13], remains in $[-1,1]$. All unchanged atom locations are within distance $2$ of it, and only the single replacement can add a distinct outlying atom. Thus the trigger is still false and $T_n$ remains the sample median in $[-1,1]$ for every one-coordinate replacement; its maximum displacement is bounded.
The absolute values in step 1.2 have supremum $1$ over $z\in\mathbb R$, so [F10] gives $\gamma^*(T,P)=1<\infty$.

Replace two coordinates by distinct values $M$ and $2M$ with $M>3$. The remaining $2r-1$ observations lie in $[-1,1]$, so the middle order statistic (position $r+1$) is still one of them and lies in $[-1,1]$; by [F13] this is the lower empirical median. Both new atom locations are more than $2$ above that median, so the trigger is true and $T_n=2M$. Letting $M\to+\infty$ makes the maximum displacement unbounded. Since step 1.4 ruled out one replacement and [F11] defines the first unbounded count, the breakdown fraction is exactly $2/n$.

Along odd $n\to\infty$, $2/n\to0$, while step 2.1 gives finite gross-error sensitivity at the fixed law $P$. Hence this functional has bounded influence and an empirical plug-in statistic whose replacement breakdown is not bounded away from zero, refuting the Statement.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix a separable real Hilbert space $H$ and an integer $k\ge1$. The rule in [[alg-geometric-median-of-block-means]] defines a single-valued Borel map $H^k\to H$: for every tuple $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)$ the function $F_m(z)=\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|$ has a nonempty closed convex minimizer set, and that set has a unique point of minimum norm. The choice-free Borel construction below does not use weak compactness or reflexivity. Countable Choice is used only for the published Hilbert projection supplier that identifies the minimum-norm point.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Every at most countable subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-countable]]) is Lebesgue measurable with

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$

so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).
In particular every singleton is null, and on the real line the set
$\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of rational reals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) satisfies
$\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$.

Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on the same measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. We say that $
u$ is **absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$**, and write
$$
u\ll\mu,$$
if every measurable $\mu$-null set is also $
u$-null:
$$\mu(E)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
u(E)=0\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
Because every measurable subset of a $\mu$-null set is again $\mu$-null, this is equivalent to requiring $
u(F)=0$ for every measurable $F\subseteq E$ whenever $\mu(E)=0$.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]],
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

derivations.claim: For each $t\in\mathbb R$, the event $\{Z=t\}$ is measurable and its singleton is Lebesgue null by [F2]. Absolute continuity [F1] gives $P(Z=t)=0$. Therefore, if $t_n\uparrow t$, the events $\{Z\ge t_n\}$ decrease to $\{Z\ge t\}$ and [F3] gives $P(Z\ge t_n)\downarrow P(Z\ge t)$. If $t_n\downarrow t$ with $t_n>t$, these events increase to $\{Z>t\}$, so [F3] gives convergence to $P(Z>t)=P(Z\ge t)$. Thus the nonincreasing tail function $S(t)=P(Z\ge t)$ is continuous at every $t$.

As $n\to\infty$, the events $\{Z\ge n\}$ decrease to the empty set and $\{Z\ge -n\}$ increase to the whole sample space. By [F3], $S(n)\to0$ and $S(-n)\to1$. Since $1-u\in(0,1)$, the set $A=\{t:S(t)\ge1-u\}$ is nonempty and bounded above; [F4] gives its finite supremum. Continuity of $S$ makes $A$ closed, so that supremum $Q_u(Z)$ belongs to $A$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space, let
$T:V\to V$ be linear, and let $\mathcal E$ be an orthonormal basis of $V$. Write

$$A=[T]_{\mathcal E}^{\mathcal E}.$$

Then:

1. $T$ is self-adjoint if and only if $A=A^*$.
2. $T$ is normal if and only if $AA^*=A^*A$.

Over $\mathbb R$, $A^*$ is just $A^{\mathsf T}$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint, and let $v\in V$ be nonzero. The **Rayleigh quotient** of $v$ for
$T$ is

$$R_T(v):=\frac{\langle Tv,v\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Because $\langle v,v\rangle>0$ for nonzero $v$ in an inner product space, this
quotient is a well-defined real number.

If $T$ is self-adjoint on a nonzero finite-dimensional real inner product space and its
eigenvalues are ordered as

$$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n,$$

then

$$\lambda_1=\max_{v\ne0} R_T(v)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \lambda_n=\min_{v\ne0} R_T(v).$$

derivations.claim: Each coordinate $X_r$ is square-integrable because $|X_r|\le\|X\|_2$, and is integrable since $|X_r|\le1+X_r^2$. Hence each $\mu_r$ is finite. Also $E[Y_r^2]\le2E[X_r^2]+2\mu_r^2<\infty$. For every $r,s$, the pointwise inequality $2|Y_rY_s|\le Y_r^2+Y_s^2$ gives $E|Y_rY_s|<\infty$, so every entry of $\Sigma$ exists. Since $Y_rY_s=Y_sY_r$, $\Sigma$ is symmetric.

For $v\in\mathbb R^d$, linearity of expectation [F2] and the finite-sum definition [F3] give $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v=E[\langle v,Y\rangle^2]\ge0$, so $\Sigma$ is positive semidefinite. Summing its diagonal entries and using linearity again yields $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=E[\sum_{r=1}^dY_r^2]=E\|Y\|_2^2$.

For nonzero $v$, [F5] identifies $\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)$ with the maximum Rayleigh quotient; pointwise Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz gives $R_\Sigma(v)=E[\langle v,Y\rangle^2]/\|v\|_2^2\le E\|Y\|_2^2=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$. Positive semidefiniteness from step 2.1 also gives $R_\Sigma(v)\ge0$, so maximizing proves $0\le\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\le\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$.

If $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=0$, step 2.1 gives $E\|Y\|_2^2=0$. By [F1], the continuous polynomial $x\mapsto\|x-\mu\|_2^2$ composed with the Borel map $X$ is measurable, so [F4] applies and gives $\|Y\|_2^2=0$ almost surely. The Euclidean norm is positive definite, hence $Y=0$ almost surely and $X=\mu$ almost surely.

space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space, let
$T:V\to V$ be linear, and let $\mathcal E$ be an orthonormal basis of $V$. Write

$$A=[T]_{\mathcal E}^{\mathcal E}.$$

Then:

1. $T$ is self-adjoint if and only if $A=A^*$.
2. $T$ is normal if and only if $AA^*=A^*A$.

Over $\mathbb R$, $A^*$ is just $A^{\mathsf T}$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint, and let $v\in V$ be nonzero. The **Rayleigh quotient** of $v$ for
$T$ is

$$R_T(v):=\frac{\langle Tv,v\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Because $\langle v,v\rangle>0$ for nonzero $v$ in an inner product space, this
quotient is a well-defined real number.

If $T$ is self-adjoint on a nonzero finite-dimensional real inner product space and its
eigenvalues are ordered as

$$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n,$$

then

$$\lambda_1=\max_{v\ne0} R_T(v)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \lambda_n=\min_{v\ne0} R_T(v).$$

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-field]]).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of [[lem-power-laws]]: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors ([[lem-of-no-zero-divisors]]).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
([[lem-of-inverse-unique]]).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ ([[def-integers]]) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]],
[[def-int-operations]]). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

Let $a, b$ be elements of a field ([[def-field]]) and let integer powers be as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$: $a^{m+n} = a^m a^n$, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$ and $(ab)^n = a^n b^n$.
2. If $a \ne 0$ then $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $a^{-m} = (a^m)^{-1}$ for every $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-int-operations]]).
3. If $a \ne 0$ and $b \ne 0$ then all three identities of claim 1 hold for all $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an integer $n\ge1$ with $n+1>\max\{a,1/a\}$. By induction from [F2], $2^n\ge n+1>a$, while $2^{-n}=1/2^n\le1/(n+1)<a$.

In the finite ordered list of integers $-n,-n+1,\ldots,n$, take the least $i$ with $2^i\ge a$; it exists because exponent $n$ qualifies and exponent $-n$ does not. Thus $i>-n$, so $i-1$ is in the list and fails the defining inequality: $2^{i-1}<a\le2^i$. The power law in [F2] gives $2^i=2\cdot2^{i-1}<2a$.

Step 2.1 covers a=1 in the finite integer search.

boundaries.reason: No degenerate object occurs.

boundaries.evidence: The half-open bracket a<=2^i<2a is proved in step 2.1.
Step 2.1 uses a least element of a finite ordered list.

The Statement is one-way.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $Z$ be a real random variable whose law is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. For $0<u<1$, define
$$
Q_u(Z)=\sup\{t\in\mathbb R:P(Z\ge t)\ge1-u\}.
$$
Then $Q_u(Z)$ is finite and
$$
P(Z\ge Q_u(Z))=P(Z>Q_u(Z))=1-u.
$$

Let $Z$ be a real random variable whose law is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. For $0<u<1$, define
$$
Q_u(Z)=\sup\{t\in\mathbb R:P(Z\ge t)\ge1-u\}.
$$
Then $Q_u(Z)$ is finite and
$$
P(Z\ge Q_u(Z))=P(Z>Q_u(Z))=1-u.
$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

For $p\in[0,1]$, a **Bernoulli$(p)$ random variable** takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, a **binomial$(n,p)$ random variable** is a sum $X=\sum_{i<n}X_i$ of $n$ mutually independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables. When $n=0$, this is the constant zero random variable.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

derivations.claim: Put $\eta=0$ and $\delta=4e^{-N/120}$. For sufficiently large $N$, $0<\delta<1$ and $\delta\ge e^{-N/4}$ because $4e^{29N/120}>1$. The theorem's definition then gives $\varepsilon=8\eta+12\log(4/\delta)/N=1/10$. Hence $p=\varepsilon/2=1/20$, $q=3\varepsilon/4=3/40$, and the asserted failure exponent is $\varepsilon/12=1/120$.

By [F1], each indicator $\mathbf1\{Z_i>Q_{19/20}(Z)\}$ has success probability $1/20$; iid sampling and [F2] give $B_N\sim\operatorname{Bin}(N,p)$ with $p=1/20$. At $q=3/40$, its relative-entropy rate is $D(q\|p)=q\log(q/p)+(1-q)\log((1-q)/(1-p))=\frac3{40}\log\frac32+\frac{37}{40}\log\frac{37}{38}$.

Let $m=qN+1$, an integer because $40\mid N$. For $p_m=m/N$, the binomial point-mass ratio $\mathbb P_{p_m}(B_N=j+1)/\mathbb P_{p_m}(B_N=j)=((N-j)/(j+1))(p_m/(1-p_m))$ is greater than $1$ at $j=m-1$ and less than $1$ at $j=m$, and decreases with $j$. Thus $m$ is a mode of $\operatorname{Bin}(N,p_m)$, whose $N+1$ masses sum to one; consequently $\mathbb P_{p_m}(B_N=m)\ge1/(N+1)$. The binomial formula and [F4] give $\mathbb P_p(B_N=m)=\mathbb P_{p_m}(B_N=m)e^{-ND(p_m\|p)}\ge e^{-ND(p_m\|p)}/(N+1)$. By continuity of $D(r\|p)$ in $r$, [F4] and step 3.1 give $D(p_m\|p)\to D(q\|p)<1/120$. Choose $c>0$ with $D(q\|p)+c<1/120$. For all sufficiently large such $N$, $D(p_m\|p)<1/120-c$ and [F5] gives $e^{cN}\ge1+cN+(cN)^2/2>N+1$. Therefore $\mathbb P_p(B_N=m)>e^{-N/120}$. Since $m>3N/40$, this mass lies in $\{B_N>3N/40\}$, disproving the displayed source bound at the admissible parameters from step 1.1.

Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let $n\ge1$, and let $1\le k\le n$ be an integer. Given $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in H^n$, put $q=\lfloor n/k\rfloor$ and $r=n-kq$. Form consecutive blocks $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ in index order, with $|B_j|=q+1$ for $j\le r$ and $|B_j|=q$ for $j>r$. Compute the block means $m_j=|B_j|^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_j}x_i$. Return the unique minimum-norm point of
$$
\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in H}\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|.
$$

The objective minimizers are called geometric medians of the block means. The minimum-norm rule makes the output single-valued. Existence, uniqueness of that selected point, and Borel measurability as a function of the input tuple are proved in [[lem-measurable-minimum-norm-geometric-median-selection]].

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

derivations.claim: Suppose at most $ak$ points satisfy $\|m_j-z\|>r$. Since $C_a^2=1+a^2/(1-2a)>1$, write $D=\|z-m\|>C_a r>r$ and $d=(z-m)/D$. For each of the at least $(1-a)k$ remaining points, $u_j=(m_j-m)/\|m_j-m\|$ is defined and $\langle u_j,d\rangle\ge(D-\|m_j-z\|)/\|m_j-m\|>0$. Put $\cos\theta_j=\langle u_j,d\rangle$. By [F2], $0<\cos\theta_j\le1$; writing $d=\cos\theta_j u_j+w_j$ with $w_j\perp u_j$, Pythagoras gives $\|w_j\|=\sin\theta_j$. The distance from $z=m+Dd$ to the line through $m$ and $m_j$ is $D\|w_j\|=D\sin\theta_j$, and is at most $\|z-m_j\|\le r$. Therefore $\cos\theta_j\ge\sqrt{1-(r/D)^2}>\sqrt{1-C_a^{-2}}=a/(1-a)$.

For $m_j\ne m$, rationalizing the difference quotient gives $\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\|m+td-m_j\|-\|m-m_j\|)/t=\langle m-m_j,d\rangle/\|m-m_j\|=-\cos\theta_j$; if $m_j=m$, the quotient is $\|td\|/t=1$. Thus the right directional derivative of $F(m+td)$ is $-\sum_{m_j\ne m}\cos\theta_j+\#\{j:m_j=m\}$. Each good point from step 1.1 contributes less than $-a/(1-a)$, and each other point contributes at most $1$ by [F2]. Since at least $(1-a)k$ points are good, the derivative is strictly less than $k-(1-a)k(1+a/(1-a))=0$. At a minimizer every right difference quotient is nonnegative, so this negative derivative is impossible. Thus more than $ak$ points lie outside the radius-$r$ ball about $z$.

Existence, uniqueness of that selected point, and Borel measurability as a function of the input tuple are proved in [[lem-measurable-minimum-norm-geometric-median-selection]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be nonempty, closed and convex, and let $x\in H$. Then there is exactly one point $p\in C$ with $\|x-p\|=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$, that is, a unique nearest point of $C$ to $x$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with closed sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and the finite intersection property as in
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. For a family $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of
$X$ write

$$\bigcap \mathcal{A} \;:=\; \{\, x \in X : x \in F \text{ for every } F \in \mathcal{A} \,\},$$

so that $\bigcap \emptyset = X$, matching the convention for the empty finite
intersection in [[def-finite-intersection-property]].

Then $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]) **if and only if** every
family $\mathcal{A}$ of closed subsets of $X$ with the finite intersection
property satisfies $\bigcap \mathcal{A} \ne \emptyset$.

No choice principle is used in either direction: complementation is a canonical
bijection, so no member of a family ever has to be selected.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

derivations.claim: Let $V=\operatorname{span}\{m_1,\ldots,m_k\}$. In the given center order, Gram–Schmidt replaces $m_j$ by $r_j=m_j-\sum_{\ell<j}\langle m_j,e_\ell\rangle e_\ell$ using the previously retained orthonormal vectors; if $r_j=0$ it is skipped, and otherwise $e=r_j/\|r_j\|$ is appended. Induction on the finite list shows the retained vectors are orthonormal and span $V$. For $d=\dim V>0$, if $v_n=\sum_{\ell=1}^d a_{n\ell}e_\ell\in V$ converges in $H$ to $v$, then [F4] gives $a_{n\ell}=\langle v_n,e_\ell\rangle\to\langle v,e_\ell\rangle$ for each $\ell$; the finite sums converge to $\sum_\ell\langle v,e_\ell\rangle e_\ell=v$, so $V$ is closed. If $d=0$, all centers are zero and $F_m(z)=k\|z\|$ has the unique minimizer $0$. For $d>0$, set $P_Vz=\sum_\ell\langle z,e_\ell\rangle e_\ell$; its residual is orthogonal to $V$. Pythagoras gives $\|z-m_j\|^2=\|P_Vz-m_j\|^2+\|z-P_Vz\|^2$, so $F_m(P_Vz)<F_m(z)$ whenever $z\notin V$. Thus every minimizer lies in $V$. The function $F_m$ is continuous and coercive because $F_m(z)\ge k\|z\|-\sum_j\|m_j\|$; its sublevel set $\{z\in V:F_m(z)\le F_m(0)\}$ is nonempty, closed and bounded in the finite-dimensional coordinate space $\mathbb R^d$, hence compact by [F3]. By [F5], $F_m$ attains a minimum there; the full minimizer set $C_m$ is nonempty, closed, bounded and compact, and it is convex because $F_m$ is convex.

By [F2], $C_m$ has a unique point $z_*(m)$ nearest to $0$, its unique minimum-norm point. If $H=\{0\}$, the selection is the constant zero map; otherwise fix a unit vector $e$ and a countable dense sequence $(d_a)_{a\ge1}$ in $H$, whose existence is given by [F8]. The countable set $D=\{\langle d_a,e\rangle:a\ge1\}$ is dense in $\mathbb R$: for each $t\in\mathbb R$, density gives $d_{a_j}\to te$, and [F4] gives $\langle d_{a_j},e\rangle\to t$. For $\lambda>0$, $G_{\lambda,m}(z)=F_m(z)+\lambda\|z\|^2$ is continuous, coercive and strictly convex. Projection to $V$ cannot increase $F_m$ and strictly decreases the squared norm off $V$, so every minimizer lies in $V$; if $d=0$ the single candidate is $0$. For $d>0$, a closed bounded sublevel set in $V$ is compact by [F3], so [F5] gives a unique minimizer $z_\lambda(m)$. By continuity and density, $h_\lambda(m)=\inf_aG_{\lambda,m}(d_a)=G_{\lambda,m}(z_\lambda(m))$. Each map $m\mapsto G_{\lambda,m}(d_a)$ is continuous, so [F7] makes their countable infimum $h_\lambda$ Borel. For $s\ge1$, set $A_{a,s}=\{m:G_{\lambda,m}(d_a)<h_\lambda(m)+1/s\}$. The countable dense set $D$ gives $A_{a,s}=\bigcup_{q\in D}\{m:G_{\lambda,m}(d_a)<q\}\cap\{m:h_\lambda(m)>q-1/s\}$ so $A_{a,s}$ is Borel; density ensures at least one such $a$ for each $m$. The least such $a$ is a Borel, countably-valued map because its level set at $a$ is $A_{a,s}\setminus\bigcup_{b<a}A_{b,s}$, and the selected point map is Borel since each open-set preimage is the union of its Borel level sets whose values lie in that open set. The selected point is within $(\lambda s)^{-1/2}$ of $z_\lambda(m)$: convexity of $F_m$ and $\|(1-t)z+ty\|^2=(1-t)\|z\|^2+t\|y\|^2-t(1-t)\|y-z\|^2$, applied at the minimizer and followed by $t\downarrow0$, give $G_{\lambda,m}(y)-G_{\lambda,m}(z_\lambda)\ge\lambda\|y-z_\lambda\|^2$. Hence the selected maps converge pointwise to $z_\lambda$. Since they are countably valued with Borel level sets, their distances to each $d_a$ are Borel and converge to $\|z_\lambda-d_a\|$; [F7] makes these limits Borel. Balls with centers $d_a$ and positive rational radii form a countable basis of the separable metric space $H$: every open neighborhood of a point contains such a ball around a sufficiently close dense center. Thus inverse images of open sets are countable unions of Borel inverse images of these balls, proving $m\mapsto z_\lambda(m)$ is Borel.

For every $s\ge1$, comparison with $z_*(m)$ in the minimization of $F_m+s^{-1}\|\cdot\|^2$ gives $\|z_{1/s}\|\le\|z_*\|$ and $F_m(z_{1/s})\le F_m(z_*)+s^{-1}\|z_*\|^2$. If $d=0$ then both points are $0$. Otherwise all $z_{1/s}$ lie in the compact ball $B_V(0,\|z_*\|)$ by [F3]. The closed tail sets $C_n=\overline{\{z_{1/s}:s\ge n\}}$ inside this ball are nonempty, nested and have the finite-intersection property, so [F6] gives $c\in\bigcap_n C_n$. For every $n$, continuity of $F_m$ and the tail bounds imply $F_m(c)\le F_m(z_*)+\|z_*\|^2/n$, while $\|c\|\le\|z_*\|$; letting $n\to\infty$ shows $c\in C_m$ is a minimum-norm minimizer, hence $c=z_*$. If the sequence did not converge to $z_*$, some $\rho>0$ would leave arbitrarily late terms at distance at least $\rho$; the closed tail closures of those terms are nonempty nested subsets of the same compact ball, so [F6] gives a point in their intersection. It lies in every $C_n$, hence equals $z_*$, but its distance from $z_*$ is at least $\rho$, a contradiction. Thus $z_{1/s}\to z_*$. By [F7] and the separable-metric basis argument of step 1.2, the pointwise limit of the Borel maps $z_{1/s}$ is Borel.

The minimizer set is nonempty, closed and convex by step 1.1, its minimum-norm point is unique by step 1.2, and step 2.1 proves the selected map is Borel. The only choice principle used is Countable Choice in [F2]; the dense sequence is supplied by separability and all subsequent approximations use least-index rules.

   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with closed sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and the finite intersection property as in
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. For a family $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of
$X$ write

$$\bigcap \mathcal{A} \;:=\; \{\, x \in X : x \in F \text{ for every } F \in \mathcal{A} \,\},$$

so that $\bigcap \emptyset = X$, matching the convention for the empty finite
intersection in [[def-finite-intersection-property]].

Then $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]) **if and only if** every
family $\mathcal{A}$ of closed subsets of $X$ with the finite intersection
property satisfies $\bigcap \mathcal{A} \ne \emptyset$.

No choice principle is used in either direction: complementation is a canonical
bijection, so no member of a family ever has to be selected.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has

$a$ and $s$ alone.

Let $d,N\ge1$ be integers, let $0\le\eta\le1/10$, and let $0<\delta<1$ satisfy $N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$. Given two observed halves $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$ in $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$
\varepsilon=\max\left\{10\eta,\frac{2560\log(2/\delta)}{N}\right\}\in(0,1].
$$
For $v\in S^{d-1}$, sort $\langle\widetilde Y_i,v\rangle$ nondecreasingly and let $\alpha_v$ and $\beta_v$ be its order statistics of ranks $\lceil\varepsilon N/2\rceil$ and $\lceil(1-\varepsilon/2)N\rceil$. Write $\phi_{a,b}(t)=\min\{b,\max\{a,t\}\}$. For $Q>0$ define
$$U_Q(v)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha_v-Q,\,\beta_v+Q}(\langle\widetilde X_i,v\rangle),\qquad \Gamma(v,Q)=\{z\in\mathbb R^d:|\langle z,v\rangle-U_Q(v)|\le2\varepsilon Q\}.$$
and $\Gamma(Q)=\bigcap_{v\in S^{d-1}}\Gamma(v,Q)$. For each $j\in\mathbb Z$, put
$$
K_j=\bigcap_{i\ge j}\Gamma(2^i),\qquad S=\{j\in\mathbb Z:K_j\ne\varnothing\}.
$$
Return the unique minimum-norm point of $K_j$ if $S$ has least element $j$; if $S=\mathbb Z$, return the unique minimum-norm point of $\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb Z}\Gamma(2^i)$; if $S=\varnothing$, return the first-half sample mean $N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\widetilde X_i$. This three-branch selector is total on the displayed input domain; its existence and Borel measurability are proved in [[lem-multivariate-trimmed-mean-selector-total-and-measurable]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with closed sets as in

$$\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i),\qquad a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Q,\quad a_i<b_i,$$

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let

Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$
